children.name: pinneapple_simulation.accelerated_foam.warm_start
children.doc:
Initial guesses for a sequence of pressure systems.

A transient pressure-velocity solver solves a new pressure system every corrector, with a matrix and a
right-hand side that change slowly. OpenFOAM starts each solve from the current pressure field. The guesses
here are never worse than that in the energy norm of the current matrix, because that field is in the space
they project on:

- :class:`ProjectionWarmStart` -- Galerkin projection on the last ``k`` solutions (Fischer 1998). This is the
  algorithm of the ``pinneWarmStart`` OpenFOAM wrapper (``guess projection``); the Python version is used
  for the offline benchmarks and to check the C++ one.
- :class:`PODWarmStart` -- Galerkin projection on a POD basis of solutions from earlier runs (a design of
  experiments, a previous simulation), plus the current field.

Both use only ``A x`` products, so they apply to any matrix the solver hands over.

classes.name: ProjectionWarmStart
classes.sig: (n_snapshots: int = 8)
classes.doc:
Galerkin projection of each new system on the span of the last ``n_snapshots`` solutions and of the
incoming field. Call :meth:`guess` before a solve and :meth:`update` with the converged solution after it.

classes.name: PODWarmStart
classes.sig: (energy: float = 0.99999, max_rank: int = 32, n_recent: int = 0)
classes.doc:
Galerkin projection on a POD basis of stored solutions (other runs or earlier steps) and the current field.

``fit`` keeps the left singular vectors that hold ``energy`` of the snapshot energy (at most ``max_rank``).
With ``n_recent > 0`` the last ``n_recent`` solutions of the current run join the basis (POD of earlier
runs + projection on the current one).

methods.name: fit
methods.doc: ``snapshots``: (n_cells, n_snapshots).

methods.name: update
methods.doc: The basis is fitted offline; only the recent solutions (``n_recent``) are kept per solve.

functions.name: galerkin
functions.sig: (system: LduSystem, basis: np.ndarray, drop: float = 1e-12) -> np.ndarray | None
functions.doc: ``x = V c`` with ``(V^T A V) c = V^T b``; dependent columns of ``V`` (n, k) are dropped. None if empty.

children.summary: Initial guesses for a sequence of pressure systems.

children.doc:
Faster implicit pressure solves for OpenFOAM, verified against plain OpenFOAM.

OpenFOAM's pressure-based solvers (PISO, PIMPLE, SIMPLE) spend most of a time step in the pressure equation.
This package changes only the *initial guess* of that linear solve and leaves the solver and its stopping test
to OpenFOAM, so the converged fields satisfy the same tolerance as a plain run:

- ``plugin/pinneWarmStart.C`` -- an OpenFOAM linear-solver wrapper (``solver pinneWarmStart;``) that projects
  each new pressure system on the span of the last solutions (Galerkin projection), or asks Python for a guess
  through named pipes, then calls the ordinary inner solver (PCG, GAMG, ...). It can also write every system
  to disk. :func:`build.build_plugin` compiles it against the installed OpenFOAM.
- :mod:`ldu` -- read those systems (lduMatrix arrays) and convert them to SciPy / PyTorch sparse matrices.
- :mod:`solvers` -- CG with Jacobi, DIC and AMG (pyamg) preconditioners and a PyTorch CG (float64 or mixed
  precision), all with OpenFOAM's normalised-residual stopping test.
- :mod:`warm_start` -- projection on past solutions and POD of earlier runs; :mod:`learned` -- a small graph
  network that corrects the guess (PyTorch).
- :mod:`guess_server` -- serve Python guesses to a running OpenFOAM solver.
- :mod:`case` -- write the benchmark cases, run them, parse logs and compare fields; :mod:`benchmark` -- the
  comparisons reported in ``docs/core_concepts/openfoam_acceleration.md``.
children.summary: Faster implicit pressure solves for OpenFOAM, verified against plain OpenFOAM.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation
pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.cavity
children.doc:
The lid-driven cavity of Ghia, Ghia and Shin (1982), built, run and compared with the published profiles (#272).

The case is the one every CFD code is checked on first: the unit square, no-slip on three walls, the lid at ``y = 1``
moving at ``U = 1``, so ``Re = U L / nu`` and ``nu = 1 / Re``. What is added here is the rest of the loop that makes
it a *validation* rather than a demonstration: the reference table (:mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.
reference`), a mesh ladder whose refinement ratio is stated, and a comparison that reports the error against the
table at the points Ghia measured, not at points that happen to be convenient.

Meshes and what the error means
-------------------------------
``n`` is the number of cells per side, uniform, thickness one cell in ``z`` with empty front and back patches — the
mesh the ``icoFoam/cavity`` tutorial uses, at a resolution the caller chooses. The measured ``u`` is taken along
``x = 0.5`` by interpolating the cell values to that column, and then to Ghia's ``y`` stations. The two stations on
the walls (``y = 0`` and ``y = 1``) are **excluded** from the error: there the answer is the boundary condition, not
a solved value, and including them would reward a case for reading its own input.

Why ``simpleFoam`` and where it stops
-------------------------------------
Ghia's tables are steady solutions, so the steady solver is the honest one to compare, and it is what makes a
three-mesh study affordable (a 64x64 cavity at Re = 100 converges in about ten seconds here). At Re = 10000 the steady
incompressible solver does not have a steady solution to find with a first-order diffusive scheme on these meshes:
:func:`study` reports ``converged=False`` rather than a number that looks like agreement, which is the honest result
the issue asks for and the reason the high-Reynolds entry is in the table at all.

classes.name: CavityRun
classes.doc: One solved cavity: its parameters, its cost, and the profiles measured at Ghia's stations.

functions.name: write_case
functions.sig: (case: str, reynolds: float, n: int = 64, *, iterations: int | None = None, residual: float = 1e-06) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Write a complete, runnable cavity case: ``n x n x 1`` cells on the unit square, laminar, ``nu = 1/Re``.

``residual`` is the normalised residual that ends the run. ``1e-6`` is the control these runs use: continuing
below it costs thousands of iterations for a change in the centreline profile in the sixth digit, which is well
under the difference between three meshes and therefore not what a mesh study is measuring.

Returns the parameters it used, so a run can record them without re-deriving them from the dictionaries on disk.
The dictionaries carry what OpenFOAM v2606 requires and nothing else — the two start-up requirements of the
incompressible solvers (a pressure reference and ``constant/turbulenceProperties``) are in
:mod:`pinneapple_data.preflight.limits`, and a case that omits them does not run.

functions.name: run
functions.sig: (case: str, reynolds: float, n: int = 64, *, timeout: float = 3600.0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
``blockMesh``, ``simpleFoam`` and ``writeCellCentres`` in ``case``; the wall time and the solver's own report.

The cell centres are asked of OpenFOAM rather than assumed: every extraction below interpolates the answer onto
the published stations, and it can only do that if it knows where the cells are.

functions.name: sample
functions.sig: (case: str, reynolds: float, *, stations: dict[str, Sequence[float]] | None = None) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
``u`` along ``x = 0.5`` and ``v`` along ``y = 0.5``, interpolated to Ghia's stations.

Returns ``{"y", "u", "x", "v"}``: the station coordinates and the measured values at them. Bi-linear: the field is
interpolated to the centreline from the two neighbouring columns (or rows) and then to the station, so the answer
is a property of the solution rather than of where the cells happen to fall.

``stations`` overrides the two station lists (``{"y": ...}`` for ``u``, ``{"x": ...}`` for ``v``). A run at a
Reynolds number Ghia did not publish needs it: the stations are the same at every column of the table, so a
solution at another ``Re`` can be read at them and put beside a model evaluated at them. Without it the lists of
the published column nearest ``reynolds`` are used, and a ``reynolds`` no column has is a :class:`KeyError` — the
case is then only readable at stations the caller names, which is what the argument is for.

functions.name: profile_error
functions.sig: (profile: Profile, measured: np.ndarray, *, interior_only: bool = True, drop_disputed: bool = True) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
The error of a measured profile against the published one: ``l2``, ``linf`` and the relative ``l2``.

``interior_only`` leaves out the two stations on the walls, where the published value is the boundary condition
and the measured one is an interpolation of the first cell off the wall. ``drop_disputed`` leaves out the stations
a run has shown the transcription to be wrong at (:attr:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.reference.Profile.
disputed`), which are recorded in the table and in the note that says what was measured there — dropping them from
the *number* is not the same as deleting them from the record. The relative norm is over the RMS of the reference
values, which is the number to quote: an absolute ``u`` error of 0.01 means little without it.

functions.name: study
functions.sig: (reynolds: float, root: str, *, meshes: Sequence[int] = MESHES, timeout: float = 3600.0, reuse: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Run the case on a ladder of meshes and compare each with the published table.

Returns the runs (one :class:`CavityRun` each, as records), the error of each against Ghia's profiles, and the
ratio of successive errors — the convergence of the *error*, which is what a mesh study is: a refinement that
halves the error is a second-order scheme, and the ladder is what shows whether that is what happened.

``reuse`` reads a case that is already solved on disk instead of solving it again, which is what a re-analysis of
a committed run needs: reading the fields back takes a second, and re-solving takes the wall time in the table.

children.summary: The lid-driven cavity of Ghia, Ghia and Shin (1982), built, run and compared with the published profiles (#272).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.cfdbench
children.doc:
The CFDBench cavity family, read off its own archive and scored against the same table our solver is (#272).

CFDBench (Luo, Chen and Zhang, 2023, arXiv:2310.05963) is a large machine-learning benchmark, and the issue that asked
for this case set asks for its numbers beside ours. Its data are on HuggingFace (``chen-yingfa/CFDBench``, licence
``apache-2.0``, read from the dataset card) as one zip per problem:

    https://huggingface.co/datasets/chen-yingfa/CFDBench/resolve/main/cavity.zip     # 786 MB, the other three too

and the loader that reads it is :mod:`pinneapple_data.datasets.cfdbench`, which is what this module goes through: a
number produced by a second reader of the archive would measure the reader as much as the data.

What "the same four problems" means here
----------------------------------------
The archive publishes ``cavity``, ``tube``, ``dam`` and ``cylinder``. Only the cavity has a table of *answers* in this
repository (Ghia's, in :mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.reference`), so only the cavity can be scored and
put in a column beside our own numbers. The tube has something weaker, and it is transcribed and used here: the paper
publishes the *operating parameters* of its cases (Table 3), which :func:`tube_against_table` holds the disk against —
that fixes which case is which, and it is all the tube can support, because the flow is a water-air two-phase one for
which the paper publishes no physical solution. The dam and the cylinder have neither: they are loaded by the same
adapter and have nothing to be wrong against here. That is recorded as it is rather than as four rows of a table.

The two things a reader of this data has to get right
-----------------------------------------------------
* **the Reynolds number includes the density.** ``case.json`` gives ``vel_top``, ``width``, ``density`` and
  ``viscosity``; the case is ``Re = rho U L / mu``. The ``prop`` family varies the density *and* the viscosity, so a
  reader that computes ``U L / nu`` reads the whole family as one Reynolds number per viscosity: measured here, the
  cases that read as ``Re = 100`` that way span 13 % to 44 % against the same column of the table, which is what a
  mislabelled Reynolds number looks like. With the density in, the cases that read ``Re = 100`` agree with each other
  to the last digit.
* **the field is a transient run on a 64 x 64 grid.** The archive stores the fields interpolated to 64 x 64 and the
  cavity cases keep only the last few frames, so the four stations nearest the moving lid (``y >= 0.9531``) — the
  layer a 64-cell grid cannot resolve — are where the difference against the table is concentrated. Both readings are
  reported: the whole column, and the column without those four stations, because quoting only the first would blame
  the data for the grid and quoting only the second would hide it.

functions.name: reynolds
functions.sig: (case: Any) -> float
functions.doc:
``Re = rho U L / mu`` of one case, from the four numbers ``case.json`` records.

The density is in the formula because the ``prop`` family varies it: dropping it (``U L / nu``) turns six different
flows into one Reynolds number, and the difference shows up as error against the table rather than as a wrong
label. ``width`` is the cavity's side, which is the length scale of the case.

functions.name: open_cases
functions.sig: (root: str | os.PathLike[str], problem: str = PROBLEM) -> list[Any]
functions.doc:
Every case of one problem under an unpacked archive, through :mod:`pinneapple_data.datasets.cfdbench`.

The zips unpack to ``bc/``, ``geo/`` and ``prop/`` at the top level, which is the shape the adapter's
``open_cases`` reads when the directory it is given *is* one problem. Raises with the URL when the directory is
missing, because a missing download is the failure this module can do nothing about.

functions.name: families
functions.sig: (root: str | os.PathLike[str]) -> dict[str, dict[str, Any] | str]
functions.doc:
Which problems of the archive are unpacked under ``root``, and how much of each one the loader opens.

The record this returns is the evidence for the part of the issue that cannot be scored: every family the same
reader opens, with its case count, its subsets and the shape of its fields — and ``"not unpacked"`` for the ones
that are not here, which is a statement about this machine rather than about the data. The cavity is the one with a
published table in this repository, so it is the one :func:`study` scores; the others are reported as loaded and
unscored.

functions.name: cases_at
functions.sig: (cases: list[Any], reynolds_number: float, *, tolerance: float = 1e-06) -> list[Any]
functions.doc:
The cases of the square cavity at one Reynolds number, sorted.

The square is required because the table is the unit square: the ``geo`` family varies the aspect ratio, and a
2 x 1 cavity compared with Ghia's profiles would report the geometry as model error.

functions.name: sample
functions.sig: (case: Any) -> dict[str, np.ndarray | float | int]
functions.doc:
The case's last frame, sampled where the table publishes its stations, in the table's own normalisation.

The archive's velocities carry the case's own lid speed (``vel_top``), which is not one: everything is divided by
it so the profile can be compared with a table that is written for ``U = 1``, and the frame index and the largest
change between the last two frames are returned with it, because "the last frame" is only the steady answer if the
run had reached one and that is the reader's to see.

functions.name: score
functions.sig: (case: Any, reynolds_number: float) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: One case as a row: its errors against the published column, and the ``u`` reading without the lid stations.

functions.name: study
functions.sig: (root: str | os.PathLike[str], reynolds_numbers: tuple[float, ...] = (100.0, 400.0, 1000.0)) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
The cavity family at the Reynolds numbers of the table: every square case at each, scored against it.

Returns the record the case's ``results/cfdbench.json`` holds. The cases at one Reynolds number are duplicates of
each other in the archive (the same flow reached through different ``density``/``viscosity``/``vel_top``
combinations), which is visible in the rows: identical profiles, and the same error to the last digit.

functions.name: tube_against_table
functions.sig: (root: str | os.PathLike[str], *, tolerance: float = 1e-09) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
The tube family held against the operating-parameter table its paper publishes (Table 3 of CFDBench).

The cavity is the one problem of this archive with a table of answers to be scored against; the tube has none, so
what can be established about it is weaker and worth stating exactly: that the cases read off the disk **are** the
cases the paper says were generated. That is a real check and not a formality — it is what catches a reader that
is subtly wrong about the data, and here it catches one thing in the data itself.

Every published value is looked for in the archive and every value in the archive is looked for in the table, for
each of the three subsets. The result carries both lists, so a mismatch reads as what it is: a value published and
absent, a value present and unpublished, or a count that disagrees with the paper's own. A value counts as found
when it is within ``tolerance`` of the published one, which is the float noise of a parameter written by a
generator as ``0.30000000000000004``.

children.summary: The CFDBench cavity family, read off its own archive and scored against the same table our solver is (#272).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.foam
children.doc:
Where OpenFOAM is on this machine, and how a validation case is run and read back (issues #272, #265, #294).

Every case in this package has the same three steps: write the dictionaries (:mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.
cfd_validation.cavity`, :mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.step`), run the solver, and read the answer back
as numbers. This module owns the middle one, so that "no OpenFOAM here" is said once, in one way, and every caller
— the tests, the example and the scripts — skips instead of failing.

Finding it
----------
``$FOAM_BASHRC`` first, then the two installs that put it somewhere predictable: the macOS cask at
``/Applications/OpenFOAM-*.app/Contents/Resources/etc/bashrc`` and the Linux packages under ``/opt``, ``/usr/lib``
and ``/usr/local``. That is the same search ``tests/test_openfoam_limits.py`` does, kept here so a validation run and
the limits test agree on what "OpenFOAM is installed" means.

Running it
----------
:func:`sh` sources the bashrc and runs one command inside the case, capturing the log text: OpenFOAM's environment
is a shell environment, and nothing about it is importable. :func:`run` is the whole sequence for the cases here —
``blockMesh``, the solver, then ``postProcess -func writeCellCentres`` so the fields come back with the cell centres
of the mesh they belong to, not an index into a grid we assumed.

Reading it back
---------------
:func:`cells` reads one time directory with :mod:`pinneapple_data.cae.foam` (the repository's own polyMesh and field
reader, so nothing here needs ParaView or a VTK install) and returns ``{"C": (n, 3), "U": (n, 3), ...}`` keyed by
field name. A case this package wrote always has ``C``: :func:`run` asks the solver for it.

functions.name: bashrc
functions.sig: () -> str | None
functions.doc:
The bashrc of the installed OpenFOAM, or ``None``. Answer the question, never raise: a caller that needs the
solver asks :func:`available` and skips, and a caller that only reports asks the same thing.

functions.name: command
functions.sig: (name: str) -> str | None
functions.doc: Absolute path of one OpenFOAM executable (``simpleFoam``, ``blockMesh``...) under the install, or ``None``.

functions.name: available
functions.sig: (*needs) -> bool
functions.doc: Whether OpenFOAM is installed **and** the named executables exist (``available("simpleFoam")``).

functions.name: sh
functions.sig: (case: str, cmd: str, *, timeout: float = 3600.0, log: str = 'log', check: bool = True) -> subprocess.CompletedProcess
functions.doc:
Run one OpenFOAM command inside ``case`` with the bashrc sourced, its output in ``log.<name>`` and returned.

``check=True`` raises :class:`RuntimeError` carrying the last lines of the log, which is where OpenFOAM says what
it did not like; ``check=False`` hands the failure back so a caller can read it (a solver that diverged is a
result to report, not an exception to swallow).

functions.name: run_case
functions.sig: (case: str, *, commands: Sequence[str], timeout: float = 3600.0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Run ``commands`` in order in ``case``; the wall time of each, and whether all of them ended cleanly.

functions.name: solver_log
functions.sig: (text: str) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
The numbers a solver run leaves in its log: iterations, whether it converged, and the last residual.

OpenFOAM prints one ``Time = n`` per outer iteration and either ``SIMPLE solution converged in N iterations`` or
just stops; reading the count from the log is the only way to know how many iterations a run took. The initial
residual of the last iteration is there for the same reason: a run that stopped without converging says how far
it got.

functions.name: case_files
functions.sig: (case: str, time: str | None = None) -> dict[str, bytes]
functions.doc:
The bytes of one case, keyed by path relative to its root — what the repository's readers take.

The mesh (``constant/polyMesh``), the ``system`` and ``constant`` dictionaries and the time directories: enough
for :func:`cells` to read the answer and for :func:`pinneapple_data.preflight.openfoam.check` to pre-flight the
case, so a case this package writes goes through the same rules as every other case in the repository before a
solver is spent on it. ``time`` selects one numeric directory (default: every one of them).

functions.name: time_dirs
functions.sig: (case: str) -> list[str]
functions.doc: The numeric time directories of a case, ascending.

functions.name: last_time
functions.sig: (case: str) -> str | None
functions.doc: The last numeric time directory, or ``None``.

functions.name: cells_available
functions.sig: (case: str) -> bool
functions.doc: Whether a case has a solved time directory with the cell centres in it (:func:`run` asks for them).

functions.name: patch_centres
functions.sig: (case: str, patch: str) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
The faces of one patch: their centres, the ``y`` extent of their *nodes*, and how many there are.

Read from ``constant/polyMesh`` rather than assumed, because a boundary value has to be placed where the mesh put
the face, in the mesh's own order. The extent comes from the nodes and not from the centres: half a cell at each
end is the difference between a profile that reaches zero at a wall and one that reaches zero at the first cell.

functions.name: patch_values
functions.sig: (case: str, field: str, patch: str, time: str | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
The boundary values of one field on one patch, as ``(n_faces, components)``.

Reads the field's ``boundaryField`` with :func:`pinneapple_data.cae.foam.read_boundary_values`, which is how a
wall-quantity the solver wrote (``wallShearStress``) comes back as numbers instead of as a file to be eyeballed.

functions.name: cells
functions.sig: (case: str, time: str | None = None, fields: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Every volume field of one time directory of ``case`` as arrays over the mesh cells, plus ``C`` (cell centres).

``time`` defaults to the last numeric time directory the solver wrote. Reads with
:mod:`pinneapple_data.cae.foam`, the repository's own ASCII/binary polyMesh and field reader, so a validation run
has no dependency beyond numpy.

children.summary: Where OpenFOAM is on this machine, and how a validation case is run and read back (issues #272, #265, #294).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.ladder
children.doc:
The low-fidelity ladder: what each rung costs, and where it stops ranking designs correctly (#294).

A design search cannot afford the fine solver for every sample, so it uses the cheapest thing that *ranks* the designs
the way the fine solver would. That is a claim about a specific family of designs and a specific quantity, and it is
either measured or it is folklore. This module measures it: one external-flow problem, several rungs of fidelity, and
a table of wall time, cells, error in ``CL`` and ``CD`` against the finest rung, and the Spearman rank correlation of
the designs — which is the column that decides whether a rung is usable for optimisation, since an error that is the
same for every design changes nothing about which one wins.

The family here
---------------
A NACA 0012 section at several angles of attack, which every rung in the repository can attempt: the thin-airfoil
rung is the closed-form answer (``CL = 2 pi sin(alpha - alpha0)``, no cells, microseconds), and the RANS rungs are
:func:`pinneapple_design.aero.case.run_case` at three :class:`~pinneapple_design.aero.mesh.GridSpec` resolutions, so
the "levels" are the same case at fewer cells rather than a different case.

Which rungs are *not* in the measured table, and why
---------------------------------------------------
The vortex lattice (:mod:`pinneapple_design.aero.vlm`) is a lifting-surface method for a finite wing: its ``CL`` is a
3-D wing's, and comparing it with a 2-D section's would put the aspect ratio's effect in the error column. The LBM
solver (:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.lbm`) is a low-Reynolds method: at the Re = 4e6 this family is
solved at, its collision model and resolution are not the same physical regime, so a number would say more about the
comparison than about the solver. Both are rungs of the ladder in the sense the issue means, and neither is on *this*
family; the table says so instead of adding a column that would mislead.

Calibration
-----------
:func:`calibrate` takes a few designs measured at the fine level and fits the offset (and the slope, if there are
enough) of a coarse rung against them, then reports the ranking with and without the correction: a bias that is the
same for every design cannot change a ranking, and a bias that varies with the design can.

classes.name: Rung
classes.doc: One fidelity level: what it is, what it costs to ask, and what it produces.

classes.name: design
classes.doc: One point of the family: a section and an angle of attack.

functions.name: thin_airfoil
functions.sig: (name: str = '0012', alpha: float = 0.0) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
The closed-form rung: ``CL = 2 pi sin(alpha - alpha0)`` and no ``CD`` (inviscid theory has none).

``alpha0`` is the zero-lift angle, which for the symmetric 4-digit sections of this family is zero. The lift slope
is the thin-airfoil one, which is exact only in the limit of a thin section at a small angle: the rung exists to be
the cheapest possible one in a cost-accuracy table, and its error is the price of that.

functions.name: rans_airfoil
functions.sig: (name: str, alpha: float, level: dict[str, Any], root: str, *, reynolds: float = 4000000.0, iterations: int = 3000, timeout: float = 3600.0, reuse: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
One RANS rung: the same case at the resolution of ``level``, returning ``CL``, ``CD`` and what it cost.

Runs with the OpenFOAM :func:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.foam.bashrc` finds, not with the fixed path
the aero module defaults to, so the ladder works wherever the case builder works.

functions.name: spearman
functions.sig: (a: Sequence[float], b: Sequence[float]) -> float
functions.doc:
Spearman's rank correlation: the correlation of the ranks, which is what a design search needs.

Ties are given their average rank. Returns ``nan`` when either column has no variation — a set of one design, or a
rung that predicts the same number for every design, which cannot rank anything (and that is the finding).

functions.name: ladder
functions.sig: (designs: Iterable[design], root: str, *, levels: Sequence[dict[str, Any]] = LEVELS, reynolds: float = 4000000.0, iterations: int = 3000, timeout: float = 3600.0, reuse: bool = False, log = print) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Run every design on every rung and return the cost-accuracy table.

``reference`` is the finest RANS level: the error column is against it, not against an experiment, because the
question the ladder answers is "which rung is a cheaper stand-in for the expensive one", not "is the expensive one
right" (that is what :mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.reference` and the TMR cases are for).

functions.name: calibrate
functions.sig: (rows: Sequence[dict[str, Any]], rung: str, *, quantity: str = 'CL', designs: Sequence[float] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Fit the offset (and slope) of one rung against the fine level on a few designs, and report the ranking twice.

A bias that is the same for every design leaves the ranking alone; one that varies does not, and the change in
Spearman after the correction is exactly the difference between the two. ``designs`` limits the fit to a few
angles of attack (the expensive runs a portfolio can afford) while the reported ranking uses all of them.

children.summary: The low-fidelity ladder: what each rung costs, and where it stops ranking designs correctly (#294).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.pinn
children.doc:
A physics-informed network for the lid-driven cavity, scored with the same ruler as the meshes (#272).

The cavity in :mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.cavity` is solved by OpenFOAM and compared with Ghia's
tables station by station. This module solves the *same* problem with a network trained on the equations alone — no
solved field is ever shown to it — and then walks through exactly the same comparison: the same 17 published
stations, the two wall stations left out, and the same relative L2, computed by
:func:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.cavity.profile_error`. A number measured here is therefore comparable
with the number the mesh table quotes at the same Reynolds number; a network scored against the solver's own field
would not be.

The equations, and what the network is asked to satisfy
------------------------------------------------------
Steady, incompressible, non-dimensional (``U = 1``, ``L = 1``, ``rho = 1``), so ``nu = 1/Re``::

    u u_x + v u_y = -p_x + nu (u_xx + u_yy)
    u v_x + v v_y = -p_y + nu (v_xx + v_yy)
    u_x + v_y = 0

on the unit square, with no-slip on the three fixed walls and ``u = 1, v = 0`` on the lid at ``y = 1``. The residual
is the strong form evaluated at collocation points by automatic differentiation, and the boundary conditions are a
penalty (:attr:`Config.bc_weight`) rather than an ansatz: an ansatz that multiplies the output by a function
vanishing on the walls cannot carry a lid moving at ``u = 1`` along the whole top edge, and the smoothed alternative
would be solving a slightly different problem. The pressure is held to zero mean, which is the gauge the equations
leave free.

The operator over Reynolds number
---------------------------------
:func:`train` with ``reynolds=None`` fits **one** network whose input carries the Reynolds number, so a single object
answers for every ``Re`` in the trained range. It is trained where the physics is defined — the collocation points
draw a Reynolds number over ``[100, 1000]`` at every step — and scored only where Ghia published a table, which is the
point of an operator: the three published columns are three *points* of one field.

Three columns are also a thin test of a claim about a whole interval, so the operator is asked twice more, at Reynolds
numbers no column of the table has (:data:`OFF_SAMPLE`, 250 and 750), and scored there against the *solver* by
:func:`against`: same stations, same exclusion of the walls, same norm, with the `simpleFoam` profile in the place of
the published one. Those two numbers are the difference between an operator over ``Re`` and three networks wearing one
hat, and they are the only measurement in this module that could have been an extrapolation — the range of the input
is fixed at training and asking outside it raises.

Where it stops
--------------
The finding this module exists to produce is the Reynolds number at which each model stops matching the reference
(:func:`stops_matching`), not the average error. A network that is good at ``Re = 100`` and useless at ``Re = 1000``
is the state of the art in this problem and is reported as measured. :attr:`Config` was chosen once, on ``Re = 100``
(where a run is cheapest), and the same configuration is used at every Reynolds number: a per-``Re`` search would
measure the search, and a configuration tuned at the hardest Reynolds number would flatter the easy one.

What is not claimed
-------------------
The network is not a solver. It has no discretisation, no residual norm that says "converged", and no guarantee that
what it returns satisfies the equations it was trained on — the physics residual at the end of training is reported
in :attr:`CavityPINN.history` as the network's own claim about itself, and the profiles at Ghia's stations as the
evidence. A run of this module costs tens of minutes of a CPU where ``simpleFoam`` takes seconds; the value of the
number is that it says how well the *method* does against the same table, not that the method is faster.

The cost of a run is recorded with it (``seconds``, ``steps``, the machine class), so it can be read next to the
solver's wall time in the same table.

classes.name: Config
classes.doc:
Everything a run is defined by, so a number can be reproduced without reading the code that produced it.

The defaults are the configuration the committed measurement used. :attr:`fourier` defaults to zero because the
random Fourier map could not be used as it stood: it multiplies the PDE residual by the square of its own
frequency, and at ``fourier_scale = 2`` the residual at the first step came out at ``8.5e1`` against ``2.1e-1``
for the plain network, so the run starts a hundred times further from a solution than the thing it was meant to
improve. Making it pay needs the output scaled to match, which was not measured — so it is not on by default, and
the README's PINN section says exactly that rather than claiming a result.

functions.name: needs_torch
functions.sig: () -> None
functions.doc: Raise if torch is missing, with the one thing a caller can do about it.

functions.name: reference_stations
functions.sig: (reynolds: float) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Ghia's own ``y`` and ``x`` stations at ``reynolds``, as the arrays a measurement is taken at.

The same two lists the OpenFOAM sampling interpolates to
(:func:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.cavity.sample`), which is what makes the two numbers comparable.

functions.name: train
functions.sig: (reynolds: float | None = None, *, config: Config | None = None, reynolds_range: tuple[float, float] = (100.0, 1000.0), on_step: object = None) -> CavityPINN
functions.doc:
Train one network: at a single ``reynolds``, or — with ``reynolds=None`` — the operator over ``reynolds_range``.

``on_step(model, step, losses)`` is called every ``config.steps // 10`` steps if given, which is how the runner
prints a training curve; it is not part of the measurement. ``reynolds_range`` only matters for the parametric
network, whose input is ``log10 Re`` mapped onto ``[-1, 1]`` over that range and whose collocation points draw a
fresh Reynolds number from it every step.

functions.name: profiles
functions.sig: (model: CavityPINN, reynolds: float | None = None) -> dict[str, np.ndarray | float]
functions.doc:
The network's ``u`` along ``x = 0.5`` and ``v`` along ``y = 0.5``, at Ghia's own stations.

``u`` is asked for at ``x = 0.5`` exactly and ``v`` at ``y = 0.5`` exactly, which the mesh cannot do (it
interpolates to the centreline from the two neighbouring columns, :func:`cavity.sample`); what has to match for
the two errors to be comparable is the *stations* and the *norm*, and both do.

functions.name: measure
functions.sig: (model: CavityPINN, reynolds: float | None = None) -> dict[str, object]
functions.doc:
One model at one Reynolds number, as the record the case's JSON holds: the stations, the values, the errors.

The errors are :func:`cavity.profile_error` of the *published* profile against what the network returned, which
is the identical call the mesh study makes on a solved field — same stations, same exclusion of the two wall
stations, same RMS of the table in the denominator.

functions.name: against
functions.sig: (model: CavityPINN, reynolds: float, solved: dict[str, np.ndarray], *, solver: str = 'simpleFoam') -> dict[str, object]
functions.doc:
The model at a Reynolds number **no published column has**, scored against a solver's field at the stations.

``solved`` is what :func:`cavity.sample` returns for a run at ``reynolds`` — ``y`` and ``u`` along ``x = 0.5``,
``x`` and ``v`` along ``y = 0.5`` — and it is the reference here because Ghia publishes nothing at this ``Re``:
the alternative is to leave the operator untested away from the three columns it is asked to reproduce, which is
exactly the claim that needs evidence. The comparison is the same one the table gets — the same stations, the
same exclusion of the two wall stations, the same :func:`cavity.profile_error` — with the solved profile in the
place of the published one, so the number reads on the same scale. The rows carry both the model's values and the
solver's, so the error can be recomputed from the record without the mesh being on disk.

functions.name: matches
functions.sig: (row: dict[str, object], tolerance: float) -> bool
functions.doc: Whether one measured row matches the reference at ``tolerance``: **both** profiles have to clear it.

functions.name: stops_matching
functions.sig: (rows: list[dict[str, object]], tolerance: float) -> dict[str, object]
functions.doc:
Where a model stops matching the reference: the last ``Re`` it clears and the first it does not.

The rows are the measured ones, sorted by Reynolds number; the answer is the *bracket* between two measured
numbers and never an interpolation, because the reference exists at the published stations only. A model that
fails at the lowest measured ``Re`` has no bracket, and says so.

functions.name: study
functions.sig: (reynolds: tuple[int, ...] = REYNOLDS, *, parametric: bool = False, config: Config | None = None, on_step: object = None, probe: tuple[float, ...] = (), solved: object = None) -> dict[str, object]
functions.doc:
Train (one network per ``Re``, or the operator) and measure every model against the published profiles.

Returns the record the case's ``results/cavity_pinn.json`` holds: what was trained, at what cost, the profiles it
produced at Ghia's stations, the errors those profiles give, and — the finding — the Reynolds number each model
stops matching the table at.

``probe`` is a set of Reynolds numbers **not** in the table, and ``solved`` the function that returns the solver's
field at one of them (:func:`cavity.sample` at :data:`OFF_SAMPLE`); the operator is then also scored there, which
is the measurement that separates an operator from three networks wearing one hat. Only the operator can be asked:
a network trained at a single ``Re`` refuses another by construction, and that refusal is the point of it.

children.summary: A physics-informed network for the lid-driven cavity, scored with the same ruler as the meshes (#272).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.reference
children.doc:
The published numbers the classical cases are measured against, transcribed as data with their citation (#272).

A validation case is only as good as the table it is compared with, so the table lives in the repository as data —
not as a comment, not as a picture, and not as a number someone remembered. Every entry below names the table it
came from, and each one is checked on import of the test suite against what the table must be true of on its own:
the endpoint values (the lid moves at ``u = 1``, a wall does not move), strictly increasing coordinates, and one
value per point. A transcription error that survives those checks would have to be a plausible number in the wrong
row, which is why the runs in ``tests/test_cfd_validation.py`` compare a real solver against these tables: a
mis-transcribed row cannot agree with a Navier-Stokes solution at 1-2 % on three meshes.

Lid-driven cavity — Ghia, Ghia and Shin (1982)
---------------------------------------------
U. Ghia, K.N. Ghia and C.T. Shin, "High-Re Solutions for Incompressible Flow Using the Navier-Stokes Equations and a
Multigrid Method", *Journal of Computational Physics* 48(3), 387-411, 1982, Table I (Re = 100, 400, 1000) and
Table II (Re = 10000); doi:10.1016/0021-9991(82)90058-4.

``u`` is the horizontal velocity along the **vertical** centreline ``x = 0.5``, as a function of ``y``; ``v`` is the
vertical velocity along the **horizontal** centreline ``y = 0.5``, as a function of ``x``. The cavity is the unit
square with the lid at ``y = 1`` moving at ``U = 1``, and ``Re = U L / nu``. Ghia's own grid was 129x129; their stated
accuracy is the last digit of the tables (three significant figures, the fourth digit interpolated).

Natural convection in a square cavity — de Vahl Davis (1983)
-----------------------------------------------------------
G. de Vahl Davis, "Natural Convection of Air in a Square Cavity: A Bench Mark Numerical Solution", *International
Journal for Numerical Methods in Fluids* 3(3), 249-264, 1983, Table I; doi:10.1002/fld.1650030305.

The benchmark Nusselt number is the mean over the hot wall, air (Pr = 0.71), insulated top and bottom, side walls at
``T_h`` and ``T_c``. The published values below are the benchmark grid-independent ones; de Vahl Davis states them to
three significant figures, and the uncertainty he quotes at Ra = 1e6 is 0.6 %.

What is deliberately not here
-----------------------------
Armaly et al. (1983, *J. Fluid Mech.* 127, 473-496) publish the reattachment length of the backward-facing step as a
figure, and the digitised table that circulates in the literature is a secondary source with no single provenance.
:data:`ARMALY_REATTACHMENT` is therefore **empty**: the case is built and run by
:mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.step`, and the reference is filled in from the paper or from a documented
digitisation rather than from memory. Pitz and Daily's profiles are in the same position.

CFDBench — Luo, Chen and Zhang (2023), the tube flow's operating parameters
--------------------------------------------------------------------------
Y. Luo, Y. Chen and Z. Zhang, "CFDBench: A Large-Scale Benchmark for Machine Learning Methods in Fluid Dynamics",
arXiv:2310.05963, Table 3 (the operating parameters of the tube flow subset). Dataset: HuggingFace
``chen-yingfa/CFDBench``, licence Apache-2.0, read from the dataset card.

This one is not a table of *answers*, and :data:`CFDBENCH_TUBE` does not pretend otherwise. The tube is a water-air
two-phase flow driven into a tube full of air and solved in Ansys Fluent, so the paper publishes **no** physical
solution to be scored against — its tube tables (Tables 12 and 13) are the NMSE of neural operators against the
archive's own fields. What Table 3 does publish is the *definition of the cases*: the baseline tube and the three
parameter sets (``bc``, ``prop``, ``geo``) with the values each one sweeps. Transcribing it is what turns "the
archive, read however the reader likes" into "the cases the paper says are there", and
:func:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.cfdbench.tube_against_table` holds the archive against it case by case.

The transcription earns its keep on the first reading. The ``prop`` family stores its density as the ten-value
*index* ``0..9``, not the ``10 .. 1000 kg/m3`` the table publishes, while its viscosity is stored as the value — so
``Re = rho U L / mu`` computed from the archive's own ``case.json`` is a hundredfold short for that family and is not
the Reynolds number of the flow. The other two families match the table exactly, value for value.

classes.name: Profile
classes.doc: One published centreline profile: the points, the values, and the table they were transcribed from.

classes.name: CaseTable
classes.doc:
A published table of *operating parameters*: the case it defines and the values each subset sweeps.

The point of the type is the provenance. A table of answers names the run that confirms it (a mistyped row cannot
agree with a Navier-Stokes solution on three meshes); a table of parameters is confirmed by the data instead —
every value it publishes has to be found in the archive, and every value in the archive has to be one it
publishes. :func:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.cfdbench.tube_against_table` is that check.

functions.name: profile
functions.sig: (case: str, quantity: str, reynolds: float) -> Profile
functions.doc: One profile by case, quantity and Reynolds number, with a message that lists what exists when it does not.

functions.name: nu_for_grashof
functions.sig: (ra: float) -> float
functions.doc:
The published mean Nusselt number at Grashof (Rayleigh) number ``ra``, with a message listing the four
benchmarks when the number is outside the published range.

functions.name: get
functions.sig: (name: str) -> Any
functions.doc: ``get("ghia-1982")`` -> the four ``u`` profiles; ``get("de-vahl-davis-1983")`` -> the Nusselt numbers.

functions.name: disputes
functions.sig: () -> list[dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc: Every station whose transcribed value our own run contradicts, as records: what, where, and why.

functions.name: as_dicts
functions.sig: () -> list[dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc: Every transcribed table as plain data, for a JSON record next to a run.

children.summary: The published numbers the classical cases are measured against, transcribed as data with their citation (#272).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.step
children.doc:
The backward-facing step and its reattachment length, built and measured (#272).

Armaly et al. (1983) made this the standard separated-flow case: a channel of inlet height ``h_i`` opening into one of
height ``H`` (their expansion ratio is 1 : 1.9423), and the quantity everyone reports is where the recirculation behind
the step closes again — ``x1 / S``, the distance from the step to the point on the lower wall where the wall shear
changes sign. It is a good validity test because the answer is one number and it is sensitive to the inlet profile,
the outlet placement and the scheme.

How the step is made
--------------------
``blockMesh`` cannot leave a hole in a block, and a hand-written block dictionary has to get the orientation of every
exposed face right. So the mesh is one block over the whole domain and the step is *cut* out of it: ``topoSet`` marks
the cells below the step, and ``subsetMesh -overwrite -patch stepWall`` removes them and turns the newly exposed faces
into the wall patch, with the orientation taken from the mesh rather than from us. Three commands instead of one, and
no face ordering to get wrong.

The geometry in cells
---------------------
The step is ``S = 1`` and ``m`` cells tall; the inlet channel is ``round(m / (expansion - 1))`` cells, so the mesh's
expansion ratio is within a cell of Armaly's 1.9423 and is recorded as ``expansion_mesh`` with every run. The Reynolds
number is Armaly's: ``Re = U_mean 2 h_i / nu`` on the hydraulic diameter of the inlet channel.

The reference is not transcribed
--------------------------------
:data:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.reference.ARMALY_REATTACHMENT` is empty, on purpose: the published
reattachment curve is a figure, and the digitisation that circulates is a secondary source with no single provenance.
:func:`study` therefore reports ``x1/S`` and its convergence with the mesh, and no ``error`` column: what does not
depend on the table is measured here, and the rest waits for the numbers to be entered from the paper itself.

classes.name: StepRun
classes.doc: One solved step case: its parameters, its cost and the reattachment length it produced.

functions.name: write_case
functions.sig: (case: str, reynolds: float, cells_per_step: int = 16, *, expansion: float = EXPANSION, lin: float = 5.0, lout: float = 30.0, iterations: int = 20000) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Write the step case: one block, then the cut. ``lin``/``lout`` are the inlet and outlet lengths in step
heights, and are this package's choice rather than Armaly's rig (recorded with every run).

functions.name: inlet_face_centres
functions.sig: (case: str, patch: str = 'inlet') -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
The faces of one patch, read from the mesh: their centres, and the ``y`` extent of their *nodes*.

Read from ``constant/polyMesh`` rather than assumed, because the profile has to be written on the faces the mesh
actually has, in the order the mesh numbers them — which is why it is written after the cut. The extent comes from
the face nodes, not from the centres: half a cell at each end is exactly the difference between a profile that
reaches zero at the walls and one that reaches zero at the first cell.

functions.name: write_inlet
functions.sig: (case: str, mean_velocity: float = 1.0, *, patch: str = 'inlet') -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Write the parabolic inlet profile over the faces the cut left, and return what it wrote.

``u(y) = 6 U s (1 - s)`` with ``s`` the fraction of the inlet height, which is the fully developed laminar channel
profile and has mean ``U``. The height is taken from the mesh, so a case whose expansion ratio came out a cell off
gets the profile of the channel it has rather than of the one intended.

functions.name: run
functions.sig: (case: str, reynolds: float, cells_per_step: int = 16, *, mean_velocity: float = 1.0, timeout: float = 3600.0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Mesh, cut the step, write the inlet profile, solve, and write the cell centres.

functions.name: reattachment_length
functions.sig: (case: str, *, step_height: float = 1.0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
``x1 / S`` behind the step: where the streamwise velocity on the first cell row changes sign.

On the first row the velocity is the wall shear up to its sign (no-slip at ``y = 0``), so the reattachment point is
that crossing, linearly interpolated between the two cell centres that bracket it. Returns ``x1_over_S``, the
interval it lies in, and ``u_min`` — the most negative velocity found, so that a run with no recirculation at all
shows it here instead of reporting a reattachment length of zero as if it were an answer.

functions.name: study
functions.sig: (reynolds: float, root: str, *, meshes: Sequence[int] = MESHES, lin: float = 5.0, lout: float = 30.0, timeout: float = 3600.0, reuse: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Run the step at ``reynolds`` on a ladder of meshes and report ``x1/S`` on each.

No error column: the published reattachment curve is not transcribed (see the module docstring), so what this
returns is the measurement and its convergence with the mesh, which is the part that does not depend on the table.

children.summary: The backward-facing step and its reattachment length, built and measured (#272).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.tmr
children.doc:
The NASA Turbulence Modeling Resource flat plate in OpenFOAM, with its grid-convergence study (#265).

The Turbulence Modeling Resource (TMR, ``https://tmbwg.github.io/turbmodels/``) publishes RANS verification cases with
the exact model definitions and grid-converged reference results from CFL3D and FUN3D. Its 2D zero-pressure-gradient
flat plate is the one that tests a turbulence model and nothing else: one wall, a known inflow, and a skin friction
that must follow the turbulent boundary layer.

What this module does, and what it does not
-------------------------------------------
It writes the case, runs it with ``SpalartAllmaras`` and ``kOmegaSST`` on a family of grids refined by two, and reports
the observed order of convergence and the Richardson-extrapolated skin friction from
:func:`pinneapple_analysis.verification.convergence.richardson_extrapolate` — the general three-grid machinery the
repository already had, applied to a turbulence case instead of reimplemented for it.

It does **not** read the TMR grids or claim agreement with the CFL3D/FUN3D numbers. The grids here are regenerated at
equivalent resolution (the TMR publishes Plot3D grids that would have to be converted, and the case page's reference
tables are not in this repository), so the comparison table waits for :func:`read_reference` to be given the TMR data
file. What is measured here is what stands without it: whether the answer converges, at what order, to what value, and
whether that value is in the place a turbulent flat plate puts it (the 1/7-power skin-friction law, to the accuracy
that law has).

Geometry and Reynolds number
----------------------------
The plate is the unit length ``x in [0, 1]`` at ``y = 0``, with the domain starting a third of a chord upstream
(``x = -1/3``) and the far boundary at ``y = 0.5``. ``Re = 5e6`` per unit length, from the TMR flat-plate case page,
and the flow is incompressible here (``simpleFoam``) rather than at the page's ``M = 0.2``: at that Mach number the
difference in skin friction is below the discretisation error of a mesh this size, and saying so is cheaper than
believing it.

classes.name: PlateRun
classes.doc: One solved flat plate: its grid, its model, its cost, and the skin friction it produced.

methods.name: at
methods.doc: The skin friction interpolated at ``x = station`` (``nan`` when the run produced nothing).

functions.name: write_case
functions.sig: (case: str, reynolds: float = PLATE_RE, *, level: dict[str, Any] = LEVELS[0], model: str = 'kOmegaSST', iterations: int = 6000) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Write the flat-plate case: graded in ``y`` from a first cell that puts ``y+`` near one at ``Re = 5e6``.

The first cell height follows ``y+ = 1`` for a flat plate, ``h1 = y+ nu / u_tau`` with ``u_tau`` from the 1/7-power
law — an estimate, and the right one to make: the wall function the models use wants its first cell inside the
log layer, and a mesh whose first cell is ten times too tall is a different (and much easier) case.

functions.name: run
functions.sig: (case: str, *, timeout: float = 3600.0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: ``blockMesh``, ``simpleFoam``, cell centres — the same three commands as every other laminar case here.

functions.name: skin_friction
functions.sig: (case: str, *, u_inf: float = 1.0, nu: float = 2e-07) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
``cf(x)`` on the plate from the wall shear stress the solver wrote: ``cf = 2 tau_w / U^2``.

``tau_w`` is the ``wallShearStress`` function object's answer — the shear the solver itself used, which is the only
value that is right when a wall function is in play. Estimating it from the first cell (``(nu + nut) du/dy``) was
measured to over-predict by 5.6x with Spalart-Allmaras and 2.0x with k-omega SST at ``y+ ~ 30``: the effective
viscosity at a log-layer cell is not the wall's. ``nu`` is kept in the signature so a caller can compare the two.

functions.name: read_reference
functions.sig: (path: str) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
A TMR ``cf`` table as ``{"x", "cf"}``: two whitespace-separated columns, one station per line.

The TMR publishes its reference results as plain text files next to each case. They are not in this repository (and
not downloadable from the machine this was built on), so the comparison is a call away rather than a number in a
README: give this the file and :func:`study` reports the difference.

functions.name: study
functions.sig: (root: str, *, reynolds: float = PLATE_RE, levels: Sequence[dict[str, Any]] = LEVELS, models: Sequence[str] = MODELS, station: float = 0.97, reference: str | None = None, timeout: float = 3600.0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Run both models on every level, and report the observed order and the Richardson-extrapolated ``cf``.

The station defaults to ``x = 0.97``: far enough downstream that the boundary layer is developed and far enough
from the trailing edge that the outlet's treatment of it does not dominate. ``reference`` is a TMR file for
:func:`read_reference`; without it the table has the extrapolated value and the 1/7-power law's estimate, and says
the comparison is pending rather than implying agreement.

children.summary: The NASA Turbulence Modeling Resource flat plate in OpenFOAM, with its grid-convergence study (#265).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.warm_start
children.doc:
Start a solver run from a surrogate's predicted field, and measure what it saved (#494).

A surrogate that predicts the flow is worth more than its fields: it is a **starting point**. Keeping the solver as
the thing that produces the answer, and using the prediction only to place the first iterate near the solution, is the
one way to get the value of a surrogate in production without trusting it — the converged answer is still the
solver's, and the measurement of the saving (iterations and wall time) is also a measurement of how good the
surrogate was. Obiols-Sales et al. (CFDNet, ICS 2020) report 1.9-7.4x for steady RANS this way.

What is here
------------
:func:`write_fields` maps a predicted field onto a case's time-zero fields **without touching the boundary
conditions**: the ``internalField`` is replaced and the ``boundaryField`` block is left exactly as it was, because the
boundary conditions are the problem statement and a surrogate has no business rewriting them.

:class:`OperatorSurrogate` is a parametric surrogate over one number — a proper orthogonal decomposition of a few
solved cases, with the mode coefficients interpolated in the parameter. It is the smallest thing that deserves the
name: it is fitted from runs (not from a formula), it predicts a whole field at a parameter it has not seen, and
:meth:`OperatorSurrogate.error` says how far its prediction is from a solver run at that parameter.

:func:`benchmark` is the experiment the issue asks for: at a parameter held out of the fit, run the case cold and run
it warm from the prediction, and report the iterations, the wall time, the speedup and the difference between the two
converged answers — which must be nothing, because they are the same equations and the same tolerance.

Where it stops
--------------
Warm starting a *steady* solve is the easy case: the iterates are a path to a fixed point and a better start is a
shorter path. A transient case has no such fixed point, and the saving depends on how fast the start-up transient
decays; the same machinery applies (write the field at ``t0`` and integrate from there) but the measurement has to be
made per case, and none is claimed here.

classes.name: OperatorSurrogate
classes.doc:
A field surrogate over one parameter: POD of the solved snapshots, coefficients interpolated in the parameter.

``fit(reynolds, snapshots)`` takes ``{re: {"U": (n, 3), "p": (n,)}}`` — the fields of cases solved on **one mesh**,
so the snapshots are the same length — and keeps ``modes`` modes per field. :meth:`predict` returns the same
structure at any parameter, interpolating the coefficients linearly between the solved ones (or holding the end
value outside the range, and saying so in :attr:`extrapolated`).

methods.name: fit
methods.sig: (snapshots: dict[float, dict[str, np.ndarray]], *, modes: int | None = None) -> OperatorSurrogate
methods.doc: Decompose each field of the snapshots and fit its coefficients against the parameter.

methods.name: predict
methods.sig: (reynolds: float, *, modes: int | None = None) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
methods.doc: The field at ``reynolds``: the mean plus the interpolated modes, in the shape the snapshots had.

methods.name: energy
methods.doc: The fraction of the snapshot energy the kept modes capture, per field.

methods.name: error
methods.sig: (reynolds: float, truth: dict[str, np.ndarray]) -> dict[str, float]
methods.doc: Relative L2 error of the prediction against a solved field at the same parameter.

classes.name: WarmStartResult
classes.doc: One cold run against one warm run: the cost of each, and whether they converged to the same answer.

functions.name: set_internal_field
functions.sig: (case: str, name: str, values: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Replace only the ``internalField`` of ``case/0/<name>``; the ``boundaryField`` is left byte for byte.

``values`` is ``(n_cells,)`` for a scalar and ``(n_cells, 3)`` for a vector. Returns what it wrote — the field,
the number of cells and the range of the values — so a run records the start it was given.

functions.name: write_fields
functions.sig: (case: str, fields: dict[str, np.ndarray]) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Map a whole predicted state onto time zero of ``case``: one :func:`set_internal_field` per field.

functions.name: internal_field
functions.sig: (case: str, name: str, time: str = '0') -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: The ``internalField`` of one field of one time directory, read back as an array (for a check or a difference).

functions.name: benchmark
functions.sig: (reynolds: float, surrogate: OperatorSurrogate, root: str, *, n: int = 64, timeout: float = 3600.0) -> WarmStartResult
functions.doc:
Solve the cavity at ``reynolds`` twice — cold, then warm from the surrogate's prediction — and compare.

The two runs are the same case: same mesh, same schemes, same residual control, same iteration cap. The only
difference is the ``internalField`` at time zero, which is uniform zero for the cold run and the surrogate's
prediction for the warm one. ``field_difference`` is the largest difference between the two converged answers,
relative to the magnitude of the field: they must agree to the tolerance, or the warm start changed the answer and
the saving is not a saving.

functions.name: snapshots
functions.sig: (root: str, reynolds: Sequence[float], *, n: int = 64, fields: Sequence[str] = ('U', 'p'), timeout: float = 3600.0) -> dict[float, dict[str, np.ndarray]]
functions.doc: Solve the cavity at each Reynolds number on one mesh and keep the converged fields as snapshots.

children.summary: Start a solver run from a surrogate's predicted field, and measure what it saved (#494).

children.doc:
Classical CFD validation cases with their published numbers, run against a real solver (issues #272, #265, #294, #494).

Every learned model and every surrogate in this repository is scored against a reference; this package is where the
reference itself is checked. It holds six things and keeps them apart:

* the published tables (:mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.reference`), transcribed as data with the table
  they came from, and never re-derived from a run;
* the cases that can be compared with them (:mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.cavity`,
  :mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.step`), which write their own OpenFOAM dictionaries and read the answer
  back as cell-centred numbers;
* the same cavity solved by a network instead of a mesh (:mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.pinn`), scored
  through the same stations and the same norm, so the two numbers can be read in one column;
* the CFDBench cavity family (:mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.cfdbench`), read from the benchmark's own
  archive and scored with that same ruler, so a published dataset's numbers can be read in that column too;
* the convergence arithmetic that turns three refined runs into an observed order and a Richardson-extrapolated value
  (:func:`observed_order`, over :func:`~pinneapple_analysis.verification.convergence.richardson_extrapolate`, which
  the repository already had for exactly this);
* the one place the solver is looked for (:mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.foam`), so a machine without
  OpenFOAM skips the runs and still gets the tables.

    import pinneapple as pp

    out = pp.cfd.validation.cavity_study(100, "runs/cavity")   # three meshes, errors against Ghia (1982)
    out["errors"][64]["u"]["l2_relative"]                       # the number to quote, at 64 x 64

    net = pp.cfd.validation.pinn_study((100, 400, 1000))        # the same case, trained (minutes on a CPU)
    net["stops_matching"]["0.05"]["stops"]                      # where it stops matching the same table

Without OpenFOAM (:func:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.foam.available`) the studies raise
:class:`OpenFOAMMissing`, which the tests turn into a skip and a caller reads as "this machine cannot run the
validation" rather than as a wrong answer. The tables in :mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.cfd_validation.reference` need no
solver at all.

classes.name: OpenFOAMMissing
classes.doc: No OpenFOAM on this machine: the case cannot be run, and that is not the same as the case being wrong.

functions.name: available
functions.sig: (*needs) -> bool
functions.doc: Whether an OpenFOAM installation (with ``needs``, e.g. ``"simpleFoam"``) is there to run the cases.

functions.name: require
functions.sig: (*needs) -> str
functions.doc: The bashrc, or :class:`OpenFOAMMissing` with the one thing a caller can do about it.

functions.name: observed_order
functions.sig: (errors: list[float], ratio: float = 2.0) -> list[float]
functions.doc:
The observed order of accuracy from the error on successive refinements: ``log(e_i/e_{i+1}) / log(r)``.

The error against a published table should fall by ``r**p`` per refinement, where ``p`` is the order of the
scheme; two errors give one estimate and three give two, and their agreement is what makes the pair believable.
A zero error gives ``inf`` (nothing left to resolve) and a growing one gives a negative order, both reported as
they are: an error that does not fall is the finding, not something to filter.

children.summary: Classical CFD validation cases with their published numbers, run against a real solver (issues #272, #265, #294, #494).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics
pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.analytic
children.doc:
Closed-form references for verifying the 2D A_z solvers.

* :func:`wire_field` -- round conductor with uniform current (Ampere's law).
* :func:`coax_field` -- coaxial cable, inner conductor ``+I``, outer ``-I``.
* :func:`magnetized_cylinder` -- uniformly magnetized cylinder (``mu_r = 1``) inside a circular
  boundary with ``A = 0``: ``A = f(r) sin(phi - alpha)``; inside the field is uniform,
  ``B = (Br/2)(1 - a^2/R^2)`` along the magnetization (``Br/2`` as ``R -> infinity``).
* :func:`skin_effect_wire` -- current density and per-unit-length impedance of a round wire carrying
  a sinusoidal current (Bessel functions of complex argument).
* :class:`RadialLayers` -- one spatial harmonic ``cos(p phi), sin(p phi)`` of a field in concentric
  layers of linear media with radially magnetized magnets and current densities: each layer obeys
  ``f'' + f'/r - p^2 f/r^2 = rhs(r)`` and the interfaces carry continuity of ``A`` and of
  ``H_phi = -nu dA/dr``. This is the subdomain (exact 2D) solution of a slotless machine, used to check
  the air-gap field and the torque of the FEM model.

All quantities SI. Torque per metre of stack in air between radii ``r`` of a field
``A = a(r) cos(p phi) + b(r) sin(p phi)`` from the Maxwell stress tensor is
``T = (p pi r / mu0) (a b' - a' b)`` (derived in :meth:`RadialLayers.torque`).

classes.name: Layer
classes.doc:
Annulus ``r_in < r < r_out`` with relative permeability ``mu_r``; radial remanence
``Br_cos cos(p phi) + Br_sin sin(p phi)`` and current density ``J_cos cos(p phi) + J_sin sin(p phi)``.

classes.name: RadialLayers
classes.sig: (layers: Sequence[Layer], p: int)
classes.doc:
Exact solution for one harmonic ``p >= 1`` in concentric layers; ``A = 0`` at the outer radius,
regular at ``r = 0`` if the first layer starts there (otherwise ``dA/dr = 0``, an ideal iron wall).

methods.name: B_polar
methods.doc: (B_r, B_phi) with B_r = (1/r) dA/dphi, B_phi = -dA/dr.

methods.name: torque
methods.doc:
Torque on everything inside radius ``r`` (an air radius), N m:
``(L/mu0) r^2 int B_r B_phi dphi = (L p pi r / mu0)(a b' - a' b)``.

functions.name: wire_field
functions.sig: (r, current: float, radius: float, R_outer: float)
functions.doc: (A_z, |B|) of a round wire (uniform J) centred in a circle of radius ``R_outer`` with A=0.

functions.name: coax_field
functions.sig: (r, current: float, a: float, b: float, c: float)
functions.doc: |B| of a coax: inner conductor radius ``a`` (+I), outer conductor ``b < r < c`` (-I).

functions.name: magnetized_cylinder
functions.sig: (x, y, Br: float, a: float, R: float, alpha: float = 0.0)
functions.doc:
A_z of a cylinder (radius ``a``, ``mu_r = 1``, remanence ``Br`` along angle ``alpha``) in air with
``A = 0`` at radius ``R``. Equivalent surface current ``K = M sin(phi - alpha)``; returns (A, B_inside).

functions.name: magnetized_ring
functions.sig: (x, y, Br: float, a: float, b: float, r0: float, R: float, alpha: float = 0.0)
functions.doc:
A_z of a uniformly magnetised ring ``a < r < b`` (``mu_r = 1``, remanence ``Br`` along ``alpha``) in air
between two circles with ``A = 0``: ``r0 < a`` and ``R > b``. Superposition of two cylinders
(:func:`magnetized_cylinder`, radii ``b`` and ``a``) plus the harmonic ``C (1/r - r/R^2) sin(phi - alpha)``
that cancels A on ``r0``.

functions.name: skin_effect_wire
functions.sig: (r, current: complex, radius: float, sigma: float, omega: float, mu: float = MU0)
functions.doc:
Phasor current density J(r) and impedance per metre Z = R + j omega L_int of a round wire.

``J = k I J0(k r) / (2 pi a J1(k a))`` with ``k^2 = -j omega mu sigma`` (time convention exp(+j omega t)).

functions.name: round_conductor_eddy_loss_low_freq
functions.sig: (B_peak: float, omega: float, sigma: float, a: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Time-averaged eddy loss per metre in a round conductor (radius ``a``, no net current) in a uniform
transverse field ``B_peak sin(omega t)``, resistance limited (field of the eddy currents neglected):
``P = pi sigma omega^2 B^2 a^4 / 8`` W/m.

Returns
-------
P : float [W/m]
    Loss per metre of conductor.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.antenna
pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.antenna.ava
children.doc:
An open parametric antipodal Vivaldi antenna (AVA) for the EMerge FEM solver, written from scratch.

Geometry (millimetres; the board lies in the x-y plane, the antenna radiates end-fire along +y, z is normal to the
board; the substrate spans ``0 <= y <= Lb``, ``|x| <= W/2``, ``0 <= z <= h``):

* top layer (z = h): a 50-ohm microstrip of width ``wf`` (Pozar, *Microwave Engineering*, 4th ed., eq. 3.197) from
  the board edge y = 0 to ``y = xs``, then the top flare towards +x: inner edge
  ``x(y) = c1 exp(R (y - xs)) + c2`` from ``-wf/2`` at ``y = xs`` to ``Wa/2`` at the mouth ``y = Lb``, outer edge a
  quarter ellipse from ``+wf/2`` to the board side ``W/2`` (semi-axis ``(Lb - xs)/2`` along y), then straight;
* bottom layer (z = 0): the ground of width ``Wg`` from y = 0 to ``y = Lo`` (the microstrip ground), a linear taper
  to ``wf`` at ``y = xs`` (the microstrip-to-parallel-strip transition, the balun), then the mirror image
  (x -> -x) of the top flare;
* optional ``nslot`` rectangular corrugations of depth ``Ls``, width ``ws`` and pitch ``ps`` cut into the outer
  straight edge of both arms, counted from the mouth;
* optional elliptical director (semi-axes ``dir_a`` along y and ``dir_b`` along x) on the top layer, centred at
  ``(0, dir_x)`` in the flare opening;
* substrate ``er`` 3.55, ``tand`` 0.003, ``h`` 1.524 mm (a hydrocarbon-ceramic laminate class, e.g. 60-mil
  RO4003C-type values; change them freely), PEC conductors of zero thickness;
* air box with a margin of ``air * lambda`` on every side and a second-order absorbing boundary on its faces; the far
  field is the Stratton-Chu integral over those faces;
* a lumped 50-ohm port across the substrate at y = 0, under the microstrip.

Per frequency :func:`simulate` returns the complex S11, the directivity, IEEE gain and realized gain at boresight
(+y) and at the pattern peak, the radiation efficiency, and saves the 3-D far field (theta, phi, E_theta, E_phi) to
``ff_<f>GHz.npz``. Definitions (IEEE Std 145): ``U = |E|^2 r^2 / (2 eta0)``; ``D = 4 pi U / P_rad`` with ``P_rad``
the integral of ``U`` over the sphere; ``G = 4 pi U / P_acc`` with ``P_acc = P_inc (1 - |S11|^2)``;
``G_realized = 4 pi U / P_inc``; ``e_rad = P_rad / P_acc = G / D``.

:func:`layout` is pure NumPy (no EMerge) and raises :class:`InvalidGeometry` for a design that cannot be built
(the DOE skips those). EMerge (GPL-2.0, ``pip install emerge``) is imported only by :func:`simulate`; it is called,
never copied. ``python -m pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.antenna.ava --freq 3 --out run/`` runs one design
from the command line (the script the :mod:`.runner` drives, one frequency per process).

classes.name: InvalidGeometry
classes.doc: The parameters do not describe a buildable antenna (overlapping metal, slots through the arm, ...).

classes.name: AVAParams
classes.doc: Design parameters, millimetres (``R`` in 1/mm, ``res`` and ``air`` in wavelengths).

classes.name: Layout
classes.doc: Conductor polygons (mm, closed, counter-clockwise not guaranteed) and the derived dimensions.

functions.name: microstrip_width
functions.sig: (z0: float, er: float, h: float) -> float
functions.doc: Width of a microstrip of impedance ``z0`` on a substrate ``er``, ``h`` (Pozar eq. 3.197, same unit as h).

functions.name: layout
functions.sig: (p: AVAParams) -> Layout
functions.doc: The conductor polygons of design ``p``; :class:`InvalidGeometry` if it cannot be built.

functions.name: use_superlu
functions.sig: () -> None
functions.doc:
Force EMerge's SuperLU direct solver.

Measured here: EMerge's PARDISO backend can die with SIGBUS when MKL is not usable; SuperLU always runs.

functions.name: nearfield_planes
functions.sig: (p: AVAParams) -> dict[str, dict[str, np.ndarray]]
functions.doc:
The two near-field cut planes of design ``p`` (mm): ``board`` (z = h/2, the substrate mid-plane) and ``axis``
(x = 0, through the end-fire axis), each ``{"origin", "u", "v", "nu", "nv"}``: points
``origin + i/(nu-1) u + j/(nv-1) v``. The extent is the board plus ``nf_margin`` on every side, the spacing
``nf_step``; it does not depend on the frequency, so the planes of every frequency share one grid.

functions.doc:
``(nv, nu, 3)`` points of a plane of :func:`nearfield_planes` (mm).

Returns
-------
points : np.ndarray [mm]
    (nv, nu, 3) points of the plane.

functions.sig: (params: AVAParams | dict, freqs_ghz, out_dir: str | None = None, *, superlu: bool = True, log: str = 'WARNING') -> list[dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:
Build the design in EMerge, solve each frequency (one mesh per frequency, size ``res * lambda``) and return
one row per frequency (the columns of :mod:`.runner`'s table).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.antenna.bounds
children.doc:
Physical limits on the directivity of a travelling-wave (end-fire) or aperture (broadside) antenna.

An end-fire antenna of length ``L`` (a Vivaldi, a Yagi, a helix, a dielectric rod) behaves like a continuous
end-fire line source of the same length. Its maximum directivity (C. A. Balanis, *Antenna Theory*, 4th ed., ch. 6,
directivity of uniform end-fire arrays with ``N d = L``) is

* ordinary end-fire (phase velocity = c): ``D ~= 4 L / lambda``;
* Hansen-Woodyard end-fire (the increased-directivity condition, slow wave): ``D ~= 1.805 * 4 L / lambda``
  (7.22 L / lambda; this module uses the rounded design value 7.28 L / lambda, 0.04 dB higher), the practical upper
  bound of a single travelling-wave antenna.

A broadside aperture of physical area ``A`` and aperture efficiency ``eta`` has ``G = eta 4 pi A / lambda^2``
(Balanis ch. 12). This is the wrong limit for an end-fire antenna, whose aperture faces along the board: a printed
Vivaldi of 100 mm x 200 mm has a large "broadside" area but its end-fire mouth is only ``W x h``. Use
:func:`endfire_directivity` for it.

:func:`min_length` inverts the end-fire limit (the shortest antenna that can reach a target gain at a frequency)
and :func:`feasibility_frequency` gives the lowest frequency at which a board of length ``L`` can reach it. Example:
10 dBi at 2 GHz needs ``L >= 10 / 7.28 * 149.9 mm = 206 mm`` in the Hansen-Woodyard limit.

functions.name: wavelength
functions.sig: (f_hz)
functions.doc: Free-space wavelength [m] at ``f_hz``.

functions.name: endfire_directivity
functions.sig: (length_m, f_hz, kind: str = 'hw')
functions.doc: Maximum directivity (linear) of an end-fire antenna of length ``length_m`` at ``f_hz``.

functions.name: endfire_directivity_dbi
functions.sig: (length_m, f_hz, kind: str = 'hw')

functions.name: aperture_gain
functions.sig: (area_m2, f_hz, efficiency: float = 1.0)
functions.doc: Broadside aperture gain (linear) ``eta 4 pi A / lambda^2``.

functions.name: aperture_gain_dbi
functions.sig: (area_m2, f_hz, efficiency: float = 1.0)

functions.name: min_length
functions.sig: (gain_dbi, f_hz, kind: str = 'hw')
functions.doc:
Shortest end-fire length [m] whose directivity limit reaches ``gain_dbi`` at ``f_hz``.

It is a lower bound for the gain too (gain <= directivity).

functions.name: feasibility_frequency
functions.sig: (gain_dbi, length_m, kind: str = 'hw')
functions.doc:
Lowest frequency [Hz] at which an end-fire antenna of length ``length_m`` can reach ``gain_dbi``.

Below it the target is out of reach for any design of that length, whatever the flare, slots or director.
