children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.mesher
children.doc:
Conforming Delaunay meshes of machine sectors and their assembly into a rotating machine mesh.

:func:`mesh_sector` triangulates one annular sector (:class:`~.geometry.SectorGeometry`) so that every edge
of every polygon, both arcs and both radial sides are edges of the mesh: boundary points are placed at the
local size ``h``, interior points on a staggered polar lattice, and any boundary segment whose diametral
circle contains another point is split (or the interior point removed) until every segment is a Gabriel edge,
which a Delaunay triangulation always contains. Elements are then named by the polygon that contains their
centroid, so the regions are the polygons exactly.

:class:`MachineMesh` copies the rotor-pole sector and the stator-slot sector around the circle (identical
elements in every pole and slot, so cogging and ripple carry no mesh noise of their own) and joins them
through the air gap with three ring layers: rotor air, moving band, stator air. Turning the rotor moves the
rotor nodes rigidly and re-triangulates only the band (:func:`~..mesh.zipper`), so rotor and stator
elements keep their indices at every angle.

methods.name: min_angle
methods.doc: Smallest interior angle of all triangles (degrees).

classes.name: MachineMesh
classes.sig: (geometry: MachineGeometry, n_gap: int = 960, h_max: float | None = None, grading: float = 0.2, smooth: int = 3, mirror: bool = True)
classes.doc:
Mesh of a complete radial-flux machine (:class:`~.geometry.MachineGeometry`).

``n_gap`` nodes on the air-gap circles (a multiple of poles and slots), element size ``h_gap`` =
``2 pi r_gap / n_gap`` at the gap growing by ``grading`` per metre away from it, at most ``h_max``.
``mirror`` meshes half a pole and half a slot pitch and reflects them (symmetric geometry assumed).
The gap is split into three equal ring layers: rotor air (turns with the rotor), moving band, stator air.
Element order: rotor, rotor air, stator, stator air, band (the band is re-triangulated at every angle).

Attributes after construction: ``n_rotor_nodes`` (rotor nodes come first and turn with the rotor),
``region_names``, ``region`` (per element), ``pole``/``slot`` index per element (-1 elsewhere),
``magnet_angle`` (per element, rotor frame, including the pole's polarity; NaN outside magnets),
``annuli``: [(r1, r2, element indices)] of the two air layers for the Maxwell-stress torque,
``boundary``: nodes of the shaft and outer circles (A = 0).

methods.name: mesh
methods.doc: The machine with the rotor turned by ``theta`` (counter-clockwise, radians).

functions.name: mesh_sector
functions.sig: (geom: SectorGeometry, size: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray] | float, n_in: int, n_out: int, smooth: int = 3, mirror: bool = False, max_rounds: int = 60) -> SectorMesh
functions.doc:
Mesh ``geom`` with element size ``size(r)`` (metres, a function of radius, or a constant); the arcs get
``n_in`` and ``n_out`` equal intervals (plus the extra nodes of ``geom.arc_nodes_in/out``). ``smooth``
rounds of Laplacian smoothing of the interior points improve the angles (boundaries stay fixed).

``mirror=True`` (geometry symmetric about the sector axis, ``n_in`` and ``n_out`` even) meshes the half
``phi < 0`` and reflects it, so the mesh itself is symmetric: a symmetric rotor in a symmetric stator then
has exactly zero torque at the aligned positions, and the cogging curve no mean offset.

functions.name: replicate_sector
functions.sig: (sm: SectorMesh, copies: int, span: float) -> Mesh2D
functions.doc:
The full circle from ``copies`` rotated copies of a sector mesh. Region index per element: the polygon
index (fill = -1 shifted to 0, polygons from 1); ``boundary``: the nodes of both arcs; extra attributes
``sector`` and ``local`` give each element's copy and its index in the sector.

children.summary: Conforming Delaunay meshes of machine sectors and their assembly into a rotating machine mesh.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.motor3d
pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.motor3d.dataset
children.doc:
The training set of the motor surrogate: a design of experiments over :data:`~.design.VARIABLES`, labelled by the
reference model and stored with its provenance.

The set is what makes the surrogate possible, and it is also the largest cost of the study: one reference design is
one electromagnetic operating point (a nonlinear magnetostatic solve over several rotor angles) plus an iron-loss
period, about a second on one core. :func:`build_dataset` therefore runs the cases in parallel processes and stores
the result, so a surrogate is trained from a file rather than from a fresh campaign.

Invalid designs (polygons that cross, a magnet that leaves its pole) are part of the record: they are marked in
``valid``, and the surrogate is trained only on the valid ones. They are also what makes the *rejection rate* of the
design space visible: at the corners of the box a large fraction of the designs cannot be built, and an optimiser
that does not know it wastes its budget.

:class:`MotorDataset` keeps the design matrix ``X`` (columns in the order of :data:`~.design.NAMES`), the outputs
``Y`` (scalars of :data:`~.model.SCALARS` and profiles of :data:`~.model.PROFILES`, flattened to ``(n, n_segments)``
columns named ``T_winding_profile_C[k]``), and a ``meta`` dictionary with the model configuration, the DOE method, the
seed, the cost and the library version. ``MotorDataset.load`` refuses a file whose design names do not match
:data:`~.design.NAMES`: a surrogate trained on a different ordering of the inputs would otherwise predict silently
wrong numbers.

The study as a :class:`~pinneapple_data.contracts.ParameterSpace`, so the same box can be sampled by the

``n`` designs of the box, labelled by the reference model.

The designs are drawn with the library's DOE (:func:`pinneapple_data.doe.design`) and filtered by the geometry

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.motor3d.design
children.doc:
Design vector of the 3-D multiphysics motor study, and the machine it builds.

The cross-section of the interior-PM rotor (:class:`~..geometry.VRotor`) is the one of the 2-D studies; this module
adds the two directions those studies do not have and the two load variables that make the problem multiphysics:

* **axial** -- stack length ``L`` and rotor skew ``skew_deg`` (mechanical degrees of twist over the stack);
* **cooling** -- coolant volume flow through the water jacket ``flow_L_min``, which sets the jacket conductance and
  therefore the winding and magnet temperatures;
* **operating point** -- peak phase current ``I_peak``, current angle ``gamma_deg`` and rotor speed ``rpm``.

:data:`VARIABLES` is the single source of the names, units and bounds: the design space of the optimiser, the
columns of the training set and the inputs of the surrogate are all built from it, so a variable that is not in it
cannot leak into one of the three by accident.

:class:`Motor3DDesign` is a frozen dataclass: a design is a value. :meth:`Motor3DDesign.geometry` returns the
cross-section the mesher takes, :meth:`Motor3DDesign.sector_errors` the reasons it cannot be meshed (empty when it
can), so an optimiser can discard a design before it costs a solve.

classes.name: DesignVariable
classes.doc: One design variable: ``name``, SI ``unit``, the box the study searches, and what it does to the machine.

methods.name: doe_group
methods.doc:
The group this variable maps to in the library's parameter-space contract (geometry, operating or
boundary: the DOE report has no separate axial or cooling group).

classes.name: Motor3DDesign
classes.doc:
One point of the study: the five rotor cross-section variables, the two axial ones, the operating point and
the cooling. Every value is SI (metres, amperes, revolutions per minute, litres per minute, degrees).

methods.name: from_mapping
methods.doc: A design from a mapping that has at least every name of :data:`VARIABLES` (extra keys are ignored).

methods.name: from_vector
methods.doc: A design from the vector in the order of :data:`NAMES` (the optimiser's ordering).

methods.name: baseline
methods.doc: The 2004 Prius design at its published operating point: the reference every result is compared with.

methods.name: clipped
methods.doc: The design moved onto the box of :data:`VARIABLES` (keeps an optimiser's proposal meshable).

methods.name: geometry
methods.doc: The cross-section: the Prius stator and winding with this design's rotor and stack length.

methods.name: sector_errors
methods.doc: Reasons the cross-section cannot be meshed (polygons crossing, leaving the pole...); empty when valid.

methods.name: omega_mech
methods.doc: Mechanical angular speed (rad/s).

methods.name: skew_factor
methods.doc:
Fundamental skew factor ``sin(x) / x`` with ``x`` half the electrical skew angle (one half of the stack
is twisted ``+skew/2`` and the other ``-skew/2``): the fraction of the fundamental flux linkage that the
twist leaves useful.

functions.sig: (designs: Sequence[Motor3DDesign]) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: ``(n, d)`` array of the designs in the order of :data:`NAMES`.

functions.doc: Designs from an ``(n, d)`` array in the order of :data:`NAMES`.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.motor3d.model
children.doc:
The multiphysics reference model of one motor design: electromagnetics, losses, cooling and temperature, coupled.

One call to :meth:`Motor3DModel.solve` runs the chain an engineer runs by hand:

1. **electromagnetic** -- nonlinear 2-D magnetostatic FEA of the cross-section at the operating point
   (:class:`~..pmsm.IPMMachine`), over a set of rotor angles, with the magnet remanence at a first-guess magnet
   temperature;
2. **skew** -- the stack is cut into ``n_segments`` axial slices twisted by ``skew_deg``: each slice contributes the
   torque of the cross-section at its own electrical angle, so the slot harmonics cancel the way they do in a skewed
   machine, and the fundamental is reduced by the skew factor;
3. **losses** -- stator and rotor iron loss from the flux density over an electrical period, resistance-limited
   magnet eddy loss, and the copper loss of the slot and end-winding parts of the winding, with the end turns of the
   axial geometry (the winding resistance depends on the stack length, so it is a 3-D quantity);
4. **cooling and temperature** -- the axial lumped network of :mod:`.thermal3d`, whose jacket conductance follows the
   coolant flow as ``flow^0.8`` (turbulent convection), giving a temperature per part and per axial segment;
5. **back to the electromagnetics** -- the magnet temperature changes the remanence (``Br(T)`` of the grade), so
   torque, iron loss (through ``B^2``) and the demagnetisation margin are corrected, and the copper loss is
   re-evaluated at the winding temperature with the network solved again until the temperatures stop moving.

Two costs are kept honest. Step 5 is a one-step fixed point around one FEA solve per design (``fea_iterations=1``);
setting it to 2 re-solves the field at the converged magnet temperature. The difference between the two is measured,
not assumed: :func:`~.workflow.check_temperature_coupling` reports it on a set of designs and the model card records
it.

Everything here is SI: metres, amperes, volts, webers, watts, degrees Celsius, kilograms. The outputs are listed in
:data:`OUTPUTS`, each with its unit and whether a better design makes it larger or smaller.

classes.name: MotorOutput
classes.doc: One output of the model: name, unit, whether a better design makes it larger, and what it is.

classes.name: Motor3DModel
classes.sig: (n_gap: int = 192, n_positions: int = 8, n_segments: int = N_SEGMENTS, magnet_T_guess: float = 90.0, fea_iterations: int = 1, coolant_flow_ref: float = 6.0, thermal: MachineThermalData | None = None, Hcj20: float = MAGNET_GRADE_HCJ, v_dc: float = 500.0, loss_steps: int = 6, magnet_T_limit: float = 180.0, name: str = 'motor3d-fea')
classes.doc:
The reference multiphysics model (see the module docstring).

``n_gap`` is the air-gap mesh of the cross-section (a multiple of twice the slot and pole counts), ``n_positions``
the rotor angles the torque is averaged over, ``n_segments`` the axial segments of the skew model and of the
thermal network, ``magnet_T_guess`` the magnet temperature the field is first solved at and
``fea_iterations`` how many times the field is re-solved at the converged magnet temperature (1 = the one-step
correction, 2 = one extra solve per design).

``count`` is the number of FEA operating points solved so far and ``seconds`` the time spent in them: a study
reports what it cost, and the point of the surrogate is the ratio between these numbers and its own.

methods.name: machine
methods.sig: (d: Motor3DDesign, magnet_temperature: float | None = None) -> IPMMachine
methods.doc: The FEA machine of a design (cached per geometry and magnet temperature: the mesh is the expensive part).

methods.name: winding
methods.doc:
Winding quantities of the axial geometry: end-turn length per side (m), the phase resistance at 20 degC
(Ohm) and its split between the slot and the ends (the resistance grows with the stack length).

methods.name: thermal_model
methods.doc: The axial network of a design, with the jacket conductance scaled by the coolant flow (``flow^0.8``).

methods.name: solve
methods.sig: (d: Motor3DDesign, keep_fields: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any]
methods.doc: Every quantity of one design, with the intermediate state (losses, node temperatures, fields).

methods.name: evaluate
methods.doc:
The outputs of every design of ``X`` (``(n, d)``, columns in the order of :data:`~.design.NAMES`), as
arrays: the scalars of :data:`OUTPUTS` and the profiles of :data:`PROFILES` (``(n, n_segments)``). Designs
the mesher cannot build come back as NaN.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.motor3d.optimize
children.doc:
The optimisation that runs on the surrogate: thousands of designs, no FEA per candidate.

The study is the one a motor designer actually asks: push torque density up, magnet mass and loss down, keep the
winding and the magnets under their temperature limits, keep the demagnetisation ratio below one and the torque
ripple below what the drive tolerates -- over the rotor cross-section, the stack length, the skew, the operating point
and the coolant flow at once.

Three functions, in the order a study uses them:

* :func:`design_problem` -- the objectives, the limits and the design space, as a
  :class:`~pinneapple_design.design_optimizer.study.DesignProblem` whose evaluator is the surrogate;
* :func:`optimize` -- NSGA-II on that problem with a budget counted in **surrogate** evaluations; the result records
  how many reference solves it cost, which is zero;
* :func:`verify_front` -- the same designs re-evaluated by the reference model, the one place where an FEA call is
  spent, so the front is not taken on the surrogate's word. A surrogate error that changes the ranking of the front
  is then visible as a number, not as a surprise.

:func:`benchmark` measures what the substitution bought: designs per second for the surrogate against designs per
second for the reference, on the same machine, in the same process.

classes.name: SurrogateEvaluator
classes.sig: (surrogate = None, check_geometry: bool = True, k_std: float = 1.0)
classes.doc:
The trained surrogate behind the design-optimiser interface: ``evaluate(X)`` returns one array per output,
the profiles flattened to their hottest segment (an optimiser constrains numbers, not curves).

methods.name: evaluate
methods.doc:
The scalars only: the optimiser constrains numbers, and the axial profiles are summarised by their
hottest segment (``T_winding_C`` and ``T_magnet_C`` already are that maximum).

methods.name: spread
methods.doc: Ensemble spread per output: how much the members disagree, in the output's unit.

functions.name: design_problem
functions.sig: (evaluator: Evaluator | None = None, *, surrogate = None, limits: dict[str, float] | None = None, objectives: Sequence[tuple[str, str]] | None = None) -> DesignProblem
functions.doc:
Maximise torque density and efficiency, minimise magnet mass; temperatures, ripple and the demagnetisation
ratio as constraints. ``evaluator`` overrides the surrogate (pass a reference evaluator to run the same problem
on the FEA); ``limits`` overrides :func:`_limits`.

functions.name: optimize
functions.sig: (problem: DesignProblem | None = None, *, budget: int = 2000, method: str = 'nsga2', seed: int = 0, surrogate = None, initial: Motor3DDesign | None = None, progress: Callable[[int, int], None] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Run ``method`` for ``budget`` surrogate evaluations and report the front, the best designs and the cost.

``budget`` counts designs, not FEA solves: the surrogate answers each one in microseconds. The result carries
``n_reference_solves`` (zero here) so the claim is checked rather than implied.

functions.name: verify_front
functions.sig: (result: dict[str, Any], *, reference: Motor3DModel | None = None, n: int = 8, limits: dict[str, float] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Re-evaluate designs of the surrogate front with the reference model and compare, output by output.

Returns the per-output error (relative and absolute) of the surrogate against the FEA-based model on exactly
those designs, whether the re-evaluated design is still feasible under the same limits, and the cost of the
check. This is the number that says whether the surrogate can be trusted for this study: it is measured on the
front, which is the region the optimiser actually chose, not on a random split.

functions.name: benchmark
functions.sig: (surrogate, reference: Motor3DModel | None = None, *, n: int = 32, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Designs per second: the surrogate against the reference model, on the same designs.

children.summary: The optimisation that runs on the surrogate: thousands of designs, no FEA per candidate.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.motor3d.surrogate
children.doc:
The surrogate of the multiphysics motor: an ensemble of networks that replaces the FEA at optimisation time.

What it predicts is every output of :data:`~.model.OUTPUTS` plus the three axial profiles of
:data:`~.model.PROFILES`, from the eleven design variables of :data:`~.design.VARIABLES` -- that is, torque, ripple,
torque density, efficiency, three loss channels, three temperatures, the demagnetisation ratio and two masses, each
resolved on the four axial segments of the thermal network.

Three things make it usable rather than merely fast, and all three are properties of this class, not of the training
script:

* **an ensemble, not a network** -- ``ensemble`` networks with different initialisations are trained on the same
  split and their spread is the model's own uncertainty. A design the networks disagree on is a design to send to
  the reference model, not one to believe;
* **a validity box and a data test** -- :meth:`MotorSurrogate3D.out_of_box` reports the design variables outside the
  box the training set was drawn from, and :meth:`MotorSurrogate3D.extrapolation` the distance to the training set
  relative to its own scale, so an optimiser that wanders off the data can see it happen;
* **a model card with the held-out numbers** -- :meth:`MotorSurrogate3D.card` carries the errors measured on data the
  networks never saw, per output, in the output's own unit. A prediction without them is a number without a claim.

Outputs are trained in a normalised space (standardised, or ``log`` for the strictly positive ones, which is what
makes a loss of 300 W and a torque of 30 N m train together): ``log_targets`` lists them, and the transforms are
stored with the weights so a saved model predicts in physical units on the way out.

classes.name: SurrogateConfig
classes.doc: Shape and training schedule of the ensemble.

``_valid`` (every design is valid for a network; the flag is what the optimiser expects).

Distance of each design from the training mean in units of the training spread (the largest over the
variables): 0 at the mean, 3 at the edge of a roughly Gaussian cloud.

methods.doc: The model card: what it was trained on, how it scored on held-out designs, what it does not know.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.motor3d.thermal3d
children.doc:
Axial-resolved lumped thermal network of the machine: the 2-D radial network of :mod:`.thermal`, cut into segments
along the stack.

:func:`~..thermal.machine_network` models one node per part (yoke, teeth, winding, end windings, rotor, magnets): the
stack is isothermal along ``z`` and the only axial information is the separate end-winding node. That is enough for a
hot-spot *level* and it is not enough for a hot-spot *place*: the middle of the stack sits between two cooled ends,
the ends of the stack sit next to the end windings, and the winding's axial conduction (copper, 390 W/m K along the
conductors) spreads heat over the whole length. This module keeps the same radial conductances and gives every part
``n_segments`` nodes along the stack, linked to their neighbours by ``k A / dz``.

The network is quasi-3-D: resolved in ``z`` and lumped in ``r`` and ``theta`` (every slot and every pole is the same).
It is solved with the steady-state solver of :class:`~..thermal.ThermalNetwork`, so all the checks of that class
apply, and the transient solver gives the thermal step response for free.

Assumptions, stated where they are used: the axial conductivity of the lamination stack is far below its in-plane one
(the sheets are insulated), so the axial conductance of the iron rings uses its own ``k_lam_axial`` (default 4 W/m K,
a typical value for a coated lamination stack; the in-plane 28 W/m K of :class:`~..thermal.MachineThermalData` is the
radial one), while copper and magnets conduct at their handbook values. The jacket is spread over the outer surface
of every yoke segment in proportion to its length.

classes.name: AxialThermalModel
classes.doc:
The nodes, their conductances and their volumes of the axial network, ready to be solved.

Attributes after construction: ``names`` (``"yoke[0]"``... in radial order per segment, then ``"end_winding"``),
``K`` (segments), ``network`` (:class:`~..thermal.ThermalNetwork`), ``volumes`` (m^3 per node, for the loss
density and the heat capacity) and ``segment_length`` (m).

methods.sig: (part: str, k: int | None = None) -> int

methods.name: powers
methods.sig: (p_yoke: float, p_teeth: float, p_winding_slot: float, p_winding_end: float, p_rotor: float, p_magnets: float) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc:
Power (W) into every node from the losses of one operating point. The stator iron is spread over the
segments in proportion to their length; the slot copper likewise; the end-winding copper goes to the single
end-winding node.

methods.name: steady
methods.doc:
Node temperatures (degC) and the summaries a design decision needs: the hottest winding and magnet node
(they are not at mid-stack when the ends are cooled) and their axial profiles.

functions.doc: The axial network of ``geometry`` (see :class:`AxialThermalModel`).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.motor3d.workflow
children.doc:
The whole study as one command: data, surrogate, optimisation, verification, figures and a report.

The workflow is what makes the pieces a product rather than a notebook:

``build-dataset``  sample the design space, label it with the reference model, store the set with its provenance
``train``          fit the ensemble, measure it on held-out designs, write the weights and the model card
``optimize``       NSGA-II on the surrogate alone; the front, the best designs and designs per second
``verify``         re-evaluate designs of that front with the reference model and report the error it finds
``check-coupling`` measure what the one-step magnet-temperature correction costs against a re-solved field
``all``            all of the above into one folder, with the figures and ``report.md``

Run it as ``python -m pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.motor3d.workflow <command> [options]`` or call
:func:`run_workflow` from Python. Every step writes its own artefact (``dataset/``, ``model/``, ``optimization.json``,
``verification.json``, ``figures/``) so a later step can be re-run without repeating the expensive one, and the report
is rebuilt from the artefacts on disk rather than from memory.

functions.name: check_temperature_coupling
functions.sig: (n: int = 6, seed: int = 0, n_gap: int = 192) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
What the one-step magnet-temperature correction costs.

The reference model solves the field once (at ``magnet_T_guess``) and then corrects torque, loss and margin for
the magnet temperature it computed (``fea_iterations=1``). With ``fea_iterations=2`` the field is re-solved at
that temperature. The two are compared here on ``n`` designs drawn from the box, so the shortcut has a number.

functions.name: figures
functions.sig: (out_dir: str | Path, opt: dict[str, Any], ver: dict[str, Any], bench: dict[str, Any], surrogate: MotorSurrogate3D, data: MotorDataset | None = None) -> list[str]
functions.doc:
The figures of the report, from the artefacts: Pareto front, thermal trade-off, axial profiles, error and
speed.

functions.name: write_report
functions.sig: (folder: str | Path) -> Path
functions.doc: Rebuild ``report.md`` from the artefacts in ``folder`` (nothing is taken from memory).

functions.name: run_workflow
functions.sig: (out_dir: str | Path, *, n_train: int = 600, seed: int = 0, workers: int = 4, budget: int = 2000, n_gap: int = 192, n_positions: int = 12, reuse: bool = True, progress = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: data -> surrogate -> optimisation -> verification -> figures -> report, into ``out_dir``.

functions.name: main
functions.sig: (argv: list[str] | None = None) -> int

children.summary: The whole study as one command: data, surrogate, optimisation, verification, figures and a report.

children.doc:
3-D multiphysics study of an interior-PM motor: reference model, pretrained surrogate, optimisation without FEA.

The pieces, in the order a study uses them:

* :mod:`.design` -- the design vector (:data:`~.design.VARIABLES`, :class:`~.design.Motor3DDesign`).
* :mod:`.thermal3d` -- the axial-resolved lumped thermal network (the stack is not isothermal: it has two cooled
  ends and a hot middle, and the winding conducts along the copper).
* :mod:`.model` -- :class:`~.model.Motor3DModel`: electromagnetic FEA, skew by axial slices, iron, magnet and copper
  loss, cooling at a coolant flow, the magnet temperature back on torque and demagnetisation, and the axial profiles.
* :mod:`.dataset` -- design of experiments over :data:`~.design.VARIABLES`, evaluated by the reference model and
  stored with its provenance.
* :mod:`.surrogate` -- :class:`~.surrogate.MotorSurrogate3D`, an ensemble of networks trained on that set with its
  held-out errors, validity box and model card, and :func:`~.surrogate.load_pretrained` for the one shipped here.
* :mod:`.optimize` -- the design problem and the search that runs **entirely on the surrogate** (no FEA per
  candidate), the Pareto front, and the re-check of the front with the reference model.
* :mod:`.workflow` -- the whole study as one command, with figures and a report.

The headline use is three lines::

    from pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.motor3d import load_pretrained, optimize
    surrogate = load_pretrained()
    front = optimize(budget=4000)["front"]        # 4000 designs, zero FEA calls

and the workflow that produced the surrogate is one more::

    python -m pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.motor3d.workflow all --out motor3d_run
children.summary: 3-D multiphysics study of an interior-PM motor: reference model, pretrained surrogate, optimisation without FEA.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.pmsm
children.doc:
Interior permanent-magnet synchronous machine: 2-D nonlinear A_z FEA and its post-processing.

    from pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines import IPMMachine, prius_2004
    m = IPMMachine(prius_2004(), n_gap=960)
    op = m.operating_point(I_peak=250.0, gamma=math.radians(50))  # torque, psi_d, psi_q over rotor positions
    T, psi_d, psi_q = op["torque_mean"], op["psi_d"], op["psi_q"]

Conventions. Rotor angle ``theta`` counter-clockwise (mechanical radians), torque on the rotor counter-clockwise
positive. The d-axis is the axis of the magnet flux linkage (found from a no-load solution,
:meth:`IPMMachine.pm_flux_angle`); the amplitude-invariant Park transform ``x_d + j x_q = (2/3)(x_a + a x_b +
a^2 x_c) e^{-j theta_e}`` with ``theta_e = p theta + phi0`` gives ``psi_d``, ``psi_q``, and phase currents
``i_k = I cos(theta_e + pi/2 + gamma - 2 pi k / 3)`` put ``i_d = -I sin(gamma)``, ``i_q = I cos(gamma)``
(``gamma = 0`` on the q-axis, ``gamma > 0`` towards -d; pyleecan's current angle ``Phi0`` is ``gamma + 90 deg``).
Electromagnetic torque from the flux linkages: ``T = 1.5 p (psi_d i_q - psi_q i_d)``; from the field:
Arkkio's Maxwell-stress torque averaged over the rotor-side and stator-side air layers.

Materials: rotor and stator iron follow a nonlinear B-H curve (stacking factor applied), magnets are linear
(``mu_r``, ``Br`` at a temperature), pockets, slot openings and slots are air for the field. The shaft is outside
the model (A = 0 on the rotor's inner circle and on the stator's outer circle: no flux leaves the
lamination there).

classes.name: Winding
classes.doc:
Phase, orientation and turns of the coil side in each slot (single layer), series turns per phase,
parallel paths. ``layout``: (phase, sign) per slot, default a 60-degree phase belt.

methods.name: solve
methods.sig: (theta: float = 0.0, currents: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), A0 = None, nu_frozen: np.ndarray | None = None, magnets: bool = True) -> MachineSolution
methods.doc:
Nonlinear magnetostatic solution at rotor angle ``theta`` with instantaneous phase ``currents`` (A).
``nu_frozen``: element reluctivities of an earlier solution, which make the problem linear (frozen
permeability); ``magnets=False`` removes the magnet sources.

methods.name: torque
methods.doc: Arkkio torque (N m), length-weighted mean over the rotor-side and stator-side air layers.

methods.name: torque_coenergy
methods.doc:
Virtual-work torque dW'/dtheta at constant currents, fourth-order differences at multiples of the
band step (identical band triangles at those angles).

methods.name: pm_flux_angle
methods.doc: Electrical angle ``phi0`` of the d-axis (pole 0, on +x at ``theta = 0``) in the frame of the winding.

methods.name: currents_dq
methods.sig: (theta: float, i_d: float, i_q: float) -> tuple

methods.name: phase_currents
methods.sig: (theta: float, I_peak: float, gamma: float) -> tuple

methods.name: load_period
methods.doc:
Mechanical period of the torque and of the dq flux linkages under sinusoidal currents: 60 electrical
degrees (a shift of one phase belt) for a three-phase winding with an integer number of slots per pole
and phase. Use a full electrical period (``2 pi / p``) for other windings.

methods.name: positions
methods.sig: (n: int, period: float | None = None, theta0: float = 0.0) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: ``n`` rotor angles over ``period`` (default :attr:`load_period`), each a multiple of the band step.

methods.name: operating_point
methods.sig: (i_d: float | None = None, i_q: float | None = None, I_peak: float | None = None, gamma: float | None = None, n_positions: int = 6, period: float | None = None, keep: bool = False) -> dict
methods.doc: Solve over ``n_positions`` rotor angles with sinusoidal currents fixed in the dq frame.

methods.name: inductances
methods.sig: (i_d: float, i_q: float, theta: float = 0.0) -> dict
methods.doc:
Frozen-permeability flux split at one operating point: the permeability of the nonlinear solution is
frozen, so the field is the sum of a magnet part and a current part (exactly, the problem being linear
with the frozen reluctivities). Returns ``psi_pm`` (magnet flux on the d-axis with the frozen
permeability), apparent ``L_d = psi_d,i / i_d``, ``L_q = psi_q,i / i_q`` from the current part, and the
cross terms of unit d and q currents.

methods.name: mtpa
methods.sig: (I_peak: float, n_positions: int = 4, bracket: tuple = (0.0, 1.4), tol: float = 0.005)
methods.doc:
Current angle gamma (rad) of maximum mean torque at current amplitude ``I_peak`` (golden section
on the FEA torque averaged over ``n_positions`` rotor angles, within ``bracket``).

methods.name: no_load
methods.sig: (n: int = 24, n_flux: int | None = None) -> dict
methods.doc:
Cogging torque at ``n`` angles over one cogging period and phase flux linkages at ``n_flux`` (default ``n``)
angles over one electrical period (for a back-EMF waveform, >= 120: the EMF carries the slot harmonics).

methods.name: back_emf
methods.sig: (psi: np.ndarray, theta: np.ndarray, rpm: float) -> dict
methods.doc:
Phase back-EMF (V) from flux linkages over one electrical period: ``e = omega dpsi/dtheta``
(spectral derivative); also the fundamental and line-to-line rms values.

methods.name: losses
methods.sig: (rpm: float, i_d: float, i_q: float, steps: int = 48, loss_model = None, n_harmonics: int | None = None) -> dict
methods.doc:
Iron loss (stator, rotor) from the flux density over one electrical period (each element in its own
frame; ``loss_model`` default: the catalogue table of the steel) and resistance-limited magnet eddy
loss (each magnet an insulated piece; segment them with ``VRotor.magnet_segments``).

methods.name: loss_components
methods.sig: (i_d: float, i_q: float, alpha: float, beta: float, steps: int = 24, n_harmonics: int | None = None) -> dict
methods.doc:
Speed-free loss data of one operating point: iron-loss sums ``S = (S_h, S_c, S_e)`` of stator and rotor
(:func:`~..postprocess.iron_loss_components`; loss ``k_h f^alpha S_h + k_c f^2 S_c + k_e f^1.5 S_e``) and
the magnet loss coefficient ``P_m / f^2`` (resistance limited), with the mean torque and dq flux.

children.summary: Interior permanent-magnet synchronous machine: 2-D nonlinear A_z FEA and its post-processing.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.robustness
children.doc:
Step skew, manufacturing tolerances and a 3-D view of the field of an IPM machine.

Step skew (multi-slice 2-D): a rotor of ``K`` axial segments, segment ``k`` turned by ``delta_k = s (k - (K-1)/2)``
(step ``s``, total skew ``(K-1) s``). Each segment is a 2-D slice of the same stator with the same phase currents,
so the torque at rotor angle ``theta`` is ``(1/K) sum_k T_2D(theta + delta_k; i_abc(theta))`` and the flux linkage
the mean of the slices (end effects and the inter-segment axial flux are neglected, as in every multi-slice model).
For a quantity with a harmonic of order ``h`` per period ``lam`` the mean over the slices multiplies that harmonic by
the step-skew factor ``|sin(K h pi s / lam) / (K sin(h pi s / lam))|`` (:func:`step_skew_factor`).

Tolerances: :func:`tolerance_model` maps samples of (remanence scale, magnet thickness, magnet width, air gap) to the
FEA mean torque and ripple; with :func:`pinneapple_analysis.uncertainty.tolerance.propagate` (JCGM 101 Monte Carlo,
Wilson interval of the yield) it gives the output distributions directly from the FEA or from a surrogate trained on
it.

3-D view: :func:`skewed_field_3d` extrudes the 2-D solution of every segment into prisms (wedges) along the stack,
each segment turned by its skew angle; :func:`~.export.write_vtu` writes it for ParaView.

functions.name: step_offsets
functions.sig: (steps: int, step_angle: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Rotor angles of the ``steps`` segments, centred on zero.

functions.name: step_skew_factor
functions.sig: (h, steps: int, step_angle: float, period: float)
functions.doc:
Factor on harmonic ``h`` (per ``period``) of the segment-mean of a quantity: ``|sin(K x) / (K sin x)|``,
``x = h pi step_angle / period``.

functions.name: skewed_no_load
functions.sig: (machine: IPMMachine, thetas: Sequence[float], steps: int, step_angle: float) -> dict
functions.doc: Cogging torque and phase flux linkages of the step-skewed rotor at the rotor angles ``thetas``.

functions.name: skewed_torque
functions.sig: (machine: IPMMachine, i_d: float, i_q: float, thetas: Sequence[float], steps: int, step_angle: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Torque of the step-skewed rotor at rotor angles ``thetas`` (mechanical), with phase currents fixed in the dq
frame of the rotor at ``theta`` (the segments see the same stator currents, turned by their offset).

Returns
-------
T : np.ndarray [N m]
    Arkkio torque at each angle (``IPMMachine.torque``).

functions.name: tolerance_model
functions.sig: (base: MachineGeometry, I_peak: float = 250.0, gamma_deg: float = 50.0, n_gap: int = 288, n_positions: int = 6, variables: Sequence[str] = TOLERANCE_VARIABLES, **machine_kw)
functions.doc:
``fn(X) -> (n, 2)`` [mean torque (N m), ripple] for rows of ``variables``: ``Br_scale`` (remanence factor),
``H3`` magnet thickness, ``W4`` magnet width (m), ``airgap`` (m, the rotor radius changes, the stator stays).
Rows whose geometry is invalid give NaN. The function counts its FEA calls in ``fn.calls``.

functions.name: skewed_field_3d
functions.sig: (machine: IPMMachine, theta: float, currents, steps: int, step_angle: float, layers_per_step: int = 1) -> dict
functions.doc:
Prism (wedge) mesh of the stack with the 2-D field of every segment: points (N, 3), wedges (M, 6), cell data
``B`` (M, 3), ``|B|`` and region index. Segment ``k`` occupies ``z`` in ``[k, k+1] L / K``.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.steel
children.doc:
Catalogue electrical steel and magnet data for machine models, with their sources.

``M400_50A``: non-oriented electrical steel grade M400-50A (EN 10106; 0.50 mm, at most 4.00 W/kg at 1.5 T,
50 Hz): the B-H curve (44 points, 0 to 2.3 T) and the specific-loss table (W/kg at 50, 100, 200, 400, 1000 and
2500 Hz, 0.1 to 1.8 T) of pyleecan's material library (``pyleecan/Data/Material/M400-50A.json``, pyleecan 1.4.2,
Apache-2.0), resistivity 4.6e-7 Ohm m, density 7650 kg/m^3. These are the data of a supplier datasheet for the
grade, not of one coil: a design should use its own supplier's curve.

``MAGNET_PRIUS``: sintered NdFeB of pyleecan's ``MagnetPrius.json``: Br = 1.24 T at 20 degC, mu_r = 1.05,
reversible Br temperature coefficient -0.1 %/K (pyleecan ``alpha_Br`` = -0.001), resistivity 1.6e-6 Ohm m.

:func:`stacked` turns a solid-steel curve into the curve of a lamination stack with stacking factor ``kf``
(``B = kf B_steel(H) + (1 - kf) mu0 H``; the flux runs in the plane of the sheets). :func:`fit_iron_loss` fits
:class:`~..postprocess.IronLossModel` (Steinmetz hysteresis + Bertotti classical and excess eddy terms) to a loss
table and returns the fit's errors; :class:`TableIronLoss` interpolates the table itself (log-log), so it
reproduces the catalogue exactly at its points.

methods.name: Hc
methods.doc: Coercivity of the linear recoil line at 20 degC (A/m).

classes.name: TableIronLoss
classes.sig: (grade: SteelGrade)
classes.doc:
Specific iron loss interpolated from a catalogue table (same interface as ``IronLossModel``).

For each tabulated frequency, ``log p`` is interpolated linearly in ``log B`` (beyond the last point:
the power law of the last two points); between frequencies, linearly in ``log f`` (beyond the table:
the power law of the two nearest frequencies).

functions.name: stacked
functions.sig: (curve: BHCurve, kf: float, n: int = 200) -> BHCurve
functions.doc: B-H curve of a lamination stack: ``B = kf B_steel(H) + (1 - kf) mu0 H``.

functions.name: fit_iron_loss
functions.sig: (grade: SteelGrade, classical_from_resistivity: bool = True, B_max: float = 1.8, f_max: float = 2500.0) -> LossFit
functions.doc:
Least-squares fit (relative errors) of ``k_h f^alpha B^beta + k_c (f B)^2 + k_e (f B)^1.5`` to the
grade's loss table. With ``classical_from_resistivity`` the classical eddy coefficient is the
thin-sheet value ``pi^2 d^2 / (6 rho_e density)`` and only ``k_h, alpha, beta, k_e`` are fitted.

children.summary: Catalogue electrical steel and magnet data for machine models, with their sources.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.thermal
children.doc:
Lumped thermal network of a radial-flux machine, and the demagnetisation check of its magnets.

:class:`ThermalNetwork` is a general network of isothermal nodes: heat capacities ``C`` (J/K), conductances ``G``
(W/K) between nodes and to fixed-temperature boundaries, heat sources ``P`` (W). Steady state solves
``(L + G_b) T = P + G_b T_b`` (``L`` the conductance Laplacian); transients use backward Euler or the trapezoidal
rule (A-stable, orders 1 and 2), with time-dependent sources.

:func:`machine_network` builds the classic seven-node model of a water-jacketed machine (stator yoke, teeth,
winding in the slots, end windings, rotor, magnets, shaft/bearing path) from the cross-section and stated material and
contact data: conduction through cylindrical shells ``G = 2 pi k L / ln(r2/r1)``, through the slot insulation
(equivalent conductivity of the winding), axially along the conductors to the end windings, and convection across the
air gap and at the end windings with given heat-transfer coefficients. The coefficients are inputs, not
correlations fitted here: a validated model needs them from measurements or a CFD study of the actual machine.

:func:`demagnetisation_margin` evaluates the FEA field inside every magnet element: the field opposing the
magnetisation, ``H_rev = -(B . m - Br) / (mu0 mu_r)``, against the intrinsic coercivity ``Hcj(T)`` of the grade (the
knee of a square-loop NdFeB magnet); margin < 0 marks elements that would demagnetise irreversibly.

methods.name: connect
methods.sig: (a: str, b: str, G: float) -> ThermalNetwork

methods.name: to_boundary
methods.sig: (a: str, G: float, T: float) -> ThermalNetwork

methods.name: matrix
methods.doc: ``K`` (W/K) and the boundary load ``b`` (W): ``C dT/dt = -K T + b + P``.

methods.name: transient
methods.sig: (P: Callable[[float], Sequence[float]] | Sequence[float], t_end: float, dt: float, T0: Sequence[float] | float, method: str = 'trapezoidal') -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
methods.doc:
Temperatures at ``t = 0, dt, ..., t_end``; ``P`` constant or ``P(t)``; ``method``: ``"euler"`` (backward)
or ``"trapezoidal"`` (Crank-Nicolson).

classes.name: MachineThermalData
classes.doc:
Material and boundary data of :func:`machine_network` (SI). Defaults are typical textbook values, stated as
assumptions: laminations radial k = 28 W/m K, winding (copper, resin, insulation) equivalent k = 1.0 W/m K across
the slot, copper k = 390 W/m K along the conductors with copper fill 0.45, air-gap h = 120 W/m^2 K, end-winding
h = 40 W/m^2 K, water jacket to stator back h A = 300 W/K with coolant at 65 degC, densities and specific heats
of steel 7650 / 460, copper 8900 / 385, NdFeB 7500 / 450.

functions.name: intrinsic_coercivity
functions.sig: (Hcj20: float, temperature: float, beta: float = -0.0055) -> float
functions.doc:
``Hcj(T) = Hcj20 (1 + beta (T - 20))`` (A/m); ``beta`` is the reversible temperature coefficient of Hcj
(typically -0.5 to -0.6 %/K for sintered NdFeB; take the grade's datasheet value).

Returns
-------
Hcj : float [A/m]
    Intrinsic coercivity at ``temperature`` (degC), for ``Hcj20`` in A/m.

functions.name: cylinder_conductance
functions.sig: (k: float, r1: float, r2: float, length: float, fraction: float = 1.0) -> float
functions.doc: Radial conduction through a cylindrical shell (or ``fraction`` of it): ``2 pi k L f / ln(r2 / r1)``.

functions.name: machine_network
functions.sig: (geometry, data: MachineThermalData | None = None, end_length: float = 0.16) -> ThermalNetwork
functions.doc: Seven-node network of a machine with a water jacket on the stator back (see the module docstring).

functions.name: reverse_field
functions.sig: (B: np.ndarray, angle: np.ndarray, Br: float, mu_r: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Field opposing the magnetisation (A/m) in linear magnet elements: ``H_rev = -(B . m - Br) / (mu0 mu_r)`` with
``m = (cos angle, sin angle)``, from ``B = mu0 mu_r H + Br m``.

functions.name: demagnetisation_margin
functions.sig: (machine, ms, Hcj: float, margin_ratio: float = 0.9) -> dict
functions.doc:
Field opposing the magnetisation in every magnet element of the solution ``ms`` of ``machine`` (an
:class:`~.pmsm.IPMMachine`), against ``Hcj`` (A/m at the magnet temperature; the knee of a square-loop NdFeB
magnet). Returns the worst reverse field, the margin ``Hcj - H_rev`` (A/m), the demagnetised area fraction
(``H_rev > Hcj``), the area fraction within ``margin_ratio`` of the knee (``H_rev > margin_ratio Hcj``; less
sensitive to single corner elements than the knee crossing), and per magnet element the element index and
``H_rev / Hcj``.

functions.name: demagnetisation_refinement
functions.sig: (geometry, magnet_temperature: float, currents_d: dict, Hcj: dict, gradings = (0.2, 0.1, 0.05, 0.025), n_gap: int = 960, margin_ratio: float = 0.9, magnet = None) -> list[dict]
functions.doc:
Mesh study of :func:`demagnetisation_margin`: the machine meshed with decreasing ``grading`` (element size
growth away from the gap, :class:`~.mesher.MachineMesh`), so the magnet elements shrink at a fixed gap mesh.
``currents_d``: label -> d-axis current (A, rotor at 0); ``Hcj``: grade -> intrinsic coercivity (A/m). Per level:
number and mean size of the magnet elements, and per case and grade the worst ``H_rev / Hcj``, the demagnetised
fraction and the fraction above ``margin_ratio``.

functions.name: magnet_temperature_sweep
functions.sig: (geometry, temperatures, I_peak: float = 250.0, n_gap: int = 960, n_positions: int = 12, n_flux: int = 24, magnet = None) -> list[dict]
functions.doc:
Machine performance against the magnet temperature (``Br(T)`` of the grade): MTPA torque and angle at
``I_peak``, torque ripple, magnet flux linkage and back-EMF constant (fundamental, from ``n_flux`` angles over an
electrical period), frozen-permeability L_d, L_q at the MTPA point.

functions.name: iron_split
functions.sig: (m, I_peak: float = 250.0, gamma_deg: float = 50.3, rpm: float = 1500.0, steps: int = 24) -> dict
functions.doc:
Fractions of the iron loss in the stator yoke, the teeth and the rotor of an
:class:`~pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.IPMMachine` at one operating point (default 250 A MTPA,
50.3 deg, 1500 rpm): how a lumped thermal network distributes the iron loss of a drive cycle.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.verification
children.doc:
Verification of the machine FEA: closed forms for the mesher and solver, internal consistency of the torque,
flux-linkage and inductance post-processing, and a cross-check against a published benchmark machine.

``run(quick=...)`` returns :class:`~..verification.CaseResult` rows (the same table format as the
electromagnetics suite); ``examples/electrodynamics/10_pmsm_prius.py --write-docs`` writes them into
docs/guides/electromagnetics.md. Published reference: torque against current angle of the 2004 Toyota Prius
motor at 250 A peak (Z. Yang, M. Krishnamurthy, I. P. Brown, "Electromagnetic and vibrational characteristic of
IPM over full torque-speed range", IEEE IEMDC 2013, pp. 295-302), values as tabulated in pyleecan's test suite
(``Tests/Validation/Electrical/test_EEC_PMSM.py``, Apache-2.0).

children.doc:
Electric machines: parametric cross-sections, conforming meshes, nonlinear 2-D FEA and post-processing.

* :mod:`.geometry` -- V-shaped interior-magnet rotors, round-bottom slots, the 2004 Toyota Prius motor.
* :mod:`.mesher` -- conforming Delaunay sector meshes copied around the circle, moving band in the air gap.
* :mod:`.steel` -- catalogue steel (M400-50A B-H and loss table), magnet grades, stacking factor, loss fits.
* :mod:`.pmsm` -- :class:`IPMMachine`: torque (Maxwell stress and co-energy), cogging, ripple, flux linkage,
  back-EMF, dq flux linkages, frozen-permeability L_d / L_q, MTPA, iron and magnet losses.

The surface-PM and reluctance model on the polar mesher is :class:`pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machine.SPMMachine`.
children.summary: Electric machines: parametric cross-sections, conforming meshes, nonlinear 2-D FEA and post-processing.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines3d
pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines3d.afpm
children.doc:
Axial-flux permanent-magnet machine in 3-D on edge elements, against quasi-3D on the same discretisation.

The machine is meshed on a structured grid in cylindrical coordinates ``(r, theta, z)``: radial and axial node
lines are chosen per region (air inside ``r_in``, the active annulus, air outside ``r_out``; rotor yoke, magnets,
gap, teeth, stator yoke, air above and below), ``theta`` covers the full circle, each grid cell is split
into six tetrahedra along its diagonal (as :func:`~..fem3d.mesh.box_mesh`) and the grid is closed at ``theta =
2 pi`` by merging the seam nodes (the split is the same in every cell, so the seam is conforming). Turning the rotor
by a whole number of steps ``2 pi / n_theta`` maps the grid onto itself: rotor angle is a relabelling of the magnet
cells, so cogging carries no remeshing noise.

``edges``: with ``"cell"`` (the default) ``theta`` is uniform and a cell is magnet, or tooth iron, when its centre
is, so the magnet arc and the slot opening move in whole steps and the rotor in even steps. With ``"fraction"`` the
tooth edges are node planes that slide with the slot opening, a cell on a magnet edge carries the share of it inside
as that share of the remanence, and the rotor turns by any angle (the magnet shares at the turned position, on the
same mesh and the same factorised stiffness).

Topologies: ``"single"`` (one rotor, one slotted stator with a yoke) and ``"double_rotor"`` (a yokeless slotted
stator between two rotors whose magnets are magnetised the same way, so the flux crosses the stator axially).

Quasi-3D (:meth:`AFPM3D.quasi3d`): the active annulus cut into ``n`` radial slices, each solved alone on its part of
the same grid with flux-parallel cylindrical faces (``n x A = 0``): the flux cannot cross radius ``r_k``, which is
the assumption of the usual quasi-3D model (a 2-D linear machine per radius, curvature kept). Summing the slices
and comparing with the full 3-D model (with air inside and outside the annulus) measures what quasi-3D neglects:
radial flux and the fringing at the inner and outer radius.

Linear iron and magnets, no winding currents: cogging torque (Maxwell stress over the gap layers) and the no-load
flux linkage of a search coil around a stator tooth (exact line integral of ``A``, :func:`.endeffects.line_integral`).

classes.name: AFPMMachine
classes.doc:
Geometry and materials (SI). Magnets and teeth are annular sectors over ``[r_in, r_out]``; ``magnet_arc``
and ``slot_fraction`` are shares of the pole pitch and of the slot pitch.

methods.name: layers
methods.doc: Axial layers from the bottom: (kind, thickness).

classes.name: AFPM3D
classes.doc:
3-D finite-difference model of the axial-flux machine ``machine``: a grid in angle (``n_theta``, a multiple of
twice the poles and twice the slots), radius (``dr``) and axis (``dz``) with air around it (``air_r``, ``air_z``),
optionally restricted to a radial band of the active annulus (quasi-3D).

methods.name: materials
solve
methods.doc: No-load field at rotor angle ``theta``: preconditioned CG, the preconditioner factorised once.

methods.name: torque
methods.doc:
Torque on the rotor(s), N m: Maxwell stress ``r B_theta B_z / mu0`` averaged over each gap layer
(volume mean times the layer area), signed by the side of the rotor.

methods.name: tooth_linkage
methods.doc:
Flux linkage (Wb) of a coil around stator tooth ``tooth`` at mid tooth height: radial sides on the
slot centre lines, arcs ``overhang`` inside ``r_in`` and outside ``r_out`` (0: on those radii), drawn as
the polygons of the grid (so on a flux-parallel boundary they add exactly nothing).

methods.name: quasi3d_models
methods.doc: ``n_slices`` radial slices of the active annulus on the same radial nodes, no radial air.

functions.name: quasi3d_slices
functions.sig: (machine: AFPMMachine, n_slices: int, n_theta: int = 240, dr: float = 0.004, dz: float = 0.002, air_z: float = 0.015, edges: str = 'cell') -> list[AFPM3D]
functions.doc:
The quasi-3D slices of :meth:`AFPM3D.quasi3d_models` without building the full 3-D model: the active
annulus has the same radial nodes (``r_in`` to ``r_out`` every ``dr`` at most) in both.
