children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines3d.afpm_design
children.doc:
Axial-flux PM machine design in two steps: a quick quasi-3D estimate, then a check in full 3-D on the same grid.

:func:`estimate` cuts the active annulus into radial slices with flux-parallel faces (the usual quasi-3D model,
:meth:`.afpm.AFPM3D.quasi3d_models`) and returns the cogging over one period, its peak-to-peak and the no-load flux
linkage of a coil around a stator tooth. :func:`verify_3d` solves the same machine in full 3-D on the same grid,
with air inside, outside, above and below, and returns the same quantities with their ratio to the estimate:
what quasi-3D leaves out (the fringing at the inner and outer radius) for this design. On the default machine the
estimate overstated the cogging by 11 to 12 % and the flux linkage by 2 to 3 %
(``examples/electrodynamics/24_afpm_quasi3d.py``); :func:`verify_3d` measures it for the design at hand.

The back-EMF constant follows from the tooth linkage: with the magnet field of one tooth varying as the
fundamental of the pole pattern, the peak EMF of one tooth coil per turn and per mechanical rad/s is
``p * lambda_tooth`` (``p`` pole pairs); :func:`estimate` and :func:`verify_3d` give it as ``ke_tooth_V_s``.

:func:`field_view_of` gives a 3-D view of ``|B|`` on the magnets, the iron and the gap layers of a solved model
(:func:`pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.fieldview.field_view`: a glTF and its description).

functions.name: grid_for
functions.sig: (machine: AFPMMachine, dr: float = 0.008, dz: float = 0.004, min_steps: int = 180, steps_per_period: int = 8) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
The coarse grid for a design: steps round the axis a multiple of twice the poles and twice the slots (pole
and slot centres on the mesh's symmetry planes), at least ``min_steps`` and at least ``steps_per_period`` steps
per cogging period. Raises when that needs more than 480 steps (a slot-pole combination with a very
short cogging period). ``AFPM3D(edges="fraction")``: the tooth edges are node planes and the magnet edges
shares of the cells they cut, so a magnet arc or slot opening between two grid steps is the one asked for, not
the nearest whole cells, and the rotor turns by any angle (:data:`SAMPLES_PER_PERIOD` angles per cogging period).

functions.name: machine_from
functions.sig: (params: dict[str, Any] | None = None) -> AFPMMachine
functions.doc: An :class:`AFPMMachine` from a dict of its fields (missing ones keep their defaults).

functions.name: estimate
functions.sig: (params: dict[str, Any] | None = None, n_slices: int = 1, grid: dict[str, float] | None = None, keep: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Quasi-3D: ``n_slices`` radial slices of the active annulus, each with flux-parallel faces, on a grid of
``grid`` (default :func:`grid_for`: 8 mm radially, 4 mm axially, 192 steps for 12 slots and 8 poles). ``keep``: also return the slice models and the solution at the
linkage angle (for :func:`field_view_of`).

functions.name: verify_3d
functions.sig: (params: dict[str, Any] | None = None, grid: dict[str, float] | None = None, against: dict[str, Any] | None = None, keep: bool = False) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Full 3-D on the same grid as :func:`estimate` (air all round); with ``against`` (an :func:`estimate`
result), the ratios estimate / 3-D of the cogging peak-to-peak and the tooth flux linkage.

functions.name: field_view_of
functions.sig: (model: AFPM3D, sol, title: str = '', max_faces: int | None = 200000)
functions.doc:
3-D view of ``|B|`` (T) on the magnets, the iron and the gap layers of ``model`` at the solution ``sol``:
a :class:`~pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.fieldview.FieldView` (``.glb()`` and ``.meta``).

children.summary: Axial-flux PM machine design in two steps: a quick quasi-3D estimate, then a check in full 3-D on the same grid.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines3d.afpm_surrogate
children.doc:
Surrogates of the axial-flux PM machine in 3-D, with calibrated uncertainty and physics checks.

The simulator is the check in full 3-D of :func:`.afpm_design.verify_3d` (with the quasi-3D estimate on the same
grid), over four design variables of :class:`.afpm.AFPMMachine` (:data:`VARIABLES`); everything else keeps its
default. Outputs per design: the cogging peak-to-peak and the tooth flux linkage in 3-D and in quasi-3D, and their
ratios (what quasi-3D overstates for that design).

The campaign, the dataset with a held-out region and the comparison of surrogate families come from
:mod:`pinneapple_autolab.study` (space-filling design, resumable runs, cross-conformal 90 % intervals, a written
selection rule). :func:`physics_checks` are what a surrogate must respect to be eligible, evaluated on a Sobol
sample of the training region:

* every predicted cogging and flux linkage is positive;
* the flux linkage rises with the magnet thickness and falls with the gap (more magnet, more flux; a wider gap,
  less), on at least 90 % of the sample when the variable moves by 5 % of its range;
* the predicted quasi-3D / 3-D ratios stay within the band the campaign measured, widened by 50 %.

functions.name: run
functions.sig: (params: Mapping[str, float]) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
One design: the quasi-3D estimate and the check in 3-D on the coarse grid of the designer
(:func:`.afpm_design.grid_for`, whose magnet and tooth edges are shares of the cells they cut, so the outputs
move continuously with ``magnet_arc`` and ``slot_fraction``), about 55 s.

functions.name: simulator
functions.doc:
A :class:`pinneapple_autolab.simulator.FunctionSimulator` of :func:`run` that refuses designs outside the
variables' bounds.

functions.name: space
functions.doc: The design space as a :class:`pinneapple_data.contracts.ParameterSpace`.

functions.name: physics_checks
functions.sig: (measured_ratios: Mapping[str, tuple[float, float]] | None = None, n: int = 256, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, list[Callable[[Callable], Any]]]
functions.doc:
``{target: [check(predict) -> Check]}`` for :func:`pinneapple_autolab.study.benchmark.benchmark`; inputs in the
unit cube of the variables (their order in :data:`VARIABLES`). ``measured_ratios``: ``{target: (min, max)}`` of
the ratios in the campaign, for the band check.

functions.name: certify
functions.sig: (board, ds, target: str, family: str | None = None, r2_min: float = 0.9, ledger = None, tool: str = 'pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines3d.afpm_surrogate') -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
The checks of one surrogate as a trust decision and as entries of an evidence ledger.

Checks: each physics check of the benchmark (critical); on the held-out test designs, ``R^2 >= r2_min``
(critical) and the coverage of the conformal 90 % interval at least ``0.9 - 2 sqrt(0.09 / n)`` (two binomial
standard deviations below nominal for ``n`` test designs); the same two on the extrapolation designs, not
critical (the region the surrogate was not fitted on). The decision is
:class:`pinneapple_analysis.trust.TrustReport`'s (APPROVED / REVIEW / REJECT); every check is recorded in
``ledger`` (a :class:`pinneapple_veriphysics.ledger.EvidenceLedger`, new if None) under ``f"{target}/..."``
with the SHA-256 of the dataset as its inputs, so a report can say "passed" only with the record of the run.

children.summary: Surrogates of the axial-flux PM machine in 3-D, with calibrated uncertainty and physics checks.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines3d.endeffects
children.doc:
End effects of a surface-PM machine against the stack length: the magnet flux a full-pitch search coil links in
3-D (stack plus air beyond each end) divided by the 2-D value times the stack length.

The search coil is a loop at a given radius (default: the middle of the slots): two axial sides a pole pitch
apart, centred on the axis of magnet 0 with the rotor aligned, joined by arcs beyond the stack ends at ``overhang``
from the end faces (0: in the end faces). Its flux linkage is the line integral of ``A`` around the loop, so it
counts the magnet flux that leaves the rotor through the end faces and enters the stator outside the 2-D
cross-section. The 2-D reference is the same stack without the end air (flux-parallel end planes, so the field
does not vary along the axis), so the ratio measures only what 2-D neglects.

functions.name: search_coil_linkage
functions.sig: (model: SPM3D, sol, radius: float | None = None, span: float | None = None, overhang: float = 0.0, n: int = 96) -> float
functions.doc:
Flux linkage (Wb) of the search coil: ``span`` (default one pole pitch) centred on angle 0, at ``radius``
(default mid-slot), the arcs ``overhang`` beyond the stack ends (they must lie inside the mesh).

functions.name: line_integral
functions.sig: (space, a: np.ndarray, P: np.ndarray, samples: int = 64) -> float
functions.doc:
``int A . dl`` along the polyline ``P`` for the edge-element field ``a``, exact: ``A`` is linear in each
tetrahedron, so every segment is cut where it crosses element faces (found by bisection between ``samples``
points per segment that lie in different elements) and each piece is integrated by the midpoint rule. A plain
midpoint rule is not enough: the tree gauge puts large gradients in ``A`` in the air, which a closed loop
cancels only if every piece is integrated exactly (400 points per side gave 0.5 % of error on the search
coil). ``samples`` must resolve the elements along a segment.

functions.name: end_effect_study
functions.sig: (machine: SPMMachine | None = None, ratios: Sequence[float] = (0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0), end_length: float = 0.03, end_layers: int = 3, layer_dz: float = 0.015, n_theta: int = 240, overhangs: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 0.01), mu_r_iron: float = 1000.0, progress: Callable[[str], None] | None = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
For each L/D (D: bore diameter ``2 r_bore``) the search-coil flux linkage in 3-D against 2-D, the
ratio ``k = lambda_3D / lambda_2D`` per overhang and the mean gap flux density in the stack. The 2-D value is
the same layered stack without end air (flux-parallel end planes: axially invariant), so ``k`` holds only the
end effect and none of the in-plane discretisation. Returns ``{"D", "rows": [...], ...}``.

children.summary: End effects of a surface-PM machine against the stack length: the magnet flux a full-pitch search coil links in 3-D (stack plus air beyond each end) divided by the 2-D value times the stack length.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines3d.extrude
children.doc:
Extrusion of a 2-D triangle mesh into tetrahedra: each triangle times each z layer is a prism cut into three
tetrahedra by the global node order, so neighbouring prisms cut their shared quadrilateral faces along the same
diagonal and the mesh is conforming.

functions.name: extrude
functions.sig: (points: np.ndarray, tris: np.ndarray, z: np.ndarray, rank: np.ndarray | None = None) -> tuple[TetMesh, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Tetrahedral mesh of ``tris`` extruded through the planes ``z`` (increasing). Node ``i`` of plane ``k`` has
index ``k * N + i``. ``rank`` (a permutation of the nodes, default the node index) is the order that decides
the cuts: a rank that alternates along a ring of nodes alternates the lean of the cuts, so the mesh has no
handedness (with ranks growing with the angle every cut leans the same way round the axis, a helical bias
that shows up as a spurious torque). Returns the mesh (one region, tag 0), and for each tetrahedron the index
of its triangle and of its z layer.

children.summary: Extrusion of a 2-D triangle mesh into tetrahedra: each triangle times each z layer is a prism cut into three tetrahedra by the global node order, so neighbouring prisms cut their shared quadrilateral ...

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines3d.load
children.doc:
Load study: the torque of a skewed surface-PM machine in 3-D against multi-slice 2-D on the same mesh.

The skew study of :mod:`.skew` is at no load, where the only torque is cogging. This one drives the machine: the
armature source of :meth:`~.spm.SPM3D.current_density` carries the instantaneous phase currents of a synchronous
drive, so each rotor angle has a mean torque and a ripple on top of it. For each skew the 3-D model gives the whole
torque curve; the multi-slice model is the mean of straight one-layer models at the same rotor offsets, each with
the same instantaneous currents, so the two differ only by what multi-slice neglects: the axial flux between
segments and the end leakage.

What is measured, per skew, is the mean torque and the ripple ``(max - min) / mean`` of the two models. The mean is
what a 2-D model is usually trusted for; the ripple at load is where the skew acts (it cancels the slot harmonics
of the armature reaction as it cancels cogging), and it is what the multi-slice approximation has to get right.

Approximations, stated: iron is linear (``mu_r_iron``); the winding is stranded, straight and uniform over the
slot, with no end turns in the mesh; the rotor is skewed and the stator is not; the currents are sinusoidal and
synchronous. What the 3-D model therefore adds over 2-D is the axial flux path and the end regions, and nothing
else.

functions.name: ripple
functions.sig: (torque) -> tuple[float, float, float]
functions.doc: ``(mean, peak-to-peak, ripple)`` of a torque curve, ``ripple = (max - min) / mean`` (a share of the mean).

functions.name: load_study
functions.sig: (model: SPM3D, totals: Sequence[float], kinds: Sequence[str] = ('step2', 'step3', 'continuous'), thetas: Sequence[float] | None = None, currents_of: Callable | None = None, slice_model: SPM3D | None = None, progress: Callable[[str], None] | None = None, checkpoint = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
Torque against total skew (radians) for each kind, 3-D and multi-slice, at the currents
``currents_of(theta)`` (A). ``thetas`` default: one cogging period in angular steps of the model (end point
excluded). Returns ``{"thetas", "period", "rows": [...]}`` with, per row, the kind, the total skew, both torque
curves and their ``mean`` / ``pkpk`` / ``ripple``, the relative difference of the means, and seconds.
``checkpoint``: a JSON-lines file; each finished row is appended, and rows already there for the same angles and
currents are reused, so an interrupted study resumes where it stopped.

children.summary: Load study: the torque of a skewed surface-PM machine in 3-D against multi-slice 2-D on the same mesh.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines3d.magnet_loss
children.doc:
Eddy-current loss in a segmented permanent magnet, 3-D against 2-D and against the closed form.

A surface magnet sees a field ripple normal to its face (slot harmonics, armature MMF harmonics). The 2-D machine
model (``postprocess.magnet_eddy_loss_resistance_limited``) lets the eddy current flow along the axis with no net
current per piece: it is the loss of an infinitely long strip, and it cannot see axial segmentation. In 3-D the
current loops in the face of the magnet and closes across its width at the ends, so short pieces lose less.

The reference is the resistance-limited loss of a thin rectangular piece ``a x b`` (thickness ``h``) in a uniform
field ``B cos(wt)`` normal to it: the current stream function solves ``lap(psi) = j w sigma B`` with ``psi = 0`` on
the edge, whose double sine series gives

    P = (h sigma w^2 B^2 / 2) sum_{m, n odd} 64 a b / (pi^4 m^2 n^2 ((m pi / a)^2 + (n pi / b)^2)),

and for ``b -> inf`` the 2-D strip, ``P / b = h sigma w^2 B^2 a^3 / 24``. The 3-D model solves the full
time-harmonic problem (:func:`~pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.fem3d.nedelec.solve_eddy`) on a structured
mesh of the segmented block in a box whose boundary carries the uniform applied field, so it also shows where the
resistance-limited assumption fails (the skin depth reaching the piece size).

functions.name: plate_loss
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float, h: float, sigma: float, f: float, B: float, terms: int = 400) -> float
functions.doc:
Time-averaged resistance-limited loss (W) of a thin ``a x b`` piece, thickness ``h``, in a uniform normal
field of peak ``B`` at ``f`` (the double sine series above, ``terms`` odd terms in each direction).

Returns
-------
P : float [W]
    Time-averaged loss of the piece.

functions.name: strip_loss
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float, h: float, sigma: float, f: float, B: float) -> float
functions.doc:
The 2-D value: an infinitely long strip of width ``a`` (axial current, no net current), over length ``b``.

Returns
-------
P : float [W]
    Time-averaged loss of the strip over length ``b``.

functions.name: loss_factor
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float, terms: int = 400) -> float
functions.doc:
``plate_loss / strip_loss``: the share of the 2-D loss a piece of width ``a`` and length ``b`` keeps.

Returns
-------
ratio : float [-]
    ``plate_loss / strip_loss``.

functions.name: segmented_block
functions.sig: (width: float, length: float, thickness: float, n_width: int = 1, n_length: int = 1, gap: float = 0.0002, h: float = 0.0015, h_thick: float | None = None, margin: float = 0.03) -> TetMesh
functions.doc:
Structured mesh of a magnet ``width x length x thickness`` (x, y, z) cut into ``n_width x n_length``
insulated pieces (``gap`` of air between them), centred at the origin in a box of air ``margin`` wide.
Regions: ``magnet`` and ``air``.

functions.name: block_loss_3d
functions.sig: (mesh: TetMesh, sigma: float, f: float, B: float, solver: str = 'auto') -> dict
functions.doc:
Eddy loss (W) in the ``magnet`` region of ``mesh`` in a uniform field ``B`` (peak, along z) at ``f``: the
box boundary carries ``n x A`` of ``A0 = B x r / 2``.

functions.name: segmentation_study
functions.sig: (width: float, length: float, thickness: float, sigma: float, B: float, segments: Sequence[tuple[int, int]], freqs: Sequence[float], h: float = 0.0015, gap: float = 0.0002, progress: Callable[[str], None] | None = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
For each ``(n_width, n_length)`` segmentation and frequency: the 3-D loss, the closed-form
resistance-limited loss of the pieces and the 2-D (infinite strip) loss, all for the whole magnet.

children.summary: Eddy-current loss in a segmented permanent magnet, 3-D against 2-D and against the closed form.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines3d.skew
children.doc:
Skew study: cogging of a skewed surface-PM machine in 3-D against multi-slice 2-D on the same mesh.

For each skew (step skew with ``K`` segments or a continuous skew, represented by one rotor offset per stack
layer) the 3-D model gives the cogging torque with the axial flux between segments and, when the model has end
regions, the end leakage; the multi-slice model is the mean of straight one-layer models at the same rotor
offsets, so the two differ only by what multi-slice neglects. The skew is symmetric about the mid-stack plane, so
the cogging is odd in the rotor angle and angles over half a cogging period suffice.

The closed-form reference for a harmonic of order ``h`` of the cogging period ``lam``: continuous skew ``s``
multiplies it by ``sin(h pi s / lam) / (h pi s / lam)``; ``K`` steps over a total skew ``s`` (step angle
``s / (K - 1)``) by :func:`~pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.robustness.step_skew_factor`.

functions.name: continuous_factor
functions.sig: (h, total: float, period: float)
functions.doc: Continuous skew factor of harmonic ``h``: ``sin(x) / x`` with ``x = h pi total / period`` (1 at x = 0).

functions.name: skew_function
functions.sig: (kind: str, total: float, length: float) -> Callable
functions.doc: ``"step<K>"`` (e.g. ``"step2"``) or ``"continuous"``.

functions.name: slice_offsets
functions.sig: (model: SPM3D, kind: str, total: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Rotor offsets of the multi-slice model: one per stack layer of ``model`` (rounded to its angular step), so
its slices hold exactly the angular content of the 3-D model's layers.

functions.name: skew_study
functions.sig: (model: SPM3D, totals: Sequence[float], kinds: Sequence[str] = ('step2', 'step3', 'continuous'), thetas: Sequence[float] | None = None, slice_model: SPM3D | None = None, progress: Callable[[str], None] | None = None, checkpoint = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
Cogging against total skew (radians) for each kind, 3-D and multi-slice. ``thetas`` default: one cogging
period in angular steps of the model (end point excluded). Returns ``{"thetas", "period", "rows": [...]}`` with,
per row, the kind, the total skew, both cogging curves, their peak-to-peak (``max - min``) and seconds.
``checkpoint``: a JSON-lines file; each finished row is appended to it, and rows already there for the same
angles are reused, so an interrupted study resumes where it stopped.

children.summary: Skew study: cogging of a skewed surface-PM machine in 3-D against multi-slice 2-D on the same mesh.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines3d.spm
children.doc:
Surface-PM machine in 3-D on edge elements: the 2-D polar mesh of
:class:`~pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machine.SPMMachine` extruded along the stack, with magnet skew,
magnet end regions and the Maxwell-stress torque.

Every node ring of the cross-section carries ``n_theta`` equally spaced nodes (the rotor core starts at
``r_inner``, a flux-tangential boundary standing in for the shaft), so turning the rotor by a whole number of
angular steps ``2 pi / n_theta`` maps the mesh onto itself. Rotor position and skew are therefore relabellings of
the rotor elements of each z layer (which tetrahedra are magnet, which are air, and the direction of their
remanence), on one mesh for every angle and every skew: cogging and its skew dependence carry no remeshing
noise, and the multi-slice 2-D model (:meth:`SPM3D.multislice`) is the same discretisation with one layer per slice.

Skew (of the magnets, relative to the stator): ``skew(z)`` gives the rotor offset of the layer at axial position
``z``, rounded to the angular step; :func:`step_skew` and :func:`continuous_skew` give the usual ones. End regions:
``end_length`` of air beyond each end of the stack (``0``: flux-parallel end planes, the 2-D condition).
Boundaries: ``n x A = 0`` (``B . n = 0``) on the inner and outer cylinders and the end planes.

Iron is linear (``mu_r_iron``) in this model; magnets are linear with ``mu_r_magnet`` and remanence ``Br``
(parallel or radial magnetisation of the 2-D machine). Two sources: the magnets, and -- when ``currents`` is given
to :meth:`SPM3D.solve` -- the armature, as the axial current density of the stranded slots
(:meth:`SPM3D.current_density`), which is the same at every rotor angle because the stator does not turn. The
winding is therefore straight and the skew is the rotor's alone; the end turns are not in the mesh, so their
leakage and their loss are not in the torque.

methods.name: labels2d
methods.doc: Region of every 2-D element with the rotor turned by ``theta`` (rounded to the angular step).

methods.name: materials
methods.sig: (theta: float, skew: Callable = no_skew) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
methods.doc: Reluctivity and remanence per tetrahedron for rotor angle ``theta`` and the magnet ``skew``.

methods.name: slot_labels
methods.doc:
``"slot<k>"`` (or the iron) of every 2-D element, at rotor angle 0. The stator does not turn, so the slots
keep their label at every angle: the armature source below is angle-independent.

methods.name: current_density
methods.doc:
``(M, 3)`` axial current density per tetrahedron, ``J = (0, 0, J_z)``, from the instantaneous phase
currents (A) of the 2-D machine (:meth:`~pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machine.SPMMachine.`
``phase_currents``): ``sign * turns * I_phase / A_slot`` in each slot of the stack, zero in the end
regions and in the iron. Stranded coil, uniform over the slot, as in the 2-D ``current_density``; the slot
area is the one of this model's own cross-section, so that the two models inject the same current density
to the accuracy of their meshes.

methods.name: solve
methods.sig: (theta: float = 0.0, skew: Callable = no_skew, a0 = None, rtol: float = 1e-10, direct = None, currents = None)
methods.doc:
Field at rotor angle ``theta``: preconditioned CG on the tree-gauged system (a few iterations:
the preconditioner is the factorised matrix of :meth:`_system`). ``direct=True`` falls back to
:func:`~pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.fem3d.nedelec.solve_magnetostatic` (ungauged CG).
``currents`` are the instantaneous phase currents in A; ``None`` is no load (magnets only).

methods.name: release
methods.doc: Free the factorised preconditioner (PARDISO holds it in MKL memory until freed).

methods.name: torque
methods.doc:
Arkkio (Maxwell-stress) torque, N m, over the two gap annuli on either side of the moving band (as in
the 2-D model), over the whole axial length of the mesh; the length-weighted mean of the two.

methods.name: gap_flux
methods.doc:
Radial flux density averaged over the gap annuli within half a pole pitch of ``pole_angle`` and over
the stack (T).

methods.name: torque_series
methods.sig: (thetas, skew: Callable = no_skew, currents_of: Callable | None = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc:
Torque at each rotor angle (warm-started CG), at no load (``currents_of=None``) or with the phase currents
``currents_of(theta)`` (A), e.g. the ``phase_currents`` of the 2-D machine: synchronous drive, the winding
common to all slices, the skew in the rotor.

methods.name: cogging
methods.doc: No-load torque at each rotor angle (warm-started CG).

methods.name: slice_model
methods.doc: One straight layer of the stack with flux-parallel end planes: the 2-D model on the same mesh.

methods.name: multislice
methods.sig: (thetas, offsets, slice_model: SPM3D | None = None, currents_of: Callable | None = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc:
Multi-slice torque: the mean over the slices at rotor offsets ``offsets`` of the straight one-layer
model, times the stack length / slice length ratio (the torque of the full stack). ``currents_of`` as in
:meth:`torque_series`: every slice carries the same instantaneous currents, the slice's own field being
solved at its own rotor offset.

functions.name: no_skew
functions.sig: (z: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray

functions.name: step_skew
functions.sig: (total: float, steps: int, length: float) -> Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
``steps`` axial segments of equal length, segment ``k`` turned by ``total (k - (steps-1)/2) / (steps-1)``
(the convention of :func:`~pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machines.robustness.step_offsets` with step
angle ``total / (steps - 1)``).

functions.name: continuous_skew
functions.sig: (total: float, length: float) -> Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray]
functions.doc: Linear skew from ``-total/2`` at ``z = -L/2`` to ``+total/2`` at ``z = +L/2``.

children.summary: Surface-PM machine in 3-D on edge elements: the 2-D polar mesh of ~pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.machine.SPMMachine extruded along the stack, with magnet skew, magnet end regions and the ...

children.doc:
3-D electric machines on the edge-element solver of :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.fem3d`.

* :mod:`.extrude` -- conforming extrusion of a 2-D triangle mesh into tetrahedra.
* :mod:`.spm` -- :class:`SPM3D`: the surface-PM machine extruded along the stack, magnet skew (step or
  continuous), end regions, Maxwell-stress torque, the armature current of the slots, multi-slice 2-D on the same
  mesh.
* :mod:`.skew`, :mod:`.endeffects` -- skew study; end effects against L/D (search-coil flux linkage).
* :mod:`.load` -- the machine at load: mean torque and ripple, 3-D against multi-slice, per skew.
* :mod:`.magnet_loss` -- eddy loss of a segmented magnet, 3-D against 2-D and the closed form.
* :mod:`.afpm` -- :class:`AFPM3D`: axial-flux PM machine (single or double rotor) in 3-D, quasi-3D on the same grid.
children.summary: 3-D electric machines on the edge-element solver of pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.fem3d.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.materials
children.doc:
Magnetic materials for 2D A_z magnetostatics: linear media, permanent magnets and nonlinear B-H curves.

A nonlinear material is described by its reluctivity as a function of ``s = |B|^2``: ``nu(s)`` with
``H = nu(s) B``, the derivative ``dnu/ds`` (for the Newton tangent ``dH/dB = nu I + 2 nu' B B^T``) and the
energy density ``w(s) = int_0^|B| H db = 0.5 int_0^s nu(t) dt`` (for the energy functional, the line
search and the co-energy torque). Both curve classes below are single-valued (no hysteresis).

``BHCurve`` interpolates measured (B, H) points with a monotone cubic (PCHIP), so H(B) stays increasing
and the energy stays convex; beyond the last point it continues with the vacuum slope ``1/mu0``.
``BrauerCurve`` is the closed form ``nu(s) = k1 exp(k2 s) + k3`` (J. R. Brauer, IEEE Trans. Magn. 11(1),
1975). ``illustrative_steel()`` is a smooth, saturating curve generated from a formula: it is NOT a
measured grade; use a supplier's data for design work.

classes.name: LinearMaterial
classes.doc: Linear, isotropic medium: relative permeability ``mu_r`` and electrical conductivity ``sigma`` (S/m).

classes.name: Magnet
classes.doc:
Linear permanent magnet: ``B = mu0 mu_r H + Br``.

``Br`` is the remanence (T). ``direction`` is ``"radial"`` (outwards, times ``polarity``),
``"parallel"`` (along the pole axis given per element by the caller) or an angle in radians in the
frame the caller supplies. ``sigma`` is used only by eddy-current post-processing.

classes.name: BHCurve
classes.sig: (B, H)
classes.doc: Single-valued B-H curve from points, monotone cubic in H(B), vacuum slope above the last point.

methods.name: dnu
methods.doc: d nu / d s with s = |B|^2: (H'(b) b - H(b)) / (2 b^3).

methods.name: energy
methods.doc: w = int_0^|B| H db (J/m^3).

classes.name: BrauerCurve
classes.sig: (k1: float, k2: float, k3: float)
classes.doc: ``nu(s) = k1 exp(k2 s) + k3`` with ``s = |B|^2`` (closed-form energy and derivative).

functions.name: illustrative_steel
functions.sig: (mu_r_init: float = 4000.0, Js: float = 2.0, n: int = 60) -> BHCurve
functions.doc:
Smooth saturating curve ``B = mu0 H + Js (2/pi) atan(pi (mu_r_init - 1) mu0 H / (2 Js))``.

Initial relative permeability ``mu_r_init``, saturation polarization ``Js`` (T). Generated from a
formula for examples and tests -- not a measured electrical-steel grade.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.media
children.doc:
Electric and magnetic media for wave problems: linear, anisotropic and dispersive (Drude, Lorentz, Debye).

Time convention. Phasors are ``Re[X exp(+j omega t)]`` throughout this package (the engineering convention of
Taflove & Hagness, Pozar and scikit-rf, and of :mod:`.eddy`), so a lossy medium has ``Im(eps_r) < 0`` and a
wave travelling towards ``+z`` is ``exp(-j k z)``. Physics texts (Jackson, Bohren & Huffman) use
``exp(-i omega t)``: their ``eps`` is the complex conjugate of the one here.

Dispersion models, relative permittivity ``eps_r(omega) = eps_inf + sum_k chi_k(omega) + sigma / (j omega eps0)``
(Taflove & Hagness, *Computational Electrodynamics*, 3rd ed., ch. 9):

* :class:`Drude` ``chi = -omega_p^2 / (omega^2 - j omega gamma)`` -- free electrons (metals, plasmas);
* :class:`Lorentz` ``chi = delta_eps omega_0^2 / (omega_0^2 + 2 j omega delta - omega^2)`` -- bound resonances;
* :class:`Debye` ``chi = delta_eps / (1 + j omega tau)`` -- orientational relaxation (water, tissue).

Each pole carries the coefficients of its auxiliary differential equation (ADE) for the FDTD solver, a
second-order accurate discretisation of the polarisation current ``J_p = dP/dt``.

:class:`Anisotropic` holds 3x3 tensors ``eps_r``, ``mu_r`` and ``sigma`` and returns the refractive indices
of a plane wave along a direction (Fresnel's equation of wave normals as a generalised eigenproblem).

classes.name: Drude
classes.doc:
``chi(omega) = -omega_p^2 / (omega^2 - j omega gamma)``; plasma frequency ``omega_p`` and collision rate
``gamma`` in rad/s. With ``gamma = 0`` it is a collisionless plasma.

methods.name: ade
methods.doc:
Coefficients of ``dJ/dt + gamma J = eps0 omega_p^2 E`` (Taflove & Hagness eq. 9.50, centred in time):
``J^{n+1} = ka J^n + kb (E^{n+1} + E^n)``.

classes.name: Lorentz
classes.doc:
``chi(omega) = delta_eps omega_0^2 / (omega_0^2 + 2 j omega delta - omega^2)``; resonance ``omega_0``
(rad/s), damping ``delta`` (1/s), strength ``delta_eps = eps_s - eps_inf``.

methods.name: ade
methods.doc:
Coefficients of ``d2P/dt2 + 2 delta dP/dt + omega0^2 P = eps0 delta_eps omega0^2 E``, centred:
``P^{n+1} = a1 P^n + a2 P^{n-1} + a3 E^n``.

classes.name: Debye
classes.doc: ``chi(omega) = delta_eps / (1 + j omega tau)``; relaxation time ``tau`` (s).

methods.name: ade
methods.doc:
Coefficients of ``tau dP/dt + P = eps0 delta_eps E``, centred (trapezoidal):
``P^{n+1} = ka P^n + kb (E^{n+1} + E^n)``.

classes.name: Medium
classes.doc:
Isotropic linear medium: ``eps_inf``, ``mu_r``, conductivity ``sigma`` (S/m), magnetic conductivity
``sigma_m`` (ohm/m, used by PMLs) and dispersive poles.

methods.name: eps_r
methods.doc: Complex relative permittivity at angular frequency ``omega`` (``exp(+j omega t)``).

methods.name: n
methods.doc: Complex refractive index ``sqrt(eps_r mu_r)`` with ``Im(n) <= 0`` (decaying ``exp(-j k z)``).

methods.name: impedance
methods.doc: Wave impedance relative to free space, ``sqrt(mu_r / eps_r)`` (``Re >= 0``).

classes.name: Anisotropic
classes.doc: Linear anisotropic medium with relative tensors ``eps_r`` and ``mu_r`` (3x3) and conductivity ``sigma``.

methods.name: uniaxial
methods.sig: (n_o: float, n_e: float, axis: Sequence[float] = (0, 0, 1)) -> Anisotropic
methods.doc: Uniaxial crystal with ordinary and extraordinary indices and optic axis ``axis``.

methods.name: is_reciprocal
methods.doc: Lorentz reciprocity holds iff eps, mu and sigma are symmetric tensors.

methods.name: indices
methods.sig: (direction: Sequence[float], omega: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: Refractive indices of the two plane waves along unit ``direction``.

functions.name: drude_metal
functions.sig: (omega_p: float, gamma: float = 0.0, eps_inf: float = 1.0) -> Medium

functions.name: is_passive
functions.sig: (medium: Medium, omegas: Sequence[float], tol: float = 1e-12) -> bool
functions.doc: Passivity of a medium under ``exp(+j omega t)``: ``Im(eps_r) <= 0`` at every given frequency.

functions.name: rotation
functions.sig: (axis: Sequence[float], angle: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Rotation matrix about ``axis`` by ``angle`` (rad), Rodrigues' formula.

Returns
-------
R : np.ndarray [-]
    3 x 3 rotation matrix.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.mesh
children.doc:
Triangle meshes for 2D magnetostatics: a polar ring mesher with a moving band, and a gmsh importer.

The polar mesher builds a mesh from concentric rings of nodes. Two consecutive rings are joined by a
"zipper" triangulation that works for any node counts and any angular offsets, so the same routine
gives quad-like layers (equal counts), coarsening towards the centre (fewer nodes inside), a fan to a
centre node, and the sliding (moving) band of a rotating machine: the rotor rings carry an angular
offset ``theta``, the stator rings do not, and only the band layer between them is re-triangulated
when the rotor turns. Rotor and stator elements keep their indices and shapes for every angle.

Geometry is resolved on the polar grid (a "staircase" in angle), so boundaries of slots, teeth and
magnets should fall on ring radii and on multiples of the angular step of their rings.

    from pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.mesh import Ring, polar_mesh
    rings = [Ring(0.0, 1), Ring(0.01, 32), Ring(0.02, 64), Ring(0.03, 64)]
    mesh = polar_mesh(rings, classify=lambda layer, r, th: "air")

classes.name: Mesh2D
classes.doc:
P1 triangle mesh with one region name per element.

points: (N, 2) coordinates in metres; tris: (M, 3) counter-clockwise node indices;
region: (M,) integer region index into ``region_names``; layer: (M,) index of the ring layer an
element belongs to (polar meshes only, -1 otherwise); boundary: (K,) nodes on the outer boundary.

methods.name: mask
methods.doc: Boolean element mask of the regions in ``names`` (unknown names select nothing).

classes.name: Ring
classes.doc:
A circle of ``n`` equally spaced nodes at radius ``r`` (``n=1`` with ``r=0`` is the centre).

``offset`` is the angle of the first node; ``rotating`` marks rings that turn with the rotor.

functions.name: zipper
functions.sig: (ia: np.ndarray, ang_a: np.ndarray, ib: np.ndarray, ang_b: np.ndarray, closed: bool = True) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Triangulate the strip between two rings of nodes (indices ``ia``/``ib``, angles ``ang_a``/``ang_b``).

Walks around both rings at once, starting at the first node of ring a, and always advances the ring
whose next node has the smaller angle, which gives ``len(ia) + len(ib)`` triangles for a closed
strip. For an open strip (a sector) the angles must be sorted ascending. Orientation is not fixed here.

functions.name: polar_mesh
functions.sig: (rings: Sequence[Ring], classify: Callable[[int, float, float], str], theta: float = 0.0, span: float = TWO_PI, region_names: Sequence[str] | None = None) -> Mesh2D
functions.doc:
Mesh the disc (or sector ``[0, span]``) between concentric rings.

``classify(layer, r, phi)`` names the region of an element from the index of its ring layer and
its centroid radius and angle; for elements between two rotating rings ``phi`` is measured in the
rotor frame (centroid angle minus ``theta``), so the rotor geometry is the same for every angle.
``theta`` turns every ring with ``rotating=True``. For a sector (``span < 2*pi``) each ring holds
``n + 1`` nodes from 0 to ``span`` (rotation is not supported for sectors).

functions.name: rect_mesh
functions.sig: (x, y, classify: Callable[[float, float], str] | None = None) -> Mesh2D
functions.doc:
Structured triangle mesh of the rectangle spanned by the node coordinates ``x`` and ``y`` (1-D, increasing;
any spacing), two triangles per cell with diagonals alternating from cell to cell, so the mesh has no preferred
direction. ``classify(xc, yc)`` names the region of each element from its centroid. Node
``i * len(y) + j`` sits at ``(x[i], y[j])``; ``boundary`` holds the nodes on the four sides.

functions.name: mesh_from_gmsh
functions.sig: (dim: int = 2, model = None) -> Mesh2D
functions.doc:
Convert the current gmsh model (already meshed) into a :class:`Mesh2D`.

Every 2D physical group becomes a region (its name, or ``"phys<tag>"``); triangles outside any
physical group are dropped. Nodes of 1D physical groups named ``"boundary"`` (or, when there is
none, of the whole mesh boundary) are returned as ``boundary``. ``gmsh`` is an optional dependency.

functions.name: boundary_nodes
functions.sig: (tris: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Nodes on edges that belong to exactly one triangle.

children.summary: Triangle meshes for 2D magnetostatics: a polar ring mesher with a moving band, and a gmsh importer.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.mie
children.doc:
Mie scattering of a plane wave by a homogeneous sphere (and a perfectly conducting one).

Implementation of the series of C. F. Bohren and D. R. Huffman, *Absorption and Scattering of Light by Small
Particles* (1983), sec. 4.4 and appendix A (BHMIE), with the logarithmic derivative ``D_n(m x)`` by downward
recurrence and the series length of W. J. Wiscombe, *Improved Mie scattering algorithms*, Appl. Opt. 19 (1980)
1505, ``n_max = x + 4 x^{1/3} + 2``.

Convention: Bohren & Huffman use ``exp(-i omega t)``, so absorbing media have ``Im(m) > 0`` there. This package
uses ``exp(+j omega t)`` (``Im(eps) < 0`` for loss); :func:`mie` accepts the relative index in this package's
convention and conjugates it internally. Efficiencies are real and convention-free.

``x = 2 pi n_medium a / lambda`` is the size parameter, ``m = n_sphere / n_medium`` the relative index.

classes.name: MieResult
classes.doc:
Mie coefficients and efficiencies of a sphere.

Attributes
----------
x : float [-]
    Size parameter.
m : complex [-]
    Relative refractive index.
qext : float [-]
    Extinction efficiency.
qsca : float [-]
    Scattering efficiency.
qback : float [-]
    Backscattering efficiency.
g : float [-]
    Asymmetry parameter <cos theta>.

methods.name: amplitudes
methods.doc: Scattering amplitudes ``S1(theta), S2(theta)`` (B&H eq. 4.74, their convention).

functions.name: mie_coefficients
functions.sig: (m_bh: complex, x: float, n_max: int | None = None)
functions.doc: ``a_n, b_n`` (n = 1..n_max) in Bohren & Huffman's convention (``Im(m_bh) >= 0`` absorbs).

functions.name: mie
functions.sig: (m: complex, x: float, n_max: int | None = None) -> MieResult
functions.doc: Efficiencies of a homogeneous sphere, ``m`` in this package's ``exp(+j omega t)`` convention.

functions.name: mie_pec
functions.sig: (x: float, n_max: int | None = None) -> MieResult
functions.doc:
Perfectly conducting sphere: ``a_n = psi_n'(x) / xi_n'(x)``, ``b_n = psi_n(x) / xi_n(x)``, the
``|m| -> infinity`` limit of the coefficients above; its small-sphere limit is ``Q_sca = (10/3) x^4``
(Jackson eq. 10.18 divided by ``pi a^2``).

functions.name: rayleigh_qsca
functions.sig: (m: complex, x: float) -> float
functions.doc: Small-sphere limit ``Q_sca = (8/3) x^4 |(m^2 - 1) / (m^2 + 2)|^2`` (B&H eq. 5.8).

children.summary: Mie scattering of a plane wave by a homogeneous sphere (and a perfectly conducting one).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.particles
children.doc:
Charged particles in electric and magnetic fields: the relativistic Boris pusher, field models, closed-form
references and ready-made studies (issue #1106).

The integrator is the Boris scheme (Boris 1970; relativistic form as in Birdsall & Langdon, *Plasma Physics via
Computer Simulation*). It advances ``u = gamma v``:

    u- = u + (q E / m) dt/2                      half electric kick
    t  = (q B / (m gamma-)) dt/2,  s = 2 t / (1 + |t|^2)
    u' = u- + u- x t,  u+ = u- + u' x s          exact-norm magnetic rotation
    u  = u+ + (q E / m) dt/2                     half electric kick
    x += u / gamma dt

It is second-order accurate and time-reversible, and in a pure magnetic field it conserves |u| (the kinetic energy)
to round-off for any step: the rotation preserves the norm. That is why it is the standard particle pusher in
plasma codes.

    from pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics import particles as P
    out = P.push(x0=[[0, 0, 0]], v0=[[1e5, 0, 0]], q=P.Q_E, m=P.M_P,
                 B=P.uniform((0, 0, 1e-3)), dt=1e-8, n_steps=4000)
    out["x"]          # (n_saved, n_particles, 3)

Field arguments are callables ``f(x, t) -> (N, 3)`` in SI (V/m, T). ``uniform``, ``magnetic_dipole``,
``magnetic_bottle`` and ``penning_trap`` build the common ones, and the Biot-Savart routines of
:mod:`.statics` can be wrapped the same way.

functions.name: uniform
functions.sig: (vector: Sequence[float]) -> Field
functions.doc: A uniform, static field (V/m for E, T for B).

functions.name: add_fields
functions.sig: (*fields) -> Field
functions.doc: The sum of several field callables.

functions.name: magnetic_dipole
functions.sig: (moment: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 0.0, -EARTH_DIPOLE_MOMENT), center: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) -> Field
functions.doc:
Field of a point magnetic dipole, B = mu0/(4 pi) (3 r_hat (m . r_hat) - m) / r^3 [T].

The default is an Earth-like dipole: the moment points to geographic south, so B points north at the equator.

functions.name: magnetic_bottle
functions.sig: (B0: float, L: float) -> Field
functions.doc:
Axisymmetric magnetic bottle (paraxial, divergence-free): Bz = B0 (1 + (z/L)^2), B_rho = -rho B0 z / L^2.

The field is weakest at z = 0 and grows to the mirror ratio R = Bz(z)/B0 = 1 + (z/L)^2.

functions.name: penning_trap
functions.sig: (V0: float, d: float) -> Field
functions.doc:
Electric field of an ideal Penning trap, Phi = V0 (2 z^2 - x^2 - y^2) / (4 d^2): E = V0/(2 d^2) (x, y, -2 z).

It confines a positive charge axially when V0 > 0. Use it with a uniform axial B.

functions.name: dipole_field_line
functions.sig: (L_shell: float, n: int = 200, longitude_deg: float = 0.0, radius: float = EARTH_RADIUS) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Points (n, 3) [m] of the dipole field line r = L R cos^2(latitude) between its two footpoints at r = R.

functions.name: push
functions.sig: (x0: Sequence[Sequence[float]], v0: Sequence[Sequence[float]], q: float, m: float, *, E: Field | None = None, B: Field | None = None, dt: float, n_steps: int, save_every: int = 1, relativistic: bool = True, t0: float = 0.0, stop: Callable[[np.ndarray, np.ndarray], np.ndarray] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Advance N particles with the (relativistic) Boris pusher.

Parameters
----------
x0, v0 : (N, 3) initial positions [m] and velocities [m/s].
q, m : charge [C] and rest mass [kg], the same for all particles (call once per species).
E, B : field callables ``f(x, t) -> (N, 3)`` [V/m], [T]; ``None`` is zero.
dt : time step [s]; n_steps : number of steps; save_every : keep every n-th state.
relativistic : advance u = gamma v (True) or v (False, the classic Boris scheme).
stop : optional ``stop(x, v) -> (N,) bool``; a particle that meets it is frozen from then on (e.g. lost through a
    mirror, hit the ground). Its index and time are reported in ``stopped``/``t_stop``.

Returns
-------
dict with ``t`` (n_saved,), ``x`` and ``v`` (n_saved, N, 3), ``gamma`` and ``kinetic_energy`` [J] (n_saved, N),
``stopped`` (N,) bool and ``t_stop`` (N,) [s] (nan when never stopped).

functions.name: lorentz_factor
functions.sig: (speed: float) -> float
functions.doc: gamma = 1 / sqrt(1 - v^2/c^2).

functions.name: cyclotron_frequency
functions.sig: (q: float, m: float, B: float, speed: float = 0.0) -> float
functions.doc: Angular gyrofrequency |q| B / (gamma m) [rad/s] (gamma from the speed; 0 gives the non-relativistic value).

functions.name: larmor_radius
functions.sig: (q: float, m: float, B: float, v_perp: float, speed: float | None = None) -> float
functions.doc: Gyroradius gamma m v_perp / (|q| B) [m]; ``speed`` (default v_perp) sets gamma.

functions.name: exb_drift
functions.sig: (E: Sequence[float], B: Sequence[float]) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: E x B drift velocity E x B / |B|^2 [m/s] (independent of charge and mass).

functions.name: gradb_drift
functions.sig: (q: float, m: float, v_perp: float, B: Sequence[float], grad_B: Sequence[float]) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Grad-B drift (m v_perp^2 / (2 q B^3)) B x grad|B| [m/s] (non-relativistic, guiding-centre limit).

functions.name: loss_cone_angle
functions.sig: (B_min: float, B_max: float) -> float
functions.doc: Loss-cone half-angle arcsin(sqrt(B_min / B_max)) [rad]: particles with a smaller pitch angle at B_min escape.

functions.name: penning_frequencies
functions.sig: (q: float, m: float, B: float, V0: float, d: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Angular frequencies [rad/s] of an ideal Penning trap: cyclotron qB/m, axial sqrt(q V0/(m d^2)),
modified cyclotron and magnetron w_pm = w_c/2 +- sqrt(w_c^2/4 - w_z^2/2) (trapped when w_c^2 > 2 w_z^2).

functions.name: guiding_center
functions.sig: (x: Sequence[Sequence[float]], v: Sequence[Sequence[float]], B: Sequence[Sequence[float]], q: float, m: float, gamma: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Guiding centre x + gamma m (v x B) / (q |B|^2) of particles at x with velocity v in the local field B.

functions.name: magnetic_moment
functions.sig: (v: Sequence[Sequence[float]], B: Sequence[Sequence[float]], m: float, gamma: float = 1.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: First adiabatic invariant mu = p_perp^2 / (2 m |B|) [J/T] (gamma m v_perp^2 / 2B non-relativistically scaled).

functions.name: pitch_velocity
functions.sig: (speed: float, pitch_deg: float, b_hat: Sequence[float] = (0, 0, 1), phase_deg: float = 0.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Velocity of the given speed at a pitch angle (degrees from b_hat) and gyrophase.

functions.name: cyclotron_study
functions.sig: (kinetic_energy_eV: float = 1000000.0, B: float = 1.0, particle: str = 'electron', steps_per_turn: int = 200, turns: int = 5) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Gyration in a uniform B (along z) at a given kinetic energy: radius, frequency and energy drift from the
Boris pusher against gamma m v / (qB), qB/(gamma m) and exact conservation.

Parameters
----------
kinetic_energy_eV : float [eV]
B : float [T]
particle : {"electron", "proton"}
steps_per_turn : int [-]
turns : int [-]

functions.name: drift_study
functions.sig: (B: float = 0.001, E: float = 100.0, grad_scale: float = 20.0, energy_eV: float = 10.0, periods: int = 20, steps_per_turn: int = 120) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
E x B drift (uniform E along y, B along z) and grad-B drift (B_z = B (1 + x/grad_scale)) of a proton,
measured from the guiding-centre motion against E/B and the grad-B formula. The grad-B formula is the
guiding-centre limit: it needs a Larmor radius much smaller than ``grad_scale`` (the result reports the ratio).

Parameters
----------
B : float [T]
E : float [V/m]
grad_scale : float [m]
energy_eV : float [eV]
periods : int [-]
steps_per_turn : int [-]

functions.name: magnetic_bottle_study
functions.sig: (B0: float = 0.01, L: float = 1.0, z_mirror: float = 2.0, energy_eV: float = 100.0, n_particles: int = 60, bounces: float = 3.0, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Protons released at the centre of a magnetic bottle at pitch angles spread over 5-90 degrees: which escape
past the mirror points at |z| = z_mirror, against the loss cone arcsin(sqrt(B0/B(z_mirror))); and how well the
magnetic moment of a trapped particle is conserved.

Parameters
----------
B0 : float [T]
L : float [m]
z_mirror : float [m]

n_particles : int [-]
bounces : float [-]

functions.name: dipole_trap_study
functions.sig: (energy_MeV: float = 10.0, L_shell: float = 2.0, pitch_deg: float = 30.0, species: str = 'proton', duration_s: float = 150.0, steps_per_gyration: int = 25, save_every: int = 50) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
A particle trapped in an Earth-like dipole field (radiation-belt picture): gyration, bounce between mirror
points and longitudinal drift around the planet. Reports the measured bounce and drift periods next to the
standard dipole approximations (Hamlin et al. 1961 / Walt 1994, for equatorial pitch angle alpha):

    T_bounce ~ 4 L R_E / v * (1.30 - 0.56 sin alpha)
    T_drift  ~ 2 pi q B_E R_E^2 / (3 L gamma m v^2) / (0.35 + 0.15 sin alpha)    [B_E: equatorial surface field]

Parameters
----------

L_shell : float [-]
pitch_deg : float [deg]
species : {"proton", "electron"}
duration_s : float [s]
steps_per_gyration : int [-]
save_every : int [-]

functions.sig: (B: float = 1.0, V0: float = 10.0, d: float = 0.005, particle: str = 'proton', x0_m: Sequence[float] = (0.0001, 0.0, 0.0001), periods: int = 40, steps_per_turn: int = 80, v0_m_s: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0)) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
A charge in an ideal Penning trap: the three eigenfrequencies measured from the motion (spectra of x and z)
against the closed forms.

V0 : float [V]
d : float [m]
particle : {"proton", "electron"}
x0_m : list of float [m]

children.doc:
Unit-cell campaigns and the equal-budget benchmark of an operator surrogate against Bayesian optimisation.

* :func:`cell_simulator` -- a :class:`~..antenna.runner.CLISimulator` on :mod:`.tcda` (one process per cell, every
  frequency and scan angle in it, SuperLU), with the peak memory and wall time of each run;
* :func:`campaign` -- a space-filling DOE of cells (:data:`CELL_RANGES`, generic) run through it;
* :func:`to_arrays` -- the (design, frequency, scan) table as ``X (n, d)`` and ``Y (n, n_f, n_scan)`` (active
  reflection in dB);
* :func:`fit_fno` -- an FNO from the design parameters to the whole (frequency x scan) map, trained with
  :mod:`pinneapple_analysis.surrogate` (its FNO candidate, budget-limited Adam, best validation checkpoint), and
  :func:`heldout` its error on cells it never saw;
* :func:`equal_budget` -- the same number of solver calls for two strategies on the worst-case active reflection
  over the band and the scan range: (a) DOE of ``budget - n_verify`` cells, an FNO, an optimiser on the FNO and the
  solver on its ``n_verify`` best candidates; (b) Bayesian optimisation calling the solver directly
  (:mod:`pinneapple_design.design_optimizer`, ``"bayesian"``). The best value is always the solver's, never the
  surrogate's. The DOE alone is reported too (random search with ``budget - n_verify`` calls).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.periodic.tcda
children.doc:
A generic tightly coupled dipole array (TCDA) unit cell for EMerge Floquet runs, written from scratch.

The cell (millimetres; infinite array in the x-y plane, E-plane = x-z): a square cell of side ``a``; the ground
plane at z = 0 (the bottom face of the cell, PEC); a dipole strip of width ``w`` along x at height ``h``, fed across
a gap ``s`` at the centre by a lumped port of ``z_port`` ohms; its arms stop ``g / 2`` from the cell edge, so
neighbouring dipoles couple capacitively across a gap ``g`` (the "tight coupling"); an optional dielectric
superstrate (``er_s``, thickness ``t_s``) at ``d_s`` above the dipole; air up to half a wavelength (at the lowest
frequency) above everything, closed by a Floquet port. Periodic boundary conditions with the phase of the scan
angle (theta, phi) close the sides.

Per scan angle and frequency the run returns the active reflection coefficient at the lumped port
(``S11`` with every element excited with the scan phase). One mesh serves every scan angle of a cell (the scan only
changes the boundary phases and the Floquet port), so a cell at several angles costs one mesh and one solve per
angle. EMerge (GPL-2.0, ``pip install emerge``) is imported only to solve; this module is called, never copies it.
SuperLU is used (PARDISO can die with SIGBUS without MKL).

``python tcda.py --params '{"h": 9}' --freq 3 4 5 6 --scan 0 30 45 --out run/`` writes ``result.json`` (the
:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.antenna.runner` format); it has no package imports, so the runner
starts it as a plain script.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.postprocess
children.doc:
Post-processing of A_z solutions: torque, flux linkage, back-EMF, iron losses, magnet eddy losses.

Torque
------
* :func:`torque_maxwell_stress` -- Maxwell stress tensor averaged over an air annulus
  ``r1 < r < r2`` (Arkkio's method, M. Arkkio, Acta Polytechnica Scandinavica EE-59, 1987)::

      T = L / (mu0 (r2 - r1)) * int_annulus r B_r B_phi dS

  Averaging the stress over the annulus instead of taking one circle removes most of the mesh noise.
* :func:`torque_coenergy` -- virtual work: ``T = dW'/dtheta`` at constant currents, by central finite
  differences of the co-energy of two solutions at ``theta +- delta`` (the caller supplies a function
  that solves at a given angle). Agreement of the two methods is a check of the whole chain.

Flux linkage and EMF
--------------------
A coil side with ``N`` turns in a region of area ``S`` and orientation ``+-1`` links
``psi = L N / S * (+-1) * int A dS``; a phase sums its coil sides (divide by parallel paths).
``e = dpsi/dt = omega_m dpsi/dtheta`` (sign convention: generator EMF is ``-e``).

Iron loss
---------
Per element, the flux density over one electrical period (stator elements in the stator frame,
rotor elements in the rotor frame) is split into Fourier harmonics; each harmonic ``n`` traces an
ellipse whose major and minor axes are treated as two alternating fields (a common engineering
approximation for rotational loss). Each alternating component of amplitude ``B`` at ``f`` adds
``k_h f^alpha B^beta + k_c f^2 B^2 + k_e f^1.5 B^1.5`` W/kg (Steinmetz hysteresis term plus Bertotti's
classical eddy and excess terms; G. Bertotti, IEEE Trans. Magn. 24(1):621-630, 1988).
Coefficients must come from fits to the material's loss data.

Magnet eddy loss (resistance limited)
-------------------------------------
In 2D each magnet piece is an infinitely long conductor without net current, so
``J = -sigma (dA/dt - <dA/dt>_piece)``; the field of these currents is neglected, valid while the
skin depth is large compared with the magnet. Use
:func:`pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.eddy.solve_time_harmonic` when it is not.

one field solution period gives the iron loss at every speed (the field waveform is fixed by the
currents in the rotor frame).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.reflector
pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.reflector.analytic
children.doc:
Closed forms that check the physical-optics code of :mod:`.po`.

* :func:`disk_on_axis` -- the exact field on the axis of a flat PEC disk carrying the PO current of a normally
  incident plane wave (``J = 2 E0 / eta`` uniform). With ``A_x = mu J (e^{-jkz} - e^{-jkR_a}) / (2 j k)``,
  ``R_a = sqrt(z^2 + a^2)``, and ``d^2 A_x / dx^2 = -(k^2 A_x + d^2 A_x / dz^2) / 2`` on the axis (Helmholtz and
  symmetry)::

      E_x(z) = -j k eta J g / 2  +  eta J a^2 e^{-jkR_a} (k^2 / R_a^2 - j k / R_a^3) / (4 j k (j k))

  with ``g = (e^{-jkz} - e^{-jkR_a}) / (j k)``, which simplifies to
  ``E_x = -E0 [e^{-jkz} - (1 + z^2 / R_a^2 + j a^2 / (k R_a^3)) e^{-jkR_a} / 2]``: the wave reflected by the plane
  plus the edge ring, whose weight tends to ``(1 + cos theta_e) / 2`` and does not vanish for a large disk (unlike
  the obliquity factor of scalar Kirchhoff diffraction). This checks the quadrature and the near-field Green's function of :func:`.po.radiate`.
* :func:`go_aperture_taper_db` -- geometrical optics of a paraboloid fed at its focus by a ``cos^q`` feed: a ray
  leaving the focus at angle ``psi`` from the feed axis reaches the aperture plane with relative amplitude
  ``sqrt(D(psi)) / rho``, ``rho = F + z`` the focus-to-surface distance (feed pattern times the space attenuation
  of the spherical wave; C. A. Balanis, *Antenna Theory*, 4th ed., ch. 15, the aperture distribution of a
  paraboloid). In a compact range the
  collimated field keeps this taper along the rays, so it is the smooth part of the quiet-zone amplitude; the PO
  field adds the ripple of the edge diffraction.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.reflector.compact_range
children.doc:
A single offset-reflector compact range: feed, reflector, quiet zone, and its parameter studies.

:class:`CompactRange` holds the design (frequency, :class:`~.geometry.OffsetReflector`, a ``cos^q`` feed of a given
gain at the focus aimed at the section centre, the quiet-zone plane, diameter and centre). :func:`evaluate` meshes
the reflector, computes the PO current and the exact near field on the quiet-zone plane (and wider, to find the
usable size) and returns the :func:`~.qz.qz_metrics` with the cost. :func:`scaled` changes the section size keeping
the clearance below it (the feed stays out of the collimated beam) and the quiet zone on the section's centre line.
:func:`sweep` runs a grid of feed gains, section sizes and roll radii into a :class:`~..antenna.runner.ResultTable`.

The default parameters are a generic example (3 GHz, F = 1.5 m, a 1.2 m section), not any particular range.

between the axis and the section's lower junction stays, the quiet zone follows the section centre line.

functions.doc:
PO field on the quiet-zone plane: ``{"xy", "E" (M, 3), "mesh", "seconds"}``; ``xy`` relative to the QZ
centre (default: a disk of ``eval_factor`` x the QZ diameter, step lambda / ``qz_step_per_wavelength``).

Every combination; returns a :class:`~pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.antenna.runner.ResultTable`
(``tag``, inputs, metrics; ``f_GHz`` constant).

PO against geometrical optics on the quiet zone: the quadratic fit of the PO amplitude (its smooth part)

lambda/``step_per_wavelength`` grid. ``ratio`` is the largest disk's.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.reflector.geometry
children.doc:
Offset paraboloid reflectors with optional rolled edges, as triangle meshes for :mod:`.po`.

The paraboloid is ``z = (x^2 + y^2) / (4F)`` (vertex at the origin, focus at ``(0, 0, F)``, reflected rays along
+z). The section is the part whose projection on the aperture plane lies inside a superellipse centred at
``(0, centre_y)`` with half sizes ``half_x``, ``half_y`` and exponent ``n`` (``n = 2``: an ellipse; large ``n``: a
rectangle with rounded corners). Past this junction contour an optional rolled edge continues the surface in each
vertical plane through the section centre: the profile leaves the paraboloid tangentially and with its curvature,
blends (``sin^2`` over the first ``blend`` fraction of the roll) to a constant curvature ``-1 / roll`` turning away
from the quiet zone, and stops when its tangent has turned to ``end_angle`` degrees (from the outward horizontal;
-90 = pointing straight back). ``roll_aspect`` stretches the roll's departure from the junction tangent line along
z (the tangent stays continuous): 1 gives the circular roll, larger values a deeper, elliptic-like one. This is a blended rolled edge in the spirit of Gupta and Burnside; the exact
profile of a given range (ellipse ratio, blending function) is a parameter, not built in.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.reflector.paired
children.doc:
The paired PO/direct experiment on the two-dimensional compact range: the sweep, the learned residual and the
multi-fidelity comparison.

The question the experiment asks is a question about numbers, not about a solver: for this design, how far is
physical optics from an exact surface-current solution, does the difference follow the design variables closely
enough to be learned, and at a fixed budget of exact solves does a learned correction beat spending them blindly.

* :func:`paired_sweep` -- every design solved twice, PO and exact (:mod:`.planar2d`), written to a JSON-lines
  checkpoint as it finishes;
* :class:`ResidualModel` / :func:`leave_out_validation` -- a Gaussian process on ``direct - PO`` and its error on
  designs it never saw, including a whole edge profile held out;
* :func:`compare_strategies` -- ``direct``, ``po`` and ``multi`` at the same number of exact solves, repeated over
  seeds;
* :func:`cost_summary` -- the measured cost of each solver, so the budget can be stated in seconds as well as in
  solves.

classes.sig: (name: str = '')
classes.doc:
Gaussian process on the residual ``direct - PO`` of one quantity, over the design inputs of
:class:`~.planar2d.Design`.

Squared-exponential kernel, one isotropic length scale and a nugget by maximum marginal likelihood over a
small grid, inputs standardised by the range of the training set. :meth:`predict` returns the mean and the
standard deviation of the residual.

functions.doc:
``PO`` against ``PO + learned residual`` on designs the model never saw.

Two splits: ``random`` (``folds``-fold over the designs, averaged over ``seeds``) and ``profile`` (one whole
edge profile -- every size and every feed of one roll/blend/aspect triple -- held out at a time, which is the
honest test of "a profile we have not built yet").

functions.name: coverage_analysis
functions.sig: (rows: Sequence[Mapping[str, Any]], metric: str = 'usable_width', *, folds: int = 5, seeds: Sequence[int] = (0, 1, 2, 3, 4)) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Do the design variables we chose cover the residual, or does the edge profile carry it?

Solves the same held-out problem with two models: a Gaussian process on ``(size, q)`` alone -- the two levers
asked for, reflector size and feed illumination -- and one on all five variables, the profile included. If the
two recover the same fraction of the PO error, the 18 profiles are redundant and the size/illumination grid is
enough; if the five-variable model is far ahead, the profile is a direction of the space that has to be in the
training set. The residual is also broken down per level of each lever, so a lever that only matters in part of
its range shows up.

above ``amp_limit`` dB and -- when ``phase_limit`` is given, in degrees of peak-to-peak phase ripple -- for the
phase ripple above it. Both tolerances are the quiet-zone spec the zone is quoted against; a design that breaks
them holds its width only where the field is quiet, so the discount is in metres per unit of violation.

children.summary: The paired PO/direct experiment on the two-dimensional compact range: the sweep, the learned residual and the multi-fidelity comparison.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.reflector.planar2d
children.doc:
A two-dimensional compact range: offset parabolic cylinder with rolled edges, ``cos^q`` line feed, physical
optics and the exact integral-equation solution of the same problem, on the same contour, with the same
quiet-zone numbers.

Why a plane model: the question these experiments ask is a question about the *difference* between physical optics
and an exact surface-current solution -- how large it is, whether it can be learned, and whether spending a few
exact solves inside an optimisation pays. That question is answered by a solver that is exact, cheap and
validatable. In two dimensions the same physics (a parabolic section, a rolled edge, an offset feed, a quiet zone
in the near field of the section) is solved by a single-layer integral equation on a contour of a few hundred
unknowns, in milliseconds, and validated against the closed-form series of a perfectly conducting circle
(:func:`validate_circle`). A three-dimensional direct solve of the production geometry is a different class of
tool: the measured cost of the operator alone at ``lambda/8`` is reported by
``examples/use_cases/antennas/direct_cost_probe.py`` and is three orders of magnitude away from PO.

Conventions: ``E = E_z z_hat`` with ``exp(+j omega t)`` (the package convention); the contour lies in the y-z plane,
the paraboloid is ``z = y^2 / (4F)`` with vertex at the origin and focus ``(0, F)``; a perfectly conducting surface
is the Dirichlet condition ``E_z = 0`` on the contour (the 2-D analogue of the 3-D ``J = 2 n x H_inc``).

Everything is per radian in 2-D, so the metrics are *relative* (taper, ripple, phase ripple, usable width): the
absolute level of a 2-D feed has no 3-D meaning and nothing here quotes it.

* :class:`Section` -- the reflector contour: an arc of the parabola between two aperture coordinates, continued
  past each end by the blended rolled edge of :func:`~.geometry._roll_profile`, sampled at a target spacing;
* :class:`Feed` -- the incident field of a directive line source at the focus: ``cos^q`` amplitude about an axis,
  ``H0^(2)(kR)`` phase, and its normal derivative (what the PO density is);
* :func:`po_metrics` / :func:`direct_metrics` -- quiet-zone metrics of the PO density and of the exact one;
* :func:`near_field_map` -- the near field both densities produce on a grid, and where they disagree;
* :func:`metrics_1d` -- the 1-D quiet-zone numbers: taper, ripple, phase ripple and usable width;
* :func:`mom_solve` -- the exact current by point-matched pulse expansion of the single-layer equation, with the
  self term integrated analytically over the log singularity;
* :func:`validate_circle` -- the exact series of a PEC circle against :func:`mom_solve`.

classes.doc:

half space, ``H0^(2)`` phase. ``q`` comes from a feed gain the same way the 3-D code does
(:func:`~.po.q_from_gain`) so the two share the parameter.

functions.doc:

pulse expansion. Returns the density and the cost.

functions.doc:

functions.sig: (obs: np.ndarray, feed: Feed, k: float) -> np.ndarray

functions.sig: (s: np.ndarray, E: np.ndarray, span: float, *, amp_tol: float = 0.5, phase_tol: float = 5.0) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Quiet-zone numbers along a cut: ``s`` positions from the zone centre, ``E`` complex along it.

``taper_dB`` the range of a quadratic fit of the amplitude (the smooth illumination taper), ``ripple_pp_dB``
the peak to peak of the residual about it, the same for the phase, and ``usable_width`` the largest centred
segment where the amplitude stays within ``+- amp_tol`` and the phase within ``+- phase_tol``.

functions.sig: (rng: Range2D, *, n_y: int = 300, n_z: int = 280, pad: float = 0.05, floor_db: float = -20.0, ceiling_db: float = 10.0, grid: Grid | None = None, solution: dict | None = None) -> dict

functions.name: validate_circle
functions.sig: (*, ka: float = 6.0, per_wavelength: float = 12.0, source_distance: float = 6.0) -> dict
functions.doc:
The exact current of a PEC circle in a cylindrical wave against :func:`mom_solve`.

The incident field of a line source at distance ``d`` from the centre is ``sum_n H_n^(2)(k d) J_n(k r)
e^{j n phi}`` (Graf's addition theorem); the scattered field is then ``sum_n a_n H_n^(2)(k r) e^{j n phi}``
with ``a_n = -H_n^(2)(k d) J_n(k a) / H_n^(2)(k a)``. Both the direct solve and PO are compared on the same
contour, in dB of the field at a point on the shadow side and on the lit side.

stays where it is), the feed ``q`` and the rolled-edge profile applied to the section.

error and the trade-off map of the quiet-zone quality.

* :func:`validate` -- the PO integrator against the closed-form field of a PO disk (:func:`.analytic.disk_on_axis`)
  at several mesh densities, the PO quiet-zone amplitude against geometrical optics (:func:`.compact_range.go_check`)
  for rolled edges of growing size, and the mesh convergence of the quiet-zone metrics;
* :func:`qz_study` -- the sweep (:func:`.compact_range.sweep`), a Gaussian process per metric over (feed gain,
  side) for each roll radius, held-out errors, and :func:`tradeoff_map`.

Every number returned is computed here; nothing is taken from elsewhere.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.reflector.study_report
children.doc:
A compact-range study that plans itself: problem -> which checks and sweeps to run -> results -> datasheet.

Given a :class:`Problem` (frequency, focal length, section, rolled edge, feed, quiet zone and, optionally, a
measured or simulated reference table and a band) this module

1. **plans** the study from the geometry alone (:func:`plan`) -- the steps, and the reason each one is there:
   a Fresnel number below two means the quiet zone is in the near field of the section and a size sweep is
   called for; a rolled edge shorter than three wavelengths means the edge diffraction needs its own sweep; a
   reference table means a comparison and a rolled-edge calibration; a spec the baseline misses means an
   optimisation at equal solver budget; no band means no bandwidth step, and the plan says so;
2. **runs** it (:func:`run`), writing every number to JSON so the document can be regenerated without solving;
3. **renders** it as a technical datasheet (:func:`report`), by number, table and figure.

No language model is involved anywhere: the steps come from thresholds on dimensionless numbers computed from
the geometry, and the sentences come from the numbers themselves.

    python -m pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.reflector.study_report --out cr_study
    python -m pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.reflector.study_report --freq 3 --focal 1.5 --section 1.2 \
        --offset 0.9 --roll 0.15 --qz 0.6 --qz-distance 3 --gain 12 --band 2 4

``(pol, z_ft, cut)`` -> ``(amp_p-p_dB, phase_p-p_deg, xpol_dB_or_None)``.

The datasheet of a compact-range study: every sentence is computed from the study's numbers.

The narrative rules are fixed here and take no model: the verdict compares the usable diameter with the
specification at the declared tolerance; the near-field remark is the Fresnel number against two; the
cut-versus-disk remark is the ratio of the two computed peak-to-peak values; the reference comparison
reports the signed differences of the rows it was given.  When a step was not run or a number is missing
the sentence says so instead of being written anyway.

functions.sig: (p, study: Mapping[str, Any], figs: Mapping[str, str]) -> Datasheet
