Reflector antennas and compact ranges by physical optics: geometry, PO currents and near fields, quiet zones.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.statics
children.doc:
Electrostatics and magnetostatics in closed form, and Biot-Savart integration of filamentary currents.

References: J. D. Jackson, *Classical Electrodynamics*, 3rd ed. (1999), ch. 1-5; D. J. Griffiths,
*Introduction to Electrodynamics*, 4th ed. (2017), ch. 2-5; the off-axis field of a circular loop in
complete elliptic integrals is Jackson's eq. 5.37 rewritten for ``B`` (Simpson et al., NASA TM 2001-210720
give the same expressions in Cartesian form).

All functions are SI and vectorised over field points.

functions.name: parallel_plate_capacitance
functions.sig: (area: float, gap: float, eps_r: float = 1.0) -> float
functions.doc:
``C = eps A / d`` (fringing neglected), F.

Returns
-------
C : float [F]
    Capacitance, for SI inputs.

functions.name: coax_capacitance
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float, eps_r: float = 1.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Per-unit-length capacitance of a coaxial line, ``2 pi eps / ln(b/a)`` (F/m).

Returns
-------
C : float [F/m]
    Capacitance per unit length.

functions.name: coax_inductance
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float, mu_r: float = 1.0) -> float
functions.doc:
External per-unit-length inductance of a coaxial line, ``mu ln(b/a) / (2 pi)`` (H/m).

Returns
-------
L : float [H/m]
    External inductance per unit length.

functions.name: spherical_capacitance
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float = math.inf, eps_r: float = 1.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Concentric spheres ``4 pi eps a b / (b - a)``; isolated sphere ``4 pi eps a`` for ``b = inf``.

Returns
-------
C : float [F]
    Capacitance, for radii in m.

functions.name: point_charge_field
functions.sig: (points, q: float, at = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), eps_r: float = 1.0)
functions.doc: (phi, E) of a point charge: ``phi = q / (4 pi eps r)``, ``E = q r_hat / (4 pi eps r^2)``.

functions.name: line_charge_field
functions.sig: (points, lam: float, eps_r: float = 1.0)
functions.doc: E of an infinite line charge on the z axis, ``lam / (2 pi eps s)`` radially (V/m).

functions.name: infinite_wire_B
functions.sig: (points, current: float)
functions.doc:
B of an infinite straight filament on the z axis carrying ``current`` towards +z: ``mu0 I / (2 pi s)``
in the azimuthal direction (T).

functions.name: polyline_segments
functions.sig: (vertices) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: Segments (start, end) of an open polyline through ``vertices`` (n, 3).

functions.name: circle_segments
functions.sig: (radius: float, n: int = 360, center = (0.0, 0.0, 0.0), z: float = 0.0)
functions.doc:
A circle of ``n`` straight segments in a plane ``z = const`` (counter-clockwise seen from +z).

The vertices lie on the circle, so the polygon is inscribed; its field converges to the circle's at
second order in ``1/n``.

functions.name: helix_segments
functions.sig: (radius: float, length: float, turns: float, n_per_turn: int = 72, z0: float | None = None)
functions.doc: A helical coil along z from ``z0`` (default ``-length/2``) to ``z0 + length``.

functions.name: biot_savart
functions.sig: (points, starts, ends, current: float | Sequence[float] = 1.0, chunk: int = 4096)
functions.doc:
B (T) at ``points`` (..., 3) from straight filament segments ``starts -> ends`` (m, 3) each carrying
``current`` (A, scalar or per segment). Exact field of each finite segment (Jackson problem 5.1 / Griffiths
eq. 5.37): ``B = mu0 I / (4 pi) (a x b)(|a| + |b|) / (|a| |b| (|a| |b| + a.b))`` with ``a = start - p``,
``b = end - p``. Points on a segment's line get zero contribution from it.

functions.name: vector_potential
functions.sig: (points, starts, ends, current: float | Sequence[float] = 1.0, chunk: int = 4096)
functions.doc:
A (T m) at ``points`` (..., 3) from straight filament segments ``starts -> ends`` (Coulomb gauge), exact
per segment: ``A = mu0 I / (4 pi) u ln((d1 + d2 + L) / (d1 + d2 - L))`` with ``u`` the unit vector of the
segment, ``L`` its length and ``d1``, ``d2`` the distances to its ends (Hanson and Hirshman, Phys. Plasmas
9, 3681 (2002), eq. 4). Away from the filaments; ``curl A`` is :func:`biot_savart`.

functions.name: flux_through_path
functions.sig: (path_starts, path_ends, starts, ends, current: float | Sequence[float] = 1.0, gauss: int = 4) -> float
functions.doc:
Magnetic flux (Wb) of filaments ``starts -> ends`` through a closed polygonal path, by Stokes' theorem
``Phi = oint A . dl`` (Gauss-Legendre with ``gauss`` points per path segment). Unlike a surface integral of B
it stays accurate when a filament pierces the spanning surface.

functions.name: loop_on_axis_B
functions.sig: (z, radius: float, current: float)
functions.doc: Axial B of a circular loop in the plane z = 0: ``mu0 I R^2 / (2 (R^2 + z^2)^{3/2})``.

functions.name: loop_field
functions.sig: (points, radius: float, current: float)
functions.doc:
B (T) of a circular loop of radius ``R`` in the plane z = 0, centred on the axis, everywhere off the
wire, with complete elliptic integrals (``m = k^2 = 4 R s / ((R + s)^2 + z^2)``)::

    B_z = mu0 I / (2 pi) / sqrt((R + s)^2 + z^2) [K(m) + (R^2 - s^2 - z^2) / ((R - s)^2 + z^2) E(m)]
    B_s = mu0 I z / (2 pi s) / sqrt((R + s)^2 + z^2) [-K(m) + (R^2 + s^2 + z^2) / ((R - s)^2 + z^2) E(m)]

functions.name: finite_solenoid_on_axis_B
functions.sig: (z, radius: float, length: float, n_turns: float, current: float)
functions.doc:
Axial B of a tightly wound finite solenoid (current sheet ``K = N I / L``) centred at z = 0:
``(mu0 N I / (2 L)) [(z + L/2) / sqrt(R^2 + (z + L/2)^2) - (z - L/2) / sqrt(R^2 + (z - L/2)^2)]``.

functions.name: helmholtz_coil_center_B
functions.sig: (radius: float, current: float, turns: int = 1) -> float
functions.doc:
Field at the centre of a Helmholtz pair (spacing = radius): ``(4/5)^{3/2} mu0 n I / R``.

Returns
-------
B : float [T]
    Field at the centre, for ``I`` in A and ``R`` in m.

functions.name: mutual_inductance_coaxial_loops
functions.sig: (r1: float, r2: float, d: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Maxwell's formula for two coaxial circular filaments at axial distance ``d``:
``M = mu0 sqrt(r1 r2) [(2/k - k) K(k^2) - (2/k) E(k^2)]``, ``k^2 = 4 r1 r2 / ((r1 + r2)^2 + d^2)``.

Returns
-------
M : float [H]
    Mutual inductance, for lengths in m.

functions.name: loop_self_inductance
functions.sig: (R: float, a: float, internal: bool = True) -> float
functions.doc:
Thin round wire loop (loop radius ``R`` >> wire radius ``a``): ``mu0 R (ln(8R/a) - 2 + Y)`` with
``Y = 1/4`` for uniform current (low frequency, ``internal=True``) and 0 at high frequency (Rosa & Grover,
*Formulas and tables for the calculation of mutual and self-inductance*, Bull. Bureau of Standards 8, 1912).

Returns
-------
L : float [H]
    Self inductance, for lengths in m.

functions.name: filament_inductance
functions.sig: (paths, wire_radius, pieces_per_metre: float = 2000.0, gauss: int = 6, mirror_z: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Inductance matrix (H) of thin conductors along polylines ``paths`` (each an (n, 3) array, closed or open;
open paths give the partial inductances of their current segments).

Neumann's double integral with the thin-wire reduced kernel ``1 / sqrt(|x - x'|^2 + g^2)``, ``g`` the geometric
mean distance of the round wire cross-section from itself (``g = a e^-1/4`` for ``wire_radius = a``): a circle of
radius R then gives ``mu0 R (ln(8 R / a) - 7/4)``, Rosa's low-frequency loop inductance
(:func:`loop_self_inductance`). The paths are cut into straight pieces; the diagonal blocks are integrated in
closed form, the others with ``gauss``-point Gauss-Legendre rules. ``wire_radius``: one value or one per path.
``mirror_z``: a plane ``z = mirror_z`` of infinitely permeable iron (the image of each element carries the same
tangential current), added to every mutual and self term.

children.summary: Electrostatics and magnetostatics in closed form, and Biot-Savart integration of filamentary currents.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.units
children.doc:
SI dimensions of electromagnetic quantities and a dimensional check of Maxwell's equations.

Every field, source and material parameter of this package is in SI. :data:`QUANTITIES` gives the SI unit of
each named quantity (parsed by :mod:`pinneapple_data.physical_units`, dimension vector over
``(m, kg, s, K, A, mol)``); :data:`EQUATIONS` writes each law as a list of terms, each a product of quantities
and derivative operators, and :func:`check_equations` verifies that all terms of every law have the same
dimension. :func:`check_units` checks user-declared units of fields against the table, so a field stored in
``V/cm`` or a permeability given in ``H/m`` mislabelled as ``T`` is caught before any residual is computed.

functions.name: dimension
functions.sig: (unit: str) -> Dim
functions.doc: Dimension vector of a unit expression.

functions.name: term_dimension
functions.sig: (term: tuple[str, ...], quantities: Mapping[str, str] = QUANTITIES) -> Dim
functions.doc: Dimension of a product of factors (see :data:`EQUATIONS`).

functions.name: check_equations
functions.sig: (equations: Mapping[str, list[tuple[str, ...]]] = EQUATIONS, quantities: Mapping[str, str] = QUANTITIES) -> list[UnitProblem]
functions.doc: Every term of every law must have the dimension of the first term; returns the violations.

functions.name: check_units
functions.sig: (declared: Mapping[str, str]) -> list[UnitProblem]
functions.doc:
Compare declared units of named quantities (``{"E": "V/m", "B": "mT"}``) with :data:`QUANTITIES`.

A different scale (``mT`` for ``B``) is reported as a scale problem only if the factor is not 1, so the
caller can convert; a different dimension is an error. Unknown names are skipped.

children.summary: SI dimensions of electromagnetic quantities and a dimensional check of Maxwell's equations.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.verification
children.doc:
Verification suite of the electromagnetics package: each case runs a solver or a reference implementation
against an independent result (closed form, a published value, another library, a limit) and reports the
measured error and, where a mesh or step is refined, the measured order of convergence.

``run()`` returns :class:`CaseResult` objects; ``to_markdown()`` renders the table of
docs/guides/electromagnetics.md, which is produced by ``examples/electrodynamics/07_em_verification.py``, so every
number in that table comes from a run. ``tests/test_em_verification.py`` asserts each case's tolerance.

Cases are registered with :func:`case`; later modules (FDTD, edge elements, particles, ...) add theirs.

functions.name: case
functions.sig: (name: str)

functions.name: observed_orders
functions.sig: (errors: Sequence[float], ratio: float = 2.0) -> list[float]

functions.name: run
functions.sig: (names: Sequence[str] | None = None, quick: bool = False) -> list[CaseResult]

functions.name: to_markdown
functions.sig: (results: Sequence[CaseResult]) -> str
functions.doc:
The verification results as a Markdown table (case, quantity, reference, error on the finest level, observed
order, status).

functions.name: write_markdown_block
functions.sig: (path, results: Sequence[CaseResult], marker: str = 'verification-table') -> None
functions.doc:
Replace the text between ``<!-- marker:start -->`` and ``<!-- marker:end -->`` in a Markdown file with the
table of ``results`` and their notes, so a page shows exactly what the last run measured.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.electromagnetics.waves

functions.name: free_space_wavelength
functions.sig: (f: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Free-space wavelength ``c / f``.

Returns
-------
wavelength : float [m]
    For ``f`` in Hz.

functions.name: fresnel
functions.sig: (n1, n2, theta_i)
functions.doc:
Amplitude reflection and transmission coefficients ``(rs, rp, ts, tp)`` at a planar interface from
medium ``n1`` to ``n2`` (non-magnetic, complex indices allowed, ``Im(n) <= 0`` for loss).

s (TE): ``rs = (n1 cos ti - n2 cos tt) / (n1 cos ti + n2 cos tt)``, ``ts = 1 + rs``.
p (TM): ratio of reflected to incident *electric* field with Born & Wolf's sign convention,
``rp = (n2 cos ti - n1 cos tt) / (n2 cos ti + n1 cos tt)``, ``tp = 2 n1 cos ti / (n2 cos ti + n1 cos tt)``.
At normal incidence ``rp = -rs``. Power coefficients: ``R = |r|^2``, ``T = Re(n2 cos tt) / Re(n1 cos ti) |t|^2``
for s (and with the same factor for p).

functions.name: brewster_angle
functions.sig: (n1: float, n2: float) -> float
functions.doc:
``atan(n2 / n1)``: p-polarised reflection vanishes.

Returns
-------
theta_B : float [rad]
    Brewster angle.

functions.name: critical_angle
functions.sig: (n1: float, n2: float) -> float
functions.doc:
``asin(n2 / n1)`` for ``n1 > n2`` (total internal reflection above it).

Returns
-------
theta_c : float [rad]
    Critical angle.

functions.name: multilayer
functions.sig: (n_layers, d_layers, wavelength, theta_i: float = 0.0, pol: str = 's', n_in: complex = 1.0, n_out: complex = 1.0) -> MultilayerResult
functions.doc:
Reflection and transmission of a stack of planar layers (indices ``n_layers``, thicknesses ``d_layers``
in m) between half-spaces ``n_in`` and ``n_out``, by Born & Wolf's characteristic matrices. ``wavelength``
may be an array (vacuum wavelength, m). Field coefficients refer to E for s and to H for p
(so ``r`` for p equals Born & Wolf's ``r_TM``, ``R`` and ``T`` are unambiguous).

functions.name: skin_depth
functions.sig: (omega, sigma: float, mu_r: float = 1.0, eps_r: float = 1.0, exact: bool = False)
functions.doc:
Skin depth (m). Good-conductor form ``sqrt(2 / (omega mu sigma))``; ``exact=True`` gives ``1 / |Im k|`` with
``k^2 = omega^2 mu eps - j omega mu sigma``, valid for any loss tangent.

functions.name: surface_impedance
functions.sig: (omega, sigma: float, mu_r: float = 1.0)
functions.doc: Surface impedance of a good conductor, ``Zs = (1 + j) / (sigma delta) = (1 + j) sqrt(omega mu / (2 sigma))``.

functions.name: rect_waveguide_cutoff
functions.sig: (m: int, n: int, a: float, b: float, eps_r: float = 1.0, mu_r: float = 1.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Cut-off frequency (Hz) of the TE_mn / TM_mn mode of an ``a x b`` rectangular guide:
``f_c = c / (2 pi sqrt(eps_r mu_r)) sqrt((m pi / a)^2 + (n pi / b)^2)``.

Returns
-------
f_c : float [Hz]
    Cut-off frequency, for ``a`` and ``b`` in m.

functions.name: rect_waveguide_modes
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float, n_modes: int = 10, eps_r: float = 1.0, max_index: int = 8)
functions.doc:
The lowest ``n_modes`` modes as ``(f_c, "TE"/"TM", m, n)`` sorted by cut-off. TE needs ``m + n > 0``,
TM needs ``m, n >= 1``.

functions.name: rect_te_mn_fields
functions.sig: (x, y, m: int, n: int, a: float, b: float)
functions.doc:
Transverse profile of TE_mn in an ``a x b`` guide (unnormalised): ``Hz = cos(m pi x/a) cos(n pi y/b)``,
``E_t`` proportional to ``(n/b cos(m pi x/a) sin(n pi y/b), -m/a sin(m pi x/a) cos(n pi y/b))``.

functions.name: circular_waveguide_cutoff
functions.sig: (kind: str, m: int, n: int, radius: float, eps_r: float = 1.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Cut-off (Hz) of TE_mn (``n``-th zero of ``J_m'``) or TM_mn (``n``-th zero of ``J_m``) of a circular guide.

Returns
-------
f_c : float [Hz]
    Cut-off frequency, for the radius in m.

functions.name: circular_waveguide_modes
functions.sig: (radius: float, n_modes: int = 10, eps_r: float = 1.0, max_m: int = 6, max_n: int = 4)

functions.name: propagation_constant
functions.sig: (f, f_cutoff: float, eps_r: float = 1.0, mu_r: float = 1.0)
functions.doc: ``beta = k sqrt(1 - (fc/f)^2)`` above cut-off; below it ``-j alpha`` (evanescent, ``exp(-j beta z)``).

functions.name: rect_cavity_resonance
functions.sig: (m: int, n: int, p: int, a: float, b: float, d: float, eps_r: float = 1.0, mu_r: float = 1.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Resonance (Hz) of mode (m, n, p) of an ``a x b x d`` PEC box:
``f = c / (2 sqrt(eps_r mu_r)) sqrt((m/a)^2 + (n/b)^2 + (p/d)^2)``.

Returns
-------
f : float [Hz]
    Resonance, for dimensions in m.

functions.name: rect_cavity_modes
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float, d: float, n_modes: int = 10, eps_r: float = 1.0, max_index: int = 6)
functions.doc:
Lowest resonances of a PEC box with multiplicity: ``(f, [labels])``. A mode exists as TE_mnp (relative to z)
if ``(m or n) and p >= 1`` and as TM_mnp if ``m, n >= 1``; at least two indices must be non-zero.

functions.name: cylindrical_cavity_resonance
functions.sig: (kind: str, m: int, n: int, p: int, radius: float, length: float, eps_r: float = 1.0) -> float
functions.doc:
TE_mnp (``p >= 1``) or TM_mnp (``p >= 0``) resonance of a closed circular cylinder (Pozar sec. 6.4).

Returns
-------
f : float [Hz]
    Resonance, for radius and length in m.

functions.name: rect_cavity_te101_q
functions.sig: (a: float, b: float, d: float, sigma: float, eps_r: float = 1.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Conductor-loss Q of the TE101 mode (Pozar eq. 6.46):
``Qc = (k a d)^3 b eta / (2 pi^2 Rs) / (2 a^3 b + 2 b d^3 + a^3 d + a d^3)``.

functions.name: hertzian_dipole_fields
functions.sig: (r, theta, current_moment: complex, omega: float)

functions.name: hertzian_dipole_power
functions.sig: (current_moment: complex, omega: float) -> float
functions.doc: Time-averaged radiated power ``eta k^2 |I l|^2 / (12 pi)`` (W, peak phasor).

functions.name: hertzian_dipole_radiation_resistance
functions.sig: (length: float, wavelength: float) -> float
functions.doc: ``R = (2 pi / 3) eta (l / lambda)^2`` = ``80 pi^2 (l/lambda)^2`` ohm with ``eta = 120 pi``.

functions.name: dipole_pattern
functions.sig: (theta, length_wavelengths: float = 0.5)
functions.doc:
Far-field E_theta pattern of a thin centre-fed dipole of length ``L`` with sinusoidal current (Balanis
eq. 4-58a): ``[cos(k L/2 cos t) - cos(k L/2)] / sin t`` (unnormalised). ``L = lambda/2`` gives
``cos(pi/2 cos t) / sin t``.

functions.name: cylinder_tm_coefficients
functions.sig: (ka: float, eps_r: complex | None, n_max: int | None = None)
functions.doc:
Coefficients ``(n, a_n, b_n)`` of the TM_z scattering by a cylinder of radius ``a`` (``ka = k0 a``):
scattered ``Ez = E0 sum j^-n a_n H_n^(2)(k rho) e^{j n phi}``, inside ``E0 sum j^-n b_n J_n(k1 rho) e^{j n phi}``
for the incident ``E0 exp(-j k x)``. ``eps_r=None`` is a perfect conductor (``a_n = -J_n(ka) / H_n(ka)``).
Continuity of ``Ez`` and ``H_phi`` (non-magnetic) at ``rho = a``.

functions.name: cylinder_scattering_tm
functions.sig: (x, y, k0: float, radius: float, eps_r: complex | None, E0: complex = 1.0, total: bool = True)
functions.doc:
Phasor ``Ez`` at points ``(x, y)`` for a plane wave ``E0 exp(-j k0 x)`` (``exp(+j omega t)``) on a circular
cylinder centred at the origin (``eps_r=None``: PEC). ``total=False`` returns the scattered field outside
(and the total field inside).

functions.name: half_wave_dipole_radiation_resistance
functions.sig: (eta: float = ETA0) -> float
functions.doc:
``R = eta / (4 pi) Cin(2 pi)`` with ``Cin(x) = gamma + ln x - Ci(x)`` (Balanis eq. 4-93): 73.08 ohm in
free space (input resistance of an infinitely thin lambda/2 dipole).

functions.name: half_wave_dipole_directivity
functions.sig: () -> float

functions.name: spp_wavenumber
functions.sig: (omega, eps_metal, eps_dielectric: float = 1.0)
functions.doc:
Surface plasmon polariton on a flat interface: ``k_sp = (omega/c) sqrt(eps_m eps_d / (eps_m + eps_d))``
(Maier eq. 2.14), with ``Im(k_sp) <= 0`` for a lossy metal under ``exp(+j omega t)``.

functions.name: plasma_dispersion_omega
functions.sig: (k, omega_p: float)
functions.doc: Transverse waves in a collisionless plasma: ``omega^2 = omega_p^2 + c^2 k^2``.

children.summary: Closed-form wave electromagnetics, exp(+j omega t) convention (see .media).

children.doc:
Electromagnetics and electrodynamics in SI: references, materials, solvers and machines.

Statics and machines (2-D, P1 triangles):

* :mod:`.mesh` -- polar ring mesher with a moving band for rotation, structured rectangles; gmsh importer.
* :mod:`.materials` -- linear media, permanent magnets, nonlinear B-H curves.
* :mod:`.hysteresis` -- Froehlich-Kennelly saturation curve, Jiles-Atherton hysteresis.
* :mod:`.fem` -- A_z magnetostatics: assembly and Newton solver with Dirichlet and (anti-)periodic constraints.
* :mod:`.electrostatics` -- -div(eps grad phi) = rho with electrodes; capacitance from the field energy.
* :mod:`.eddy` -- time-harmonic eddy currents in solid conductors with imposed net currents.
* :mod:`.postprocess` -- Maxwell-stress and co-energy torque, flux linkage, back-EMF, iron and magnet losses.
* :mod:`.machine` -- surface-PM / reluctance machine model (cogging, torque vs current angle, losses,
  rotor design sensitivities).

Fields, waves and references:

* :mod:`.constants` -- CODATA 2022 constants; :mod:`.units` -- SI dimensions and a dimensional check of
  Maxwell's equations.
* :mod:`.media` -- isotropic, anisotropic and dispersive (Drude, Lorentz, Debye) media, ``exp(+j omega t)``.
* :mod:`.statics` -- capacitors, Biot-Savart, loops, solenoids, inductances in closed form.
* :mod:`.waves` -- Fresnel, multilayers, skin depth, waveguides, cavities, dipoles, cylinder scattering,
  surface plasmons.
* :mod:`.mie` -- Mie series for dielectric and conducting spheres.
* :mod:`.analytic` -- closed-form references of the machine solvers (wire, coax, magnetised cylinder,
  skin effect, subdomain solution of a slotless machine).
* :mod:`.particles` -- charged particles in E and B fields: relativistic Boris pusher, dipole / bottle / Penning
  fields, closed forms (Larmor radius, drifts, loss cone, Penning frequencies) and checked studies.

Physics checks of any field (Gauss, Faraday, Ampere-Maxwell, Poynting, reciprocity, passivity) are in
:mod:`pinneapple_physics.maxwell_checks` and ``pinneapple check`` (``physics = "maxwell"``). See
docs/guides/electromagnetics.md.
children.summary: Electromagnetics and electrodynamics in SI: references, materials, solvers and machines.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.events
children.doc:
Simulação orientada a evento: ``pp.Event(condition=..., action=...)`` (#210).

Um impacto, uma mudança de fase, uma válvula que abre, um contato, um limiar de reação: são todos a mesma coisa em
termos de integração — em algum instante ``t*`` uma condição sobre o estado cruza zero, e no instante seguinte a
dinâmica é outra. Integrar com passo fixo e testar a condição **depois** do passo erra o instante por até um passo
inteiro (e num impacto, errar o instante é errar a energia); integrar com passo fixo e simplesmente refletir a
velocidade quando o estado ficou abaixo do chão *cria* energia, porque o rebote acontece em ``h < 0``.

Este módulo faz o que um integrador de eventos faz: detecta a troca de sinal da condição dentro do passo, localiza o
instante por bissecção até a tolerância pedida, aplica a ação **naquele** instante e retoma a integração com o passo
que sobrou. O instante que sai no registro é o localizado, com a largura final do intervalo de bissecção junto — é o
que permite comparar com o tempo analítico.

    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> from pinneapple_simulation.events import Event, reflect, run_events
    >>> g, h0 = 9.81, 1.0
    >>> floor = Event(name="floor", condition=lambda t, y, p: y[0], action=reflect(component=1, factor=-1.0))
    >>> trace = run_events(lambda t, y, p: np.array([y[1], -g]), [h0, 0.0], (0.0, 2.0), 0.01, [floor])
    >>> round(trace.first("floor"), 5), round(float(np.sqrt(2 * h0 / g)), 5)   # o tempo analítico da queda
    (0.45152, 0.45152)

Por que a condição é uma função e não um número: ``condition(t, y, params) -> float`` é a função de cruzamento, e o
evento dispara onde ela muda de sinal na direção pedida (``falling`` por omissão: de positivo para negativo, que é o
caso de um objeto que chega ao chão). ``action(t, y, params) -> Reaction`` devolve o estado novo, muda parâmetros ou
para a simulação — as três coisas que uma ação de verdade faz.

Limites declarados, porque um benchmark os encontra:

* a trajetória entre dois instantes é integrada por um passo de Runge-Kutta 4, o mesmo do integrador principal; a
  localização do evento herda essa aproximação (não há interpolação densa de ordem superior aqui);
* a detecção é o teste de sinal **nos extremos do passo**: um evento cujo cruzamento inteiro cabe dentro de um passo
  não é visto. Num rebote isso acontece quando o voo entre dois quiques fica menor que ``dt`` — e é por isso que o
  passo tem de resolver o evento, não o contrário: com ``dt`` grande demais a bola "atravessa" o chão em silêncio no
  `run_events`, o que é o mesmo erro que qualquer integrador de passo fixo comete;
* um evento que dispara sem parar (chattering: a condição continua satisfeita logo depois da própria ação) estoura
  ``max_events`` e o módulo levanta :class:`EventLimit` em vez de girar para sempre. O caso de Zeno (bola com
  restituição menor que 1 quicando cada vez mais rápido) tem o mesmo fim *se* o passo ainda o resolver; mais cedo,
  ele cai na limitação anterior — use ``reflect(stop_below=...)`` para fechá-lo por física em vez de por contagem;
* depois de disparar, o evento é desativado por omissão (``repeat=False``), que é o que a maioria dos casos quer; um
  rebote que deve repetir declara ``repeat=True`` e um piso de velocidade na ação (ver ``reflect(stop_below=...)``).

classes.name: EventLimit
classes.doc: An event fired more times than ``max_events`` allowed -- the case is chattering or Zeno, and this says so.

classes.name: Reaction
classes.doc:
O que uma ação faz no instante do evento: novo estado, parâmetros alterados, ou parar.

Qualquer combinação é válida. ``state=None`` mantém o estado; ``params`` é mesclado; ``stop=True`` encerra a
simulação **naquele** instante, e o registro diz por quê em ``reason``.

classes.name: Event
classes.doc:
Uma condição de cruzamento e a ação que ela dispara.

``condition(t, y, params) -> float`` é a função de cruzamento: o evento dispara onde ela troca de sinal na
direção pedida. ``action(t, y, params) -> Reaction`` diz o que passa a valer dali em diante.

methods.name: crosses
methods.doc: A condição passou para o outro lado, na direção pedida, entre os dois valores?

fields: condition: Callable[[float, np.ndarray, Mapping[str, Any]], float]
action: Callable[[float, np.ndarray, Mapping[str, Any]], Reaction] | Reaction

classes.name: Trigger
classes.doc: Um disparo, com o instante localizado, a largura do intervalo e quantas avaliações custou.

classes.name: EventTrace
classes.doc: O que a simulação deixou: a trajetória, os disparos e se ela parou por ação de um evento.

methods.name: first
methods.doc: O primeiro instante em que o evento ``name`` disparou; ``KeyError`` se ele nunca disparou.

methods.name: state_at
methods.doc: O estado registrado no instante mais próximo de ``time`` (a grade é a dos passos dados).

functions.name: reflect
functions.sig: (component: int, factor: float, *, stop_below: float | None = None, speed_component: int | None = None) -> Callable[[float, np.ndarray, Mapping[str, Any]], Reaction]
functions.doc:
A ação de um impacto: multiplica uma componente do estado por ``factor`` (``-1`` = rebote elástico).

``stop_below`` para a simulação quando ``|y[speed_component]|`` (por omissão a própria componente) fica abaixo
dele — é o que fecha um caso de Zeno com ``restitution < 1`` em vez de deixá-lo girar.

functions.name: set_params
functions.sig: (**values) -> Callable[[float, np.ndarray, Mapping[str, Any]], Reaction]
functions.doc: A ação de uma válvula que abre, de uma bomba que liga: altera parâmetros que o lado direito lê.

functions.name: stop_simulation
functions.sig: (reason: str = '') -> Callable[[float, np.ndarray, Mapping[str, Any]], Reaction]
functions.doc: A ação de um limiar de falha: a simulação termina no instante do evento.

functions.name: chain
functions.sig: (*actions) -> Callable[[float, np.ndarray, Mapping[str, Any]], Reaction]
functions.doc: Aplica as ações em ordem, acumulando estado e parâmetros (a última que pedir para parar decide).

functions.name: run_events
functions.sig: (rhs: Callable[[float, np.ndarray, Mapping[str, Any]], np.ndarray], y0: Any, t_span: Sequence[float], dt: float, events: Sequence[Event], *, params: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, max_events: int = 1000, min_step: float = 1e-12) -> EventTrace
functions.doc:
Integra ``dy/dt = rhs(t, y, params)`` de ``t_span[0]`` a ``t_span[1]``, parando em cada evento.

``rhs(t, y, params)`` devolve o lado direito (o mesmo ``params`` que as ações alteram). O passo é ``dt``; quando
um evento é localizado dentro do passo, a integração é retomada exatamente no instante localizado, com o resto do
passo, em vez de recomeçar do fim do passo.

Levanta :class:`EventLimit` quando os disparos passam de ``max_events`` (chattering/Zeno) e ``ValueError`` para
``dt <= 0``, ``t_span`` invertido ou passo menor que ``min_step``.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers
pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.ansys
pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.ansys.journal_builder
children.doc:
ANSYS Fluent batch-mode journal (``.jou``) generation.

Fluent has no Python/REST scripting surface used here -- like every other
"drive a real external solver" integration in this repository
(``external_solvers/openfoam/runner.py`` shells out to real OpenFOAM
executables), the only way to actually run it non-interactively is its
documented Text User Interface (TUI), invoked in batch mode with a journal
file of TUI commands (``fluent 3ddp -g -i run.jou``). The TUI command set
used below (``/file/read-case``, ``/solve/initialize/initialize-flow``,
``/solve/iterate``, ``/solve/dual-time-iterate``,
``/file/write-case-data``, ``/file/binary-files``, ``exit``) is Fluent's
own public, documented command-line interface -- the same commands that
appear throughout ANSYS's own Fluent Text Command List documentation and
in essentially every publicly published Fluent journal-file tutorial. This
is knowledge of a standard tool's documented CLI (like knowing ``git
commit -m``), not anything reverse-engineered or proprietary.

Confidence level, command by command
-------------------------------------
High confidence (these are the commands used by virtually every public
Fluent journal example and have been stable across Fluent versions for
decades):
  - ``/file/read-case <path>``
  - ``/file/binary-files no`` (ASCII/text I/O toggle)
  - ``/solve/initialize/initialize-flow``
  - ``/solve/iterate <n>``
  - ``/file/write-case-data <path>``
  - ``exit`` / ``yes``

Medium confidence (documented, but with more version-to-version drift in
exact prompt sequencing than the commands above):
  - ``/solve/dual-time-iterate <n-time-steps> <max-iterations-per-step>``
    for transient runs.
  - ``/solve/monitors/residual/convergence-criteria <values...>`` -- the
    number and order of prompted values depends on which equations
    (turbulence, energy, species, ...) are active in the case, which this
    module cannot know without reading the case file. See
    ``FluentCaseConfig.residual_convergence`` docstring for the narrow,
    explicit assumption made here (a fixed 4-slot laminar flow/continuity
    + 3 velocity components ordering).
  - ``/define/boundary-conditions/set/<zone-type> <zone> () <field> no
    <value> quit`` -- this "set" shorthand (zone list, empty parens for
    "no additional zones", field keyword, "no" to skip profile/expression
    input, a literal value, ``quit`` to close the per-zone menu) is the
    idiom used in numerous public Fluent journal tutorials for setting a
    single scalar BC value without walking the full interactive panel.
    Deliberately limited to exactly two BC kinds for this reason -- see
    below.

Deliberately NOT implemented (left out due to insufficient confidence,
per this module's honesty policy -- do not guess at TUI syntax you are not
sure of):
  - Any boundary condition beyond velocity-inlet velocity-magnitude and
    pressure-outlet gauge-pressure (e.g. mass-flow-inlet, wall
    temperature/heat-flux, turbulence intensity/length-scale, species
    fractions, multiphase BCs). These involve longer, model-dependent
    prompt sequences this module cannot generate reliably without a real
    Fluent session to verify against.
  - Turbulence/physics model selection (``/define/models/...``) -- the
    input case file is assumed to already have the desired model set up.
  - Mesh quality/adaption commands.
  - Parallel partitioning TUI commands (processor count is a Fluent
    *launch* flag, ``-t<n>``, handled by ``ansys.runner``, not a journal
    command).

None of this has been exercised against a real Fluent installation (see
``ansys/runner.py`` and ``tests/test_ansys_fluent_runner.py`` for why:
this environment has no licensed ``fluent`` binary). Only the generated
journal *text* is tested here, against the documented command syntax
above.

classes.name: FluentCaseConfig
classes.doc:
Configuration for one basic batch Fluent run.

Exactly one of ``case_file`` / ``mesh_file`` must be given: an existing
Fluent case (``.cas``/``.cas.h5``, read via ``/file/read-case``) or a
raw mesh to import (via ``/file/import/fluent-mesh``) when no case has
been set up yet. A case file is strongly preferred -- it already
carries model/BC-type setup that a bare mesh does not.

functions.name: build_journal
functions.sig: (config: FluentCaseConfig) -> str
functions.doc:
Generate Fluent TUI journal-file text for ``config``.

Command order: read case/mesh -> (optional) force ASCII output ->
boundary-condition overrides -> (optional) convergence criteria ->
(optional) flow initialization -> solve (steady iterate or transient
dual-time-iterate) -> write case+data -> exit.

children.summary: ANSYS Fluent batch-mode journal (.jou) generation.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.ansys.runner
children.doc:
ANSYS Fluent live-solver coupling: launches a real ``fluent`` batch-mode
process against a generated journal file and drives an actual solve, then
hands the result off to the existing ``cfd_formats.fluent_mesh_reader``
UPD bridge.

Mirrors ``external_solvers/openfoam/runner.py``'s shape (a frozen
``RunConfig``-style dataclass, subprocess invocation of a real external
executable, explicit failure if the executable isn't found) rather than
inventing a different structure for this second live-solver integration.

Fluent's batch-mode command line (``fluent <precision> -g -i
<journal>.jou [-t<nprocs>]``) is Fluent's own public, documented launch
syntax -- ``-g`` (no GUI), ``-i <journal>`` (run a journal file
non-interactively), ``-t<n>`` (processor count) are all in ANSYS's own
Fluent User's Guide / Text Command List documentation and used throughout
publicly published Fluent batch-run tutorials and HPC cluster job
scripts.

Honesty note
------------
This environment has no licensed ANSYS Fluent installation (``fluent`` is
not on PATH here -- confirmed via ``shutil.which`` at import/use time, not
assumed). This module has therefore only been exercised, and can only be
tested in this repository, along two paths:

  1. Journal-text generation (``journal_builder.build_journal``) --
     fully real logic, fully testable with no Fluent install.
  2. The "executable not found" error path here -- also fully real and
     testable, and it is the actual path a caller hits in this
     environment.

The subprocess-invocation and log-capture code itself is straightforward
and follows the same pattern as the OpenFOAM runner (which *is* exercised
against a real OpenFOAM install elsewhere in this repo's test suite), but
the specific claim "fluent 3ddp -g -i journal.jou correctly drives a real
solve end-to-end" is NOT verified locally -- consistent with this
repository's existing convention for external tools that aren't installed
here (see e.g. ``pinneapple_design/geometry/io/iges.py`` for gmsh, or
``cfd_formats/abaqus_reader.py``'s ``.odb`` bridge for Abaqus).

classes.name: FluentRunConfig
classes.doc:
Mirrors ``openfoam.runner.OpenFOAMRunConfig``'s role: how to invoke
the external binary, not what to simulate (that's ``FluentCaseConfig``).

functions.name: run_fluent_case
functions.sig: (case_config: FluentCaseConfig, run_config: Optional[FluentRunConfig] = None) -> FluentRunResult
functions.doc:
Build a journal from ``case_config``, launch a real Fluent batch
process against it, and package the resulting case/data file via the
existing ``fluent_mesh_to_upd`` bridge (imported, not reimplemented).

Raises ``FileNotFoundError`` immediately (before touching the
filesystem beyond validating ``case_config``) if the ``fluent``
executable can't be located -- this never silently no-ops.

children.summary: ANSYS Fluent live-solver coupling: launches a real fluent batch-mode process against a generated journal file and drives an actual solve, then hands the result off to the existing ...

children.doc:
ANSYS Fluent live-solver coupling: launches a real ``fluent`` batch-mode
process (journal-file driven, ``fluent <precision> -g -i run.jou``) and
drives an actual simulation, then hands the result off to the existing
``cfd_formats.fluent_mesh_reader`` UPD bridge.

This is distinct from -- and complements -- ``cfd_formats.fluent_mesh_reader``,
which only reads ``.msh``/``.cas`` files Fluent has already produced and
has no live-solver coupling of its own. See ``runner.py``'s module
docstring for the honesty note on what could and couldn't be tested
locally (no licensed Fluent installation is available in this
environment).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.backends
children.doc:
The solver implementations this repository already had, behind the one contract of :mod:`.contract`.

Nothing is reimplemented here. Each backend calls the module it wraps -- ``openfoam.campaign``/``openfoam.field_reader``,
``calculix.inp``/``frd``/``runner``, ``ansys.runner``/``journal_builder``, ``numerical_solvers.fenics_bridge``,
``matlab.runner`` -- and adds only the four things the contract asks of it: what it needs (:meth:`_requirements`),
how a neutral :class:`~.contract.SolverCase` becomes its input (``prepare``), how it starts (``_start``), and which
log lines mean converged or diverged (``converged_markers`` / ``divergence_markers`` fed to
:func:`~.contract.classify_run`).

Two of the six are the pair the cross-backend test runs: :class:`CalculiXBackend` (the ``ccx`` binary or the bundled
Docker image) and :class:`SolidFEMBackend` (the in-process hexahedral elasticity solver of
``numerical_solvers.solid_fem``, which needs no executable and no licence). They take the same
:meth:`~.contract.SolverCase.cantilever`, and their displacement fields arrive in the same schema with provenance
naming each backend and its version -- which is what makes two solvers comparable rather than merely both installed.

COMSOL is not among them on purpose: no implementation of it exists in this repository, its Python coupling needs a
licensed commercial client and its model files are binary, so it cannot be exercised here -- see the module docstring
of :mod:`.contract` and ``docs/guides/external_solver_contract.md``.

classes.name: BackendMissing
classes.doc: A backend module is missing although its own check said it was there (an extra is required).

classes.name: OpenFOAMBackend
classes.sig: (workdir: str | Path | None = None, *, solver: str = 'icoFoam', bashrc: str | None = None, commands: Sequence[str] | None = None, edits: Sequence[dict] | None = None, fields: Sequence[str] = ('p', 'U'), case_subdir: str = 'case', patterns: Sequence[str] | None = None, environ: dict[str, str] | None = None, log_name: str = 'solver.log')
classes.doc:
OpenFOAM: a case directory, the mesh command, the solver, the log.

``check_environment`` asks the environment itself rather than trusting ``PATH``: a distribution package puts
``blockMesh`` on the path but the binaries only run with the OpenFOAM environment sourced, so the probe sources
the ``bashrc`` (:mod:`.openfoam.environment`) and reports what it provides. The one case it stages is
:data:`~.contract.OPAQUE` (``SolverCase.case_directory``): the case files are OpenFOAM's own, and rewriting them
from a neutral description would be a mesher, not a contract.

classes.name: CalculiXBackend
classes.sig: (workdir: str | Path | None = None, *, job: str = 'case', threads: int = 1, backend: str | None = None, image: str | None = None, platform: str | None = None, log_name: str = 'solver.log')
classes.doc:
Implicit structural FEM through ``ccx``: the native binary when it is on ``PATH``, else the bundled Debian image.

The deck comes from a neutral :meth:`~.contract.SolverCase.cantilever` through ``calculix.inp``; the answer comes
back from ``calculix.frd``. A run whose ``.frd`` holds non-finite displacements is reported ``diverged`` even when
the log looks clean -- a NaN field is what a diverged structural solve leaves behind, and calling it converged
because the process exited 0 is how a wrong number reaches a report.

classes.name: SolidFEMBackend
classes.doc:
3-D linear elasticity in-process (``numerical_solvers.solid_fem``: 8-node hexahedra with incompatible modes, the
element Abaqus calls C3D8I), with no executable and no licence to check.

It is the second half of the cross-backend test: the same ``SolverCase.cantilever`` as :class:`CalculiXBackend`,
with a different element, a different solver and the same schema out -- so the contract is shown to be a layer and
not a renaming of one program.

classes.name: FEniCSxBackend
classes.doc:
Plane elasticity and steady conduction through ``numerical_solvers.fenics_bridge`` (DOLFINx, or legacy FEniCS
when that is what the machine has).

The bridge forms plane stress/strain with a body force and Dirichlet boundaries -- no traction term -- so the
neutral cases it takes are :meth:`~.contract.SolverCase.plane_cantilever`, whose uniform load becomes the body
force ``q / h``, and :meth:`~.contract.SolverCase.conduction`, whose closed form the field can be measured against.
Its labels come from the bridge's own supported kinds: anything else is :class:`~.contract.CaseUnsupported`.

Read the plane case for what it is: P1 triangles lock in bending, so a slender cantilever comes back far too stiff
(L/h = 10 under-predicts the tip deflection by an order of magnitude here). That is a property of the discretisation,
not of the contract -- measure this backend against a closed form (the conduction case) and use
:mod:`.openfoam`/:class:`CalculiXBackend` for the structural claims, which are checked against beam theory.

The DOLFINx API is pinned by a version requirement, not discovered by a crash: the bridge calls
``dolfinx.fem.petsc.LinearProblem``, which DOLFINx 0.10 removed. A newer DOLFINx is reported as a missing version
with the pin in the fix, because "installed" and "usable" are different answers.

classes.name: AnsysFluentBackend

ANSYS Fluent in batch mode: a journal from the neutral case, ``fluent <precision> -g -i run.jou``.

The licence is part of :meth:`check_environment` and not of the run: ANSYS is licence-gated, and a machine without
``ANSYSLMD_LICENSE_FILE`` (or ``LM_LICENSE_FILE``) is a machine that will fail at start, so the report says so

classes.name: MatlabBackend

MATLAB in ``-batch`` mode: the neutral case is a script (or a function call with its arguments), the results are
the ``.mat`` file it writes.

The licence is checked by the launcher, not by us: a machine can have ``matlab`` on ``PATH`` and still fail
checkout. That requirement is therefore reported unverified, and the launcher's refusal ("License checkout
failed") lands in the run's log where the status carries it as evidence.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.calculix.contact.cases
children.doc:
Contact problems with friction, as decks with a closed-form answer: the case library.

Each case is one geometry, one contact interface and one question that has an exact answer independent of the solver:

===========================  ==========================================================================
``bloco_plano``              a slider pushed sideways on a fixed plate: the joint transmits ``mu*N`` and no
                             more, so the tangential force saturates exactly there
``junta_dupla``              a plate pulled between two clamped plates: two interfaces share the load, so the
                             pull at slip is ``2*mu*N`` while each support carries ``mu*N``
``cilindro_hertz``           a rigid cylinder pressed into a plate: a non-conforming pair, so the peak pressure
                             and the half-width follow Hertz instead of the nominal contact area
``rampa``                    the same slider on an inclined interface: it stays put while ``tan(theta) <= mu``
                             and slides when it does not — the self-locking (autotravamento) test
``parafuso_pretensao``       two plates clamped by a ``*PRE-TENSION SECTION`` whose head and nut are footprints
                             joined by ``*DISTRIBUTING COUPLING``: the clamp force is the preload
``plastificacao_hertz``      the Hertz cylinder on an elastic-perfectly-plastic plate: yield begins at
                             ``p0 = k*sigma_y``, and ``k`` is Johnson's factor, not 1
===========================  ==========================================================================

Every case writes a deck PrePoMax opens unchanged, and every case declares the tolerance its comparison is judged by.
The parameters are the engineer's (mm, N, MPa), the meshes are structured hexahedra the solver can resolve the patch
with, and nothing here is specific to one problem size: the closed form is evaluated at the numbers the run reports,
so changing the load moves both sides of the comparison.

functions.name: get
functions.sig: (case_id: str | None, cases: Mapping[str, Case] | None = None) -> Case
functions.doc:
The case ``case_id`` (the default when None), out of ``cases`` or out of this module's own library.

``cases`` is how a caller adds its own problems to the menu without copying the readers: the same lookup, the same
error message, over a wider dict.

functions.name: catalog
functions.sig: (cases: Mapping[str, Case] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: The menu: every case with its parameters, its closed-form reference and what it assumes.

functions.name: build
functions.sig: (case_id: str | None, raw: dict[str, Any] | None, cases: Mapping[str, Case] | None = None) -> tuple[Case, dict[str, float], Built]

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.calculix.contact.deck
children.doc:
Writing the CalculiX deck — the file PrePoMax opens.

Everything here is a keyword CalculiX defines and PrePoMax writes and reads itself, so a deck assembled from these
blocks imports into PrePoMax as a model with its contact definitions intact (surface interaction, friction, contact
pairs, rigid bodies) and runs unchanged under ``ccx``. The two files agree by construction, which is the point: the
deck an engineer inspects in PrePoMax is the deck that produced the evidence.

Units are the engineer's, kept consistent: **mm, N, MPa (= N/mm²), s**. ``E`` in MPa, pressures in MPa, forces in N —
the same convention PrePoMax uses when its unit system is set to mm-N-s.

classes.name: Deck
classes.doc: A deck under construction: a title, then keyword blocks in the order CalculiX requires them.

functions.name: geometry
functions.sig: (deck: Deck, blocks: Sequence[tuple[str, Grid]]) -> None
functions.doc: ``*NODE`` once for every block, then one ``*ELEMENT`` per block, each in its own element set.

functions.name: node_set
functions.sig: (deck: Deck, name: str, ids: Sequence[int]) -> None

functions.name: element_set
functions.sig: (deck: Deck, name: str, ids: Sequence[int]) -> None

functions.name: surface
functions.sig: (deck: Deck, name: str, faces: Iterable[tuple[int, int]]) -> None
functions.doc: ``*SURFACE, TYPE=ELEMENT`` from ``(element id, face number)`` pairs, as :meth:`mesh.Grid.faces` returns them.

functions.name: interaction
functions.sig: (deck: Deck, name: str, friction: float, k_normal: float = 100000.0, c0: float = 0.0, stick_slope: float = 10000.0) -> None
functions.doc:
``*SURFACE INTERACTION`` with a linear pressure-overclosure and Coulomb friction.

``PRESSURE-OVERCLOSURE=LINEAR`` and a finite ``k_normal`` are what PrePoMax and CalculiX both recommend for
contact that starts closed: ``HARD`` is silently reduced to linear by ``ccx`` anyway (with a default stiffness
of about 1e7 N/mm³), and a very stiff interface converges slowly. ``stick_slope`` is the tangential stiffness
before slip; too small a value lets a "stuck" contact creep, too large a one slows every iteration down.

functions.name: contact_pair
functions.sig: (deck: Deck, name: str, slave: str, master: str, interaction_name: str, kind: str = 'SURFACE TO SURFACE') -> None
functions.doc: A contact pair. The slave is the softer, finer surface — the one whose nodes report contact results.

functions.name: material
functions.sig: (deck: Deck, name: str, E: float, nu: float) -> None

functions.name: section
functions.sig: (deck: Deck, elset: str, material_name: str) -> None

functions.name: plastic
functions.sig: (deck: Deck, sigma_y: float, hardening: float = 0.0) -> None
functions.doc:
``*PLASTIC`` under the material just declared, as an elastic-**perfectly** plastic card.

The curve is written with two points and no slope between them (``sigma_y`` at zero plastic strain and the same
stress at 1.0), which is what "perfectly plastic" means: the material carries ``sigma_y`` and no more, however far
it is pushed. It has to follow the ``*ELASTIC`` of the same material — a ``*PLASTIC`` card attaches to the
preceding ``*MATERIAL``, and writing another material in between silently gives the yield to the wrong body.

functions.name: distributing_coupling
functions.sig: (deck: Deck, elset: str, element: int, ref: int, weights: dict[int, float]) -> None
functions.doc:
``*DISTRIBUTING COUPLING``: a load put at ``ref`` spread over the listed nodes instead of entering at one.

The keyword needs an element set holding exactly one ``DCOUP3D`` element, whose single node is the reference;
what is applied there — a force by ``*CLOAD`` or a displacement by ``*BOUNDARY`` — is distributed over the nodes
below it with the weights given. Area weights (each node's tributary area) make the traction uniform, which is
the point when the coupling stands for a bolt head or a nut face: a single node dents the plate, a weighted
footprint presses it.

CalculiX builds one multiple point constraint per direction with every listed node in it, so the equation is
fully populated and the manual recommends staying under about 50 nodes — a footprint, not a whole face.

functions.name: plane_strain
functions.sig: (deck: Deck, faces: Sequence[int], dof: int = 3) -> None
functions.doc:
``*BOUNDARY`` inside the step that holds the out-of-plane displacement on both thickness faces.

A one-element-thick block whose two faces cannot move out of plane behaves exactly as a plane-strain section, and
that is what the two-dimensional closed-form references (Hertz line contact) describe. It is written as an
ordinary boundary so it reads in PrePoMax like any other support — no equations to maintain.

functions.name: outputs
functions.sig: (deck: Deck, totals_set: str, displacement_set: str | None = None, contact: bool = True, stress: bool = False) -> None
functions.doc:
The requests that make a run checkable: reaction totals in the ``.dat`` (equilibrium and friction force) and
contact results in the ``.frd`` (pressure, shear, opening, slip per node), which is also what PrePoMax plots.

functions.name: interference_fit_pressure
functions.sig: (*, interference_m: float, interface_radius_m: float, ring_outer_radius_m: float, shaft_inner_radius_m: float, ring_young_pa: float, ring_poisson: float, shaft_young_pa: float, shaft_poisson: float, plane_strain: bool = True) -> float

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.calculix.contact.mesh
children.doc:
Structured hexahedral blocks and CalculiX's brick face numbering: the geometry every contact case is built from.

A case is a handful of blocks (a base plate, a slider, a rigid indenter) meshed as grids of C3D8 bricks. Nothing here
knows about contact: a block is nodes, elements and the faces/ node sets its case asks for, selected by *geometry* —
the plane a face lies in, and which side of that plane the element sits on — instead of by a face number typed into
the deck by hand. That matters: picking the wrong local face loads or contacts the wrong side of a body, and the
solver reports a converged, wrong answer. Every surface a case uses is therefore derived from coordinates.

The face table is CalculiX's brick convention (``*SURFACE, TYPE=ELEMENT``), with local nodes numbered the way
:class:`Grid` builds them: 1-4 around the bottom face, 5-8 around the top, both counter-clockwise seen from +z.

classes.name: Grid
classes.doc:
A rectilinear block of C3D8 bricks.

``shift`` moves every node as a function of its x coordinate — the parabolic crown of a cylinder, or the tilted
plane of an incline — so a case can keep a rectangular grid while presenting a curved or inclined surface.

``polar`` reads the first two axes as radius and angle (radians) and places the nodes in Cartesian coordinates
``(r cos t, r sin t)``: a ring, a shaft or a quarter of either, still meshed as bricks. The faces then have to be
selected by radius (:meth:`faces_where`), not by a plane — which is what a cylindrical surface needs.

``warp`` moves a node as a function of its position on the surface — the sphere cap of an indenter, whose height
over a grid cell depends on both in-plane coordinates, which ``shift`` (a function of ``x`` alone) cannot express.
It is applied last, so a block stays a block of bricks with a curved face, and the curved face is still selected
by :meth:`faces` with a ``curved`` test.

methods.name: next_node
methods.doc: The first node id this block did not use: where the next one starts.

methods.name: faces
methods.sig: (plane: str, value: float, side: int | None = None, tol: float = TOL, curved: Callable[[tuple[float, float, float]], float] | None = None) -> list[tuple[int, int]]
methods.doc: ``(element id, face number)`` for every face lying in ``plane = value``.

methods.name: faces_where
methods.sig: (test: Callable[[tuple[float, float, float]], bool], tol: float = TOL) -> list[tuple[int, int]]
methods.doc:
``(element id, face number)`` for every face whose four nodes satisfy ``test`` — the way a cylindrical
surface is named (by its radius), since it lies on no plane.

methods.name: nodes_at_radius
methods.doc: Node ids on a cylinder of that radius (distance from the z axis).

methods.name: nodes_on
methods.sig: (plane: str, value: float, tol: float = TOL) -> list[int]
methods.doc: Node ids whose ``plane`` coordinate is ``value`` (within ``tol``).

methods.name: area
methods.sig: (plane: str, value: float, tol: float = TOL) -> float
methods.doc: The exact area of that plane of the block, for the load a pressure produces.

fields: shift: Callable[[float], tuple[float, float, float]] | None = None
warp: Callable[[tuple[float, float, float]], tuple[float, float, float]] | None = None
nodes: dict[int, tuple[float, float, float]] = field(default_factory=dict, init=False)

functions.name: axis
functions.sig: (x0: float, x1: float, n: int, grading: float = 1.0, cluster: str = 'low') -> list[float]
functions.doc:
``n + 1`` coordinates from ``x0`` to ``x1``. ``grading`` > 1 clusters the cells towards one end — the end the
contact patch is at, which is what makes a curved-on-flat case affordable: fine where the pressure is, coarse
where the body only carries it away.

functions.name: mirror
functions.sig: (values: Sequence[float]) -> list[float]
functions.doc: A one-sided axis turned into the symmetric one around 0 (``[0, .5, 1]`` -> ``[-1, -.5, 0, .5, 1]``).

functions.name: merge
functions.sig: (*grids) -> tuple[dict[int, tuple[float, float, float]], list[tuple[int, list[int]]]]
functions.doc: The node table and the ``(element id, its eight nodes)`` list of a set of blocks, in deck order.

functions.name: nset
functions.sig: (ids: Sequence[int], per_line: int = 16) -> list[str]
functions.doc:
An ``*NSET`` body. CalculiX refuses more than 16 entries on a line, and a hand-written deck that breaks the
rule stops with a message about the *next* keyword, which is why this is a helper and not a detail of each case.

children.summary: Structured hexahedral blocks and CalculiX's brick face numbering: the geometry every contact case is built from.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.calculix.contact.run
children.doc:
One contact run, end to end: build the deck, solve it with the ``ccx`` PrePoMax ships, read the results back through
:mod:`pinneapple_data.cae` and compare them with the closed form of :mod:`.verify`.

Nothing here decides on its own whether a run is good. It produces the deck, the solver's own files, the numbers as
read and the comparisons; the caller writes the report and the evidence record from those. The result files are read
by the data layer and not here, so a value that a report shows and a value a verification compares come from the same
fixed columns.

classes.name: SolverMissing
classes.doc: No ``ccx`` to run: the deck is still written and the run says so instead of guessing a result.

functions.name: ccx_binary
functions.sig: (explicit: str | None = None) -> str | None
functions.doc: Where the solver is: the setting when it names a file, else ``ccx`` on ``PATH``. None when there is none.

functions.name: version
functions.sig: (binary: str) -> str | None
functions.doc: The CalculiX version, read from the banner ``ccx -v`` prints (it exits 0 on every version we know of).

functions.name: solve
functions.sig: (deck_path: Path, binary: str, timeout: float, workdir: Path) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Run ``ccx`` on the deck in its own directory and read back whatever it wrote.

The solver reads its argument as a file stem in the working directory, writes ``.dat``/``.frd``/``.sta`` beside it,
and asks on stdin for another file when the deck ends early — hence the closed stdin: without it a malformed deck
would hang instead of failing.

functions.name: read_results
functions.sig: (deck_path: Path, times: dict[str, float] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Everything a verification reads out of one run, through :mod:`pinneapple_data.cae`.

``contact_until`` and ``stress_until`` hold the contact state and the stress field at each step time a case asks
for, which is how a two-step case reads what the preload did apart from what the pull did — and what the material
had already done by then.

functions.name: run_case
functions.sig: (case_id: str | None, params: dict[str, Any] | None, out_dir: Path, binary: str | None = None, timeout: float = 600.0, cases: Mapping[str, C.Case] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Build, solve, read and verify one case. ``out_dir`` receives the deck and the solver's files.

The return value is what a report and an evidence record are written from: the resolved parameters, the closed
form, the deck, the solver, the measured numbers as read, and the checks. No Markdown is produced here — that is
the caller's, and it must not be able to change a number the checks saw.

functions.name: measured
functions.sig: (parsed: dict[str, Any], built: C.Built) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: The numbers the run produced, as read — never adjusted towards the reference.

functions.name: footprint
functions.sig: (parsed: dict[str, Any], built: C.Built) -> list[dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc:
The contact pressure under the footprint a load spreads over, in distance from its axis.

It is the table that shows a head is an area and not a point: a load entering at one node leaves a spike at
``r = 0`` and a tail everywhere else, while a footprint presses with a pressure. It reads the state the checks
read — the end of the preload step when the case has one, because a joint that is pulled afterwards has two
reasons for its pressure and the table should name the one the head produced.

children.summary: One contact run, end to end: build the deck, solve it with the ccx PrePoMax ships, read the results back through pinneapple_data.cae and compare them with the closed form of .verify.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.calculix.contact.verify
children.doc:
The checks a contact run is judged by: closed-form comparisons, the Coulomb cone and the Hertz profile fit.

A contact analysis that converges is not a contact analysis that is right — a wrong master surface, a friction
coefficient applied to the wrong interface or a load transferred through the wrong path all converge, and the plot in
PrePoMax looks plausible. What settles it is a number computed independently: ``|F_t| = mu*N`` for a sliding joint,
``p0`` and the half-width for a non-conforming pair, ``T/N = min(tan(theta), mu)`` for an interface on a slope.

Three rules hold everywhere here:

* every comparison names the closed-form value, its formula and how it was obtained;
* a value that could not be measured makes the check ``inconclusive`` — never a pass;
* tolerances are declared by the case, not tuned until it passes. A mesh that does not resolve the contact patch
  fails the check, and the report says the tolerance it missed.

classes.name: Check
classes.doc: One verification, in the shape the job's evidence record reads.

functions.name: finite
functions.sig: (*values) -> bool

functions.name: relative
functions.sig: (value: float | None, reference: float | None) -> float | None
functions.doc: ``(value - reference) / reference``, or None when either is missing, non-finite or the reference is 0.

functions.name: compare
functions.sig: (name: str, value: float | None, reference: float | None, tol: float, source: str, unit: str = '', what: str = '') -> Check
functions.doc: ``value`` against a closed-form ``reference``, passing inside a declared relative ``tol``.

functions.name: at_most
functions.sig: (name: str, value: float | None, limit: float | None, tol: float, source: str, unit: str = '', what: str = '') -> Check
functions.doc: ``|value| <= limit`` (an inequality, such as the Coulomb cone), with the same declared slack.

functions.name: between
functions.sig: (name: str, ratio: float | None, low: float, high: float, source: str, what: str = '') -> Check
functions.doc: A ratio expected inside a band — the shape of a contact-pressure profile, for instance.

functions.name: contact_nodes
functions.sig: (contact: dict[int, dict[str, float]], nodes: Iterable[int] | None = None, min_pressure: float = 0.0) -> list[tuple[int, dict[str, float]]]
functions.doc: The nodes actually carrying pressure, restricted to the interface that was asked about.

functions.name: peak_pressure
functions.sig: (contact: dict[int, dict[str, float]], nodes: Iterable[int] | None = None) -> float | None

functions.name: hertz_fit
functions.sig: (points: Sequence[tuple[float, float]]) -> tuple[float, float, float] | None
functions.doc:
Fit ``p(x) = p0 * sqrt(1 - (x/b)^2)`` to a measured contact-pressure profile: ``(p0, b, r2)``.

The fit is linear in ``p^2`` against ``x^2`` (``p^2 = p0^2 - (p0^2 / b^2) x^2``), which needs no optimiser and
gives the peak pressure and the half-width directly — the two numbers Hertz's line-contact solution predicts.
``None`` when the profile has fewer than three distinct positions or does not fall away from the centre (a
contact patch the mesh did not resolve).

functions.name: hertz_line
functions.sig: (P: float, R: float, length: float, E: float, nu: float, rigid: bool = True) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Hertz line contact: half-width ``b`` and peak pressure ``p0`` for a total load ``P`` over ``length``.

``b = sqrt(4 P R / (pi L E*))``, ``p0 = 2 P / (pi b L)``, with ``1/E* = (1 - nu^2)/E`` for a rigid indenter and
``(1 - nu1^2)/E1 + (1 - nu2^2)/E2`` for two elastic bodies.

functions.name: von_mises
functions.sig: (sx: float, sy: float, sz: float, sxy: float = 0.0, syz: float = 0.0, szx: float = 0.0) -> float
functions.doc:
The equivalent (von Mises) stress of a stress state, tension positive — the quantity ``*PLASTIC`` compares
with the yield stress.

functions.name: hertz_line_axis
functions.sig: (zeta: float, nu: float = 0.3) -> tuple[float, float, float]
functions.doc:
The principal stresses on the loaded axis under a 2-D Hertz line contact, in units of ``p0``.

``zeta = z/b``, ``z`` measured from the surface into the body, compression negative. The classical field
(Johnson, *Contact Mechanics*, 1985) written out on the axis, where the shear vanishes and the three principal
stresses are ``sigma_x`` (across the contact), ``sigma_y = nu (sigma_x + sigma_z)`` (out of plane, plane strain)
and ``sigma_z`` (into the body).

functions.name: first_yield_factor
functions.sig: (nu: float = 0.3, steps: int = 4000, z_max: float = 4.0) -> float
functions.doc:
``p0 / sigma_y`` at the onset of yield in a 2-D Hertz line contact — Johnson's classic factor.

The peak of the equivalent stress sits *below* the surface, so the factor is not ``1``: the field above is
scanned along the axis and the factor is ``1 / max(von Mises / p0)``. For ``nu = 0.3`` it comes out **1.79** by
von Mises (the criterion CalculiX uses), with the peak at ``z = 0.70 b``; by Tresca it is 1.67 ``sigma_y``, the
peak shear being ``0.30 p0`` at ``z = 0.79 b``. Same numbers as Johnson, *Contact Mechanics* (Cambridge, 1985),
the section on the onset of yield.

functions.name: lame_shrink_fit
functions.sig: (interference: float, a: float, b: float, c: float, E: float, nu: float, plane_strain: bool = True, *, E_ring: float | None = None, nu_ring: float | None = None) -> float
functions.doc:
Interface pressure of a ring shrunk onto a hollow shaft.

With ``E_ring``/``nu_ring`` omitted the ring and the shaft share the material.

Lamé: the radial interference is the sum of the ring's expansion and the shaft's contraction,
``delta = p a [(c^2+a^2)/(c^2-a^2) + (a^2+b^2)/(a^2-b^2)] / E'`` — the Poisson terms cancel for a single
material, which is why the pressure depends on ``nu`` only through ``E'``. In **plane strain** (a long fit, which
is what a one-element-thick model with its faces held is) ``E' = E/(1 - nu^2)``, and that is a 10 % difference at
``nu = 0.3``: a plane-stress formula against a plane-strain model misses by more than the mesh does.

functions.name: coulomb_ratio
functions.sig: (contact: dict[int, dict[str, float]], nodes: Iterable[int] | None, min_fraction: float = 0.05) -> float | None
functions.doc:
The largest ``|tau| / p`` over the loaded nodes: 0 when nothing is stuck or sliding, ``mu`` at the limit.

Nodes below ``min_fraction`` of the peak pressure are left out: there the pressure is a rounding error and the
ratio it produces says nothing about friction.

functions.name: tributary_areas
functions.sig: (coords: dict[int, tuple[float, float, float]], nodes: Iterable[int], plane: str = 'y') -> dict[int, float]
functions.doc:
The area each node of a structured surface stands for, so a nodal field can be integrated into a force.

On a grid the rule is the vertex one: a node owns half of each cell edge it sits on, so its weight is the product
of the half-spans to its neighbours. For a bilinear field that is the exact integral (each cell hands a quarter of
itself to each corner), which is what makes ``sum(p_i * A_i)`` the contact force rather than an estimate of it.

functions.name: resultant

functions.doc: ``sum(field * area)`` over the loaded nodes: the force the interface transmits in that direction.

functions.name: slip_range
functions.sig: (contact: dict[int, dict[str, float]], nodes: Iterable[int] | None) -> float | None
functions.doc: How far the interface actually slid: the spread of the tangential slip over the loaded nodes.

children.summary: The checks a contact run is judged by: closed-form comparisons, the Coulomb cone and the Hertz profile fit.

children.doc:
Contact, as a capability of the library: seven cases with a closed-form answer, and the decks PrePoMax opens
unchanged. Six are friction cases; the seventh lets the plate yield.

Each case is one geometry, one contact interface and one question that has an exact answer independent of the solver:

===========================  ==========================================================================
``bloco_plano``              a slider pushed sideways on a fixed plate: the joint transmits ``mu*N`` and no more,
                             so the tangential force saturates exactly there
``junta_dupla``              a plate pulled between two clamped plates: two interfaces share the load, so the
                             pull at slip is ``2*mu*N`` while each support carries ``mu*N``
``cilindro_hertz``           a rigid cylinder pressed into a plate: a non-conforming pair, so the peak pressure
                             and the half-width follow Hertz instead of the nominal contact area
``rampa``                    the same slider on an inclined interface: it stays put while ``tan(theta) <= mu``
                             and slides when it does not — the self-locking test
``parafuso_pretensao``       two plates clamped by a bolt whose preload is a ``*PRE-TENSION SECTION``, so the clamp
                             force is the preload and the slip load is ``mu`` times the preload *measured*
``ajuste_forcado``           a ring shrunk onto a hollow shaft: the interference is geometric and the interface
                             pressure is Lamé's, not load/area
``plastificacao_hertz``      the Hertz cylinder on an elastic-perfectly-plastic plate: yield begins at
                             ``p0 = k*sigma_y`` with Johnson's ``k``, and the equivalent stress then stops there
===========================  ==========================================================================

The pieces are separable on purpose: :mod:`.mesh` (structured blocks and CalculiX's brick face numbering),
:mod:`.deck` (the keyword blocks PrePoMax reads), :mod:`.verify` (the closed forms and the comparisons) and
:mod:`.run` (the solver, with the results read by :mod:`pinneapple_data.cae`, never by a parser of its own).

    from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.calculix.contact import CASES, build, run_case
    case, params, built = build("bloco_plano", {"friccao": 0.3})
    result = run_case("bloco_plano", {"friccao": 0.3}, "runs/bloco")

``run_case`` returns the numbers as read and the checks; a report, a route and an evidence record are written from it
and cannot change what the checks saw. Without a ``ccx`` binary the deck is still written and the result says so.
children.summary: Contact, as a capability of the library: seven cases with a closed-form answer, and the decks PrePoMax opens unchanged.

CalculiX ``.frd`` results: reader (ASCII) and writer.

The writer is the heart of the drop-in idea: a PINN or surrogate that predicts displacements
(and stresses) on the mesh of an engineer's ``.inp`` can write a ``.frd`` that cgx, PrePoMax,
ccx2paraview or any FRD reader opens exactly like a CalculiX result. Format: CalculiX GraphiX
manual, "Result Format" (fixed-width ASCII records: ``2C`` nodes, ``3C`` elements, ``100CL``
result blocks with ``-4`` header, ``-5`` components, ``-1`` data lines, ``-3`` end).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.calculix.inp
children.doc:
CalculiX ``.inp`` decks: a small model container, a writer and a reader.

Only the keywords a linear static structural model needs are handled (``*NODE``, ``*ELEMENT``,
``*NSET``/``*ELSET``, ``*MATERIAL`` + ``*ELASTIC`` + ``*DENSITY``, ``*SOLID SECTION``,
``*BOUNDARY``, ``*CLOAD``, ``*STEP``/``*STATIC``, ``*NODE FILE``/``*EL FILE``). Everything else in
a deck written by a pre-processor is ignored by the reader, so an engineer's own deck (PrePoMax,
cgx, FreeCAD FEM) can still be read for its mesh, material, supports and point loads.

Keyword syntax: CalculiX User's Manual (G. Dhondt, www.calculix.de), section 7.

Nodes set ``FIXED`` (x = 0) and ``TIP`` (x = L). Node numbering and element connectivity follow
CalculiX's C3D8/C3D20 conventions (User's Manual §6.2.4, §6.2.10).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.calculix.runner
children.doc:
Run CalculiX (``ccx``): native binary if on PATH, else the bundled Docker image.

The image is built from ``Dockerfile`` next to this module (Debian's official ``calculix-ccx`` package on the official
Debian image, pulled from the AWS mirror of the Docker library to avoid Docker Hub's anonymous rate limit), tag
``pinneapple/calculix:local``: no third-party container is pulled.

The image is multi-platform: the same ``Dockerfile`` builds for :data:`PLATFORMS` (an x86 server or CI runner and an
Apple-silicon laptop), and :func:`build_for` tags each build with the architecture it is for. :func:`image_smoke`
builds one platform and runs a real cantilever through it -- the gate CI runs (``.github/workflows/calculix-image.yml``)
and, while the repository's runners are unavailable, ``scripts/calculix_docker_smoke.py`` runs locally.

functions.name: docker_available
functions.sig: () -> bool

functions.name: host_platform
functions.sig: () -> str
functions.doc: The platform ``docker build`` produces by default on this machine, as a Docker platform string.

functions.name: platform_tag
functions.sig: (platform: str, image: str = IMAGE) -> str
functions.doc:
``pinneapple/calculix:local`` + ``linux/arm64`` -> ``pinneapple/calculix:local-arm64``: one tag per platform, so
the two images can live in the same store instead of overwriting each other.

functions.name: ensure_image
functions.sig: (image: str = IMAGE, attempts: int = 3, platform: str | None = None, rebuild: bool = False) -> str
functions.doc:
Build the image if it is missing, for ``platform`` (the host's by default). The build downloads the base image
and the Debian package, so a failed attempt is retried, each time from the next registry of :data:`BASE_IMAGES`
(registry or mirror hiccups and rate limits); the last failure is raised with Docker's own output.

``rebuild`` builds even when an image of that name exists: a gate that tests whatever image happens to be in the
store is testing an older Dockerfile. Docker's layer cache keeps that cheap when nothing changed.

functions.name: build_for
functions.sig: (platform: str, image: str = IMAGE, attempts: int = 3, rebuild: bool = True) -> str
functions.doc:
Build the image for one platform under its own tag (:func:`platform_tag`) and return that tag. The multi-platform
entry point: on an arm64 machine ``linux/amd64`` is built under emulation (Docker Desktop's qemu or Rosetta), which
is how the x86 image gets tested from a laptop.

functions.name: ccx_backend
functions.sig: () -> str | None
functions.doc: 'native', 'docker' or None.

functions.name: ccx_command
functions.sig: (workdir: str, job: str, *, threads: int = 1, backend: str | None = None, image: str | None = None, platform: str | None = None) -> list[str]
functions.doc:
The command line that runs ``ccx -i <job>`` in ``workdir`` for the backend in use: the ``ccx`` binary, or the
bundled image with the directory mounted at ``/work``.

It exists as its own function because two callers need the same line for different reasons: :func:`run_ccx` waits
for it, and a caller that wants to watch the process itself (the solver contract's ``status()``/``cancel()``)
builds the same argv instead of a second, quietly different one.

functions.name: run_ccx
functions.sig: (workdir: str, job: str, *, threads: int = 1, timeout: float = 3600.0, backend: str | None = None, image: str | None = None, platform: str | None = None) -> CcxRun
functions.doc:
Run ``ccx -i <job>`` in ``workdir`` (which must contain ``<job>.inp``). ``backend='docker'`` runs it in
``image`` (the bundled one by default), for ``platform`` when given: with two architectures of the same name in
the store, the flag is what says which one.

functions.name: image_version
functions.sig: (image: str = IMAGE, platform: str | None = None) -> str
functions.doc: The ``ccx`` version the image reports (``ccx -v``), e.g. ``'2.20'``; '' when it cannot be read.

functions.name: image_arch
functions.sig: (image: str = IMAGE, platform: str | None = None) -> str
functions.doc:
The architecture the image is really built for: the ``Dockerfile`` writes ``dpkg --print-architecture`` into
``/etc/pinneapple-arch`` at build time, so this is a fact about the bytes and not the declaration a build argument
would be (under the plain docker driver BuildKit's ``TARGETPLATFORM`` never arrives).

functions.name: image_smoke
functions.sig: (platform: str, image: str = IMAGE, timeout: float = 1800.0) -> dict
functions.doc:
The gate: build the image for one platform, run a real CalculiX case in it -- a C3D20R cantilever 1 x 0.1 x
0.05 m under a 1 kN tip load, whose deflection Timoshenko's theory fixes to 1 % -- and compare. Returns what it
measured; ``ok`` is the verdict. The workflow and the local script call this same function, so "the image is
tested" means one thing in both places.

children.summary: Run CalculiX (ccx): native binary if on PATH, else the bundled Docker image.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.calculix.study
children.doc:
CalculiX studies in a few lines: a mesh (structured hexahedra, gmsh tetrahedra from CAD-like geometry, or an
engineer's deck), node and face sets picked by geometry, one analysis step, ``ccx``, and the results back as arrays.

    from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.calculix.study import FEModel, Material, Static, Frequency, solve
    m = FEModel.from_box(1.0, 0.1, 0.1, 40, 4, 4, element="C3D8I")          # or FEModel.from_gmsh(geo, size=...)
    m.material = Material("steel", E=210e9, nu=0.3, density=7850.0)
    root, tip = m.nodes_where(lambda X: X[:, 0] < 1e-9), m.faces_where(lambda C: C[:, 0] > 1.0 - 1e-9)
    res = solve(m, Static(fix={root: (1, 2, 3)}, pressure={tip: 1e6}), "work/beam")
    res.u, res.stress, res.von_mises, res.reactions
    res = solve(m, Frequency(6, fix={root: (1, 2, 3)}), "work/modes")
    res.frequencies, res.modes                                                # Hz, one (n, 3) shape per mode

Steps: ``Static`` (point loads, pressure on faces, gravity; nonlinear geometry and plasticity with increments),
``Frequency`` (eigenfrequencies and mode shapes), ``Buckle`` (buckling load factors and shapes), ``Heat``
(steady conduction with fixed temperatures, film convection and surface flux). Keyword syntax: CalculiX User's
Manual (G. Dhondt), section 7. Faces follow its numbering (hexahedra 1-6, tetrahedra 1-4).

methods.sig: (geo: str, size: float, order: int = 2, workdir: str | None = None, optimize: bool = True) -> FEModel
methods.doc:
Tetrahedra (C3D10 for ``order`` 2, C3D4 for 1) of a gmsh .geo script (OpenCASCADE kernel allowed); only
the volume elements are kept. Needs the ``gmsh`` executable.

methods.doc: Indices of the nodes whose coordinates satisfy ``pred(X) -> bool mask``.

methods.name: boundary_faces
methods.doc: (element index, CalculiX face number 1.., corner nodes) of every boundary face.

methods.name: faces_where
methods.doc: Boundary faces whose centroid satisfies ``pred(C) -> bool mask``: (element indices, face numbers).

methods.doc: Corner-node polygons of the boundary, ordered so that their normal points out of the body.
