methods.doc: Corner-node polygons of the boundary (quads or triangles) for drawing.

classes.name: Static
classes.doc:
Linear (or nonlinear) static step. ``fix``: [(nodes, dofs)] or {...}; ``loads``: [(nodes, (Fx, Fy, Fz))] a
total force shared by the nodes; ``pressure``: [((elements, faces), p)] positive into the body; ``gravity``:
(gx, gy, gz) in m/s^2. ``nlgeom`` and ``increments`` (initial, total) for nonlinear geometry or plasticity.
fields: gravity: tuple[float, float, float] | None = None

classes.doc: Eigenfrequencies and mode shapes (needs a density).

classes.name: Buckle
classes.doc: Linear buckling: load factors of the given reference loads, and the buckling shapes.

classes.name: Heat

Steady heat conduction (needs a conductivity). ``temperature``: [(nodes, T)]; ``film``: [((elements, faces),
(T_sink, h))]; ``flux``: [((elements, faces), q)] W/m^2 into the body; ``body``: uniform heat generation
W/m^3 in every element.

methods.doc: Duck type of solid_fem.HexMesh for the post-processor figures (boundary polygons, nodes).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.calculix.virtual_ccx
children.doc:
A drop-in ``ccx``: same command line, same ``.inp`` in, same ``.frd`` out, fields from a model.

Idea (user request, 2026-09-25): CalculiX (implicit) and OpenRadioss (explicit) already hide FEM
from engineers behind a deck -> solver -> results workflow. Putting a PINN/surrogate *where the
solver is* makes it usable from the tools engineers already have (PrePoMax, cgx, FreeCAD FEM,
ccx2paraview) with no new UI. Replacing the Fortran core of ccx is not practical; replacing the
executable at its input/output interface gives the same effect: point the pre-processor's
"CalculiX executable" setting at ``pinneapple-ccx`` (see :func:`main`).

Guard rail: a model only answers inside its validity envelope (bounding box of the geometry it
was trained on, and the load cases it covers, as declared by the model). Outside it, the real
``ccx`` runs (``--fallback``) or the call fails loudly; a silent extrapolation is never written.

A predictor is any callable ``predict(model: CalculixModel, coords: (N,3)) -> {"DISP": (N,3),
optional "STRESS": (N,6)}`` with an optional ``envelope`` attribute:
``{"bbox": [[xmin,ymin,zmin],[xmax,ymax,zmax]], "E": [lo, hi], "load": [lo, hi]}``.

functions.name: check_envelope
functions.sig: (model: CalculixModel, coords: np.ndarray, envelope: dict | None, tol: float = 1e-06) -> None

functions.name: predict_to_frd
functions.sig: (inp_path: str, predictor: Callable, frd_path: str | None = None) -> str
functions.doc: Read ``inp_path``, predict nodal fields, write the matching ``.frd``; returns its path.

functions.name: load_predictor
functions.sig: (spec: str) -> Callable
functions.doc: ``"package.module:attr"`` -> the predictor object (a callable, optionally with ``envelope``).

functions.name: main
functions.sig: (argv = None) -> int
functions.doc:
``pinneapple-ccx -i job [--predictor pkg.mod:obj] [--fallback]`` (mirrors ``ccx -i job``).

The predictor can also come from ``PINNEAPPLE_CCX_PREDICTOR`` so that a pre-processor that only
passes ``-i job`` can still use it.

children.summary: A drop-in ccx: same command line, same .inp in, same .frd out, fields from a model.

children.doc:
CalculiX (implicit structural FEM) bridge: decks, runs, results, and a drop-in virtual ccx.

CalculiX is to implicit problems what OpenRadioss (``..openradioss``) is to explicit ones:
the engineer's deck-based FEM workflow. This package reads and writes ``.inp`` decks, runs
``ccx`` (native or the bundled Debian-based Docker image), reads ``.frd``/``.dat`` results, and
provides ``virtual_ccx``: the same command line and file formats with the fields coming from a
PINN/surrogate, behind a validity-envelope guard that falls back to the real solver.

Validated: a C3D20R cantilever (1 x 0.1 x 0.1 m, steel, 1 kN tip load) gives a tip deflection
within 1 % of Timoshenko beam theory (tests/test_calculix_bridge.py).
children.summary: CalculiX (implicit structural FEM) bridge: decks, runs, results, and a drop-in virtual ccx.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.campaign_cases
children.doc:
Case files for a planned simulation campaign: one directory per case, ready for the solver.

=====================================  ==============================================================================
``write_case_tables``                  ``cases.csv`` / ``.parquet`` / ``.json`` with the parameter space as sidecar
``write_python_runner``                ``run_cases.py``: loops over the cases, calls your ``simulate``, writes results
``write_openfoam_airfoil``             OpenFOAM simpleFoam cases of CST airfoils (``pinneapple_design.aero.case``)
``write_openfoam_from_base``           copies of your base case with dictionary edits per case
                                       (``openfoam.campaign.edit_file``) and the ``plan.json`` of
                                       ``python -m pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.campaign``
``write_calculix_cantilever``          CalculiX decks of a tip-loaded cantilever (``calculix.study.FEModel``)
``write_calculix_from_template``       your ``.inp`` with ``{parameter}`` placeholders filled per case
``write_campaign``                     all of the above that apply, plus the contracts (``space.json``,
                                       ``study.json``, ``dataset.skeleton.json``) and a README
=====================================  ==============================================================================

Presets used by the Campaign Planner app: :func:`airfoil_space` (+ :func:`airfoil_feasible`,
:func:`airfoil_existing`: the 436 OpenFOAM runs of the zoo dataset ``airfoil_rans_cst_re4e6``) and
:func:`cantilever_space`.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.cfd_formats
pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.cfd_formats.abaqus_reader
children.doc:
Abaqus mesh (``.inp``) reader, and an ``.odb`` results bridge.

Two genuinely different problems, handled two different ways
---------------------------------------------------------------
**``.inp`` (input deck: mesh, materials, BCs, step definitions)** is a
plain, stable, publicly-documented text keyword format (Abaqus Keywords
Reference). ``read_abaqus_inp_mesh`` below parses the ``*NODE`` and
``*ELEMENT`` blocks directly -- genuinely implementable and testable
without any Abaqus installation, same as this repository's other
open-format readers.

**``.odb`` (output database: the actual solved result fields)** is a
proprietary binary format with no public specification at all, and
reading it requires Abaqus's own bundled Python and its ``odbAccess``
module -- there is no independent, open way to parse an ``.odb`` file
(unlike CGNS/Exodus, which are open formats this repository can implement
directly; unlike OpenFOAM's binary format, whose byte layout is
documented and was reverse-engineerable). Writing a from-scratch binary
``.odb`` parser here would be guessing at an undocumented, versioned,
proprietary format with zero ability to validate the guess -- exactly the
kind of unverifiable code this repository is trying to avoid, not add.

So ``.odb`` support here is a **bridge**, not a parser: :func:`export_odb_fields`
shells out to a real local Abaqus installation's own Python interpreter
(``abaqus python <script>``, i.e. the standard way any external tool
reads odb data) running a small script (installed alongside this module,
``_odb_export_script.py``) that uses the genuine ``odbAccess`` API to dump
the requested step/frame/field data to a plain ``.npz`` file, which
:func:`load_exported_odb_npz` then reads back with ordinary numpy -- no
proprietary code executes inside this process, only inside Abaqus's own
interpreter, which is the only thing actually licensed and guaranteed to
read its own file format correctly. This requires the caller to have
Abaqus installed and licensed; there is no way around that for ``.odb``,
by design of the format.

functions.name: read_abaqus_inp_mesh
functions.sig: (path: str)
functions.doc:
Parse ``*NODE`` and ``*ELEMENT`` blocks out of an Abaqus ``.inp``
keyword file.

Returns
-------
dict with ``"node_ids"`` (N,), ``"coords"`` (N, 3), and
``"elements"`` (``{element_type: {"ids": (M,), "connectivity": (M, k)}}``,
one entry per ``*ELEMENT, TYPE=...`` block encountered). Multi-line
continuation (a trailing comma with more data on the next line, common
for higher-order elements) is handled.

functions.name: abaqus_inp_to_upd
functions.sig: (path: str)
functions.doc:
Package an ``.inp`` mesh (geometry + connectivity, no result
fields -- ``.inp`` is a pre-processor input deck, not a results file;
see :func:`export_odb_fields` for actual field data) as a UPD
``PhysicalSample``.

functions.name: export_odb_fields
functions.sig: (odb_path: str, out_npz_path: str, *, step_name: str | None = None, frame_index: int = -1, field_outputs: Sequence[str] = ('U', 'S'), abaqus_executable: str = 'abaqus', timeout: int = 1800) -> str
functions.doc:
Export field data from an ``.odb`` to a plain ``.npz`` file by
running Abaqus's own Python (``odbAccess``) as a subprocess.

Requires a local, licensed Abaqus installation with ``abaqus`` (or
``abaqus_executable``) on ``PATH``, or an executable path pointing at
one. This is the only correct way to read ``.odb`` data without
Abaqus's proprietary format specification -- see the module docstring.

Parameters
----------
odb_path : path to the .odb file.
out_npz_path : where to write the exported .npz (node coords under
    ``"coords"``, each requested field under its own name).
step_name : step to read; last step in the odb if None.
frame_index : frame within the step (-1 = last, the converged/final
    result -- the common case for a steady analysis).
field_outputs : Abaqus field-output identifiers to export (e.g.
    ``"U"`` displacement, ``"S"`` stress, ``"NT11"`` temperature).
abaqus_executable : the Abaqus command-line entry point.
timeout : seconds to allow the subprocess before giving up.

Returns
-------
``out_npz_path``, once the export subprocess has completed
successfully.

Raises
------
FileNotFoundError
    If ``abaqus_executable`` is not found on PATH (no local Abaqus
    installation -- there is no fallback, by design; see module
    docstring for why).
RuntimeError
    If the Abaqus subprocess itself fails (bad odb path, licensing
    issue, unknown step/field name, ...); the subprocess's own stderr
    is included in the message.

functions.name: load_exported_odb_npz
functions.sig: (npz_path: str)
functions.doc:
Load a ``.npz`` produced by :func:`export_odb_fields` as a UPD
``PhysicalSample``.

children.summary: Abaqus mesh (.inp) reader, and an .odb results bridge.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.cfd_formats.cgns_reader
children.doc:
CGNS (CFD General Notation System) reader, via the CGNS/HDF5 mapping.

Validation status
------------------
**Validated against a real CGNS file.** A small file was written by a C
program linked directly against the real, official CGNS Mid-Level Library
(``libcgns`` 4.5.2, via ``brew install cgns``) calling its public API
(``cg_open``/``cg_zone_write``/``cg_field_write``/...) -- not any code
from this repository -- and was independently confirmed spec-valid by the
CGNS project's own reference validator (``cgnscheck``, 0 errors) before
this module was pointed at it. It read the file correctly on the first
attempt: node coordinates and two vertex fields matched their known-exact
values exactly, no bug found. See
``tests/fixtures/cfd_formats/README.md`` and
``tests/test_cfd_format_readers.py`` for the fixture, exact commands used
to produce it, and the reproducible test.

This covers a single unstructured zone, ``Vertex``-location
``FlowSolution_t`` fields, and ``TETRA_4`` elements -- **not** covered:
multi-zone bases, ``CellCenter`` solutions, structured zones, or other
element types; treat those as still unverified against this exact reader.
Please open an issue with a reproducer file if one of those (or anything
else) misparses.

Format background
------------------
A CGNS/HDF5 file is a plain HDF5 file where the CGNS node tree is mapped
onto nested HDF5 groups. Every CGNS node is one HDF5 group carrying two
attributes -- ``label`` (the CGNS/SIDS node type, e.g. ``"CGNSBase_t"``,
``"Zone_t"``, ``"GridCoordinates_t"``, ``"FlowSolution_t"``,
``"DataArray_t"``) and ``type`` (the CGNS data-type code, e.g. ``"R8"``
double, ``"I4"`` 32-bit int, ``"C1"`` char) -- and, for a leaf/data node, one
HDF5 dataset named literally ``" data"`` (with the CGNS-mandated leading
space) holding the actual numeric payload.

This reader walks that tree looking for the standard SIDS layout:
``CGNSBase_t -> Zone_t -> GridCoordinates_t -> DataArray_t`` (node
coordinates, conventionally named ``CoordinateX``/``Y``/``Z``) and
``Zone_t -> FlowSolution_t -> DataArray_t`` (solution fields, at whichever
grid location -- Vertex or CellCenter -- the writer used; both are
returned, the caller's ``fields`` argument selects by name regardless of
location).

functions.name: read_cgns_mesh_and_fields
functions.sig: (path: str, *, fields: Sequence[str] | None = None, zone_index: int = 0)
functions.doc:
Read node coordinates and solution fields from a CGNS/HDF5 file.

Parameters
----------
path : path to the .cgns file.
fields : field (DataArray_t) names to extract from every
    FlowSolution_t container found in the zone; all are returned if
    None.
zone_index : which Zone_t under the first CGNSBase_t to read (CGNS
    supports multiple zones/blocks per base; multi-zone assembly is
    not attempted here -- read each zone separately and combine
    yourself if you need the whole domain).

Returns
-------
dict with keys ``"coords"`` (N, 3) and ``"fields"``
(``{name: array}``, each ``(N,)`` or ``(N, k)``, at whatever grid
location -- vertex or cell-center -- the writer used; the two are not
distinguished or interpolated onto a common set here).

functions.name: cgns_to_upd
functions.sig: (path: str, *, fields: Sequence[str] | None = None, zone_index: int = 0)
functions.doc:
Read a CGNS/HDF5 file and package it as a UPD ``PhysicalSample``
(``domain={"type": "mesh"}``, ``geometry.nodes`` = node coordinates --
same contract ``openfoam.field_reader.openfoam_case_to_upd`` produces,
see ``mesh_reader.MeshGeometry``).

children.summary: CGNS (CFD General Notation System) reader, via the CGNS/HDF5 mapping.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.cfd_formats.cgns_writer
children.doc:
CGNS (CFD General Notation System) writer, through the CGNS/HDF5 mapping (#115).

This is the other half of ``cgns_reader.py``: what that module reads, this one writes. A CGNS/HDF5 file is a plain
HDF5 file where every CGNS node is one HDF5 group carrying a ``label`` attribute (the SIDS node type) and a
``type`` attribute (the CGNS data-type code, ``I8``/``R8``/``C1``/``MT``), and, for a leaf, one dataset named
literally ``" data"`` -- leading space included -- holding the payload. The layout written here is the one the
reference implementation produces for a single unstructured zone:

    CGNSLibraryVersion  (R4)
    Base                (CGNSBase_t, I4 [cell dim, phys dim])
      Zone1             (Zone_t, I8 [[n vertices], [n elements], [0]])
        ZoneType        (C1 "Unstructured")
        GridCoordinates (MT)
          CoordinateX/Y/Z  (DataArray_t, R8)
        Elements        (Elements_t, I4 [element type, 0])
          ElementRange  (IndexRange_t, I8 [first, last])
          ElementConnectivity (DataArray_t, I8, 1-based)
        FlowSolution    (MT, + GridLocation when not Vertex)
          <field>       (DataArray_t, R8)

The tree was matched node for node against ``tests/fixtures/cfd_formats/real_cgns_mll.cgns``, which was written by
a C program linked against the official CGNS Mid-Level Library, and the files this writer produces pass the CGNS
project's own ``cgnscheck`` validator (see ``tests/test_cgns_writer.py``).

Covered: one unstructured zone, ``TETRA_4``/``HEXA_8``/``PENTA_6``/``PYRA_5``/``TRI_3``/``QUAD_4``/``BAR_2``/
``NODE`` elements, and vertex or cell-centre flow solutions. **Not** covered, and not pretended: multiple zones per
base, structured (``SIDS``) zones, boundary conditions, and the ADF (non-HDF5) backend -- CGNS 3.x files. A file
written here is CGNS 3.4+/HDF5, which is what ParaView, SU2 and the CGNS tools read.

functions.name: write_cgns
functions.sig: (path: str | Path, points: Any, cells: Any, fields: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, *, cell_type: str = 'TETRA_4', base_name: str = 'Base', zone_name: str = 'Zone1', location: str = 'Vertex') -> Path
functions.doc:
Write one unstructured zone to a CGNS/HDF5 file, 1-based connectivity included.

Parameters
----------
points : (n, 3) node coordinates, written as ``R8`` so they round-trip without loss.
cells : (m, k) connectivity, **0-based** like every other array in this library; the 1-based numbering CGNS
    requires is applied here, in one place.
fields : ``{name: values}`` at the nodes (``location="Vertex"``, the default) or the cells
    (``location="CellCenter"``); ``(n,)`` for a scalar, ``(n, k)`` for a vector, flattened as CGNS stores it.
cell_type : one of :data:`ELEMENT_CODES`; the whole zone is one element block, which is what the reader reads.

Raises ``ValueError`` for what would otherwise become a file a solver rejects: an unknown element type, a
connectivity matrix whose column count does not match it, node indices outside the point array, non-finite
coordinates, and a field with the wrong length for the location it claims.

functions.name: mesh_to_cgns
functions.sig: (path: str | Path, mesh: Any, *, cells: Iterable[int] | None = None, **kwargs) -> Path
functions.doc:
Write a ``pinneapple_data.cae.Mesh`` (its points, one cell block and its point fields) as one CGNS zone.

``cells`` selects which block of the mesh to write -- the first by default. A mesh with a polyhedral
(OpenFOAM) representation has no single element type and is refused with that sentence rather than silently
written as something else.

children.summary: CGNS (CFD General Notation System) writer, through the CGNS/HDF5 mapping (#115).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.cfd_formats.convert
children.doc:
Format dispatch for CFD / FEM / CAD files: a portable point bundle from any supported file, a triangle surface
from the formats that carry connectivity, and repair / simplification on the way out.

* :func:`detect_format` -- file suffix to format name (``.cgns``, ``.exo``/``.e``, ``.inp``, ``.msh`` (Fluent),
  ``.step``/``.stp``, ``.stl``, ``.obj``, ``.ply``).
* :func:`read_point_bundle` -- node coordinates + every field array + the reader's provenance string, for the
  volume formats (CGNS, Exodus II, Abaqus ``.inp``, Fluent ASCII mesh), through the readers of this package. The
  CGNS, Exodus and Fluent readers were written to the published specs and not yet checked against a file from
  the real writers (see the package docstring); their element connectivity is not returned, so these files give
  points, not surfaces.
* :func:`read_surface_mesh` -- a ``MeshData`` triangle surface for STL / OBJ / PLY (trimesh), STEP (CadQuery
  tessellation, optional ``cadquery``) and Abaqus ``.inp``: triangle shell elements (S3, STRI3, M3D3, ...) as they
  are, tetrahedra (C3D4, C3D10: corner nodes) reduced to their boundary faces (faces used by one tet only).
  Node ids are mapped to row indices.
* :func:`convert_surface` -- read, optionally repair (``pinneapple_design.geometry.ops.repair.repair_mesh``:
  duplicate and degenerate faces, normals) and simplify (``simplify_mesh``), and write STL / OBJ / PLY.

Moved here from the PINNeAPPle-apps ``cfd_format_converter`` product (MeshBridge), with two fixes: Abaqus
connectivity used the node ids as row indices, and a tetrahedral mesh was turned into one face per tet instead of
its boundary.

functions.name: detect_format
functions.sig: (filename: str) -> str
functions.doc: Format name for ``filename``'s suffix; ``ValueError`` listing the supported ones otherwise.

functions.name: read_point_bundle
functions.sig: (path: str, fmt: str | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: ``{"coords": (N, d), "fields": {name: array}, "provenance": str, "format": fmt}`` for a volume format.

functions.name: tet_boundary_faces
functions.sig: (tets: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Triangles used by exactly one tetrahedron (the boundary of a conforming tet mesh), outward ordering not
guaranteed (repair fixes the winding).

functions.name: read_surface_mesh
functions.sig: (path: str, fmt: str | None = None)
functions.doc: A ``MeshData`` triangle surface for STL / OBJ / PLY / STEP / Abaqus ``.inp``.

functions.name: convert_surface
functions.sig: (path: str, out_path: str, *, fmt: str | None = None, repair: bool = False, simplify_target_faces: int | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Read a surface, optionally repair and simplify it, write ``out_path`` (suffix .stl / .obj / .ply).

children.summary: Format dispatch for CFD / FEM / CAD files: a portable point bundle from any supported file, a triangle surface from the formats that carry connectivity, and repair / simplification on the way out.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.cfd_formats.exodus_reader
children.doc:
Exodus II (``.exo``/``.e``) reader, via the classic-NetCDF layer.

Validation status
------------------
**Validated against a real classic-NetCDF Exodus file.** Written by
``meshio`` 5.3.5's real Exodus writer (itself using the real ``netCDF4``
package to do the actual encoding), forced to classic NetCDF-3 -- read
correctly, node coordinates and two vertex fields matched their
known-exact values exactly. See ``tests/fixtures/cfd_formats/README.md``
and ``tests/test_cfd_format_readers.py`` for the fixture and test.

This process also surfaced a real bug: pointing this reader at the
*other* real, valid Exodus file the same writer produces by default
(NetCDF-4/HDF5-based, no format override -- also genuine Exodus, many
modern solvers default to it for large meshes) raised a confusing raw
``scipy`` ``TypeError`` instead of a clear, actionable error. Fixed --
this now raises ``NotImplementedError`` naming the actual problem (HDF5
container, not classic NetCDF) and the ``netCDF4``/``h5netcdf`` fallback,
still true to the "raise on that failure rather than silently returning
nothing" contract below, just with a message that says why. Element
connectivity is still not read (see "Variables read" below); that part
remains unverified.

Format background
------------------
Exodus II (Sandia National Laboratories) is a schema layered on top of
classic NetCDF -- an ``.exo``/``.e`` file is a NetCDF file with a fixed set
of conventionally-named dimensions and variables. This reader uses
``scipy.io.netcdf_file`` (already a PINNeAPPle dependency via ``scipy``),
which reads the *classic* NetCDF format without any extra dependency; a
64-bit-offset or NetCDF-4/HDF5-based Exodus file (large meshes) needs
``netCDF4`` or ``h5netcdf`` instead and is out of scope here (raise on
that failure rather than silently returning nothing).

Variables read (Exodus II data model): ``coord`` (or ``coordx``/``coordy``/
``coordz`` when split), ``vals_nod_var<k>`` (nodal field ``k``, one array
per time step) and ``name_nod_var`` (their names, as a fixed-width char
array), and ``time_whole`` (the time values). Element-block connectivity
(``connect<k>``) is not read by this module -- only the node cloud and
nodal fields, which is what a PINN training pipeline needs; a caller
wanting cell/element structure can extend this reader with the
``connect<k>``/``eb_prop1`` variables the same way.

functions.name: read_exodus
functions.sig: (path: str, *, fields: Sequence[str] | None = None, time_index: int = -1)
functions.doc:
Read node coordinates and nodal fields from a classic-NetCDF Exodus
II file.

Parameters
----------
path : path to the .exo/.e file.
fields : nodal variable names to extract (from Exodus's own
    ``name_nod_var`` list); all are returned if None.
time_index : which time step's nodal-variable values to read (Exodus
    stores one array per (variable, time step) pair); -1 = last.

Returns
-------
dict with keys ``"coords"`` (N, 3), ``"fields"`` (``{name: (N,)}``),
and ``"time"`` (the time value read, or None if the file has no
``time_whole`` variable).

functions.name: exodus_to_upd
functions.sig: (path: str, *, fields: Sequence[str] | None = None, time_index: int = -1)
functions.doc:
Read an Exodus II file and package it as a UPD ``PhysicalSample``
(same ``domain={"type": "mesh"}`` / ``geometry.nodes`` contract as
``openfoam.field_reader.openfoam_case_to_upd``).

children.summary: Exodus II (.exo/.e) reader, via the classic-NetCDF layer.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.cfd_formats.fluent_mesh_reader
children.doc:
ANSYS Fluent / Gambit neutral mesh (``.msh``) reader -- node coordinates
only.

Validation status
------------------
**Validated against a real ASCII Fluent/TGrid ``.msh`` file.** Written by
``meshio`` 5.3.5's ``ansys`` writer (``binary=False``) -- meshio's own
module docstring for that writer cites the same TGrid user-guide appendix
this reader implements section 10 (node coordinates) from. Read
correctly: node coordinates matched their known-exact values exactly, no
bug found. See ``tests/fixtures/cfd_formats/README.md`` and
``tests/test_cfd_format_readers.py`` for the fixture and test. This only
exercises section 10 -- cells/faces/zones/BCs remain unimplemented (see
"Scope, deliberately narrow" below) and the binary encoding remains
untested (this reader raises `NotImplementedError` on it by design, not
tested against a real binary file).

Scope, deliberately narrow
---------------------------
A full Fluent case (``.cas``/``.dat``) is a much larger, partly
undocumented format: dozens of section types (nodes, faces, cells, zones,
periodic-shadow face pairs, boundary condition records, solver settings,
...), an optional binary encoding per section, and no publicly published
authoritative specification (what's known comes from reverse-engineering
by third-party tools, e.g. meshio's Fluent reader, and Gambit/Fluent's own
older public neutral-format docs). Writing a *complete, correct* reader
for that is a multi-week reverse-engineering effort in its own right (the
same scale of work this repository's OpenFOAM binary reader took, and that
one had a real 244 MB reference case to validate every byte-layout
decision against end-to-end -- this format has no equivalent reference
file available here).

What is implemented, and kept deliberately small so it can actually be
trusted: **ASCII-encoded node coordinates only** (section index ``10``,
Fluent/Gambit's mesh-node section) -- the single most immediately useful
piece for a PINN training pipeline that just needs a spatial point cloud,
and the one section whose ASCII grammar is simple enough to parse
correctly without a reference file to check against. Cells (section
``12``), faces (section ``13``), zones and BC records, and any binary-
encoded section, are NOT parsed -- reading one of those raises
``NotImplementedError`` rather than silently returning nothing, so a
caller finds out immediately rather than getting a mesh that looks
plausible but is missing all its topology.

Format background (section 10 only)
------------------------------------
A Fluent/Gambit ``.msh`` file is ASCII text, structured as parenthesised
sections ``(<section-id> ...)``. A node section looks like::

    (10 (zone-id first-index last-index type nd)
    (
    x1 y1 z1
    x2 y2 z2
    ...
    ))

with ``zone-id 0`` used for a "declaration" header section (no coordinate
data follows) and any other ``zone-id`` introducing an actual coordinate
block. ``nd`` (present in 3D files) is the number of spatial dimensions.

functions.name: read_fluent_mesh_nodes
functions.sig: (path: str)
functions.doc:
Read the node coordinates out of a Fluent/Gambit ASCII ``.msh``
file's section-10 blocks.

Returns
-------
(N, 3) numpy array of node coordinates (z filled with 0 for a 2D mesh).

Raises
------
NotImplementedError
    If the file appears to be binary-encoded (Fluent's binary section
    marker) -- not supported by this reader.
ValueError
    If no section-10 coordinate block is found at all.

functions.name: fluent_mesh_to_upd
functions.sig: (path: str)
functions.doc:
Read a Fluent/Gambit ASCII ``.msh`` file's node coordinates and
package them as a UPD ``PhysicalSample`` with an empty field set (this
reader extracts geometry only -- see the module docstring) --
``domain={"type": "mesh"}`` / ``geometry.nodes``, same contract as
``openfoam.field_reader.openfoam_case_to_upd``.

children.summary: ANSYS Fluent / Gambit neutral mesh (.msh) reader -- node coordinates only.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.cfd_formats.starccm_reader
children.doc:
Siemens Simcenter STAR-CCM+ readers: CGNS export (delegated to the real
``cgns_reader``) and plain-text table/CSV export (implemented here). The
proprietary native ``.sim``/``.ccm`` binary format is explicitly NOT
supported -- see "What is NOT supported" below.

What IS supported, and why it's legitimate
--------------------------------------------
STAR-CCM+ does not require reading its native project file to get mesh and
field data out of it -- it has two real, documented export paths that leave
its own proprietary binary format entirely:

1. **CGNS export.** STAR-CCM+ can export a region's mesh and solution
   fields to CGNS (CFD General Notation System) via its own
   ``Export > CGNS...`` action -- an open, standardised interchange format
   (the same one ``cgns_reader.py`` already reads, validated against a real
   CGNS Mid-Level Library file; see that module's docstring). A STAR-CCM+
   CGNS export is ordinary CGNS/HDF5 laid out per the standard SIDS schema
   (``CGNSBase_t -> Zone_t -> GridCoordinates_t`` / ``FlowSolution_t``) --
   nothing STAR-CCM+-specific about the bytes on disk. So :func:`starccm_cgns_to_upd`
   below is a thin, honest re-export of :func:`cgns_reader.cgns_to_upd`
   under a name that documents *why* it applies to STAR-CCM+ output,
   **not** a reimplementation -- reusing already-validated logic rather
   than duplicating (and risking drifting from) it.

2. **Plain-text table/CSV export.** STAR-CCM+'s ``Plot > Export`` /
   ``Table > Export`` action writes scalar/vector field data (e.g. probe
   points, an XY plot's underlying data, a derived-part table) as a plain
   delimited text file: one header row of quoted column names -- often
   carrying a unit suffix, e.g. ``"X (m)"``, ``"Temperature (K)"`` -- then
   one data row per point/sample, comma- or tab-delimited. This is a real,
   commonly-used, simple, and fully documented export path (STAR-CCM+ User
   Guide, "Exporting Plot and Table Data"), genuinely different from the
   proprietary ``.sim``/``.ccm`` binary and *not* just guessed at here --
   :func:`read_starccm_table` below is a real, working parser for it, not a
   stub.

What is NOT supported, and why
--------------------------------
STAR-CCM+'s native project files (``.sim``, and the older ``.ccm``) are a
**proprietary, undocumented binary format** with no public specification
and no independently-implementable open encoding (unlike CGNS/Exodus/Fluent
ASCII, which this package's sibling modules implement directly from
published specs). Siemens does not publish the ``.sim``/``.ccm`` byte
layout, and the only reliable way to read one is Siemens' own Simcenter
STAR-CCM+ installation (interactively, or via its bundled Java macro API,
analogous to how ``abaqus_reader.py``'s ``.odb`` bridge shells out to a
real, licensed Abaqus installation rather than guessing at that format).
This module deliberately does **not** attempt to reverse-engineer or guess
at ``.sim``/``.ccm`` -- doing so would produce a reader that looks like it
works but silently misparses on the first file that doesn't match the
guess, which is worse than refusing outright. There is no
``starccm_sim_to_upd`` (or similar) function here, and none should be added
without a real, licensed STAR-CCM+ installation to validate against (the
same bar ``export_odb_fields`` was held to for Abaqus).

If you have a real ``.sim``/``.ccm`` file: export it to CGNS or a table/CSV
from within STAR-CCM+ first (both are standard menu actions), then use one
of the two functions in this module.

functions.name: read_starccm_cgns
functions.sig: (path: str, *, fields: Sequence[str] | None = None, zone_index: int = 0)
functions.doc:
Read a STAR-CCM+ CGNS export. Thin re-export of
:func:`cgns_reader.read_cgns_mesh_and_fields` -- a STAR-CCM+ CGNS export
is standard CGNS/HDF5, so the existing, already-validated reader applies
unchanged; see the module docstring for why this is legitimate reuse
rather than a separate implementation.

functions.name: starccm_cgns_to_upd
functions.sig: (path: str, *, fields: Sequence[str] | None = None, zone_index: int = 0)
functions.doc:
Read a STAR-CCM+ CGNS export and package it as a UPD
``PhysicalSample``. Thin re-export of :func:`cgns_reader.cgns_to_upd` --
STAR-CCM+'s CGNS export is standard CGNS/HDF5 (see module docstring), so
this calls straight through to the same, already-validated CGNS parser
rather than duplicating it under a new name.

functions.name: read_starccm_table
functions.sig: (path: str, *, coord_names: Sequence[str] = ('X', 'Y', 'Z'))
functions.doc:
Parse a STAR-CCM+ plain-text table/CSV export (``Plot > Export`` /
``Table > Export``): one header row of (optionally quoted, optionally
unit-suffixed) column names, then one data row per point.

Parameters
----------
path : path to the exported ``.csv``/``.txt`` table file.
coord_names : column-name prefixes (case-insensitive, unit suffix like
    ``" (m)"`` ignored) treated as spatial coordinates, in order. Any
    column not matched here is returned as a field. Missing trailing
    coordinates (e.g. a 2D export with only X/Y) are zero-padded to 3D.

Returns
-------
dict with ``"coords"`` (N, 3), ``"fields"`` (``{name: (N,)}`` for every
non-coordinate column), and ``"column_names"`` (the original header row,
unit suffixes included, for reference/round-tripping).

Raises
------
FileNotFoundError
    If ``path`` does not exist.
ValueError
    If the file has no header row, no data rows, or no column matches
    any of ``coord_names`` at all.

functions.name: starccm_table_to_upd
functions.sig: (path: str, *, coord_names: Sequence[str] = ('X', 'Y', 'Z'))
functions.doc:
Read a STAR-CCM+ plain-text table/CSV export and package it as a UPD
``PhysicalSample`` (``domain={"type": "mesh"}``, ``geometry.nodes`` =
point coordinates -- same contract as
``openfoam.field_reader.openfoam_case_to_upd``; no cell/face topology
since a table export is a scattered point/sample set, not a mesh).

children.summary: Siemens Simcenter STAR-CCM+ readers: CGNS export (delegated to the real cgns_reader) and plain-text table/CSV export (implemented here).

children.doc:
Open-format CFD/FEM readers beyond OpenFOAM: CGNS, Exodus II, Fluent
mesh (ASCII, geometry-only), an Abaqus .inp/.odb bridge, and STAR-CCM+
(CGNS export delegation + table/CSV export).

Validation status differs sharply by module -- read each one's own
docstring before trusting its output for anything important:

- ``openfoam`` (sibling package, not here): validated byte-for-byte
  against a real 244 MB LES case.
- ``cgns_reader``, ``exodus_reader``, ``fluent_mesh_reader``: implement
  their documented open-format specs precisely, but were NOT checked
  against a real file from a real writer (none was available) -- treat as
  unverified until exercised against one.
- ``abaqus_reader``'s ``.inp`` mesh parser: an open text format, parsed
  directly, same confidence level as the OpenFOAM/CGNS/Exodus readers.
- ``abaqus_reader``'s ``.odb`` bridge: correctness depends entirely on a
  local, licensed Abaqus installation's own ``odbAccess`` API -- this
  repository does not and cannot implement the (undocumented, proprietary)
  ``.odb`` binary format itself.
- ``starccm_reader``'s CGNS path: delegates entirely to ``cgns_reader``
  (no separate implementation to validate). Its table/CSV parser is a
  real, implemented parser tested against a hand-constructed synthetic
  fixture (no real STAR-CCM+ file was available); its ``.sim``/``.ccm``
  native binary format is explicitly NOT supported -- see the module
  docstring for why.
children.summary: Open-format CFD/FEM readers beyond OpenFOAM: CGNS, Exodus II, Fluent mesh (ASCII, geometry-only), an Abaqus .inp/.odb bridge, and STAR-CCM+ (CGNS export delegation + table/CSV export).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.contract
children.doc:
One interface every external solver is reached through.

The problem: OpenFOAM, CalculiX, Fluent, FEniCSx and MATLAB each arrived with their own case layout, their own health
check, their own log parsing and their own idea of what "finished" means, so wiring a fourth solver meant reading the
third one's code. The gap was never coverage, it was the contract (PINNeAPPle#1476).

Every backend answers the same six questions::

    check_environment()  what is missing here -- executable, version, licence, environment, Python module; never raises
    prepare(case)        materialise the input from a neutral :class:`SolverCase`; returns the run directory
    run()                start it, return a :class:`RunHandle`
    status()             queued / running / converged / diverged / failed / cancelled, with the evidence
    results()            fields and scalars in one schema, provenance naming the backend and its version
    cancel()             idempotent

:func:`classify_run` is *the* one definition of "finished": a divergence marker in the log outranks the exit code (a
diverged run usually exits non-zero and would otherwise read as a plain failure), then the exit code, then the
artefact the solver was supposed to write, then the solver's own end marker. A backend that diverges therefore never
looks like a backend that crashed.

The contract is a layer over the implementations, not a rewrite: :mod:`.backends` maps each existing bridge onto it,
and ``pinneapple_core.workflows.adapters`` asks it for the environment verdict, so the workflow surface and this one
cannot disagree about whether a solver is installed::

    from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers import SolverCase, check_all, get_solver

    for name, report in check_all().items():
        print(report.explain())                    # every solver: what it needs, what this machine lacks, the fix

    solver = get_solver("calculix", workdir="run")
    solver.check_environment().raise_if_missing()  # a readable diagnosis instead of a crash mid-run
    solver.prepare(SolverCase.cantilever(P=1000.0))
    solver.run()
    solver.status()                                # -> converged / diverged / failed, with the log lines
    sample = solver.results().to_upd()             # the neutral scientific schema (UPD), provenance included

A new backend subclasses :class:`ExternalSolver`, supplies ``_requirements``, ``prepare``, ``_start``, ``_results`` and
declares its log markers, then registers itself with :func:`register_solver`.

What is *not* here, deliberately: **COMSOL**. This interface does not pretend to cover it. There is no COMSOL
implementation in this repository and there cannot be an honest one here -- its Python coupling (``mph``/LiveLink)
needs the commercial client installed and licensed, and its model files are binary and proprietary, so nothing about it
could be exercised or verified by this repository's tests. A backend nobody can run is worse than no backend: it moves
the failure from :meth:`ExternalSolver.check_environment` to the middle of a run, which is the problem this contract
exists to fix. COMSOL is therefore out of scope until a licensed client can be exercised (see
``docs/guides/external_solver_contract.md``), and adding it later is one class plus :func:`register_solver` --
``get_solver("comsol")`` says so today with a ``KeyError`` that names the backends which do exist.

classes.name: SolverCase
classes.doc:
A case in neutral terms: the physics, the geometry, the material, the mesh, the boundary conditions and the
loads -- nothing about a backend's file layout. ``prepare`` turns it into whatever the backend runs.

``parameters`` carries what only some backends read (solver name, commands, edits, end time); ``source`` points at
an existing case directory or deck when the neutral description is a pointer (physics :data:`OPAQUE`).

methods.name: cantilever
methods.sig: (*, L: float = 1.0, b: float = 0.1, h: float = 0.1, E: float = 210000000000.0, nu: float = 0.3, P: float = 1000.0, nx: int = 20, ny: int = 2, nz: int = 2) -> SolverCase
methods.doc:
A box cantilever clamped at ``x = 0`` and pulled down (``-z``) on the ``x = L`` face: the case a structural
FEM backend and CalculiX both take, so the two results are numbers of the same physical quantity.

methods.name: plane_cantilever
methods.sig: (*, L: float = 1.0, h: float = 0.1, b: float = 0.1, E: float = 210000000000.0, nu: float = 0.3, q: float = 100.0, nx: int = 40, ny: int = 8) -> SolverCase
methods.doc:
The same cantilever as a 2-D plane-stress rectangle ``L x h`` of thickness ``b`` under a uniform downward
load ``q`` (N/m along the beam, so the tip deflection is ``q L^4 / (8 E I)`` with ``I = b h^3 / 12``).

methods.name: conduction
methods.sig: (*, L: float = 1.0, H: float = 1.0, k: float = 1.0, source: float = 0.0, T_left: float = 0.0, T_right: float = 1.0, nx: int = 16, ny: int = 16) -> SolverCase
methods.doc:
Steady conduction through a rectangle: ``-div(k grad T) = source`` with the vertical sides held at
``T_left`` and ``T_right``.

methods.name: case_directory
methods.sig: (path: str | Path, *, physics: str = OPAQUE, **parameters) -> SolverCase
methods.doc: A case that already exists on disk (a case directory, a deck, a script): the backend stages it its own way.

classes.name: Requirement
classes.doc:
One thing a solver needs before it can run, and what this machine found.

``ok`` is the answer; ``detail`` is the evidence (the path found, or what is missing and why); ``fix`` is what the
reader does about it. ``verified=False`` marks a check that cannot be made without starting the solver (a licence
the launcher alone can validate): it never counts as missing, and ``explain`` prints it with a ``?`` so nobody
reads it as a pass.

classes.name: EnvironmentReport
classes.doc: What :meth:`ExternalSolver.check_environment` returns: never an exception, always an answer with its evidence.

methods.name: version
methods.doc:
The version the probe actually read -- a placeholder ("not read ...") is unverified and gives None, so it
never ends up in provenance as if it were a version.

methods.name: why
methods.doc: One line naming every missing item with its fix; empty when nothing is missing.

methods.name: explain
methods.doc: The whole verdict, one requirement per line -- the diagnosis a caller shows instead of a traceback.

methods.name: raise_if_missing
methods.doc: Raise :class:`SolverUnavailable` with :meth:`explain` as the message; return ``self`` when ready.

classes.name: SolverState
classes.doc:
The terminal states are :attr:`CONVERGED`, :attr:`DIVERGED`, :attr:`FAILED` and :attr:`CANCELLED`; the other two
are what a live run is.

classes.name: SolverStatus
classes.doc:
Where a run stands, with the evidence that says so: ``evidence`` holds the log lines (a divergence marker, the
solver's end marker, the fatal error) and ``reason`` the one sentence a person needs.

classes.name: SolverResults
classes.doc:
Fields and scalars of one converged run, in one schema whoever produced them.

``fields`` maps a name to an array whose first axis is the points of the domain; ``scalars`` holds the numbers a
person reads off (tip displacement, last time, cell count); ``provenance`` names the backend and its version, which
is what makes two backends' answers comparable rather than merely similar. :meth:`to_upd` hands it to the rest of
the library as a ``PhysicalSample``.

methods.name: to_upd
methods.doc: The neutral scientific schema of the library (``pinneapple_data.physical_sample.PhysicalSample``).

methods.name: summary
methods.doc: A JSON-able digest for a step's outputs: the scalars, the field names and shapes, the provenance.

classes.name: RunHandle
classes.doc:
What :meth:`ExternalSolver.run` returns: the run's identity, its directory, its log and (when it is a process)
the process itself, so ``status``/``cancel`` do not need the solver to be asked twice about the same run.

methods.name: new
methods.sig: (backend: str, workdir: str | Path, *, argv: Sequence[str] = (), log_path: str | Path | None = None, process: Any | None = None, status: SolverStatus | None = None) -> RunHandle

methods.name: poll
methods.doc: The exit code, or None while the process runs (a finished in-process run keeps its recorded status).

methods.name: wait
methods.doc: Block until the process ends (or ``timeout``); returns the exit code, or None if it is still running.

methods.name: cancel
methods.doc: Stop the process if it is still running; True when this call is what stopped it.

classes.name: SolverError
classes.sig: (diagnosis: str)
classes.doc: Base of everything this module raises deliberately; ``diagnosis`` is the readable text for the caller.

classes.name: SolverUnavailable
classes.sig: (solver: str, report: EnvironmentReport)
classes.doc: The environment cannot run the solver: carries the :class:`EnvironmentReport` that says what is missing.

classes.name: CaseUnsupported
classes.doc: The backend cannot express this neutral case (a physics, a dimension or a geometry it does not implement).

classes.name: RunUnusable
classes.sig: (status: SolverStatus)
classes.doc: ``results()`` was asked for a run that did not converge; carries the :class:`SolverStatus` that says why.

classes.name: ExternalSolver
classes.sig: (workdir: str | Path | None = None, *, log_name: str = 'solver.log')
classes.doc:
One external solver behind one contract. Subclasses fill in the fives hooks and set :attr:`name`.

``check_environment``, ``status`` and ``cancel`` are implemented here once, so every backend answers the same way;
a backend only decides *what it needs* (``_requirements``), *how the case becomes input* (``prepare``), *how it
starts* (``_start``), *what it reads back* (``_results``), and *which log lines mean converged or diverged*.

methods.name: key
methods.doc: The registry key: :attr:`kind` when set, else :attr:`name`.

methods.name: check_environment
methods.doc: What this machine lacks for the solver to run (executable, version, licence, environment, module).

methods.name: version
methods.doc: The version the environment probe found, for provenance. This asks the machine (once).

methods.name: prepare
methods.doc: Materialise ``case`` in :attr:`workdir` the way this backend runs it; returns the run directory.

methods.name: run
methods.doc: Start the prepared case; returns the handle ``status``/``cancel``/``results`` speak about.

methods.name: status
methods.doc:
Where the run stands. ``queued`` before ``run()``, ``running`` while the process lives, then the verdict of
:func:`classify_run` -- cached on the handle, so asking twice gives the same answer.

methods.name: wait
methods.doc: Block until the run ends (or ``timeout``) and return its status.

methods.name: results
methods.doc: Fields and scalars of the run, in the one schema; raises :class:`RunUnusable` unless it converged.

methods.name: cancel
methods.doc: Stop the run; idempotent -- a second call (or a call after the run ended) reports the same state.

functions.name: conduction_profile
functions.sig: (case: SolverCase, x: Any) -> Any
functions.doc:
The closed-form temperature of a :meth:`SolverCase.conduction` case at ``x``.

``T(x) = T0 + (T1 - T0) x / L + source x (L - x) / (2 k)``: the solution of ``-k T'' = source`` with ``T(0) = T0``
and ``T(L) = T1``, which is what a backend's field is measured against. Raises :class:`CaseUnsupported` when the
case is not a conduction case, so a call that cannot have a closed form says so instead of returning numbers.

functions.name: classify_run
functions.sig: (*, backend: str, log: str, returncode: int | None, converged: Sequence[str] = (), divergence: Sequence[str] = (), artefacts: Mapping[str, bool] | None = None, elapsed_s: float | None = None, progress: dict[str, Any] | None = None, version: str | None = None) -> SolverStatus

functions.name: register_solver
functions.sig: (factory: Callable[..., ExternalSolver], *, key: str | None = None, replace: bool = False) -> Callable[..., ExternalSolver]
functions.doc: Make ``factory(**options)`` reachable as :func:`get_solver` under ``key`` (its class's ``kind`` by default).

functions.name: solver_names
functions.sig: () -> list[str]
functions.doc: Every registered backend, by key.

functions.name: get_solver
functions.sig: (name: str, **options) -> ExternalSolver
functions.doc:
An instance of the backend ``name`` (``openfoam``, ``calculix``, ``fenicsx``, ``ansys-fluent``, ``matlab``,
``solid-fem``); it does not check the environment -- :meth:`ExternalSolver.check_environment` is that question, and
it answers instead of raising.

functions.name: check_all
functions.sig: (**options) -> dict[str, EnvironmentReport]
functions.doc: ``check_environment()`` for every registered backend: what this machine can run, and what it cannot.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.fenics
pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.fenics.solver
children.doc:
FEniCS integration — workflow layer on top of ``numerical_solvers.fenics_bridge``.

The low-level bridge (``numerical_solvers.fenics_bridge.FEnicsBridge``) does the FEM assembly and solve. This module
adds:

  FEniCSConfig     — structured configuration dataclass
  solve_and_package — one-call solve + UPD packaging
  dof_to_upd       — convert raw DOF vector + mesh coords to PhysicalSample
  FEniCSWorkflow   — convenience wrapper for repeated solves (e.g. parametric sweeps)

The bridge takes a *problem spec* (``kind``, ``domain_bounds``, ``conditions``, ``parameters``); :class:`FEniCSConfig`
says the same thing in this module's vocabulary, so :func:`solve_and_package` translates one into the other. That
translation is the whole of the wrapper's work: a wrapper that names a class or a keyword that does not exist fails on
the first call, and nobody notices while the import stays lazy.

For the one-interface-every-solver route use the solver contract instead
(``pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.get_solver("fenicsx")``), which wraps the same bridge with
``check_environment()``, a status with the log evidence and results in the same schema as the other backends.

classes.name: FEniCSConfig
classes.doc:
Configuration for a FEniCS solve.

Parameters
----------
pde : PDE identifier understood by FEniCSBridge
    e.g. "heat_equation_steady", "linear_elasticity_plane_stress"
domain : domain specification dict accepted by FEniCSBridge
    e.g. {"type": "rectangle", "x": [0, 1], "y": [0, 1], "nx": 32, "ny": 32}
bcs : list of boundary condition specs accepted by FEniCSBridge
params : PDE parameter values (conductivity k, Young's modulus E, etc.)
solver_opts : additional solver options forwarded to FEniCSBridge

classes.name: FEniCSUnavailable
classes.doc: FEniCS (DOLFINx or legacy FEniCS) is not importable, so there is nothing to solve with.

classes.name: FEniCSWorkflow
classes.sig: (base_config: FEniCSConfig) -> None
classes.doc:
Convenience wrapper for repeated FEniCS solves over a parameter space.

Useful for generating training datasets for surrogate models or PINNs.

Examples
--------
>>> base_cfg = FEniCSConfig(pde="heat_equation_steady", domain=..., bcs=...)
>>> wf = FEniCSWorkflow(base_cfg)
>>> samples = wf.sweep({"k": [0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0]})

methods.name: solve
methods.doc: Run a single solve with optional parameter override.

methods.name: sweep
methods.doc: Solve for each combination in a parameter grid.

functions.name: problem_spec
functions.sig: (config: FEniCSConfig) -> Any
functions.doc:
The bridge's problem spec (``kind``, ``domain_bounds``, ``conditions``, ``parameters``) for a config.

``domain`` is the rectangle ``{"x": [x0, x1], "y": [y0, y1], "nx": n, "ny": n}`` the bridge's mesher builds;
``bcs`` become boundary objects with ``type``, ``side`` and ``value``; ``params`` is passed through as the PDE
parameters (``k`` and ``f`` for the heat equation, ``E``/``nu``/``f`` for elasticity).

functions.name: solve_and_package
functions.sig: (config: FEniCSConfig)
functions.doc:
Run a FEniCS solve and return a UPD PhysicalSample.

Returns
-------
PhysicalSample with ``state`` = the field vectors, ``domain`` = the coordinates of their degrees of freedom (so a
value and its point stay together), ``provenance`` = the backend, its version and the PDE.

Raises ``FEniCSUnavailable`` when neither DOLFINx nor legacy FEniCS is installed -- the fix is in the message.

functions.name: dof_to_upd
functions.sig: (dof_vector: np.ndarray, mesh_coords: np.ndarray, field_name: str = 'u')
functions.doc:
Package a raw FEniCS DOF vector and mesh coordinates as a UPD PhysicalSample.

Parameters
----------
dof_vector : (N,) or (N, F) array of DOF values
mesh_coords : (N, d) array of node coordinates
field_name : name for the field in the PhysicalSample

Returns
-------
PhysicalSample

children.summary: FEniCS integration — workflow layer on top of numerical_solvers.fenics_bridge.

children.doc:
FEniCS integration for PINNeAPPle.

This subpackage wraps pinneapple_solvers.fenics_bridge (low-level FEM) and adds
a workflow layer with structured configuration and UPD packaging.

Quick start
-----------
>>> from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.fenics import FEniCSConfig, solve_and_package
>>> cfg = FEniCSConfig(
...     pde="heat_equation_steady",
...     domain={"type": "rectangle", "x": [0, 1], "y": [0, 1], "nx": 32, "ny": 32},
...     bcs=[{"type": "dirichlet", "boundary": "left", "value": 0.0},
...          {"type": "dirichlet", "boundary": "right", "value": 1.0}],
...     params={"k": 1.0},
... )
>>> sample = solve_and_package(cfg)

For parametric sweeps:
>>> from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.fenics import FEniCSWorkflow
>>> samples = FEniCSWorkflow(cfg).sweep({"k": [0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 5.0]})
children.summary: FEniCS integration for PINNeAPPle.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.fluidx3d
children.doc:
Bridge to FluidX3D (lattice Boltzmann CFD on GPUs, OpenCL; Dr. Moritz Lehmann).

FluidX3D is not open source in the OSI sense: its license allows public research, education and personal use, and
forbids commercial and military use (https://github.com/ProjectPhysX/FluidX3D/blob/master/LICENSE.md). PINNeAPPle
does not ship or import any of its code. This module only:

- writes a ``main_setup()`` for a wind tunnel (STL body or sphere) in the user's own FluidX3D checkout, using the setup
  API its documentation describes (``units.set_m_kg_s``, ``LBM``, ``voxelize_stl``, ``object_force``,
  ``write_device_to_vtk``), and switches on the extensions it needs in ``src/defines.hpp`` (both files are backed up);
- compiles and runs it with the checkout's ``make.sh`` (an OpenCL device is required);
- reads the force history it prints and the ``.vtk`` fields it exports (:func:`read_vtk` from ``lbm_tunnel``, which
  also reads PINNeAPPle's own LBM output), into arrays or PhysicalSamples.

Using it is subject to FluidX3D's license: check that your use is allowed before running it.

    from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.fluidx3d import WindTunnelSetup, run_fluidx3d, read_results
    s = WindTunnelSetup(stl="car.stl", length_m=4.5, velocity_m_s=30, nu_m2_s=1.5e-5, rho_kg_m3=1.2,
                        box=(1.0, 3.0, 0.75), memory_mb=2000, time_s=0.5, export_every_s=0.1, floor=True)
    run_fluidx3d(s)                                  # FLUIDX3D_HOME=/path/to/FluidX3D
    res = read_results()                             # forces [N] over time, last exported u/rho fields

classes.name: WindTunnelSetup
classes.doc:
Wind tunnel around an STL body (or a sphere when ``stl`` is None), flow along +y (FluidX3D's convention in its
examples). Lengths in metres, velocity in m/s; ``length_m`` is the body length along the flow (or the sphere
diameter). ``box`` is the tunnel size relative to its x extent (aspect ratio passed to ``resolution``).

functions.name: fluidx3d_home
functions.sig: () -> str | None

functions.name: fluidx3d_available
functions.sig: () -> bool
functions.doc: A checkout is configured and an OpenCL ICD is installed (FluidX3D still needs a working device).

functions.name: write_setup
functions.sig: (setup: WindTunnelSetup, home: str | None = None) -> str
functions.doc:
Replace the active ``main_setup()`` of ``src/setup.cpp`` by the generated one: the original file is kept as
``setup.cpp.pinneapple.bak`` and only the generated function is compiled (the file's other setups stay commented
out as FluidX3D ships them).

functions.name: enable_features

functions.doc:
Uncomment ``#define <feature>`` lines in ``src/defines.hpp`` (backup ``defines.hpp.pinneapple.bak``) and comment
out ``BENCHMARK``, which would otherwise run the benchmark instead of the setup.

Write the setup and the defines (when ``setup`` is given), then compile and run with ``make.sh``.
Output goes to ``<home>/<log>``; raises RuntimeError on a non-zero exit.

functions.doc: Rows (t [s], Fx, Fy, Fz [N]) printed by the generated setup.

functions.sig: (home: str | None = None, log: str = 'log.pinneapple', export_dir: str | None = None) -> dict
functions.doc: Force history from the log and the last exported field of each quantity (``bin/export/<q>-<step>.vtk``).

functions.sig: (results: dict, source: str = 'fluidx3d') -> list
functions.doc: One PhysicalSample with the last exported fields on their regular grid (positions from origin/spacing).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.genesis
pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.genesis.adapter
children.doc:
Adapters from Genesis AI trajectory dicts to PINNeAPPle's UPD format.

genesis_traj_to_upd    — single trajectory dict → PhysicalSample
genesis_trajs_to_upd   — list of trajectory dicts → list[PhysicalSample]

functions.name: genesis_traj_to_upd
functions.sig: (traj: dict, time_array: Optional[np.ndarray] = None, field_map: Optional[Dict[str, str]] = None, meta_extra: Optional[dict] = None, dt: Optional[float] = None)
functions.doc:
Convert a Genesis AI trajectory dict to a UPD PhysicalSample.

Parameters
----------
traj : output from GenesisRunner.simulate().
    Keys are field names (e.g. "robot_pos", "robot_vel", "step").
time_array : (T,) float array of simulation timestamps.
    If None and "step" is present, the time coordinate is derived from
    the step index (see ``dt``).
field_map : optional rename map {traj_key: upd_field_name}.

children.doc:
Genesis AI integration for PINNeAPPle.

Provides a structured workflow over the genesis-world physics engine
(Genesis-Embodied-AI/Genesis) for robotics, embodied AI, and multi-physics
simulation, with output conversion to PINNeAPPle's UPD (PhysicalSample) format.

Sub-modules
-----------
scene_builder — GenesisConfig, EntitySpec, build_scene()
runner        — GenesisRunner (step loop, trajectory collection)
adapter       — genesis_traj_to_upd(), genesis_trajs_to_upd()

Quick start — rigid body simulation
-------------------------------------
>>> from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.genesis import (
...     GenesisConfig, EntitySpec, GenesisRunner, genesis_traj_to_upd
... )
>>> cfg = GenesisConfig(
...     backend="gpu",
...     n_steps=500,
...     entities=[
...         EntitySpec(morph={"type": "Plane"}),
...         EntitySpec(
...             morph={"type": "URDF", "file": "robot.urdf", "fixed": True},
...             material={"type": "Rigid"},
...             name="robot",
...         ),
...     ],
... )
>>> runner = GenesisRunner(cfg)
>>> traj = runner.simulate()              # dict of numpy arrays
>>> sample = genesis_traj_to_upd(traj)   # → PhysicalSample (UPD)

Quick start — MPM soft-body with differentiable simulation
-----------------------------------------------------------
>>> cfg = GenesisConfig(
...     backend="gpu",
...     requires_grad=True,
...     mpm_options={"lower_bound": (-1, -1, 0), "upper_bound": (1, 1, 2)},
...     entities=[
...         EntitySpec(morph={"type": "Sphere", "radius": 0.1}, material={"type": "MPM.Elastic", "rho": 500}),
...     ],
... )

Parallel environments (RL / dataset generation)
------------------------------------------------
>>> cfg = GenesisConfig(backend="gpu", n_envs=512, n_steps=200, entities=[...])
>>> runner = GenesisRunner(cfg)
>>> trajs = runner.collect_trajectories(n_rollouts=1)  # each step batched over 512 envs

Custom controller injection (PINN-in-the-loop)
----------------------------------------------
>>> def ctrl(scene, entities, step_idx):
...     robot = entities["robot"]
...     robot.control_dofs_position(pinn_policy(step_idx))
>>> runner = GenesisRunner(cfg, controller_fn=ctrl)

children.doc:
Bridge to GeoTaichi (MPM, DEM / level-set DEM, FEM, IGA and their couplings; Taichi; GPL-3.0).

GeoTaichi is run as a separate program: PINNeAPPle never imports or ships its code. Point ``GEOTAICHI_HOME`` at a
GeoTaichi checkout (installed with its own requirements), run one of its scripts, and read the particle frames it
writes (``<path>/particles/MPMParticle<NNNNNN>.npz`` or ``DEMParticle``) into arrays or PhysicalSamples for
training and checks. The same reader reads the frames of PINNeAPPle's own ``geo_mpm`` solver, so a GeoTaichi run
and a PINNeAPPle run of the same problem can be compared point for point.

    from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.geotaichi import run_geotaichi, read_geotaichi, frames_to_samples
    run_geotaichi("examples/mpm/column_collapse/DPmaterial.py", workdir="runs/collapse")
    frames = read_geotaichi("runs/collapse/OutputData")          # list of {position, velocity, volume, ...}
    samples = frames_to_samples(frames, source="geotaichi")

FMI import compatibility: run FMUs through :func:`simulate_fmu` in every interface they offer and record what
worked, as the table the FMI tools list asks for (exporting tool, FMI version, platform, FMU, interface).

    from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.modelica.fmi_compat import check_fmus, markdown_table
    rows = check_fmus(sorted(Path("Reference-FMUs/2.0").glob("*.fmu")), exporter="Reference-FMUs 0.0.39")
    print(markdown_table(rows))

A run passes when it reaches the stop time with finite outputs. For the ``Dahlquist`` test model (x' = -k x) the
trajectory is also compared with the exact solution exp(-k t): within 1e-3 through Model Exchange (the importer's
integrator) and within 0.1 through Co-Simulation, where the FMU integrates with its own fixed-step explicit Euler.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.modelica.fmu_export
children.doc:
Export a validated surrogate as an FMU: a package another simulator loads and co-simulates.

The library already reads FMUs (:mod:`fmi_runner`, :mod:`fmu_inspect`); this is the reverse path. A surrogate that
passed its validation becomes an FMI 2.0 Co-Simulation archive that Simulink, OpenModelica, Dymola or fmpy can load,
with its validity envelope carried inside the package and in the model description, so the tool on the other side
receives the numbers *and* the range the numbers are allowed to answer.

What the package contains
-------------------------

``modelDescription.xml``
    FMI 2.0, one ``CoSimulation`` interface. Every input is a ``causality="input"`` Real with its validated
    ``min``/``max`` as attributes; every output is a ``causality="output"`` Real; ``envelope_ok`` is a Boolean
    output that reads 0 when the inputs handed to the slave are outside the validated box. The envelope, the
    validation decision and the hashes of the surrogate's coefficient tables are in ``VendorAnnotations`` (the slot
    FMI 2.0 reserves for exactly this), so an importer that only parses the XML still sees the range.
``sources/surrogate_fmu.c``
    the whole slave: the FMI 2.0 Co-Simulation entry points with the surrogate's coefficients baked in as
    ``static const double`` tables. No FMI header is needed -- the ABI types are declared in the file -- so `cc` is
    the only thing a rebuild takes.
``resources/validated_surrogate.json``
    the same coefficients, the envelope and the evidence as data, for a rebuild on another platform, for a reader
    that does not compile, and for whoever has to check that the binary and the validation are the same model.
``binaries/<platform>/<identifier>.<ext>``
    the compiled slave, when this machine has a compiler that can produce it (:func:`export_fmu` with
    ``build=True``).

What is *not* produced, and why
-------------------------------

- **A binary for another platform than the one that built the package.** An FMU ships one binary per target; the
  package written here carries the binary of the machine that ran it. Windows and Linux binaries need a compiler (or
  a cross toolchain) on that platform: run the same export there, or rebuild from ``sources/`` and ``resources/``.
- **FMI 3.0.** The 3.0 interface changes the value-reference model, the step API and the binary platform tags;
  emitting both here would double the surface for the benefit of the newest tools only. FMI 2.0 is what Simulink and
  the Modelica tools load, and 3.0 can wait for a real request.
- **State or dynamics of its own.** A surrogate is an algebraic map from inputs to outputs; the slave recomputes it
  at every ``fmi2DoStep`` and holds no state beyond the last inputs. An FMU that integrated something would be
  claiming a model of the physics that this one does not have.
- **A step that refuses to extrapolate.** When the inputs leave the validated box the slave sets ``envelope_ok`` to
  false and logs a warning, and the step still returns ``fmi2OK``. FMI 2.0 has no "refuse this input" that does not
  end somebody's simulation, and a boundary case a tenth of a percent outside the box should not kill a run that is
  otherwise fine; the flag, the log line and the ``min``/``max`` on the variables are what a caller acts on.

The one gate worth naming: :func:`export_fmu` refuses a surrogate whose evidence does not read ``validated`` (or
``approved``). Shipping a model that failed, or that is still under review, into another engineer's Simulink is how a
surrogate gets used outside the envelope it was checked in, and the refusal is cheaper than that.

    >>> from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.modelica.fmu_export import (
    ...     Port, RbfForm, SurrogateExport, export_fmu)
    >>> form = RbfForm.fit(design, values)                       # the surrogate, in a form that compiles
    >>> export = SurrogateExport(model=form, inputs=(Port("u", "m/s", 0.0, 30.0),),
    ...                          outputs=(Port("drag", "N"),), evidence=assessment.to_dict())
    >>> print(export_fmu(export, "drag.fmu").summary())          # refuses unless evidence reads "validated"

classes.name: UnvalidatedSurrogate
classes.doc: The evidence attached to a surrogate does not say it was validated, so it is not exported.

classes.name: Port
classes.doc:
One input or output of the surrogate, with the range it is defined on.

``minimum``/``maximum`` are the validated range for an input (written as the FMI ``min``/``max`` attributes) and
are left empty for an output, where they would be a claim about the result rather than a limit on the question.

classes.name: Envelope
classes.doc: The box the surrogate was validated in: one :class:`Port` per input and output.

methods.name: contains
methods.doc: A boolean per row of ``design``: every input inside its validated range.

classes.name: RbfForm
classes.doc:
A kernel expansion: ``y = output_scale * (bias + sum_j exp(-|x - c_j|^2 / 2l^2) w_j)``.

This is the form a kernel-ridge surrogate, a Gaussian-process posterior mean, or the correction of a
co-kriging model takes once its hyperparameters are fixed: a weighted sum of radial bumps, which is a handful of
arrays and the same handful of lines in C. ``centers`` and ``length_scale`` are in the *scaled* input space (the
inputs divided by ``input_scale``), which is how a design in metres and one in Mach number end up on the same
footing -- the same convention :mod:`pinneapple_data.multifidelity` uses.

methods.name: fit
methods.sig: (design, values, *, ridge: float = 1e-08, length_scale: float | None = None, input_scale = None, output_scale = None) -> RbfForm
methods.doc:
Kernel ridge with an RBF kernel, in closed form -- the estimator of
:class:`pinneapple_data.multifidelity.KernelRidge`, returned in the shape that compiles.

classes.name: MlpForm
classes.doc:
A fully connected network with ``tanh`` on every hidden layer and a linear output layer.

The parameters are plain arrays, so the weights of a small trained network -- the kind that fits on a handful of
simulation runs -- become a few dozen lines of C instead of a dependency on a deep-learning runtime inside
somebody else's simulator.

classes.name: SurrogateExport
classes.doc:
A validated surrogate, its interface, and the evidence that lets it out.

``model`` is one of the compiling forms (:class:`RbfForm`, :class:`MlpForm`); ``inputs``/``outputs`` are the
ports, in the column order the model's tables use -- the exporter checks the counts, because a port list that is
out of order would name the numbers wrongly on the other side and nothing inside the FMU could tell.

methods.name: guid
methods.doc: A GUID that changes with the coefficients, the interface or the envelope: an FMU's identity.

methods.name: predict
methods.doc: The surrogate's own numbers, the ones the compiled slave has to reproduce.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.modelica.fmu_inspect
children.doc:
FMU preflight: check that a compiled FMU can actually be loaded *before* a
sweep or a twin depends on it.

``fmi_runner`` / ``sweep`` hand an ``.fmu`` to fmpy and find out it is broken
only when instantiation fails, often minutes into a campaign. This module
opens the archive statically (nothing is loaded or executed) and reports:

- FMI version, model name, ``modelIdentifier`` per interface (ME / CS / SE);
- which platform binaries are shipped (``binaries/<platform>/<id>.<ext>``);
- for ELF64 shared objects (Linux), the **exported** symbol table, compared
  with the functions the FMI standard requires for the declared interfaces;
- cheap modelDescription consistency checks (unique value references,
  outputs listed in ``ModelStructure`` are declared ``causality="output"``).

Function lists: taken from the FMI standard headers ``fmi2FunctionTypes.h`` /
``fmi3FunctionTypes.h`` (Modelica Association, BSD-2-Clause), grouped by the
interface they belong to. The FMI specification requires an FMU to export
every function of each interface type it declares.

How this was built: REA (``inspect-artifact``, ``inspect-binary-layout``) was
run on the binaries of the Modelica Reference-FMUs to confirm what a correct
FMU exports; REA's deep native analysis (``open_binary``) needs a Hopper /
Ghidra / IDA provider, which was not available, so function bodies were not
analysed. PE (Windows ``.dll``) and Mach-O (``.dylib``) symbol tables are not
parsed here and are reported as ``unchecked``.

functions.name: elf_exported_functions
functions.sig: (data: bytes) -> list[str]
functions.doc:
Names of defined, global/weak, default-visibility FUNC symbols in the
``.dynsym`` table of a little-endian ELF64 object. Raises ValueError for
anything else.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.mujoco.batch
children.doc:
Thread-parallel MuJoCo rollouts: many simulations of one model, for training data.

``mujoco.batch`` (MuJoCo 3.17+, and 4.0) steps N independent simulations of a model on a thread pool, with results
bit-identical to a loop over one ``MjData`` per simulation at any thread count. It runs on CPU (no JAX, no GPU) and
lets each simulation carry its own model parameters — mass, friction, gains — which is what turns one MJCF into a
design-of-experiments campaign.

    cfg = MuJoCoConfig(model_path="hopper.xml", dt=2e-3)
    runner = BatchRunner(cfg, n_envs=256)
    runner.randomize("body", "torso", "mass", 0.8, 1.2)        # domain randomisation, per environment
    batch = runner.rollout(n_steps=500)                          # {"qpos": (256, 500, nq), ...}
    samples = runner.rollout_to_upd()                             # one PhysicalSample per environment

For closed-loop policies (the control depends on the state) use :meth:`BatchRunner.roll_loop`, which binds the state
arrays and lets the policy write ``ctrl`` between steps. For GPU/TPU and differentiable physics use
:class:`~.mjx_backend.MJXParallelRunner` (``mujoco-mjx`` + JAX).

nthread : worker threads; ``0`` (default) uses every CPU.

Raises

children.doc:
MuJoCo model loading and data initialization for PINNeAPPle.

Wraps ``mujoco.MjModel`` / ``mujoco.MjData`` construction with a structured config so the rest of the pipeline stays
framework-agnostic, and hides the differences between the MuJoCo 3.x and 4.x wheels:

* 4.0 split the distribution: ``mujoco`` (bindings) now depends on ``mujoco-core`` (engine) and ``mujoco-studio``,
  and MJX moved out into its own ``mujoco-mjx`` package (``from mujoco import mjx`` still works once it is installed).
* 4.0 requires Python ≥ 3.11; 3.17 is the last line that installs on 3.10.
* ``mujoco.batch`` (thread-pool batch stepping) exists since 3.17, so both lines can use
  :class:`~.batch.BatchRunner`.

classes.name: MuJoCoConfig
classes.doc:
Configuration for a MuJoCo simulation.

Parameters
----------
model_path : path to a ``.xml`` (MJCF/URDF) or ``.mjb`` binary model file.
    Mutually exclusive with ``model_xml``.
model_xml : raw XML string (MJCF). Mutually exclusive with ``model_path``.
assets : dict mapping virtual filenames to bytes — forwarded to ``mujoco.MjModel.from_xml_string`` when
    using ``model_xml`` (meshes and textures referenced by the XML).
dt : override for ``model.opt.timestep`` (seconds). ``None`` keeps the model default.
n_steps : number of ``mj_step`` calls per :meth:`~.runner.MuJoCoRunner.simulate` run.
n_substeps : how many ``mj_step`` calls to batch per loop iteration (``mj_step(..., nstep=n_substeps)``).
gravity : override gravity vector (3-tuple). ``None`` keeps the model default.
keyframe : name or index of the ``<keyframe>`` the runner resets to. ``None`` resets to ``qpos0``.
record_energy : turn on ``mjENBL_ENERGY`` so the runner records potential and kinetic energy per step.
record_contacts : record the number of active contacts per step.
extra_opts : additional key-value pairs written into ``model.opt`` before the simulation runs.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.mujoco.mjx_backend
children.doc:
MJX (JAX/GPU) backend for massively parallel MuJoCo rollouts.

MJX uploads a MjModel to JAX device memory and runs thousands of environments simultaneously using ``jax.vmap``.
This is the GPU path for generating large training datasets for surrogate models and PINNs.

Requirements
------------
MuJoCo 3.x shipped MJX inside the ``mujoco`` wheel; **4.0 moved it to the separate ``mujoco-mjx`` package** (the
import path is still ``mujoco.mjx``):

    pip install mujoco-mjx jax          # CPU
    pip install mujoco-mjx "jax[cuda12]"  # NVIDIA GPU

Usage
-----
    from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.mujoco import MJXParallelRunner, MuJoCoConfig

    cfg = MuJoCoConfig(model_path="robot.xml", n_steps=500)
    runner = MJXParallelRunner(cfg, n_envs=1024)
    batched_traj = runner.rollout()              # {"qpos": (1024, 500, nq), ...}
    samples = runner.rollout_to_upd()            # one PhysicalSample per environment

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.mujoco.robot_backend
children.doc:
MuJoCo as a PINNeAPPle robot simulator.

:class:`MuJoCoRobotSim` gives MuJoCo 4.0 the same interface as
:class:`~pinneapple_simulation.robot_sim.sim.RobotSim` (NVIDIA Newton) and
:class:`~pinneapple_simulation.robot_sim.sim.IsaacSimBackend`: build a robot from an :class:`ArticulationSpec`, an
MJCF file, a URDF file or an XML string, run it with a torque controller, and get back the same
:class:`~pinneapple_simulation.robot_sim.sim.RobotRun` — joint positions, velocities, delivered torques, body poses,
body velocities and mass properties — so the PINNeAPPle checks (energy balance, torque replay, actuator limits,
``imu``) run unchanged, and the same study can be solved by two independent engines.

    from pinneapple_simulation.robot_sim.arms import TwoLinkArm
    from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.mujoco import MuJoCoRobotSim

    arm = TwoLinkArm(payload=5.0)
    sim = MuJoCoRobotSim.from_spec(arm.spec(), ground=False)
    run = sim.run(0.8, 5e-4, controller=lambda t, q, qd: kp * (q_ref(t) - q) - kd * qd)
    run.energy(), run.actuator_work(), run.imu("link2")

The controller is ``controller(t, q, qd) -> tau`` (joint torques, clipped to each joint's effort limit; the clipping
is counted in ``run.saturated``), exactly as in Newton's ``RobotSim.run``.

Parameters
----------

gravity : gravity magnitude [m/s^2]; ignored for a model loaded from a file (its ``<option>`` wins).

MJCF text for an :class:`~pinneapple_simulation.robot_sim.spec.ArticulationSpec`.

Boxes and cylinders become MuJoCo geoms (MuJoCo cylinders are along z, so the spec's y-axis cylinders are turned),
each joint becomes a hinge at the child link frame, each drive an effort ``motor`` with the joint's force limit as
its control range, and a ground plane is added when ``spec.ground`` is set (or ``ground`` overrides it).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.mujoco.runner
children.doc:
MuJoCo simulation runner for PINNeAPPle.

:class:`MuJoCoRunner` executes the ``mj_step`` loop and records the trajectory (``qpos``, ``qvel``, ``ctrl``,
body poses, body velocities, sensors, energy and contact count) into a :class:`~.trajectory.MuJoCoTrajectory`, ready
for surrogate / PINN training or for the checks in :mod:`.validation`.

Controller injection
--------------------
Pass a callable ``controller(model, data) -> None`` that writes ``data.ctrl`` before each step. This closes the loop
with a PINN-predicted or RL-policy controller:

    def my_ctrl(model, data):
        data.ctrl[:] = pinn_policy(data.qpos, data.qvel)

    runner = MuJoCoRunner(config, controller=my_ctrl)
    traj = runner.simulate()

Reading the state
-----------------
Each record is taken with the derived fields in sync with the state (``mj_forward`` runs after every step when
``sync_derived`` is on), so ``xpos``, ``cvel`` and ``sensordata`` in row ``k`` all describe time ``t[k]`` — MuJoCo's
own ``mj_step`` leaves them one substep behind. ``simulate`` records ``n_steps + 1`` rows, the initial state included.

Run a MuJoCo model and collect a trajectory.

Parameters

config : MuJoCoConfig
controller : optional callable ``(model, data) -> None`` executed before every step.
sync_derived : run ``mj_forward`` after each step so every record is internally consistent (default ``True``).
    Turn it off for speed when only ``qpos``/``qvel`` are used, and call ``mj_forward`` yourself before reading
    derived fields.

methods.doc: Reset the simulation to the configured keyframe (or the model's ``qpos0``).
