children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.mujoco.trajectory
children.doc:
Recorded MuJoCo trajectories as one object.

:class:`MuJoCoTrajectory` is what :class:`~.runner.MuJoCoRunner` and :class:`~.batch.BatchRunner` return: the state
per recorded time together with the model's mass properties, so a trajectory can be checked (energy, contacts) and
exported to PINNeAPPle's UPD (:meth:`MuJoCoTrajectory.to_upd`) without carrying the ``MjModel`` around.

Times and states follow MuJoCo's conventions: ``qpos``/``qvel`` are generalized coordinates and velocities, body
quaternions are ``(w, x, y, z)``, ``cvel`` is ``(angular, linear)`` in the world frame about each body's centre of
mass. Positions and quaternions are for the body frame origin, as ``MjData.xpos`` / ``xquat`` give them.

classes.name: MuJoCoTrajectory
classes.doc:
States recorded from one MuJoCo run.

Attributes
----------
t : (T,) simulation times [s].
qpos : (T, nq) generalized positions.
qvel : (T, nv) generalized velocities.
ctrl : (T, nu) actuator controls.
xpos : (T, nbody, 3) body frame origins, world frame [m].
xquat : (T, nbody, 4) body orientations ``(w, x, y, z)``.
cvel : (T, nbody, 6) world-frame ``(angular, linear)`` velocity about each body's centre of mass.
sensordata : (T, nsensordata) sensor readings (empty when the model has no sensors).
ncon : (T,) number of active contacts (empty when contacts were not recorded).
energy_rows : (T, 2) potential and kinetic energy [J] (empty when energy was not recorded).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.mujoco.validation
children.doc:
Analytic checks of a MuJoCo run — the PINNeAPPle trust layer for rigid-body simulation.

Each case builds a minimal MJCF whose answer is known in closed form, runs it through :class:`~.runner.MuJoCoRunner`
and compares. When a case fails, the model, the time step or the contact settings are wrong — not the paper — so the
checks are run before a MuJoCo-generated dataset is trusted as training data.

Cases
-----
``free_fall``        z(t) = z0 - g t^2 / 2 and v = -g t for a free body.
``pendulum_period``  small-oscillation period T = 2 pi sqrt(L / g), measured from the zero crossings.
``sliding_friction`` stopping distance v0^2 / (2 mu g) of a box sliding on a plane.
``gravity_torque``   the torque a pendulum needs to be held at an angle, m g L sin(theta), against ``qfrc_bias``.
``torque_free_spin`` kinetic energy and angular momentum of a free body, with no torque acting on it.
``resting_contact``  a box settled on a plane stays put (no sinking, contacts present).

functions.name: free_fall
functions.sig: (dt: float = 0.001) -> dict
functions.doc: A body in free fall for 0.3 s: position and velocity against the closed form.

functions.name: pendulum_period
functions.sig: (dt: float = 0.001, length: float = 0.5, amplitude: float = 0.05) -> dict
functions.doc: Small-oscillation period of a point mass on a massless rod, from the zero crossings of the angle.

functions.name: sliding_friction
functions.sig: (dt: float = 0.001, mu: float = 0.4, v0: float = 2.0) -> dict
functions.doc: Stopping distance of a box sliding on a plane, v0^2 / (2 mu g).

functions.name: gravity_torque
functions.sig: (theta_deg: float = 30.0, length: float = 0.5, dt: float = 0.001) -> dict
functions.doc: Generalized torque a pendulum needs to be held at ``theta``: m g L sin(theta), read from ``qfrc_bias``.

functions.name: torque_free_spin
functions.sig: (dt: float = 0.001, duration: float = 1.0) -> dict
functions.doc: A free body spinning with no torque: kinetic energy and angular momentum stay constant.

functions.name: resting_contact
functions.sig: (dt: float = 0.001) -> dict
functions.doc: A box dropped from 1 cm settles on the plane and then does not sink or bounce.

functions.name: validate
functions.sig: (cases: Sequence[str] | None = None, dt: float = 0.001, log = None) -> list
functions.doc:
Run the analytic cases and return one row per case ``{"case", "value", "limit", "passed", "note"}``.

``cases`` defaults to every entry of :data:`CASES`; ``log`` is called with each row when given.

functions.name: summary
functions.sig: (rows: Sequence[dict]) -> dict
functions.doc: Pass/fail roll-up of :func:`validate`: ``{"decision", "passed", "failed"}``.

children.doc:
MuJoCo integration for PINNeAPPle.

A workflow layer over the MuJoCo Python bindings (google-deepmind/mujoco) for **MuJoCo 4.0**, with a fallback to the
3.17 line on Python 3.10: structured model configuration, recorded trajectories, analytic checks, CPU thread-pool
rollouts (``mujoco.batch``), GPU rollouts (MJX), and the same robot interface PINNeAPPle already gives NVIDIA Newton.

What changed in MuJoCo 4.0 (released 2026-11-06)
------------------------------------------------
* MJX left the ``mujoco`` wheel: install ``mujoco-mjx`` (the import path is still ``mujoco.mjx``).
* ``mujoco.batch`` (3.17+) steps many simulations of one model on a thread pool, with per-simulation model
  parameters and bit-identical results — the CPU path for dataset generation, no JAX needed.
* Python 3.10 is no longer supported; ``pip install "pinneapple[mujoco]"`` picks the right line per interpreter.
* New physics this layer exposes through the model (nothing to configure here): speculative contacts
  (``<option flag="speculative">``), elasto-plastic flexes and springs, ``mujoco.sysid``.

Sub-modules
-----------
loader          MuJoCoConfig, load_model/make_data/reset_data, MjSpec, version probes
trajectory      MuJoCoTrajectory (states, energy, contacts) and its UPD export
runner          MuJoCoRunner: one ``mj_step`` loop, controller injection, keyframes
batch           BatchRunner: ``mujoco.batch`` thread-pool rollouts and domain randomisation
validation      analytic checks (free fall, pendulum, friction, torque, spin, resting contact)
robot_backend   MuJoCoRobotSim: ``run() -> RobotRun``, the interface Newton's RobotSim uses
mjx_backend     MJXParallelRunner: JAX/GPU rollouts (needs ``mujoco-mjx`` + ``jax``)

Quick start
-----------
>>> from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.mujoco import MuJoCoConfig, MuJoCoRunner, validate
>>> cfg = MuJoCoConfig(model_path="robot.xml", n_steps=500, dt=0.002)
>>> traj = MuJoCoRunner(cfg).simulate()
>>> traj.qpos.shape, traj.energy()["total"][:3]
>>> sample = traj.to_upd()                      # → PhysicalSample (UPD)
>>> rows = validate()                           # are these settings physically right?
>>> summary(rows)["decision"]

Parallel rollouts on CPU (no JAX):
>>> from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.mujoco import BatchRunner
>>> runner = BatchRunner(cfg, n_envs=256)
>>> runner.randomize("body", "torso", "mass", 0.8, 1.2)
>>> samples = runner.rollout_to_upd()

Robotics, same interface as Newton's ``RobotSim``:
>>> from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.mujoco import MuJoCoRobotSim
>>> sim = MuJoCoRobotSim.from_mjcf("arm.xml")
>>> run = sim.run(0.8, 5e-4, controller=lambda t, q, qd: -kp * q - kd * qd)

classes.doc: Recorded states. Quaternions are ``(w, x, y, z)``; velocities are of the centre of mass, world frame.

methods.doc: Kinetic, potential (m g z of the centre of mass) and total energy per recorded time [J].

methods.name: to_rigid_body_state
methods.doc: State at record ``k`` as the PyTorch :class:`RigidBodyState` used by the differentiable solver.

methods.name: to_upd
methods.doc: The trajectory as a PINNeAPPle :class:`PhysicalSample` (time coordinate, one field per quantity).

functions.name: simulate
functions.sig: (scene: RigidScene, duration: float, dt: float = 0.001, solver: str = 'xpbd', iterations: int = 8, record_every: int = 10, device: str = 'cpu', log = None, wrenches = None) -> RigidTrajectory
functions.doc:
Integrate ``scene`` for ``duration`` seconds with step ``dt`` and record every ``record_every`` steps.

``solver``: ``"xpbd"`` (position-based, robust contacts, default), ``"semi_implicit"`` (penalty contacts,
needs a small ``dt``), ``"featherstone"`` (reduced coordinates, best for joint chains) or ``"mujoco"``
(MuJoCo-Warp, needs the ``newton[sim]`` extra). The first call on a device compiles Warp kernels
(seconds to a minute on CPU); later calls reuse the cache.

``wrenches``: constant external loads ``{body index: (force [N], torque [N m])}`` in the world frame, the torque
taken about the body's centre of mass, applied at every step (e.g. a steady push).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.newton_physics.scene
children.doc:
Scene description for the Newton rigid-body backend.

A :class:`RigidScene` is a plain Python description (bodies, shapes, joints, ground) that does not import
Newton or Warp until :meth:`RigidScene.build` is called, so scenes can be created, saved and inspected on a
machine without the solver installed.

Conventions: SI units, the z axis points up, gravity is ``-g`` along z, and quaternions are given as
``(w, x, y, z)`` like :class:`pinneapple_simulation.particle_dynamics.rigid_body.RigidBodyState` (Newton
stores ``(x, y, z, w)``; the conversion happens here and in the runner).

classes.name: Shape
classes.doc: One collision shape of a body, in the body frame (centred on the body origin).

classes.name: RigidScene
classes.doc:
Bodies, joints and an optional ground plane, built into a Newton model on demand.

>>> scene = RigidScene()
>>> scene.ground(mu=0.4)
>>> box = scene.box("crate", (0.2, 0.2, 0.2), pos=(0, 0, 0.2), vel=(2.0, 0, 0))

methods.doc: A closed triangle mesh (e.g. from an STL of the part), vertices in the body frame [m].

methods.name: compound
methods.doc:
One rigid body made of several boxes ``[(half_extents, position in the body frame, mass), ...]``; its mass,
centre of mass and inertia follow from the boxes (``mass`` / ``density`` keywords are not used).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.newton_physics.validation
children.doc:
Checks of a Newton solver against closed-form rigid-body results.

Each case builds a small scene, runs it and compares one quantity with its analytic value. Run them before
trusting a solver setting (``dt``, iterations, solver) for a study: ``validate()`` returns one row per case
with the simulated value, the reference, the error and whether it is within the stated tolerance.

functions.name: free_fall
functions.sig: (solver = 'xpbd', dt = 0.001, **kw) -> dict
functions.doc: Sphere released from rest, no ground: z(t) = z0 - g t^2 / 2. Error = max |dz| / drop height.

functions.name: sliding_friction
functions.sig: (solver = 'xpbd', dt = 0.001, mu = 0.4, v0 = 2.0, **kw) -> dict
functions.doc: Box sliding on the ground with Coulomb friction stops after v0^2 / (2 mu g).

functions.name: pendulum_period
functions.sig: (solver = 'xpbd', dt = 0.001, length = 1.0, amp_deg = 5.0, **kw) -> dict
functions.doc: Small sphere on a hinge, small amplitude: T = 2 pi sqrt(I_pivot / (m g L)).

functions.name: bounce
functions.sig: (solver = 'xpbd', dt = 0.0001, e = 0.5, **kw) -> dict
functions.doc: Ball dropped on the ground with restitution e: first rebound height = e^2 x drop height.

functions.name: torque_free_spin
functions.sig: (solver = 'xpbd', dt = 0.001, **kw) -> dict
functions.doc: Box spinning about a tilted axis without gravity: the angular momentum vector is conserved.

functions.name: resting_contact
functions.sig: (solver = 'xpbd', dt = 0.001, **kw) -> dict
functions.doc: Box at rest on the ground for 2 s: it should neither sink nor drift.

functions.name: validate
functions.sig: (solver: str = 'xpbd', cases: list[str] | None = None, log = print, **kw) -> list[dict]
functions.doc: Run the analytic checks for one solver; returns rows (without the trajectories) and logs a table.

children.summary: Checks of a Newton solver against closed-form rigid-body results.

children.doc:
NVIDIA Newton rigid-body backend for PINNeAPPle.

`Newton <https://github.com/newton-physics/newton>`_ (Apache-2.0, built on NVIDIA Warp) is a GPU-ready physics
engine with several rigid-body solvers: XPBD (position based, robust contacts), semi-implicit Euler with
penalty contacts, Featherstone (reduced coordinates for joint chains) and MuJoCo-Warp. It runs on CPU too.

Sub-modules
-----------
scene      — RigidScene: bodies (sphere, box, capsule, cylinder, mesh), revolute / fixed joints, ground
runner     — simulate() -> RigidTrajectory (positions, quaternions, velocities, energy, UPD export)
validation — analytic checks (free fall, friction, pendulum, restitution, torque-free spin, resting contact)

Quick start
-----------
>>> from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.newton_physics import RigidScene, simulate, validate
>>> scene = RigidScene().ground(mu=0.4)
>>> scene.box("crate", (0.1, 0.1, 0.1), pos=(0, 0, 0.1), vel=(2.0, 0, 0), mu=0.4)
>>> traj = simulate(scene, duration=1.0, dt=1e-3)         # stops 0.51 m further, as v0^2 / (2 mu g)
>>> rows = validate("xpbd")                                 # check the solver settings first

Install: ``pip install newton`` (core) or ``pip install "newton[examples]"`` (viewer, importers, MuJoCo-Warp).
children.summary: NVIDIA Newton rigid-body backend for PINNeAPPle.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam
pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.binary_reader
children.doc:
Binary-format OpenFOAM FoamFile primitives.

``field_reader.py``'s ``_read_internal_field`` only understands ASCII
FoamFiles (a regex over UTF-8 text). Most real OpenFOAM cases -- anything
run with the (very common) ``writeFormat binary;`` control-dict setting --
cannot be read by it at all: a binary field/mesh file's payload is a raw
little-endian byte blob, not text, so the ASCII regexes either raise
``ValueError`` or silently mis-parse. There is also no reader anywhere in
PINNeAPPle for ``constant/polyMesh`` (points/faces/owner/neighbour), binary
or ASCII, so cell connectivity/positions could not be recovered at all
without an OpenFOAM installation's own ``writeCellCentres`` function
object having been run.

This module implements just enough of the binary (and, where a field
happens to be hand-written or exported as ASCII despite the case's
declared format, ASCII) FoamFile layout to read what a training pipeline
actually needs:

- scalar / vector / symmTensor / tensor volField ``internalField`` blocks
  (uniform and nonuniform, in either format).
- ``labelList`` (``constant/polyMesh/owner``, ``neighbour``).
- ``vectorField`` (``constant/polyMesh/points``).
- ``faceCompactList`` (``constant/polyMesh/faces``): an offsets labelList
  followed by an indices labelList -- the default face-storage format
  since OpenFOAM 4.

Binary layout (``arch "LSB;label=32;scalar=64"``, the default and by far
the most common OpenFOAM build configuration): a decimal ASCII count,
then ``(``, then the raw little-endian payload (no separators between
elements), then ``)``. Only 32-bit label / 64-bit scalar, little-endian
archives are supported; a big-endian or ``label=64`` build is out of
scope for this module.

See ``mesh_reader.py`` for cell-center/volume reconstruction built on top
of this module's polyMesh primitives.

functions.name: read_header
functions.sig: (data: bytes) -> FoamFileHeader
functions.doc: Locate the end of the ``FoamFile {...}`` block and parse its keys.

functions.name: read_binary_block
functions.sig: (data: bytes, pos: int, n_components: int, dtype = _SCALAR_DTYPE) -> tuple[np.ndarray, int]
functions.doc:
Read ``<count>\n(<raw bytes>)`` starting at *pos*.

Returns the array (shape ``(count,)`` if ``n_components == 1`` else
``(count, n_components)``) and the byte offset just past the closing
``)``.

functions.name: read_label_list
functions.sig: (data: bytes, path_hint: str = '') -> np.ndarray

functions.name: read_vector_field_points
functions.sig: (data: bytes, path_hint: str = '') -> np.ndarray

functions.name: read_face_compact_list
functions.sig: (data: bytes, path_hint: str = '') -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Read a ``faceCompactList``: an offsets array (len nFaces+1) followed
by a flat point-index array (len offsets[-1]).

functions.name: read_internal_field
functions.sig: (data: bytes, path_hint: str = '') -> tuple[np.ndarray, bool, int | None]
functions.doc:
Read the ``internalField`` entry of a vol{Scalar,Vector,SymmTensor,...}Field.

Returns ``(values, is_uniform, n_components)``. When uniform,
``values`` has shape ``(n_components,)`` (or a 1-element array for a
scalar) and the caller must broadcast it to the mesh's cell count
itself (the field file alone does not carry the cell count).

A field file's own ``FoamFile.format`` can differ from the case's
``controlDict`` default -- e.g. a hand-written initial-condition field
generated by a Python pre-processing script is commonly ASCII even
when the solver writes binary for every later time -- so the format is
read per-file from its own header, never assumed from the case.
Matching is scoped to the ``internalField ... ;`` statement specifically
(not the whole file), since a boundaryField patch can carry its own
``value uniform (...);`` entry that a whole-file search would wrongly
latch onto first.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.campaign
children.doc:
Parameter campaigns of OpenFOAM runs, split over any number of machines.

A campaign is one verified base case and a list of runs, each a set of input parameters. Every run:
1. copies the base case (a directory or a .tar.gz), optionally with another mesh;
2. applies the parameters: dictionary edits with values computed from the parameters, an optional patch rebuilt
   to a given area (an inlet diameter as an input), and an optional Python hook;
3. runs the pre-processing commands, decomposes the case and runs the solver with MPI;
4. samples lines while the solver runs (``LiveLineSampler``, so no function objects are needed and old times can
   be deleted to bound disk use);
5. writes ``<results>/<id>.json``: parameters, solver health from the log (Courant number, phase-fraction bounds,
   phase volume, end reached) and the time-mean profiles on the lines.

The same plan file runs on one workstation or on many machines. Each machine takes its share with ``--worker`` (the
runs tagged with that worker) or ``--shard i/n`` (round robin), skips the runs whose result already exists, and
claims a run with a lock file, so machines sharing a disk never run the same case. Results can be committed and
pushed to a git branch as each run finishes (``--publish-git``), which is how machines that share nothing, such as
cloud sessions, return their results.

    python -m pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.campaign plan.json --commands 5   # one line per machine
    python -m pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.campaign plan.json --shard 2/5 --procs 4 --publish-git

Plan (JSON; relative paths are relative to the plan file)::

    {"name": "jet sweep", "base": "base_case.tar.gz", "solver": "interFoam", "procs": 4, "end_time": 30,
     "pre": ["checkMesh", "setFields"],
     "derived": {"Uy": "U*cos(radians(theta))", "Uz": "U*sin(radians(theta))"},
     "edits": [{"file": "0/U", "key": "boundaryField/inlet/value", "value": "uniform (0 {Uy} {Uz})"}],
     "area_patch": {"patch": "inlet", "area": "pi*(d/1000)**2/4", "centre": [0, -7.4, -1.3], "normal": [0, -1, 0],
                    "from": ["inlet", "wall"], "rest": "wall"},
     "sample": {"fields": ["k", "alpha.water"], "keep_every": 10, "average_from": 0,
                "lines": [{"name": "L1", "start": [0, -7.4, -2.2], "end": [0, 15.3, -2.2], "n": 101}]},
     "runs": [{"id": "T01", "params": {"U": 8.6, "theta": 5.0, "d": 109}, "worker": "1"},
              {"id": "D1", "params": {"U": 10, "theta": 10, "d": 85}, "mesh": "mesh_deflector.tar.gz"}]}

Expressions (``derived``, ``area``) may use the parameters, earlier derived values, numbers, + - * / ** and the
functions and constants of ``math``; nothing else is evaluated. Edit values are templates filled with them
(``{Uy}``, or ``{Uy:.3f}``); a list value is written as an OpenFOAM vector ``(a b c)``.

methods.doc:

functions.doc:
Set ``a/b/c`` (slash-separated, e.g. ``boundaryField/inlet/value``) to ``value``; missing levels are

functions.doc:
Set ``key`` to ``value`` in an OpenFOAM dictionary file. With ``root``, the file must lie inside it (the edit
list of a campaign comes from the user).

functions.name: reset_nonuniform
functions.sig: (case: str | Path, n_cells: int) -> list[str]
functions.doc:
After a mesh swap, set every ``0/`` field whose internalField does not have ``n_cells`` values to its most
common value (``setFields`` or the solver rebuilds the rest). Returns the fields changed.

functions.name: n_cells
functions.sig: (case: str | Path) -> int

functions.name: area_patch
functions.sig: (case: str | Path, patch: str, area: float, centre: Sequence[float], normal: Sequence[float], from_patches: Sequence[str] | None = None, rest: str = 'wall', plane_tol: float = 0.03, bashrc: str | None = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
Rebuild boundary patch ``patch`` with the faces of the plane through ``centre`` (outward ``normal``) that are
nearest to ``centre``, until their area reaches ``area``: a circular inlet of a chosen diameter cut from a
larger opening or from the wall. Faces of the old ``patch`` left out go to ``rest``. ASCII meshes.

functions.doc:
decomposeParDict for ``n`` ranks. ``auto`` uses scotch when the installation has it, else ``simple``
slices along the longest side of the mesh. Returns the method used.

Health of a transient run from its log: last time, Courant numbers, phase-fraction bounds and volume
history (VOF solvers), whether it ended normally, and the first fatal error.

functions.doc: One shell line per machine: shard i of n, in the background, logging to campaign_<i>.log.

Where OpenFOAM is and which version: the installation paths, the ``bashrc`` that has to be sourced, and a probe of

One place for it, because two surfaces ask the same question: the workflow step (``pinneapple_core.workflows.adapters``,
which has to find a ``bashrc`` before running ``blockMesh``) and the solver contract's OpenFOAM backend (whose
``check_environment()`` answers *executable*, *version* and *environment* out of the same probe). A distribution
package puts ``blockMesh`` on PATH but the binaries only run with the environment loaded, so presence on PATH is not
enough -- the probe sources the ``bashrc`` and asks the environment itself.

functions.sig: (explicit: str | None = None, *, patterns: tuple[str, ...] | list[str] = FOAM_BASHRCS, environ: dict[str, str] | None = None) -> str | None

directory and the path of each executable asked for (empty when the environment does not have it).

``sourced=False`` with the error in ``error``, which is the diagnosis a caller wants.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.field_reader
children.doc:
OpenFOAM field extraction → UPD PhysicalSample.

Moved from pinneapple_geom/io/openfoam.py: field reading is a data concern,
not a geometry concern, and requires pinneapple_data imports.

Internal-field parsing is delegated to ``binary_reader.read_internal_field``,
which handles both ASCII and binary FoamFiles (detected per-file from each
file's own header, since a case's declared ``writeFormat`` and an
individual field file's actual format can differ -- e.g. a hand-written
initial condition is commonly ASCII even when the solver writes binary for
every later time). This replaced an ASCII-only regex parser that raised or
silently mis-parsed on any binary-format field, which is the OpenFOAM
default for most real cases.

When ``constant/polyMesh`` is present, cell centers/sizes are now
reconstructed directly from the mesh (``mesh_reader.load_mesh``) instead of
requiring the case to have been run with ``writeCellCentres`` -- and the
returned ``PhysicalSample`` is tagged ``domain={"type": "mesh"}`` with a
proper ``geometry`` object (a ``.nodes`` array), not ``{"type": "grid"}``.
The previous "grid" tag was wrong for finite-volume cell data (an
unstructured point cloud, not a structured grid) and broke
``pinneapple_data.dataloaders.build_physical_sample_dataloader``'s own
grid-vs-mesh branch, which expects an ``xr.Dataset`` on the grid path and
never got one from this function.

functions.name: openfoam_case_to_upd
functions.sig: (case_dir: str, *, time: str | None = None, fields: Sequence[str] = ('p', 'U'))
functions.doc:
Read OpenFOAM internalField data and package as a UPD PhysicalSample.

Parameters
----------
case_dir : path to the OpenFOAM case directory
time : time directory name; uses latest if None
fields : field names to extract (must exist in the time directory)

Returns
-------
PhysicalSample with fields dict and provenance metadata. ``domain`` is
``{"type": "mesh", ...}`` with a populated ``geometry.nodes`` when
``constant/polyMesh`` is present (the common case, and now readable
whether it is ASCII or binary); it falls back to the previous
``{"type": "grid", "coords": {...}}`` shape (populated only if a ``C``
cell-centers field exists) when no polyMesh is found, unchanged from
before for callers relying on that path.

children.summary: OpenFOAM field extraction → UPD PhysicalSample.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.mesh_reader
children.doc:
Cell-center / cell-size reconstruction from a binary OpenFOAM polyMesh.

PINNeAPPle has no ``constant/polyMesh`` reader anywhere: cell-center
coordinates were only ever recoverable via an optional ``C`` field, which
only exists if the case was run with OpenFOAM's ``writeCellCentres``
function object -- i.e. never, for an arbitrary case someone hands you.
This module reconstructs per-cell positions and sizes directly from the
mesh itself (``points``, ``owner``, ``neighbour``, ``faces``), no solver
run required beyond ``blockMesh``/``snappyHexMesh`` having produced the
mesh files.

Method
------
For every face, sum the coordinates of its vertices and add that sum to
the owner cell's accumulator, and to the neighbour cell's accumulator for
internal faces. For an axis-aligned hexahedral cell (true for any
``blockMesh``-graded structured/rectilinear mesh -- channels, pipes,
ducts, and similar canonical cases) each of the 8 distinct vertices of a
cell is shared by exactly 3 of its 6 faces, so summing all face-vertices
with equal weight and dividing by the total count already equals the mean
of the 8 distinct vertices, i.e. the exact centroid of a rectangular box,
with no need to de-duplicate vertices per cell. The same running min/max
over face-vertex coordinates gives the cell's axis-aligned bounding box,
whose extents equal the true cell ``(dx, dy, dz)`` for these box-shaped
cells.

For a general (non-box) cell this centroid/bounding-box are the common,
cheap face-vertex-average approximation of the true (face-decomposition)
centroid/volume, not an exact finite-volume computation -- adequate for
placing training samples and sizing an LES filter width, not for
finite-volume accounting. A proper arbitrary-polyhedron centroid/volume
(tet-decomposition from face centers) is straightforward to add on top of
the same ``points``/``owner``/``neighbour``/``faces`` arrays this module
already parses, if a future caller needs it.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.splash_packer
children.doc:
Pack a finished OpenFOAM case directory into a ``.splash`` archive.

No writer for this format existed anywhere in PINNeAPPle before this
module -- ``binary_reader.py``/``mesh_reader.py``/``field_reader.py`` are
all read-only, built to open ``.splash`` files (or plain case
directories) that already exist. A ``.splash`` file is nothing exotic: a
zip of a standard OpenFOAM case directory (``system/``, ``constant/``,
time directories, optionally ``postProcessing/``) plus one extra
top-level ``splash-manifest.json`` recording per-file size/sha256 and a
small summary block -- this module writes exactly that, so any case this
package's own tools (or plain ``blockMesh``/... run by hand) produce can
be packed into something ``field_reader``/``mesh_reader`` can read back.

Manifest schema (reverse-engineered from a real, externally-produced
``.splash`` archive, since no spec ships anywhere in this codebase)::

    {
      "format": 1,
      "splash_version": "<free-form string>",
      "case_name": "<string>",
      "generated_by": "<string>",
      "files": {"<relative/path>": {"size": <int>, "sha256": "<hex>"}, ...},
      "summary": {<caller-supplied dict, e.g. solver/cells/physical params>}
    }

functions.name: pack_splash_archive
functions.sig: (case_dir: str, out_path: str, *, case_name: Optional[str] = None, summary: Optional[Dict[str, Any]] = None, generated_by: str = 'pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.openfoam.splash_packer', splash_version: str = '1.0-pinneapple', exclude: Optional[Callable[[str], bool]] = None) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Zip ``case_dir`` (a finished OpenFOAM case: ``system/``,
``constant/``, time directories, ...) into a ``.splash`` archive at
``out_path``, with a ``splash-manifest.json`` listing every packed
file's size and sha256 plus a caller-supplied ``summary`` block.

Parameters
----------
case_dir : path to the case directory to pack.
out_path : where to write the ``.splash`` zip.
case_name : recorded in the manifest; defaults to ``basename(case_dir)``.
summary : free-form dict merged into the manifest's ``"summary"`` key
    (e.g. solver name, cell count, physical parameters) -- whatever a
    reader of this archive later would want without opening a case
    file.
exclude : optional ``(relative_path) -> bool``; files it returns True
    for are skipped. Defaults to excluding ``processor*`` directories
    (decomposed-run artifacts that shouldn't ship in the packed case)
    and ``case.foam`` (a ParaView placeholder file with no data).

Returns
-------
The manifest dict that was written (also embedded in the archive).

functions.name: read_splash_manifest
functions.sig: (splash_path: str) -> Dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Read just the ``splash-manifest.json`` entry out of a ``.splash``
archive, without extracting anything else.

functions.name: verify_splash_archive
functions.sig: (splash_path: str) -> Iterable[str]
functions.doc:
Yield a description for every file whose recorded sha256/size in
the archive's own manifest doesn't match its actual packed content --
empty if the archive is internally consistent. Cheap integrity check
before trusting a ``.splash`` file (e.g. after copying/transferring
one) without needing the original case directory.

children.summary: Pack a finished OpenFOAM case directory into a .splash archive.
OpenFOAM cases: build, run, read meshes and fields (ASCII and binary), sample and export.

pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.pict.case
children.doc:
The case description PICT needs: a wall-refined grid, a lid-driven cavity, and its PISOtorch domain.

Everything here except :func:`build_cavity_domain` runs without PICT installed: the grid is built with numpy and
checked (spacing monotone, geometric ratio, corners exact), and the case validates itself before any CUDA call.

classes.name: PICTAvailability
classes.doc: What is present and what is missing, one line each. ``available`` is the AND of all of it.

classes.name: CavityCase
classes.doc:
A lid-driven cavity in ``[0, 1]^2``: no-slip walls, the lid moving at ``lid_velocity`` in +x.

``Re = lid_velocity * L / viscosity`` with ``L = 1``, so ``viscosity = lid_velocity / Re``. The Ghia et al.
(1982) reference profile used by :mod:`~pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.pict.validation` assumes the lid
at the **y+** wall moving in **+x**; moving the lid elsewhere mirrors the profile and the check will say so.

methods.name: viscosity
methods.doc: Kinematic viscosity in m^2/s for this Reynolds number (``L = 1 m``).

methods.name: walls
methods.doc: The walls to refine towards: all four when ``refine`` is set.

methods.name: check
methods.doc: Problems with the description, before any solver is touched. Empty when it is usable.

methods.name: grid
methods.doc: Vertex coordinates in PICT's layout, ``(1, 2, ny+1, nx+1)``.

functions.name: pict_available
functions.sig: () -> bool
functions.doc: ``True`` when PICT could run here (both modules import and a CUDA device is visible).

functions.sig: (nx: int, ny: int, *, bounds: tuple[float, float, float, float] = (0.0, 0.0, 1.0, 1.0), refine: tuple[str, ...] = ('-x', '+x', '-y', '+y'), base: float = 1.1) -> np.ndarray

Vertex coordinates of a structured, wall-refined quad grid, in PICT's layout ``(1, 2, ny+1, nx+1)``.

``bounds`` is ``(x0, y0, x1, y1)``. ``refine`` names the walls the cells are packed towards (``"-x"`` is the low-x
wall). ``base`` is the ratio between the widths of neighbouring cells.

PICT ships its own generator inside its example scripts (``lib/data/shapes.py``), which is not part of the
package it installs; this one is ours, and `tests/test_pict_bridge.py` checks its spacing, its symmetry and its
corners instead of trusting it.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.pict.local_solver
children.doc:
A local incompressible solver, so the cavity runs without an NVIDIA GPU (this MacBook, CI, any CPU box).

PICT cannot run here: its kernels are CUDA, Apple Silicon has no CUDA. This module is **not** PICT and does not
pretend to be -- it is a vorticity-streamfunction solver written for this repository, run by numpy/scipy, and every
result it produces is labelled ``engine="local"``. It exists for two reasons: a Mac or a CI machine can then exercise
the whole bridge end to end (case, run, checks, ``PhysicalSample``), and the Ghia et al. (1982) comparison that
:mod:`.validation` implements gets a solver to be compared *with*, on a machine that has no GPU.

Method: vorticity-streamfunction, uniform square grid, second-order central differences, explicit Euler in time
(to steady state, where the time integrator stops mattering), Thom's wall-vorticity condition, and the streamfunction
Poisson problem solved exactly with a sparse LU factorised once per grid. Pressure is recovered afterwards from the
pressure Poisson equation with the steady wall condition ``dp/dn = -(1/Re) dw/ds``, and the result reports the
momentum residual that pressure leaves, so a wrong pressure is visible instead of implied.

Why not :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.stable_fluids`: that one is a graphics solver (semi-Lagrangian
advection with an FFT projection for a periodic domain). Its advection is too diffusive and its domain has no walls,
so it cannot be held to Ghia. Why not a finite-volume PISO of our own: that is what PICT is for; the point of this
module is a second, independent, cheap path, not a replacement.

Limits, stated rather than discovered:
- **Uniform grid only** (``CavityCase(refine=False)``): the wall-refined grid changes the finite-difference stencils,
  and a second discretisation with no reference behind it is how silent errors get in.
- **Lid at the +y wall moving in +x** (``lid_side="+y"``), the Ghia et al. configuration.
- It is a **steady** solver in practice: it marches the transient, records the initial and final fields, and stops on
  the residual. The transient is not an accurate time history and is not offered as one.
- Cost grows as ``nx^4`` (explicit stability limits dt while the Poisson solve grows with ``nx^2``): 64x64 is seconds,
  128x128 is about a minute, 256x256 is an afternoon.

classes.name: LocalSolverConfig
classes.doc:
How the local solver marches.

``cfl`` sets the time step through ``dt = min(cfl * h / |u|_max, viscosity * h^2 / 5)``: the second bound is the
explicit diffusion limit, and 5 is a safety factor over the 2-D stability limit of 4. ``steady_tol`` is the
relative change of vorticity per step that ends the march; ``max_steps`` and ``max_time_s`` are the guards that
turn a run that will not converge into an answer that says so.

functions.name: solve_cavity_local
functions.sig: (case: CavityCase, config: LocalSolverConfig | None = None)
functions.doc:
March the cavity to steady state on the CPU and return a :class:`~.runner.PICTResult` with ``engine="local"``.

The result is a cavity result like any other, so :func:`~.validation.cavity_checks` applies unchanged -- that is
the point: the checks and the reference data are the same, only the engine differs, and the result says which.

children.summary: A local incompressible solver, so the cavity runs without an NVIDIA GPU (this MacBook, CI, any CPU box).

``substeps`` is either a positive number of substeps per output step or ``"ADAPTIVE"`` (PICT's CFL-based split).
``differentiable`` records the steps on the torch graph, which is what a network trained through the solver

What a cavity run left behind: the recorded velocity and pressure, and the case they came from.

``engine`` is ``"pict"`` or ``"local"``: a result always says which solver produced it, and no number here is
ever relabelled. The class is the shared currency of both engines, which is what lets
:func:`~.validation.cavity_checks` apply to either without knowing which ran.

``velocity`` is ``(snapshots, 2, ny, nx)`` in the order PICT stores a field (channels first), ``velocity[0]``
being the x component; ``pressure`` is ``(snapshots, ny, nx)`` and is the pressure PICT reports, whose datum is
arbitrary (only differences drive the flow).

methods.name: component
methods.doc: ``"u"`` or ``"v"``: ``(snapshots, ny, nx)``.

methods.name: cell_centers
methods.doc: Coordinates of the recorded samples: the cell centres, or the nodes when ``layout="nodes"``.

methods.name: checks
methods.doc: The physics checks of :func:`~pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.pict.validation.cavity_checks`.

methods.name: to_upd
methods.doc: The recorded fields as a PINNeAPPle ``PhysicalSample`` (time, x, y and the three fields).

functions.name: run_cavity
functions.sig: (case: CavityCase, config: PICTRunConfig | None = None, *, engine: str = 'auto') -> PICTResult
functions.doc:
Run ``case`` and record velocity and pressure; ``engine`` selects the solver and the result says which ran.

``"pict"`` requires PICT and raises :class:`ImportError` naming the missing part when it cannot run -- nothing is
invented for a machine without it. ``"local"`` uses this repository's vorticity-streamfunction solver (CPU, no
CUDA): see :mod:`.local_solver` for what it is and what it is not. ``"auto"`` is PICT when it is available and the
local engine otherwise, and ``result.engine`` always names the one that produced the numbers.

children.summary: Run a PICT case and bring its fields back as arrays PINNeAPPle can check and store.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.pict.validation
children.doc:
The checks a PICT cavity result is held to: continuity, the boundary conditions, and Ghia et al. (1982).

The reference data are the values in Ghia, Ghia and Shin, *High-Re solutions for incompressible flow using the
Navier-Stokes equations and a multigrid method*, Journal of Computational Physics 48 (1982) 387-411, Tables I and II,
as reproduced by PICT's own validation suite (``tests/validations.py``, Apache-2.0). They are the u velocity along the
vertical centreline and the v velocity along the horizontal centreline, at the y and x stations in the tables -- not
a dense profile, so a computed field is interpolated onto those stations before comparing.

Nothing here needs PICT installed: the reference data, the reductions and the comparison can all be exercised on an
array (``tests/test_pict_bridge.py`` does exactly that). :func:`validate` is the only function that runs the solver,
and it says so instead of returning numbers when the solver is missing.

functions.name: ghia_profile
functions.sig: (reynolds: int, component: str = 'u') -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
``(stations, values)`` of the Ghia table for ``reynolds``; ``component`` is ``"u"`` (along y) or ``"v"``.

Raises :class:`KeyError` naming the Reynolds numbers the table has instead of interpolating between them.

functions.name: centerline
functions.sig: (field: np.ndarray, *, direction: str = 'vertical') -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
The middle column (``"vertical"``, along y) or middle row (``"horizontal"``, along x) of a 2-D field.

For an even number of cells the two middle lines are averaged: the comparison is against a point on the centre,
and a single line would bias it by half a cell.

functions.name: compare_to_ghia
functions.sig: (computed: np.ndarray, stations: np.ndarray, *, reynolds: int = 100, component: str = 'u', tol: float = 0.05) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Interpolate ``computed`` (sampled at ``stations``) onto the Ghia table and report rms, max and the verdict.

``tol`` is the rms the result must stay under, in units of the lid velocity; it is a parameter because the
accuracy a run owes depends on its grid -- 32x32 cells at Re = 1000 is a screenshot, 256x256 is a result.

functions.name: spacing_from_summary
functions.sig: (summary: dict[str, Any]) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: Cell sizes ``(dx, dy)`` of the grid the case built, from the summary in the result.

functions.name: divergence_max
functions.sig: (u: np.ndarray, v: np.ndarray, dx: np.ndarray, dy: np.ndarray, *, nodes: bool = False) -> float
functions.doc:
``max |du/dx + dv/dy|`` over the whole field, central differences inside and one-sided at the border.

``dx`` and ``dy`` are the distances between consecutive samples along each axis (so they have one entry fewer than
the field). ``nodes=False`` means the samples are cell centres and ``dx``/``dy`` are the cell widths; ``nodes=True``
means they are the node spacings. The border is included on purpose: in a cell-centred field the largest divergence
sits right below the moving lid, and an interior-only difference would never look there.

functions.name: spacing_for
functions.sig: (result) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, bool]
functions.doc: ``(dx, dy, nodes)`` matching the field of ``result``: the description of the grid it was recorded on.

functions.name: stations
functions.sig: (result) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: Normalised ``(x, y)`` of the recorded samples, in units of the cavity side.

functions.name: cavity_checks
functions.sig: (result, *, tol_div: float = 0.01, tol_wall: float = 0.05, tol_ghia: float = 0.05, snapshot: int = -1) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
The checks a recorded cavity run has to pass, each with the number it was decided on.

- ``continuity``: the largest discrete divergence of the velocity, normalised by ``U / L`` (PISO enforces it to
  the pressure tolerance; a value of order 1 means the field is not a solution of the equations).
- ``lid``: the u velocity on the top row against the lid velocity.
- ``walls``: the largest speed on the three closed walls -- the bottom row and the side columns below the lid
  (a no-slip wall must be still).
- ``ghia_u`` / ``ghia_v``: the centreline profiles against Ghia et al. (1982) at the run's Reynolds number, when
  the table has one.

The checks read the field where the engine put it (``result.layout``): a node-based field has the walls in its
first and last rows, a cell-centred one has them half a cell outside -- and there the ``lid`` line measures the
top *cell centre*, which on a coarse grid is not the lid velocity. That is why a PICT run that reports a low
``lid`` value on a coarse grid is read together with its grid, not as a boundary-condition failure.

functions.name: validate
functions.sig: (*, reynolds: tuple[int, ...] = (100, 1000), nx: int = 32, ny: int = 32, iterations: int = 100, tol_ghia: float = 0.05, engine: str = 'auto') -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Run the cavity at each Reynolds number and check it; the report says which engine produced the numbers.

``engine="auto"`` uses PICT when it can run here and this repository's local solver otherwise (a Mac, a CI box,
any machine without CUDA). Nothing is relabelled: every row carries the engine that ran, and the report names it
at the top. ``nx``/``ny`` must be large enough for the Reynolds number being claimed -- a 32x32 grid at Re = 1000
is a smoke test, and the rms against Ghia says so rather than a footnote.

children.summary: The checks a PICT cavity result is held to: continuity, the boundary conditions, and Ghia et al.

children.doc:
PICT: a differentiable multi-block PISO solver on CUDA, driven from PINNeAPPle.

`PICT <https://github.com/tum-pbs/PICT>`_ (Franz, Wei, Guastoni and Thuerey, *A differentiable, GPU-accelerated
multi-block PISO solver for simulation-coupled learning tasks in fluid dynamics*, Journal of Computational Physics
544 (2026) 114433, Apache-2.0) solves the incompressible Navier-Stokes equations with PISO on structured, deformed
multi-block grids. Its fields are plain PyTorch tensors and every step supports autograd through hand-written CUDA
backward kernels, which is what makes it useful here: a network can sit inside a CFD solve and be trained by
backpropagating through it.

What this wrapper is, and what it is not
----------------------------------------
It is a bridge: it builds the grid, the domain, the boundaries and the ``PISOtorch_simulation.Simulation``
configuration from a description in SI units, runs it, records the velocity and pressure fields it read back, and
returns them as a :class:`PICTResult` and a PINNeAPPle ``PhysicalSample``. It adds no physics of its own.

It is **not** a reimplementation and it does not fake a run. PICT needs Linux, an NVIDIA GPU and its own compiled
extensions (``extensions/setup.py``, CUDA 12.8 as the paper's environment); on a machine without them
``run_cavity(..., engine="pict")`` raises with the missing part named. Nothing in this repository has been executed
against PICT -- state that plainly when reporting a PICT number. What *is* checked without the solver is the grid
generator, the case validation, the reference data and the reduction of a field to the quantities the checks need
(``tests/test_pict_bridge.py``).

``engine="local"`` runs the cavity here instead, with this repository's own vorticity-streamfunction solver
(:mod:`.local_solver`, numpy/scipy, no GPU): the same case, the same result type, the same Ghia comparison, and a
result that says ``engine="local"`` so the two are never confused. ``engine="auto"`` (the default) picks PICT when it
can run and the local engine when it cannot.

Sub-modules
-----------
case       — availability, the wall-refined grid, the lid-driven cavity case and its PISOtorch domain
runner     — PICTRunConfig, run_cavity() -> PICTResult (velocity, pressure, times) and its PhysicalSample
validation — Ghia et al. (1982) centreline reference data, the checks of a cavity result, and validate()

Quick start (on a machine with PICT installed)
----------------------------------------------
>>> from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.pict import CavityCase, PICTRunConfig, run_cavity
>>> result = run_cavity(CavityCase(nx=32, ny=32, Re=1000), PICTRunConfig(iterations=100), engine="auto")
>>> result.engine                               # "pict" (CUDA) or "local" (this repository's CPU solver)
>>> result.velocity.shape                     # (snapshots, 2, ny, nx)
>>> checks = result.checks()                   # continuity, lid and wall boundary conditions, Ghia profile
>>> print(checks["ghia_u"]["rms"], checks["ghia_u"]["passed"])

Install: ``git clone https://github.com/tum-pbs/PICT.git``, then ``cd extensions && python setup.py install`` (see
the project's installation guide; the Python side also needs ``torch`` with CUDA).
children.summary: PICT: a differentiable multi-block PISO solver on CUDA, driven from PINNeAPPle.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.turbodesigner
pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.turbodesigner.bridge
children.doc:
TurboDesigner integration — analytical mean-line solver as a PINN data source.

The low-level bridge wraps the ``turbodesigner`` Python package
(pip install turbodesigner) and exposes:

  TurboDesignerConfig  — structured configuration dataclass (mirrors the
                         TurboDesigner JSON design format)
  run_turbodesigner    — one-call analytical solve, returns field arrays
  turbodesigner_to_upd — packages solve results as a UPD PhysicalSample
  TurboDesignerWorkflow — convenience wrapper for parametric sweeps

The workflow is:
  1. Define a design with ``TurboDesignerConfig``.
  2. Call ``run_turbodesigner(cfg)`` → dict of numpy arrays (station fields).
  3. Feed the arrays as ``DataConstraint`` into a PINN training run so the
     network learns residual corrections on top of the analytical solution.

Example
-------
>>> from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.turbodesigner import (
...     TurboDesignerConfig, run_turbodesigner, TurboDesignerWorkflow
... )
>>> cfg = TurboDesignerConfig(
...     pressure_ratio=3.0,
...     num_stages=5,
...     mass_flow_rate=4.37,
...     rpm=10_000,
... )
>>> data = run_turbodesigner(cfg)
>>> print(data["T_t_K"].shape)   # (num_stations,)

classes.name: TurboDesignerConfig
classes.doc:
Parameters for one TurboDesigner axial compressor solve.

All fields map directly to the ``definition`` block of a TurboDesigner
JSON design file (see turbodesigner CLI ``design schema``).

Parameters
----------
pressure_ratio          : overall total-to-total pressure ratio
num_stages              : number of compressor stages
mass_flow_rate          : kg/s
rpm                     : shaft speed (rev/min)
inlet_total_pressure    : Pa
inlet_total_temperature : K
isentropic_efficiency   : stage isentropic efficiency (0–1)
hub_to_tip_ratio        : inlet hub-to-tip radius ratio
axial_velocity          : mean axial velocity (m/s)
gamma                   : specific heat ratio (default 1.4 for air)
gas_constant            : J/(kg·K) (default 287 for air)
num_streams             : spanwise stream count for free-vortex analysis
aspect_ratio            : {"rotor": ..., "stator": ...}
stage_reaction          : list of per-stage reaction values (len = num_stages)
extra_params            : any additional definition keys forwarded as-is

methods.name: to_turbodesigner_dict
methods.doc: Serialise to the TurboDesigner JSON ``definition`` schema.

classes.name: TurboDesignerWorkflow
classes.sig: (base_config: TurboDesignerConfig) -> None
classes.doc:
Convenience wrapper for repeated TurboDesigner solves over a parameter space.

Useful for generating PINN training datasets that cover a range of
operating conditions (off-design, multi-point training).

Examples
--------
>>> wf = TurboDesignerWorkflow(TurboDesignerConfig(num_stages=5))
>>> samples = wf.sweep({"pressure_ratio": [2.0, 3.0, 4.0, 5.0]})
>>> samples = wf.sweep({"rpm": [8000, 10000, 12000], "pressure_ratio": [2.5, 3.0]})

methods.name: solve
methods.sig: (param_override: dict[str, Any] | None = None, **run_kwargs) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
methods.doc: Run a single TurboDesigner solve with optional parameter override.

methods.name: solve_upd
methods.doc: Run a single solve and return a UPD PhysicalSample.

methods.name: sweep
methods.sig: (param_grid: dict[str, list[Any]], as_upd: bool = False, **run_kwargs) -> list[Any]
methods.doc: Solve for each combination in a parameter grid.

functions.name: run_turbodesigner
functions.sig: (cfg: TurboDesignerConfig, *, fallback_if_missing: bool = True) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Run an axial compressor mean-line analysis with TurboDesigner.

Attempts to use the ``turbodesigner`` package for a full mean-line +
free-vortex solve.  If the package is not installed and
``fallback_if_missing=True``, a simplified analytical calculation is
performed instead (suitable for quick prototyping).

Parameters
----------
cfg : TurboDesignerConfig
fallback_if_missing : bool
    When True, fall back to a pure-Python approximation if turbodesigner
    is not importable.  When False, raise ImportError instead.

Returns
-------
dict with keys:
  s             : normalised streamwise coordinate, shape (S,)
  T_t_K         : total temperature at each station, shape (S,)
  p_t_Pa        : total pressure at each station, shape (S,)
  rho_kg_m3     : density at each station, shape (S,)
  u_axial_m_s   : axial velocity at each station, shape (S,)
  c_theta_m_s   : tangential velocity at each station, shape (S,)
  stage_work_J_kg : work input per stage, shape (num_stages,)  [if available]

functions.name: turbodesigner_to_upd
functions.sig: (cfg: TurboDesignerConfig, **run_kwargs)
functions.doc:
Run TurboDesigner and package results as a UPD PhysicalSample.

Returns
-------
PhysicalSample with:
  - coords : {"s": array}
  - fields : {"T_t": tensor, "p_t": tensor, "rho": tensor,
              "u": tensor, "c_theta": tensor}

children.summary: TurboDesigner integration — analytical mean-line solver as a PINN data source.

children.doc:
TurboDesigner external solver bridge.

Wraps the ``turbodesigner`` package (pip install turbodesigner) to generate
analytical mean-line compressor data for PINN training.

If ``turbodesigner`` is not installed, a built-in analytical fallback is used
automatically — the bridge remains importable at all times.

Public API
----------
TurboDesignerConfig   — design configuration dataclass
run_turbodesigner     — one-call analytical solve → dict of numpy arrays
turbodesigner_to_upd  — solve + package as UPD PhysicalSample
TurboDesignerWorkflow — convenience wrapper for parametric sweeps

Quick start
-----------
>>> from pinneapple_simulation.external_solvers.turbodesigner import (
...     TurboDesignerConfig, TurboDesignerWorkflow
... )
>>> cfg = TurboDesignerConfig(pressure_ratio=3.0, num_stages=5, rpm=10_000)
>>> wf = TurboDesignerWorkflow(cfg)
>>> data = wf.solve()           # single operating point
>>> samples = wf.sweep(         # parametric sweep
...     {"pressure_ratio": [2.0, 3.0, 4.0]},
...     as_upd=True,
... )
children.summary: TurboDesigner external solver bridge.

children.doc:
External tool integrations for PINNeAPPle.

Subpackages
-----------
openfoam  — case staging, execution, field sampling, and UPD packaging
matlab    — MATLAB Engine API wrapper, subprocess runner, .mat I/O
modelica  — FMU simulation (fmpy) and OpenModelica (OMPython)
fenics    — workflow layer on top of pinneapple_solvers.fenics_bridge
mujoco    — MuJoCo 4.0 (google-deepmind/mujoco): trajectories + UPD, analytic checks, mujoco.batch
            thread-pool rollouts, MJX (mujoco-mjx) and a robot backend for pinneapple_simulation.robot_sim
genesis   — Genesis AI (Genesis-Embodied-AI/Genesis) multi-physics robotics simulation
newton_physics — NVIDIA Newton rigid-body solvers (XPBD, Featherstone, MuJoCo-Warp) with analytic checks
pict      — PICT (tum-pbs), a differentiable multi-block PISO solver on CUDA: cavity case, runner, Ghia checks

contract  — one interface every external solver is reached through (``check_environment``, ``prepare``, ``run``,
            ``status``, ``results``, ``cancel``) and ``backends``: the six implementations of it (OpenFOAM, CalculiX,
            FEniCSx, ANSYS Fluent, MATLAB, and the in-process hexahedral FEM), so a solver is added by writing one class
            instead of reading the previous one's case layout. See :mod:`.contract`.

All subpackages use lazy / optional imports so that the base package remains
importable even when a specific external tool is not installed.
children.summary: External tool integrations for PINNeAPPle.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.flight
pinneapple_simulation.flight.aero
children.doc:
Quasi-steady aerodynamics of a whole aircraft for flight simulation, from the vortex lattice of
:mod:`pinneapple_design.aero.vlm`.

At every evaluation the lattice of wing + horizontal tail is solved with the local relative air velocity at each
control point (flight velocity, rotation p, q, r and the wind / gust at that point), so the lift, pitching and rolling
moments, the pitch and roll damping, the downwash at the tail, the dihedral effect and the response to a gust that
differs from one wing to the other all come from the same linear potential-flow model. The influence matrix depends
only on the geometry: it is LU-factorised once. Control surfaces rotate the normals of their panels (thin-airfoil
flap effectiveness tau). Forces: Kutta-Joukowski on the bound legs with the local velocity.

Added by component build-up (the lattice has neither): zero-lift drag from the parasite-drag build-up passed in
(``cd0``), induced drag K CL^2 with K from the lattice's Trefftz-plane drag (and McCormick's ground-effect factor), the
vertical tail as a lifting line at its aerodynamic centre (Helmbold lift slope with the effective aspect ratio
1.55 AR for the end-plate effect of fuselage and tailplane; rudder through tau), and the fuselage Munk moments in
pitch and yaw (Raymer, Aircraft Design, 6th ed., eqs. 16.25 and 16.47).

Axes: the lattice uses the airframe axes A (x aft, y right, z up), the dynamics the body axes B (x forward, y right,
z down); B = T (A - cg) with T = diag(-1, 1, -1), a proper rotation, so forces and moments map with T as well.

Limits (quasi-steady): no stall (the angle of attack at the section cl max is reported by the caller), no unsteady
lift build-up (Wagner, Kussner), no downwash lag (Cm_alpha_dot), no aeroelasticity, ground effect on induced drag only.

classes.name: ControlSurface
classes.doc:
Panels of the lattice moved by one control: ``surface`` 0 wing / 1 tail, spanwise range |eta| in
[eta_in, eta_out] of that surface's half-span, ``sign`` per side (+1 symmetric, -1 antisymmetric: right side
gets +delta), chord ratio for the effectiveness. A positive deflection is trailing edge down on the right side.

classes.name: Fin
classes.doc:
Vertical tail as one lifting line: area [m^2], height [m], aerodynamic centre in airframe axes, rudder chord
ratio, quarter-chord sweep [deg].

classes.name: AeroModel
classes.doc: Built by :meth:`from_airframe`; :meth:`loads` gives forces and moments about the CG in body axes.

methods.name: circulation
methods.doc: Bound circulation [m^2/s] for relative air velocities at the control points (N, 3) in A axes.

methods.name: loads
methods.sig: (v_b: np.ndarray, omega_b: np.ndarray, rho: float, wind_b_strips: np.ndarray | None = None, wind_b_fin: np.ndarray | None = None, wind_b_cg: np.ndarray | None = None, deflections: dict[str, float] | None = None, height_agl: float = np.inf, gear_down: bool = False) -> dict[str, object]
methods.doc: Aerodynamic force and moment about the CG in body axes.

methods.name: panel_dcp
methods.doc: Pressure-coefficient jump across each panel, dCp = rho Gamma V |dl| / (q area) = 2 Gamma / (V dx).

methods.name: panel_quads
methods.doc: (N, 4, 3) corner points of every panel in airframe axes (for visualisation of the loading).

functions.name: flap_effectiveness
functions.sig: (cf_c: float, correction: float = 0.85) -> float
functions.doc:
Thin-airfoil flap effectiveness d(alpha_0)/d(delta) for a plain flap of chord ratio cf/c:
tau = 1 - (theta_f - sin theta_f) / pi, cos theta_f = 2 cf/c - 1, times an empirical ``correction`` for real
viscous flow at moderate deflections (an assumption; 0.7-0.9 is the usual range).

functions.name: helmbold_lift_slope
functions.sig: (aspect_ratio: float, sweep_half_chord_deg: float = 0.0, eta: float = 0.95) -> float
functions.doc: Lift-curve slope [/rad] of a finite wing (Helmbold / DATCOM form, Raymer eq. 12.6, subsonic, M ~ 0).

functions.name: fuselage_munk_factor
functions.sig: (wing_qc_fraction: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Raymer's K_fus [per degree] against the wing root quarter-chord position as a fraction of the fuselage length
(Aircraft Design fig. 16.14), interpolated between the two values the aero-optimizer models use (0.012 at 30 %,
0.025 at 45 %): an approximation of the chart, clipped to that range.

functions.name: fuselage_moments
functions.sig: (length: float, max_width: float, volume: float, wing_area: float, mac: float, span: float, depth: float, wing_qc_fraction: float)
functions.doc:
(Cm_alpha, Cn_beta) of the fuselage [/rad]: Raymer eq. 16.25 Cm_a = K_f W_f^2 L_f / (c S) (per degree x
57.3) and eq. 16.47 Cn_b = -1.3 (volume / (S b)) (D_f / W_f) (sign: body axes, a positive Cn_beta is stable,
the fuselage is unstable so the value is negative).

children.summary: Quasi-steady aerodynamics of a whole aircraft for flight simulation, from the vortex lattice of pinneapple_design.aero.vlm.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.flight.aircraft
children.doc:
The aircraft as a 6-DOF rigid body: mass properties, vortex-lattice aerodynamics, engines and landing gear.

:class:`Aircraft` evaluates the total force and moment about the CG for a state (13-vector of
:mod:`.rigid_body`), the controls and a wind field (:mod:`.turbulence`), and the state derivative. Atmosphere: ISA
(:func:`pinneapple_design.aero.airliner3d.isa`) at the geometric altitude above the runway plus ``field_elevation``.

classes.name: Controls
classes.doc:
Positive elevator / rudder / aileron / flap = trailing edge down on the right side (elevator down = nose
down, rudder: trailing edge left = nose left, aileron: right aileron down = roll left), radians; throttle and
brake 0..1; steer = nose-wheel angle [rad], positive turns right.

methods.name: stall_speed
methods.sig: (rho: float = 1.225, clmax: float | None = None) -> float

methods.name: evaluate
methods.sig: (t: float, x: np.ndarray, u: Controls, wind = None, ground_z: float = 0.0) -> dict[str, Any]

methods.name: sample_points
methods.sig: (x: np.ndarray, C: np.ndarray | None = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: NED positions of the wind sample points (lattice strips, fin, CG) for state x.

methods.name: specific_force_at
methods.sig: (ev: dict[str, Any], x: np.ndarray, r_b: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: Specific force [m/s^2] in body axes at body point r_b: f_cg + omega_dot x r + omega x (omega x r).

methods.name: derivative
methods.sig: (t, x, u: Controls, wind = None) -> np.ndarray

children.summary: The aircraft as a 6-DOF rigid body: mass properties, vortex-lattice aerodynamics, engines and landing gear.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.flight.catalog
children.doc:
Four aircraft for flight simulation, built from the library's parametric geometry and weight / drag models.

=====================  ============================================================================================
``light_ga``           Cessna 172-class single piston (the aero optimizer's baseline ``Airframe`` and ``Aircraft``)
``regional_turboprop`` ATR 72-600-class high-wing twin turboprop (planform and gear from the ``turboprop_atr72``
                       geometry-library entry, its mesh for the visuals)
``a320``               A320-class single-aisle twin turbofan (the aero optimizer's baseline ``Airliner``)
``motor_glider``       high-aspect-ratio self-launching motor glider (Stemme S10-class span, area and mass)
=====================  ============================================================================================

Every number is either computed by the library from the geometry (spans, chords, tail sizes, lattice, wing / tail
weights by the Raymer equations the aero optimizer uses, drag build-up) or listed in ``Aircraft.info["published"]``
with its source, or in ``Aircraft.info["assumptions"]`` as an assumption. Nothing here is fitted to a flight test.

classes.name: ExplicitAirframe
classes.doc:
An :class:`Airframe` whose wing height and tails are given explicitly (for a high wing on a T-tail aircraft,
whose tail the parametric sizing rules would put on the fuselage).

functions.name: profile_cd0
functions.sig: (re: float, tc: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Turbulent flat-plate friction (0.074 Re^-0.2) x thickness form factor (1 + 2 t/c + 60 (t/c)^4), both sides,
on the planform area (the glider-wing template's model, :mod:`pinneapple_design.intent.templates.glider_wing`).

functions.name: light_ga
functions.sig: () -> Aircraft

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.flight.control
children.doc:
Pilot and autopilot models: pitch-attitude, altitude, speed, wings-level / heading hold, yaw damper, and the
take-off schedule (ground roll on the centreline, rotation at V_R, climb-out at a target speed).

The inner loops are designed per aircraft from its own control derivatives (:func:`.trim.stability_derivatives`) and
inertias, and scheduled with the dynamic pressure: the elevator for a pitch loop of natural frequency w and damping
zeta is

    d_e = d_e,trim + I_yy (w^2 (theta_c - theta) - 2 zeta w q + w_i int(theta_c - theta)) / (q S c Cm_de)

(roll with I_xx, Cl_da, b; yaw with I_zz, Cn_dr, b). The airframe's own stiffness and damping add to these, so the
closed loop is at least as stiff and damped as designed. Gains use a floor on the dynamic pressure so they stay finite
at low speed (the surfaces then saturate at their limits).

classes.name: InnerLoops
classes.sig: (ac: Aircraft, derivs: dict[str, float], design: LoopDesign | None = None)
classes.doc: Attitude loops of one aircraft: :meth:`elevator`, :meth:`aileron`, :meth:`rudder` give surface increments.

classes.name: StickFixed
classes.sig: (controls: Controls)
classes.doc: Controls frozen at the trim values.

classes.name: Autopilot
classes.sig: (ac: Aircraft, trim, derivs: dict[str, float], design: LoopDesign | None = None, altitude: float | None = None, heading: float | None = None, speed: float | None = None, omega_h: float = 0.25, tau_heading: float = 8.0, washout: float = 2.0, autothrottle: bool = True)
classes.doc:
Altitude hold (through pitch attitude), wings level / heading hold (through bank), yaw damper (washed-out yaw
rate), autothrottle on airspeed, about a trim state. ``loops`` scales the attitude bandwidths.

classes.name: TakeoffPilot
classes.sig: (ac: Aircraft, sched: TakeoffSchedule, derivs: dict[str, float], design: LoopDesign | None = None)
classes.doc:
Full throttle and the take-off flap from brake release; on the ground the nose wheel and the rudder hold the
runway centreline (y = 0 in NED for a north runway, ``runway_heading`` otherwise) and the ailerons keep the wings
level; at airspeed V_R the pitch attitude is commanded up at ``rotation_rate`` to ``theta_rotation``; once
airborne and ``h_climb`` above the runway the pitch attitude is adjusted (at most 2 deg/s) to fly ``V_climb``;
in the air the track is held along the runway by bank and the yaw damper keeps the turn coordinated. Records the
events (t, x, V at V_R, lift-off) in ``events``.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.flight.encounter
children.doc:
Turbulence and gust encounters in flight, and their load-factor statistics.

:func:`turbulence_encounter` trims the aircraft at a speed and altitude, flies it through a wind field (by default a
frozen 3-D von Karman field, so the two wings meet different gusts) stick-fixed or under the autopilot, and returns
the history with :func:`encounter_metrics`: RMS and peak of the vertical load-factor increment at the CG and at each
cabin station, lateral load factor, bank and pitch excursions, airspeed and angle-of-attack excursions.

Checks against closed forms:

* :func:`gust_sensitivity`: the quasi-steady load-factor response to a vertical gust, A = rho V CL_alpha / (2 W/S)
  per m/s of gust; A sigma_w is the RMS increment of a rigid wing that does not move and has no lift lag (an upper
  bound: plunge and pitch relieve it, unsteady lift build-up too);
* :func:`discrete_gust` + :func:`pratt_check`: the full 1-cosine gust of half-length H = 12.5 MAC, compared with the
  Pratt-Walker formula (alleviation factor K_g from the mass ratio mu, which also accounts for unsteady lift build-up
  the quasi-steady model leaves out).

functions.name: gust_sensitivity
functions.sig: (ac: Aircraft, V: float, rho: float, cl_alpha: float) -> float
functions.doc: dn / dw_gust [1/(m/s)] of a fixed wing in quasi-steady flow.

functions.name: stall_angle
functions.sig: (ac: Aircraft, trim_alpha: float, trim_CL: float, cl_alpha: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Angle of attack [rad] at which the linear lift reaches the aircraft's clean CLmax (``ac.clmax_clean``, an
assumption of the catalog): alpha_trim + (CLmax - CL_trim) / CL_alpha. Beyond it the linear lattice is outside
its validity (no stall in the model).

functions.name: encounter_metrics
functions.sig: (ac: Aircraft, hist: FlightHistory, t_skip: float = 5.0, alpha_stall: float | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Statistics after ``t_skip``. With ``alpha_stall`` [rad] the run is also checked against the model's validity:
the fraction of time above the stall angle and ``departed`` (bank beyond 90 deg or alpha 10 deg past stall), in
which case the numbers describe a loss of control the quasi-steady linear model cannot represent.

functions.name: turbulence_encounter
functions.sig: (ac: Aircraft, V: float, altitude: float, spec: TurbulenceSpec | None = None, wind = None, duration: float = 60.0, dt: float = 0.01, controller: str = 'autopilot', field: str = '3d', seed: int = 0, record_gamma: bool = False, record_every: int = 1, design: LoopDesign | None = None, t_skip: float = 5.0)

functions.name: discrete_gust
functions.sig: (ac: Aircraft, V: float, altitude: float, U: float, H: float | None = None, duration: float | None = None, dt: float = 0.005)
functions.doc:
Stick-fixed response to an up-gust of amplitude U [m/s] (full 1-cosine, half-length H, default 12.5 MAC)
starting 2 s ahead of the aircraft. Returns (history, dnz_max).

functions.name: pratt_check
functions.sig: (ac: Aircraft, V: float, altitude: float, U_de: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Simulated peak dn for a 12.5-MAC 1-cosine gust against the Pratt-Walker formula at the same equivalent gust
and speed. The model is quasi-steady, so its peak sits between Pratt (with K_g) and the unalleviated value.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.flight.gear
children.doc:
Landing-gear contact with a flat runway: spring-damper legs with rolling, braking and tyre side forces.

Each leg is a vertical spring-damper at a wheel contact point fixed in the airframe (its unloaded position). With
penetration d of that point below the runway (NED z = ``ground_z``) and its vertical velocity d_dot, the normal force
is N = max(0, k d + c d_dot). Along the wheel heading (the body x axis, turned by the steering angle for a steerable
leg) the tyre gives a rolling (and braking) resistance -(mu_roll + brake mu_brake) N, across it a side force
-mu_side N tanh(slip / slip_ref) (slip the tyre slip angle: a linear cornering stiffness mu_side N / slip_ref that
saturates at the friction limit). Both are regularised near zero speed so the aircraft can stand still.

Defaults (assumptions, not measured tyre data): mu_roll 0.02 (dry hard runway, brakes off), mu_brake 0.40, mu_side
0.7, slip_ref 0.10 rad, static compression 0.25 m and damping ratio 0.6 of the sprung mass (:func:`size_gear`).

functions.name: size_gear
functions.sig: (legs: Sequence[GearLeg], mass: float, cg: np.ndarray, static_compression: float = 0.25, zeta: float = 0.6, g: float = 9.80665) -> list[GearLeg]
functions.doc:
Spring and damper of every leg so that the static compression under its share of the weight is
``static_compression``; the shares come from moment balance about the CG in x (nose / mains) and split equally
between legs at the same x station (left / right).

functions.name: gear_forces
functions.sig: (legs: Sequence[GearLeg], x: np.ndarray, C: np.ndarray, cg: np.ndarray, steer: float = 0.0, brake: float = 0.0, ground_z: float = 0.0)
functions.doc: (F_b, M_b, normal loads list) of all legs for state x (13-vector) and body->NED matrix C.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.flight.mass
children.doc:
Mass, centre of gravity and inertia tensor from a component breakdown.

Each :class:`Component` has a mass, a centroid in airframe axes (x aft, y right, z up) and its own inertia about its
centroid (from simple shapes: point, slender rod, thin plate, solid cylinder). :func:`mass_properties` sums them by
the parallel-axis theorem and returns the inertia tensor in body axes (x forward, y right, z down) about the CG.
:func:`balance` moves one component along x so the CG lands at a chosen station (the loading of the aircraft).

functions.name: point
functions.sig: (name, mass, center) -> Component

functions.name: rod
functions.sig: (name, mass, center, length, axis: int = 0) -> Component
functions.doc: Slender rod of ``length`` along airframe axis ``axis``.

functions.name: plate
functions.sig: (name, mass, center, span, chord, taper: float = 1.0) -> Component
functions.doc:
Thin plate in the x-y plane: ``span`` along y, ``chord`` along x (a wing, a tailplane, wing fuel). With
``taper`` < 1 the mass per unit span follows the local chord (linear taper from the root to the tips):
Ixx = m (b/2)^2 (1 + 3 taper) / (6 (1 + taper)), m b^2 / 12 for a rectangular plate.

functions.name: fin_plate
functions.sig: (name, mass, center, height, chord) -> Component
functions.doc: Thin plate in the x-z plane (a vertical tail).

functions.name: cylinder
functions.sig: (name, mass, center, length, radius, shell: bool = False) -> Component
functions.doc: Cylinder along x (a fuselage, a nacelle); ``shell=True`` for a thin-walled one.

functions.name: mass_properties
functions.sig: (components: Sequence[Component]) -> tuple[float, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: (mass, cg in airframe axes, inertia about the CG in body axes).

functions.name: balance
functions.sig: (components: Sequence[Component], x_target: float, movable: str) -> list[Component]
functions.doc: Shift the component named ``movable`` along x so that the CG is at ``x_target`` (airframe axes).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.flight.propulsion
children.doc:
Engines for flight simulation: thrust against speed and altitude, and where it acts.

* :class:`Turbofan`: installed thrust lapse of a high-bypass turbofan, Mattingly (Aircraft Engine Design, 2nd ed.,
  2002, eq. 2.45a): T / T_SL = delta_0 (1 - 0.49 sqrt(M)), delta_0 = p_t / p_SL (total pressure ratio).
* :class:`Propeller`: shaft power P(h) (piston: Gagg-Ferrar P/P_SL = 1.132 sigma - 0.132; turboprop: sigma^0.75, an
  assumption for a flat-rated engine below its flat-rating altitude is not modelled) driving a propeller with
  efficiency eta: T = eta P / sqrt(V^2 + V0^2), V0 = eta P / T_static, so T -> T_static at rest and eta P / V in
  flight; static thrust from momentum theory with a figure of merit: T_static = (FM P)^(2/3) (2 rho A)^(1/3).

Positions in airframe axes (x aft, y right, z up); the thrust acts along the body x axis tilted by ``cant_deg``
(nose-up positive). Propeller torque, P-factor and slipstream are not modelled.

methods.sig: (V: float, rho: float, a: float, throttle: float = 1.0) -> float

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.flight.rigid_body
children.doc:
6-DOF rigid-body equations in body axes with a unit quaternion for the attitude.

Frames: earth NED (x north, y east, z down, flat non-rotating earth), body (x forward, y right wing, z down). The
attitude quaternion q = [q0, q1, q2, q3] (scalar first) rotates body vectors into NED: v_ned = C(q) v_body. Euler
angles (yaw psi, pitch theta, roll phi, 3-2-1 order) are only an output: the quaternion has no singularity at
theta = +-90 deg, and :func:`quat_to_euler` stays finite there (it clips the pitch sine and splits yaw / roll by the
quaternion, not by the division that blows up).

State vector (13): position NED [m], velocity in body axes (u, v, w) [m/s], quaternion, angular velocity in body axes
(p, q, r) [rad/s]:

    x_dot = C(q) v_b
    v_b_dot = F_b / m - omega x v_b              (F_b includes gravity)
    q_dot = 1/2 q (x) [0, omega] - k (|q|^2 - 1) q
    omega_dot = I^-1 (M_b - omega x I omega)

The last term of q_dot pulls the quaternion back to unit norm (Baumgarte-type); :func:`rk4_step` also renormalises.

functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray

functions.doc: Rotation matrix body -> NED (columns: the body axes in NED).

functions.name: euler_to_quat
functions.sig: (phi: float, theta: float, psi: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Roll, pitch, yaw [rad] (3-2-1: yaw, then pitch, then roll) -> quaternion body -> NED.

(phi, theta, psi) [rad]. At the gimbal lock (|theta| = 90 deg) only phi -+ psi is defined: the split puts it
all in psi (phi = 0), so the result stays finite and round-trips the attitude.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.flight.simulate
children.doc:
Time integration of an :class:`~.aircraft.Aircraft` with a controller and a wind field, and the recorded history.

    hist = simulate(ac, x0, controller, t_end=30.0, dt=0.01, wind=field)

``controller(t, x, last)`` returns :class:`~.aircraft.Controls` held over the step (zero-order hold); ``last`` is the
previous step's evaluation (or None). RK4 with quaternion renormalisation. Everything a figure, a table or a 3-D scene
needs is recorded per step (or every ``record_every`` steps): state, Euler angles, airspeed, alpha, beta, load factor
at the CG and at the cabin stations, gear loads, controls, wind at the CG and, when ``record_gamma``, the lattice
circulation (for the surface loading in the viewer).

functions.sig: (ac: Aircraft, x0: np.ndarray, controller: Callable[[float, np.ndarray, dict | None], Controls], t_end: float, dt: float = 0.01, wind = None, record_every: int = 1, record_gamma: bool = False, stop: Callable[[float, np.ndarray, dict], bool] | None = None, t0: float = 0.0, hold_wind: bool = True) -> FlightHistory
functions.doc:
``hold_wind``: sample the wind at the aircraft's sample points at the start of each step and at their
predicted end-of-step positions, and interpolate linearly in time over the RK stages (two field evaluations per
step instead of four; second order in the step). False samples the field at every stage.

functions.doc:
Energy and momentum consistency of the integrator with the aerodynamics, engines and gear off (a body in
vacuum under gravity, spinning): kinetic + potential energy and the angular momentum in NED are conserved.
