children.name: pinneapple_simulation.flight.takeoff
children.doc:
Take-off: ground roll, rotation at V_R, lift-off, climb-out over the 35 ft screen, and a closed-form check.

:func:`simulate_takeoff` runs the 6-DOF model from brake release (on its gear at rest, full throttle) with the
:class:`~.control.TakeoffPilot` and any wind field (crosswind, gusts, turbulence); :func:`takeoff_metrics` reads off
the ground-roll distance, lift-off speed, pitch attitude and angle of attack at lift-off, the distance to 35 ft (lowest
wheel), the speed there, the climb gradient after the screen, tail and wing-tip clearances and the lateral deviation.

:func:`raymer_takeoff` is the closed-form estimate of Raymer (Aircraft Design: A Conceptual Approach, section 17.8):

    S_G  = 1 / (2 g K_A) ln((K_T + K_A V_LOF^2) / K_T),  K_T = T/W - mu,  K_A = rho / (2 W/S) (mu CL - CD0 - K CL^2)
    S_R  = t_R V_LOF                                     (rotation: ~1 s small aircraft, ~3 s large)
    S_TR = R sin(gamma_climb),  R = V_TR^2 / (0.2 g),  V_TR = 1.15 V_stall,  h_TR = R (1 - cos gamma_climb)
    S_C  = (h_obs - h_TR) / tan(gamma_climb)             (or S_TR = sqrt(R^2 - (R - h_obs)^2) if h_TR > h_obs)

with the thrust taken at 0.7 V_LOF and the ground-roll CL, CD0, K from the same aircraft model.

functions.name: default_schedule
functions.sig: (ac: Aircraft, kind: str = 'transport') -> TakeoffSchedule
functions.doc:
V_R = 1.05 x the take-off-flap stall speed (CLmax_TO of the aircraft), climb at 1.25 V_s (between V2 = 1.13
V_SR and V2 + 10 kt for a transport), rotation at 3 deg/s to 12 deg (transport) or 6 deg/s to 11 deg (light); an
assumption of a typical technique, not a certified schedule.

functions.name: takeoff_derivatives
functions.sig: (ac: Aircraft, V: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc: Control derivatives for the pilot's gain design: about a trimmed climb-out at V with the take-off flap.

functions.name: simulate_takeoff
functions.sig: (ac: Aircraft, schedule: TakeoffSchedule | None = None, wind = None, t_max: float = 90.0, dt: float = 0.01, h_stop: float = 400 * FT, design: LoopDesign | None = None, record_gamma: bool = False, record_every: int = 1, kind: str = 'transport') -> FlightHistory
functions.doc:
Simulate the whole take-off of the aircraft, from the ground equilibrium to the stopping height ``h_stop``;
returns the flight history.

functions.name: takeoff_metrics
functions.sig: (ac: Aircraft, hist: FlightHistory) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
The take-off metrics from a flight history: distances, speeds and times (or ``lifted_off: False`` when it did
not lift off).

functions.name: raymer_takeoff
functions.sig: (ac: Aircraft, V_LOF: float | None = None, mu: float = 0.02, t_rotation: float = 3.0, h_obstacle: float = SCREEN, theta_ground: float = 0.0) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Raymer's closed-form take-off distance with this aircraft's thrust, lift and drag (see the module text).
``V_LOF`` defaults to 1.1 V_stall (take-off flap). Ground-roll lift and drag from the lattice at the ground
attitude with the take-off flap and the gear down, ground effect on the induced drag at the wing height.

functions.name: raymer_variants
functions.sig: (ac: Aircraft, metrics: dict[str, float], kind: str = 'light') -> dict[str, dict[str, float]]
functions.doc:
The two closed-form references the take-off results quote (Raymer, Aircraft Design, sec. 17.8):

* ``raymer_1p1Vs``: V_LOF = 1.1 V_stall and Raymer's rotation time, 1 s for light aircraft, 3 s for transports;
* ``raymer_sim_VLOF``: the simulated lift-off speed and rotation time (``metrics`` from :func:`takeoff_metrics`),
  so only the closed-form ground roll, transition and climb differ from the simulation.

Each carries ``sim_over_raymer``: the simulated distance to the 35 ft screen over the closed form.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.flight.turbulence
children.doc:
Atmospheric turbulence and gusts for flight simulation (MIL-F-8785C / MIL-HDBK-1797).

Intensities and scale lengths (:func:`turbulence_spec`):

* low altitude, h < 1000 ft: sigma_w = 0.1 W20, sigma_u = sigma_v = sigma_w / (0.177 + 0.000823 h)^0.4,
  L_w = h, L_u = L_v = h / (0.177 + 0.000823 h)^1.2 (h, L in ft; W20 the wind speed at 20 ft: 15 / 30 / 45 kt for
  light / moderate / severe);
* medium / high altitude, h > 2000 ft: isotropic, sigma from the probability-of-exceedance chart (light 1e-2, moderate
  1e-3, severe 1e-5), L = 1750 ft (Dryden) or 2500 ft (von Karman);
* in between, intensities and lengths are interpolated linearly between their values at 1000 ft and 2000 ft.

The scale lengths follow MIL-F-8785C (L_u = L_v at low altitude, all equal above 2000 ft). MIL-HDBK-1797 writes the
same spectra with half lengths for v and w (L_v -> 2 L_v); the two forms are the same functions of frequency.

Spectra (one-sided in the spatial frequency Omega [rad/m], integral over 0..inf = sigma^2, :func:`psd`):

    Dryden       Phi_u = s_u^2 2L_u/pi / (1 + (L_u W)^2)
                 Phi_v = s_v^2 L_v/pi (1 + 3 (L_v W)^2) / (1 + (L_v W)^2)^2            (w as v with L_w)
    von Karman   Phi_u = s_u^2 2L_u/pi / (1 + (1.339 L_u W)^2)^(5/6)
                 Phi_v = s_v^2 L_v/pi (1 + 8/3 (1.339 L_v W)^2) / (1 + (1.339 L_v W)^2)^(11/6)

Generators, all frozen in space (Taylor's hypothesis: the aircraft flies through a field that does not change while
it crosses it), validated against the target spectra and variances in ``tests/test_flight_turbulence.py``:

* :class:`FrozenLine`: one realisation along the flight path by spectral synthesis (random phases, exact spectral
  amplitudes), any of the two forms; the same gust is met by the wing and, later, by the tail;
* :class:`DrydenFilter`: the MIL-HDBK-1797 forming filters driven by white noise, discretised exactly (Van Loan), for
  streaming / real-time use at one point;
* :class:`FrozenField3D`: an isotropic, divergence-free 3-D von Karman field from random Fourier modes (Kraichnan
  1970), evaluated at any points: a large aircraft sees different gusts on each wing (rolling moment from the
  spanwise gust gradient);
* :class:`DiscreteGust`: the 1-cosine gust (MIL-F-8785C ramp form, or the full 1-cosine shape of length 2H used for
  the Pratt formula and CS-25.341);
* :class:`ShearWind`: mean wind with the MIL-F-8785C logarithmic profile near the ground.

Every field returns the wind velocity in the earth frame NED (x north, y east, z down) in m/s at points given in the
same frame, from ``velocity(t, points)``. The turbulence components u (longitudinal), v (lateral) and w (vertical) are
taken along the flight path heading ``heading_deg`` (u horizontal along it, v to its right, w down).

Sources: MIL-F-8785C (1980), Military Specification, Flying Qualities of Piloted Airplanes, section 3.7; MIL-HDBK-1797
(1997), Flying Qualities of Piloted Aircraft, section 4.9 and appendix; the high-altitude intensity chart (MIL-F-8785C
Figure 7) as tabulated in ``HIGH_ALTITUDE_SIGMA_FT_S``. Random Fourier modes: Kraichnan, R. H. (1970), Phys. Fluids 13,
22-31; Smirnov, Shi and Celik (2001), J. Fluids Eng. 123, 359-371.

classes.name: TurbulenceSpec
classes.doc:
RMS intensities [m/s] and scale lengths [m] of the three turbulence components, and the spectral form.

Attributes
----------
sigma_u, sigma_v, sigma_w : float [m/s]
    RMS gust intensities (longitudinal, lateral, vertical).
L_u, L_v, L_w : float [m]
    Scale lengths.
model : str
    ``dryden`` or ``von_karman``.
altitude : float [m]
    Altitude the spec was made for.
severity : str
    ``light`` / ``moderate`` / ``severe``.

classes.name: WindField
classes.doc: A wind field: ``velocity(t, points)`` -> (M, 3) NED wind [m/s] at (M, 3) NED points [m].

classes.name: ConstantWind
classes.doc: Uniform steady wind ``ned`` [m/s] (the velocity of the air, e.g. (0, -10, 0) blows towards the west).

classes.name: ShearWind
classes.doc:
Mean wind with the MIL-F-8785C logarithmic profile W(h) = W20 ln(h / z0) / ln(20 ft / z0); ``from_deg`` the
direction the wind comes from (meteorological, degrees from north), ``z0`` the roughness length (0.15 ft = 0.046 m
for category C flight phases, MIL-F-8785C 3.7.2.1). Below z0 the wind is zero; ``ground_z`` is the NED z of the
ground (h = ground_z - z).

classes.name: FrozenLine
classes.doc:
One frozen realisation of the three components along a straight line through ``origin`` with heading
``heading_deg``, length ``length`` [m] at spacing ``dx`` [m], by spectral synthesis: each Fourier coefficient has
the exact target amplitude sqrt(Phi dOmega) and a random phase, so the periodogram of the whole line equals the
target spectrum and the variance equals the integral of the spectrum over the represented band. The line is
periodic with period ``length``; take it several scale lengths long. Points off the line take the value at their
projection on it (no lateral variation: use :class:`FrozenField3D` for that).

methods.name: components
methods.doc: (len(s), 3) u, v, w at path coordinates s [m] (linear interpolation, periodic).

classes.name: DrydenFilter
classes.sig: (spec: TurbulenceSpec, V: float, dt: float, seed: int | None = 0)
classes.doc:
MIL-HDBK-1797 Dryden forming filters, driven by white noise, for one point flying at true airspeed V:

    H_u(s) = s_u sqrt(2 L_u / (pi V)) / (1 + L_u/V s)
    H_v(s) = s_v sqrt(L_v / (pi V)) (1 + sqrt(3) L_v/V s) / (1 + L_v/V s)^2        (w as v)

The white noise has a two-sided spectral density pi so the output has the one-sided MIL spectrum; the state-space
filters are discretised exactly for the step ``dt`` (Van Loan), so the variance is exact at any step. ``step()``
returns the next (u, v, w) sample in path axes.

methods.name: series
methods.doc: (n, 3) consecutive samples (the same sequence as n calls of :meth:`step`).

classes.name: FrozenField3D
classes.doc:
Isotropic, divergence-free von Karman turbulence in 3-D from random Fourier modes:
u(x) = sum_n a_n sigma_n cos(k_n . x + phi_n), with |k_n| on log-spaced shells between ``k_min`` and ``k_max``,
directions uniform on the sphere (``n_dirs`` per shell), sigma_n a random unit vector normal to k_n (so
div u = 0) and a_n = 2 sqrt(E(k_n) dk_n / n_dirs) (kinetic energy = integral of E over the band).

The scale length is ``spec.L_w`` and the reference intensity ``spec.sigma_w``; the u, v, w components (path axes
of ``heading_deg``) are then scaled by sigma_u / sigma_w and sigma_v / sigma_w (this keeps the low-altitude
intensities but not their different scale lengths: an assumption, isotropy holds above 2000 ft). ``k_max``
defaults to pi / (2 * dx_min) with ``dx_min`` the smallest length the aircraft must resolve (a chord); the
fraction of the variance in the band is ``variance_fraction``. Evaluates at any (M, 3) points: cost M x modes.

methods.name: components
methods.doc: (M, 3) u, v, w at points given in path axes (u along the heading, v right, w down) [m].

classes.name: DiscreteGust
classes.doc:
1-cosine gust met by the aircraft when its path coordinate s (along ``heading_deg`` from ``origin``) passes
``start``. ``shape="ramp"``: MIL-F-8785C 3.7.4, v = V_m/2 (1 - cos(pi x / d_m)) for 0 <= x <= d_m and V_m beyond;
``shape="full"``: v = V_m/2 (1 - cos(pi x / H)) for 0 <= x <= 2H and 0 elsewhere (CS-25.341, Pratt), with
H = ``length``. ``direction``: unit vector in path axes (u, v, w), (0, 0, -1) an up-gust.

functions.name: turbulence_spec
functions.sig: (altitude: float, severity: str = 'moderate', model: str = 'von_karman', *, w20: float | None = None, probability: float | None = None) -> TurbulenceSpec
functions.doc:
Intensities and scale lengths at ``altitude`` [m] (above ground level for the low-altitude model) for a
severity ``light`` / ``moderate`` / ``severe``. ``w20`` [m/s] overrides the 20 ft wind of the severity (low
altitude), ``probability`` the exceedance probability (medium / high altitude, a key of
``HIGH_ALTITUDE_SIGMA_FT_S``).

functions.name: psd
functions.sig: (spec: TurbulenceSpec, Omega, component: str = 'w') -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: One-sided spatial PSD [(m/s)^2 / (rad/m)] of component u, v or w at spatial frequency Omega [rad/m].

functions.name: psd_temporal
functions.sig: (spec: TurbulenceSpec, omega, V: float, component: str = 'w') -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: One-sided temporal PSD [(m/s)^2 / (rad/s)] seen at true airspeed V (frozen field: Omega = omega / V).

functions.name: welch_psd
functions.sig: (x: np.ndarray, d: float, nseg: int = 16)
functions.doc:
One-sided PSD of a sampled signal against angular frequency (rad per unit of the sample spacing ``d``):
Welch's method with a Hann window, 50 % overlap. Returns (Omega, Phi) with integral of Phi dOmega = variance.

functions.name: path_axes
functions.sig: (heading_deg: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Rows: the u (along the heading, horizontal), v (to the right) and w (down) unit vectors in NED.

functions.name: von_karman_energy
functions.sig: (k, L: float, sigma: float = 1.0)
functions.doc:
Isotropic von Karman energy spectrum E(k) = C sigma^2 L (a L k)^4 / (1 + (a L k)^2)^(17/6) [m^3/s^2],
a = 1.339, with C fixed numerically so that the kinetic energy (integral of E) is 3 sigma^2 / 2. Its
one-dimensional longitudinal and transverse spectra are then the MIL von Karman Phi_u and Phi_w with scale length
L (checked by quadrature in ``tests/test_flight_turbulence.py``).

functions.name: isotropic_line_spectra
functions.sig: (k1, L: float, sigma: float = 1.0)
functions.doc:
One-sided longitudinal (F11) and transverse (F22) spectra [(m/s)^2 / (rad/m)] of the isotropic field with
the energy spectrum :func:`von_karman_energy`, by quadrature of E(k) (Batchelor 1953):
F11(k1) = int_k1^inf E(k)/k (1 - k1^2/k^2) dk, F22(k1) = 1/2 int_k1^inf E(k)/k (1 + k1^2/k^2) dk.

functions.name: pratt_gust_load
functions.sig: (wing_loading: float, cl_alpha: float, mac: float, U_de: float, V_e: float, rho0: float = 1.225, rho: float = 1.225, g: float = 9.80665)
functions.doc:
Pratt-Walker gust load factor increment (FAR 25.341 before amendment 25-86, CS-23.341):

    mu = 2 (W/S) / (rho c a g),  K_g = 0.88 mu / (5.3 + mu),  dn = K_g rho0 U_de V_e a / (2 W/S)

with W/S [N/m^2], a [/rad], c the mean geometric chord [m], U_de and V_e equivalent speeds [m/s] and rho the
density at altitude. Returns dict(mu, K_g, dn, dn_unalleviated).

Flight dynamics: a 6-DOF rigid aircraft driven by vortex-lattice aerodynamics, thrust, gravity and landing-gear
contact, with trim, stability derivatives, a pilot / autopilot, take-off and turbulence-encounter simulations, and
3-D scenes of the flights.

    from pinneapple_simulation import flight
    ac = flight.catalog.build("a320")                       # also light_ga, regional_turboprop, motor_glider
    tr = flight.trim(ac, V=128.0, altitude=3000.0)
    hist = flight.simulate_takeoff(ac)                      # ground roll, rotation at V_R, climb over 35 ft
    m = flight.takeoff_metrics(ac, hist); cf = flight.raymer_takeoff(ac)
    hist, m, *_ = flight.turbulence_encounter(ac, 128.0, 3000.0, flight.turbulence_spec(3000.0, "severe"))
    scene = flight.visuals.flight_scene(ac, hist)           # pp.viz.web_viewer(scene, "viewer/") / Blender

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.geophysics
pinneapple_simulation.geophysics.energy_balance
children.doc:
Two-layer energy-balance model of global-mean surface warming (Held et al. 2010, J. Climate 23:2418; Geoffroy et
al. 2013a, J. Climate 26:1841; efficacy of deep-ocean heat uptake: Geoffroy et al. 2013b, J. Climate 26:1859):

    C  dT/dt  = F - lambda T - eps gamma (T - T0)        (upper ocean + atmosphere + land)
    C0 dT0/dt = gamma (T - T0)                            (deep ocean)

Units: T in K, F in W m-2, time in years, heat capacities in W yr m-2 K-1, lambda and gamma in W m-2 K-1.

* :meth:`TwoLayerEBM.simulate` integrates exactly for forcing that is constant over each step (matrix exponential), so
  annual forcing series need no small step;
* :meth:`TwoLayerEBM.step_response` is the closed-form response to an abrupt forcing step: a fast mode (years) and
  a slow mode (centuries), as in Geoffroy et al. (2013a);
* :meth:`TwoLayerEBM.ecs` and :meth:`TwoLayerEBM.tcr` give the equilibrium climate sensitivity F2x/lambda and the
  transient response at year 70 of a 1 %/yr CO2 increase;
* :func:`fit_two_layer` estimates the parameters from a temperature series and its forcing by least squares, with
  standard errors from the Jacobian (an inverse problem: observed warming -> feedback and ocean heat uptake).
  Identifiability: an abrupt-forcing run constrains every parameter; a historical ramp constrains the transient
  response (TCR) well but trades lambda against the deep-ocean capacity, so lambda and ECS come back with large
  errors. The returned correlation matrix shows it.

methods.name: simulate
methods.sig: (forcing: Sequence[float], dt: float = 1.0, T_init: float = 0.0, T0_init: float = 0.0) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
methods.doc:
Exact integration with forcing[k] held over [k dt, (k+1) dt]. Returns T and T0 at the step ends, and the
top-of-atmosphere imbalance N = F - lambda T - (eps - 1) gamma (T - T0).

methods.name: modes
methods.doc:
Time scales and amplitudes of the fast and slow modes of the step response, from the eigen-decomposition
of the system matrix (valid for any efficacy): T(t) = T_eq [1 - a_f exp(-t/tau_f) - a_s exp(-t/tau_s)], with
a_f + a_s = 1. For eps = 1 these are the time scales and amplitudes of Geoffroy et al. (2013a).

methods.name: step_response
methods.doc: Surface warming after an abrupt, constant forcing F applied at t = 0 (closed form, two exponentials).

methods.name: tcr
methods.doc: Warming at year 70 of a 1 %/yr CO2 increase (forcing grows linearly to F2x at year 70).

functions.name: fit_two_layer
functions.sig: (T_obs: Sequence[float], forcing: Sequence[float], dt: float = 1.0, fit_eps: bool = False, guess: TwoLayerEBM | None = None, sigma: float | None = None) -> dict[str, object]
functions.doc:
Least-squares fit of (lambda, gamma, C, C0[, eps]) to a warming series driven by ``forcing``.

Parameters are fitted in log space (all positive). Returns the fitted model, standard errors (from J^T J and the
residual variance, or ``sigma`` if the observation error is known), the residual RMS and the derived ECS and TCR
with first-order (delta-method) errors.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.geophysics.richards
children.doc:
Unsaturated flow in soil: the Richards equation in 1-D with the classical water-retention / conductivity models.

Retention and conductivity (h = pressure head [L], negative when unsaturated; Se = effective saturation):

* :class:`VanGenuchten` (van Genuchten 1980, SSSAJ 44:892) with Mualem's conductivity (Mualem 1976, WRR 12:513):
  Se = [1 + |alpha h|^n]^-m, m = 1 - 1/n;  K = Ks Se^l [1 - (1 - Se^(1/m))^m]^2, l = 0.5.
* :class:`BrooksCorey` (Brooks & Corey 1964, Hydrology Paper 3): Se = (h_b/h)^lambda for h < h_b;
  K = Ks Se^((2 + 3 lambda)/lambda).
* :class:`ClappHornberger` (Clapp & Hornberger 1978, WRR 14:601; the same power laws as Campbell 1974, Soil Sci.
  117:311): theta/theta_s = (psi_s/h)^(1/b); K = Ks (theta/theta_s)^(2b + 3).
* :class:`Gardner` (Gardner 1958, Soil Sci. 85:228): K = Ks exp(alpha h), Se = exp(alpha h); the model with an exact
  steady infiltration profile (:func:`gardner_steady_infiltration`), used to verify the solver.

Solver (:func:`solve_richards`): mixed-form (theta-h) equation, z positive upward,

    d theta/dt = d/dz [ K(h) (dh/dz + 1) ] - S(z, t),

cell-centred finite volumes, backward Euler in time and the modified Picard iteration of Celia, Bouloutas & Zarba
(1990, WRR 26:1483). The mixed form makes the scheme mass-conservative: the mass-balance ratio reported with each
result is 1 to the Picard tolerance, unlike the h-form. Boundary conditions: prescribed head, prescribed flux
(positive upward), or free drainage (unit gradient) at the bottom. Time step adapts to the Picard iteration count.

methods.name: C
methods.doc: Specific moisture capacity d theta / dh.

classes.name: Boundary
classes.doc:
``kind``: "head" (value = h), "flux" (value = Darcy flux, positive upward, i.e. infiltration < 0) or
"free_drainage" (bottom only). ``value`` may be a function of time.

functions.name: solve_richards
functions.sig: (soil, depth: float, n_cells: int, h0: float | np.ndarray, t_end: float, top: Boundary, bottom: Boundary, dt0: float = 1.0, dt_min: float = 1e-06, dt_max: float | None = None, t_out: np.ndarray | None = None, tol: float = 1e-06, max_picard: int = 30, sink: Callable[[np.ndarray, float], np.ndarray] | None = None) -> RichardsResult
functions.doc:
Column from z = -depth (bottom) to z = 0 (surface). ``h0``: initial head (scalar or per cell, bottom first).
``sink(z, t)``: volumetric sink [1/T] (root water uptake). Returns profiles at ``t_out`` (default: 11 times).

functions.name: gardner_steady_infiltration
functions.sig: (soil: Gardner, z_above_table: np.ndarray, q0: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Exact steady head profile above a water table (h = 0 at z = 0) under a constant infiltration rate q0 > 0
(downward) for the Gardner model: K(z) = q0 + (Ks - q0) exp(-alpha z), h = ln(K/Ks)/alpha.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.geophysics.sphere_shallow_water
children.doc:
Shallow-water equations on the rotating sphere: spectral-transform solver and the Williamson et al. test suite.

Model: vorticity-divergence form on a Gaussian grid with triangular truncation T_N (the spectral-transform method of
the NCAR shallow-water model, Hack & Jakob 1992, NCAR/TN-343+STR):

    dzeta/dt = -div(eta V)                         eta = zeta + f
    ddelta/dt = k.curl(eta V) - lap(Phi + Phi_s + |V|^2/2)
    dPhi/dt  = -div(Phi V)                          Phi = g h (fluid layer), Phi_s = g h_s (topography)

Transforms use normalised associated Legendre functions (orthonormal on [-1, 1]) and Gauss-Legendre quadrature, so
the analysis of grid products is exact up to the 2N alias-free limit (nlat >= (3N+1)/2, nlon >= 3N+1). Divergence and
curl of a flux vector are analysed directly (integration by parts against the Legendre derivative), which keeps the
global mean of Phi exactly constant: mass is conserved to round-off. Time stepping is classical RK4 (explicit; the time
step follows the gravity-wave CFL, see :func:`stable_dt`), with optional implicit del^4 hyper-diffusion.

Test cases (Williamson, Drake, Hack, Jakob & Swarztrauber 1992, J. Comput. Phys. 102:211-224):
* case 2: steady zonal geostrophic flow (exact solution = initial state), optionally rotated by alpha;
* case 5: zonal flow over an isolated mountain (no analytic solution);
* case 6: Rossby-Haurwitz wave of wavenumber 4.

Diagnostics: total mass, total energy and potential enstrophy, which the continuous equations conserve, and the
normalised l1, l2, l_inf height errors of Williamson et al. (their eqs. 82-84).

classes.name: SphericalHarmonics
classes.sig: (trunc: int, nlat: int | None = None, nlon: int | None = None, radius: float = EARTH['a'])
classes.doc:
Scalar and vector spectral transforms for triangular truncation ``trunc`` on a Gaussian grid.

Earth-system building blocks, each verified against an exact solution or a standard test:

* ``sphere_shallow_water``: spectral-transform shallow-water model on the sphere and the Williamson et al. (1992)
  test cases 2, 5 and 6, with mass / energy / potential-enstrophy diagnostics;
* ``richards``: 1-D Richards equation (mixed form, Celia et al. 1990) with van Genuchten-Mualem, Brooks-Corey,
  Clapp-Hornberger/Campbell and Gardner soils;
* ``energy_balance``: two-layer energy-balance model of global warming (Held et al. 2010; Geoffroy et al. 2013) with
  exact integration, closed-form step response, ECS/TCR and parameter fitting.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.granular
pinneapple_simulation.granular.bonds
children.doc:
Bonded elements that break: a brittle agglomerate made of rigid bodies joined by beams.

This is the ``bonded elements`` half of the multiphysics DEM picture: a block, a tablet, a rock or an ore particle is
built from bodies whose pairs are joined by a short beam with axial, shear, bending and torsional stiffness
(Potyondy & Cundall 2004, *A bonded-particle model for rock*, Int. J. Rock Mech. Min. Sci. 41:1329-1364, which is
the parallel-bond formulation this follows).  A bond carries a load until its extreme-fibre stress passes the
material strength and then disappears -- and because the bodies are still there, a broken aggregate keeps moving as
fragments instead of vanishing.

Fragments are the connected components of the intact bond graph (union-find), reported by mass and by the sieve size
a comminution engineer expects: the equivalent-sphere diameter ``d = (6 V / pi)^(1/3)`` of each fragment, and its
``P80``.  That is what turns a DEM run into a product curve (see
:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.granular.equipment` for the mill that produces it).

The bond frame is fixed at creation (small-strain assumption), which is the usual bonded-particle idealisation: the
element size is small compared with the deformation at which the bond fails, so the error stays well below the
scatter in the strength parameters.

classes.sig: (E: float = 2000000000.0, nu: float = 0.25, sigma_max: float = 2000000.0, tau_max: float = 1000000.0, radius_ratio: float = 0.5) -> None
classes.doc: Elastic and strength parameters of the bond (not of the bodies).

functions.doc: Turn the ``add_bond`` records into arrays of bond geometry, stiffness and strength.

functions.doc: Forces and torques every intact bond applies to its two bodies, and the break decision for this step.

functions.name: fragment_ids

functions.doc: Connected components of the intact-bond graph (``-1`` for bodies with no bond at all).

functions.doc: 80 % passing size: the diameter below which 80 % of the mass lies (linear interpolation).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.granular.contacts
children.doc:
Contact materials, force laws and walls for the granular solver.

Two normal-force laws are available and they differ in *what the overlap measures*:

``volume`` (default, and the only one for polyhedral particles)
    ``F_n = k_v * V_overlap`` -- the force is proportional to the volume two bodies share, exactly as it is in the
    volume-based contact model of the GPU DEM literature (Govender et al., the BLAZE-DEM line of work).  A corner
    entering a face, or two faces lying on each other, then behave the same way per unit shared volume, which a
    penetration-depth law does not give you: the depth of a corner-face contact and of a face-face contact differ by
    a large factor for the same shared volume.

``hertz`` (spheres only)
    ``F_n = (4/3) E* sqrt(R* delta) delta`` -- the classical Hertz law.  Kept because it is the standard DEM
    benchmark and because the stiffness follows from a Young's modulus directly instead of from a fitted ``k_v``.

Tangential (Cundall & Strack 1979, Memory: "A discrete numerical model for granular assemblies", Geotechnique
29:47-65) keeps a per-pair spring vector, capped by Coulomb friction, so static friction -- and therefore an angle
of repose -- exists.  Rolling resistance is a moment proportional to ``mu_roll * F_n * R_eff`` opposing relative
spin (Ai et al. 2011, Powder Technology 206:205-211).

Units are SI throughout: metres, kilograms, seconds, pascals, newtons, and radians.

classes.name: Material
classes.doc: Bulk elastic and tribological properties of one species of body.

methods.name: G
methods.doc: Shear modulus [Pa].

methods.name: K
methods.doc: Bulk modulus [Pa].

methods.name: effective_modulus
methods.doc: ``1 / E*`` of the Hertz contact of two different materials.

classes.name: ForceModel
classes.doc:
How contacts become forces.

``mode``        ``"volume"`` (F = k_v * V_overlap) or ``"hertz"`` (spheres only).
``volume_stiffness``  ``k_v`` in N/m^3; ``None`` derives it from the material and the smallest particle so that
               a body resting under its own weight sinks by ``rest_penetration`` of its own volume.
``damping``     fraction of critical damping (``None`` uses each pair's restitution).
``friction``    overrides the pair friction coefficient when not ``None``.
``kt_ratio``    tangential stiffness as a fraction of the secant normal stiffness.

methods.sig: (mass: np.ndarray | float, volume: np.ndarray | float) -> float
methods.doc: ``k_v`` that lets the heaviest body rest on another with a penetration of ``rest_penetration * radius``.

classes.name: Obstacle
classes.doc:
A finite convex body fixed to a wall's frame (a mill lifter, a baffle, a screw flight).

Half-space planes are the right tool for a *surface*, but not for a body of finite size: the half-space of a
20 mm lifter flank would cut through the whole mill.  An obstacle is a real convex polyhedron, so a particle is
pushed out of the body itself and everything else stays open.

methods.name: placed
methods.doc: World rotation and position for a wall frame turned by ``R`` and shifted by ``t``.

classes.name: Wall
classes.doc:
A rigid set of half-space constraints ``normal . x <= offset`` that can rotate and translate.

The planes are stored in the wall's own frame; ``theta`` turns the body about ``axis`` through ``pivot``, which
is how a mill barrel, its lifters and a screw shaft all move.  ``omega`` is the angular velocity used for
friction: the wall surface at a point ``p`` moves with ``omega x (p - pivot)``.

methods.name: rotation
methods.doc: Rotation matrix of the wall frame at turned angle ``theta``.

methods.name: planes
methods.doc: World normals and offsets at turned angle ``theta``.

methods.name: surface_velocity
methods.doc: Velocity of the wall material at world ``points`` (``(n, 3)``), for friction and power draw.

methods.sig: (radius: float, length: float, facets: int = 48, *, material: Material | None = None, omega: float = 0.0, axis: np.ndarray | None = None, pivot: np.ndarray | None = None, end_caps: bool = True, name: str = 'barrel') -> Wall
methods.doc: The inner surface of a cylinder, as ``facets`` planes plus two end caps.

methods.name: with_lifters
methods.sig: (count: int, height: float, thickness: float, radius: float, length: float) -> Wall
methods.doc: Add ``count`` rectangular lifters standing ``height`` off the barrel wall.

functions.name: restitution_to_damping
functions.sig: (restitution: float) -> float
functions.doc: Viscous damping ratio that gives the requested coefficient of restitution (log-decrement inversion).

functions.name: hertz_normal_force
functions.sig: (E_star: float, R_star: float, penetration: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Hertz normal force ``(4/3) E* sqrt(R* delta^(3/2))`` for a non-negative penetration array.

functions.name: rayleigh_timestep
functions.sig: (radius: float, material: Material, safety: float = 0.2) -> float
functions.doc:
A stable DEM time step: ``safety`` times the Rayleigh surface-wave time of a body of ``radius``.

``t_R = pi R sqrt(rho / G) / (0.1631 nu + 0.8766)`` follows from the Rayleigh wave speed of an elastic sphere and
is the usual upper bound for the DEM step (Johnson 1985, *Contact Mechanics*; O'Sullivan, *Particulate Discrete
Element Modelling*).  ``safety`` of 0.1-0.2 keeps a stiff contact comfortably resolved.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.granular.coupling
children.doc:
Two-way-capable fluid drag on a granular assembly: the particle side of a DEM-CFD coupling.

A mill runs wet as often as dry, and the drag a fluid exerts on the charge is what decides whether the slurry
carries the fines or the charge settles.  This module adds the particle side of that coupling to a
:class:`~pinneapple_simulation.granular.world.World`: the fluid velocity is a callable (an analytic field, a SPH
solution resampled onto the particle positions, or a field read back from an OpenFOAM run), and the drag force
follows the Schiller-Naumann correlation already used by
:func:`pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.particles.terminal_velocity`, so a single settling body has to
reproduce that function's answer -- that is the check in ``tests/test_granular_coupling.py``.

    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> from pinneapple_simulation.granular import Sphere, World
    >>> from pinneapple_simulation.granular.coupling import FluidCoupling
    >>> world = World(gravity=(0.0, -9.81, 0.0))
    >>> _ = world.add(Sphere(1.0e-3, density=2500.0))
    >>> world.finalize()
    >>> coupling = FluidCoupling(velocity=lambda x: np.zeros_like(x), rho=998.0, mu=1.0e-3)
    >>> coupling.attach(world)                                  # doctest: +ELLIPSIS
    0
    >>> coupling.drag_force(world).shape
    (1, 3)

The porosity factor ``eps^-chi`` (Di Felice 1994, *The voidage function for fluid-particle interaction systems*,
Int. J. Multiphase Flow 20:153-159) is applied when ``porosity=True`` and uses the local solids fraction measured on
a grid of cells about four particle diameters wide.  It is off by default: the voidage function describes a *bed*,
and applying it to a lone particle is a modelling choice rather than a correction -- with a dilute assembly it
returns the single-particle drag to within the grid's resolution.

classes.name: FluidCoupling
classes.doc:
Drag of a carrier fluid on the bodies of a world.

``velocity`` is either a constant ``(3,)`` array or a callable ``positions (n, 3) -> velocities (n, 3)``.
``porosity`` adds the Di Felice voidage correction from the local solids fraction; ``chi`` is its exponent
(3.7 is the usual value for the whole Reynolds range).

methods.name: solids_fraction
methods.doc: Local solids fraction at each body, on a grid of cells about two particle diameters wide.

methods.name: drag_force
methods.doc: Fluid force on every body [N]: the drag on the slip, plus buoyancy when enabled.

methods.name: attach
methods.doc: Register the drag as a force source of ``world`` (returns its index in ``world.force_sources``).

methods.name: detach
methods.doc: Remove the drag source again (e.g. to run the same world dry).

fields: velocity: Callable[[np.ndarray], np.ndarray] | np.ndarray = field(default_factory=lambda: np.zeros(3))

functions.name: schiller_naumann_drag
functions.sig: (reynolds: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Drag coefficient ``24/Re (1 + 0.15 Re^0.687)`` (valid to Re ~ 1000, extended to 800 by the source).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.granular.equipment
children.doc:
Process equipment: a rotating drum / tumbling mill, its charge, and the numbers a plant asks for.

The mill here is the shape the industry actually runs -- a barrel with lifters and a charge of particles that
cascades and cataracts -- and the measurement that matters is the one every mill circuit is designed around: the
mechanical power drawn through the shell, ``P = torque . omega``, taken from the contact torques on the wall rather
than from a fitted correlation.  With bonded particles in the charge the same run returns a product curve (the
``P80`` of the fragments), which is how a DEM comminution model is used in practice.

    >>> from pinneapple_simulation.granular.equipment import RotatingDrum, cascade_power
    >>> drum = RotatingDrum(radius=0.15, length=0.04, rpm=30.0, lifters=6)
    >>> w = drum.build(n_particles=120, particle_radius=0.01, seed=0)
    >>> result = drum.run(w, steps=400, dt=2.0e-5)          # doctest: +SKIP
    >>> result["power"] > 0.0                               # doctest: +SKIP
    True

The charge is placed on a jittered close packing inside the barrel, neither poured nor settled: a short settle
phase (``RotatingDrum.settle``) is enough for a power number, and a longer one is what a quantitative comparison
against a plant measurement needs.

A non-overlapping packing of up to ``n_particles`` spheres inside a cylinder along ``z``.

Candidates come from a jittered lattice; a candidate is kept only if it clears every already-placed body by
``2.04 radius``.  Starting a run with interpenetrating bodies is the classic way to make a DEM run explode, so
the packing is screened here instead of being cleaned up by a repulsive phase in the solver.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.granular.lattice
children.doc:
From a crystal lattice to a material and a particle shape -- the ``Atoms to Material`` chain.

A DEM run needs a Young's modulus, a density and a particle shape.  All three follow from the crystal structure and
the interatomic potential when the material is a simple one, and this module computes them rather than asking for
them:

1. **Lattice constant** -- minimise the cohesive energy per atom over the cubic lattice constant ``a``;
2. **Elastic constants** ``C11``, ``C12``, ``C44`` -- second derivatives of the energy density under homogeneous
   strain.  For a monatomic Bravais lattice the affine (homogeneous) deformation is the exact response, so no
   internal relaxation is missing;
3. **Polycrystal moduli** -- Voigt / Reuss bounds and their Hill average, then ``E`` and ``nu``;
4. **Crystal shape** -- surface energies per facet from the broken-bond count and a Wulff construction, which
   returns a :class:`~pinneapple_simulation.granular.shapes.ConvexPolyhedron` that the contact model uses directly.

Two physics checks come for free and are asserted in the tests: a central-force potential at zero stress obeys the
**Cauchy relation** ``C12 = C44`` (Born & Huang, *Dynamical Theory of Crystal Lattices*), and the elastic constants
must satisfy the **Born stability** inequalities (Born 1940, Math. Proc. Cambridge Philos. Soc. 36:160-172).  A
potential or a structure that fails either is reported, not smoothed over.

    >>> from pinneapple_simulation.granular.lattice import Crystal, LennardJones
    >>> crystal = Crystal("fcc", LennardJones(epsilon=1.0, sigma=1.0, cutoff=3.0))
    >>> a = crystal.relaxed_lattice_constant()
    >>> 1.0 < a < 1.3
    True
    >>> constants = crystal.elastic_constants(a)
    >>> bool(constants["cauchy_rel_error"] < 1e-3)
    True

Units are reduced: ``sigma`` for lengths, ``epsilon`` for energies, so elastic constants come out in
``epsilon / sigma^3``.  :func:`material_from_lattice` rescales them to SI with a ``sigma`` in metres and an
``epsilon`` in joules, which is all a real material needs.

classes.name: LennardJones
classes.doc:
``4 epsilon [(sigma/r)^12 - (sigma/r)^6]`` truncated at ``cutoff * sigma``.

The truncation is the shifted-force form by default: the energy *and* the force are made continuous at the
cutoff (``phi(r) - phi(rc) - (r - rc) phi'(rc)``).  A plain truncation leaves a step of ~5e-3 epsilon in the
energy, and a second derivative of a discontinuous function is noise -- which shows up as a broken Cauchy
relation and meaningless elastic constants, so it is not an option for this module.

classes.name: Crystal
classes.doc: A cubic crystal structure with a pair potential.

methods.name: neighbor_vectors
methods.doc: Bond vectors from one atom to every neighbour inside the potential cutoff (each direction once).

methods.name: energy_per_atom
methods.sig: (a: float, vectors: np.ndarray | None = None, deformation: np.ndarray | None = None) -> float
methods.doc: Cohesive energy per atom of the (possibly homogeneously strained) lattice.

methods.name: relaxed_lattice_constant
methods.sig: (a_lo: float = 0.8, a_hi: float = 1.6, tol: float = 1e-10) -> float
methods.doc: Lattice constant that minimises the cohesive energy (golden-section search on ``a``).

methods.name: elastic_constants
methods.sig: (a: float | None = None, step: float = 0.002) -> dict
methods.doc: ``C11``, ``C12``, ``C44`` from central differences of the energy density, plus their physical checks.

methods.name: surface_energy
methods.doc: Broken-bond surface energy for the facet with the given normal [energy / area].

methods.name: facet_energies
methods.sig: (normals = None, a: float | None = None) -> dict

methods.name: wulff_shape
methods.sig: (a: float | None = None, facets = None) -> ConvexPolyhedron
methods.doc: The equilibrium crystal shape: the Wulff construction over the facet surface energies.

functions.name: wulff_polyhedron
functions.sig: (facet_energies: dict) -> ConvexPolyhedron
functions.doc:
Wulff construction: the polytope ``{x : n . x <= gamma(n)}`` for the given facets.

Wulff (1901, Z. Kristallogr. 34:449-530): the equilibrium shape of a crystal is the intersection of half-spaces
placed at a distance proportional to each facet's surface energy.  Facets with a low energy therefore grow and
the high-energy ones are cut away -- which is why an fcc metal is octahedral at ``(111)`` and not a cube.

functions.name: cubic_polycrystal_moduli
functions.sig: (C11: float, C12: float, C44: float) -> dict
functions.doc: Voigt / Reuss / Hill moduli of a random cubic polycrystal (Voigt 1928; Reuss 1929; Hill 1952).

functions.name: material_from_lattice
functions.sig: (crystal: Crystal, sigma_m: float = 3.4e-10, epsilon_J: float = 1e-21, atomic_mass_kg: float = 6.63e-26, a: float | None = None, facet_normals = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
Rescale a reduced-unit crystal into SI and return a DEM :class:`Material` plus a particle shape.

``sigma_m`` and ``epsilon_J`` set the length and energy scale of the potential (for argon, 3.40e-10 m and
1.66e-21 J respectively); ``atomic_mass_kg`` sets the density.  Nothing else is fitted.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.granular.overlap
children.doc:
Exact overlap geometry for convex bodies: the separating axis, and the volume two bodies share.

This is the part of the granular solver that makes it a *volume-based* contact model instead of a penetration-depth
one.  For two convex bodies the intersection is again convex, so the shared volume can be computed exactly by
clipping one body's face loops against the other's face planes and integrating the divergence theorem over what is
left.  The force magnitude is then a function of that volume (see
:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.granular.contacts`), which is what keeps a polyhedral particle from sinking into its
neighbour differently depending on which corner meets which face.

Three quantities come out of one call and are all used downstream:

* ``volume``  -- the force magnitude,
* ``centroid`` -- the contact point, so torque and the wear patch land where the material actually is,
* ``normal``/``depth`` -- the minimum-translation axis from the separating axis theorem, so the normal force pushes
  along the direction that separates the pair fastest.

    >>> from pinneapple_simulation.granular import box
    >>> from pinneapple_simulation.granular.overlap import overlap_volume
    >>> a = box(1.0, 1.0, 1.0).transformed(translation=[0.0, 0.0, 0.0])
    >>> b = box(1.0, 1.0, 1.0).transformed(translation=[0.5, 0.0, 0.0])
    >>> round(overlap_volume(a, b)[0], 12)
    0.5

All routines work in world coordinates: a body is passed already rotated and translated (``ConvexPolyhedron`` keeps
its own body frame, the caller does the rigid motion).

classes.name: SeparatingAxis
classes.sig: (overlap: bool, normal: np.ndarray, depth: float) -> None
classes.doc: Result of :func:`separating_axis`: ``overlap`` is ``False`` when a gap exists along ``normal``.

functions.name: separating_axis
functions.sig: (a: ConvexPolyhedron, b: ConvexPolyhedron, Ra: np.ndarray | None = None, Rb: np.ndarray | None = None, ta: np.ndarray | None = None, tb: np.ndarray | None = None, tol: float = 0.0) -> SeparatingAxis

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.granular.shapes
children.doc:
Convex rigid shapes for the granular solver: convex polyhedra and spheres.

Every shape is stored in its own body frame, centred on its centre of mass, so a rigid motion is a rotation matrix
and a translation.  Polyhedra carry closed face loops with outward winding, which the volume-overlap contact model
in :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.granular.overlap` clips directly -- that is the whole reason this module works on
``(vertices, faces)`` rather than on half-spaces or triangle soups.

    >>> from pinneapple_simulation.granular import box, faceted_sphere
    >>> cube = box(0.02, 0.02, 0.02)
    >>> round(cube.volume, 12) == round(0.02 ** 3, 12)
    True

The volumes, centroids, surface areas and inertia tensors are exact for a convex polyhedron: volume and first and
second moments come from the divergence theorem over the face loops, not from a voxel or sampling approximation.
Sphere-sphere geometry is analytic elsewhere (:mod:`pinneapple_simulation.granular.contacts`).

classes.name: ConvexPolyhedron
classes.doc:
A closed convex polyhedron given by vertices (``(n, 3)``) and face loops (indices, outward-wound).

Positions are measured from the centre of mass, so ``vertices.mean(0)`` is not zero in general but the volume
centroid is.  Faces may have any number of vertices and need not be coplanar in a first guess: each face's
normal is the area-weighted (Newell) normal of its loop.

methods.doc: Convex hull of ``points`` (triangulated faces with outward winding).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.granular.wear
children.doc:
Liner wear: the impulse wear model, and fitting its coefficient to a measured (laser-scanned) profile.

A mill liner loses thickness where the charge keeps hitting it, and DEM is used for exactly one reason there: to
turn a liner profile measured after a campaign into a wear law that predicts the next one.  The model here is the
impulse form of Archard's wear law, which is what DEM wear studies use when the liner is discretised into patches
(Cleary 1998, *Predicting charge motion, power draw, segregation and wear in ball mills using discrete element
methods*, Minerals Engineering 11:1061-1080):

    depth_patch = k_w * I_patch / (H * A_patch)

with ``I`` the normal impulse the patch received over the run [N s], ``H`` the liner hardness [Pa] and ``A`` the
patch area [m^2].  ``k_w`` is a dimensionless wear coefficient; it is the one number a measured profile is used to
calibrate, and :func:`fit_wear_law` does that by least squares through the origin and reports the ``R^2`` of the fit
so a poor calibration is visible rather than assumed.

The impulse form assumes the mean sliding speed at the contact is comparable between the calibration campaign and
the prediction -- true for a mill run at the same speed and fill, and the reason the fit is reported per speed band
rather than once for a whole circuit.

    >>> from pinneapple_simulation.granular.wear import fit_wear_law
    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> impulse = np.array([1.0, 2.0, 3.0]); areas = np.full(3, 0.01); hardness = 2.0e9
    >>> depth = 3.0e-9 * impulse / (hardness * areas)
    >>> round(fit_wear_law(impulse, areas, depth, hardness)["k_wear"], 9)
    3e-09

classes.name: WearTracker
classes.doc: Accumulates the impulse each patch sees and converts it to a wear depth.

methods.name: update
methods.doc: Add the impulse of the last step (already cumulative in the world) and return the per-patch depth.

functions.name: patch_areas
functions.sig: (wall) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Area of every wall plane [m^2] (the barrel facets of a :class:`Wall`, which set their own areas).

functions.name: fit_wear_law
functions.sig: (impulse: np.ndarray, areas: np.ndarray, depth: np.ndarray, hardness: float) -> dict
functions.doc:
Least-squares wear coefficient through the origin, with the fit quality.

``x = I / (H A)`` has units of metres, so ``k_wear = sum(x y) / sum(x^2)`` is dimensionless; ``r2`` is computed
on the same one-parameter model and a value well below one says the scanned profile is not explained by the
impact distribution alone (a different liner material, a changed speed, or a patch too coarse to resolve).

functions.name: linear_wear_profile
functions.sig: (areas: np.ndarray, rate: np.ndarray, hours: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: A synthetic ``target`` liner profile from per-patch wear rates [m/h] -- the stand-in for a laser scan.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.granular.world
children.doc:
The granular world: bodies, neighbour search, contacts, time integration and the measurements that matter.

A :class:`World` holds rigid bodies (spheres and convex polyhedra) plus rigid walls, resolves contacts with the
volume-based (or Hertz) laws of :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.granular.contacts`, and integrates a semi-implicit
scheme: the velocity is updated with the forces of the current configuration and the position then follows.  That
is the standard choice for stiff DEM (Cundall & Strack 1979; O'Sullivan, *Particulate Discrete Element Modelling*).

Plain NumPy over flat arrays: the sphere-sphere, sphere-wall and polyhedron-wall kernels are vectorised over all
pairs at once; only polyhedron-polyhedron pairs (whose exact overlap volume needs a clipping pass) run in a Python
loop.  On one core this carries a few thousand particles at the ~10 microsecond step a DEM run needs, and the same
arrays are what a GPU port would upload -- the next step listed in ``docs/granular_dem.md``.

Contact bookkeeping follows the array convention of production DEM codes: contacts are identified by integer keys,
the tangential spring vector of each contact is carried over by a sorted-key lookup (not a Python dictionary) for
the vectorised kernels, so static friction survives from step to step at no per-contact Python cost.

    >>> from pinneapple_simulation.granular import World, Material, Sphere
    >>> w = World(gravity=(0.0, -9.81, 0.0))
    >>> _ = w.add(Sphere(0.01, density=2500.0), position=(0.0, 0.20, 0.0))
    >>> w.finalize()
    >>> hist = w.run(steps=50, dt=2.0e-5)
    >>> hist["kinetic_energy"][0] < 1.0e-9 and hist["kinetic_energy"][-1] > 0.0
    True

children.summary: The granular world: bodies, neighbour search, contacts, time integration and the measurements that matter.

children.doc:
Granular DEM with volume-based contact for convex polyhedra, bonded breakage, mills, wear and fluid drag.

This package is PINNeAPPle's answer to GPU-native granular multiphysics: a discrete element solver whose contact law
acts on the **volume two bodies share** instead of on a penetration depth, so a polyhedral particle behaves the same
per unit of shared volume whether it meets a neighbour corner-to-face or face-to-face.  That is the method the GPU
DEM line of work (BLAZE-DEM / Govender et al.) is built on, and it is what makes angular particles usable for a
mill, a tablet or an ore without rounding everything into spheres.

Layers, bottom up:

============================  ==================================================================================
:mod:`.shapes`                convex polyhedra (exact volume, centroid, inertia), spheres and shape factories
:mod:`.overlap`               separating axis, exact overlap volume and contact point by half-space clipping
:mod:`.contacts`              materials, the volume and Hertz laws, Cundall-Strack friction, walls and obstacles
:mod:`.world`                 bodies, neighbour search, vectorised contact kernels, integration, measurements
:mod:`.bonds`                 bonded elements that break, and the fragment / ``P80`` statistics of a breakage run
:mod:`.equipment`             rotating drum / mill, the charge, power draw and the product curve
:mod:`.wear`                  impulse wear law on liner patches, fitted to a measured profile
:mod:`.coupling`              fluid drag (Schiller-Naumann + Di Felice) as a force source, the particle side of CFD
:mod:`.lattice`               crystal lattice -> elastic constants -> Wulff particle shape ("atoms to material")
============================  ==================================================================================

    >>> import numpy as np
    >>> from pinneapple_simulation.granular import World, Material, box
    >>> world = World(gravity=(0.0, -9.81, 0.0))
    >>> _ = world.add(box(0.01, 0.01, 0.01, density=2500.0), position=(0.0, 0.05, 0.0),
    ...               material=Material(density=2500.0))
    >>> world.finalize()
    >>> history = world.run(steps=100, dt=2.0e-5)
    >>> history["time"][-1] > 0.0
    True

What it is not: a GPU solver.  The kernels are plain NumPy (see ``docs/granular_dem.md`` for the measured speed and
for what a CUDA port would have to replace), and the fluid coupling is one-way -- the fluid pushes the particles,
the particles do not yet push the fluid back.
children.summary: Granular DEM with volume-based contact for convex polyhedra, bonded breakage, mills, wear and fluid drag.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.hemodynamics
pinneapple_simulation.hemodynamics.aorta
children.doc:
Pulsatile flow in the library's thoracic aorta (``aortic_arch``) with three-element Windkessel outlets, in
OpenFOAM.

* :func:`find_caps` finds the flat caps of a closed vessel surface (connected sets of exactly coplanar triangles
  that are discs), the inlet and outlets; :func:`aorta_stl` writes the aorta as a multi-solid STL with the patches
  ``inlet``, ``outlet_desc`` (descending aorta), ``outlet_rsa``, ``outlet_rcca``, ``outlet_lcca``, ``outlet_lsa``
  (right subclavian, right / left common carotid, left subclavian) and ``wall``;
* :func:`setup_case` meshes it (blockMesh + snappyHexMesh, through
  :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.pipelines.freecad_openfoam`) and writes a laminar ``pimpleFoam`` case: the inflow
  ``Q(t)`` imposed with ``flowRateInletVelocity`` (plug profile), fixed pressure on each outlet;
* :class:`CoupledRun` couples the outlets to :class:`~.windkessel.Windkessel` models from Python: the solver runs
  one window ``dt_couple`` at a time, then each outlet's flux (from ``phi``) advances its Windkessel exactly
  (piecewise-constant flow) and the new outlet pressure is written into the latest time before the next window.
  OpenFOAM v1912 from Ubuntu has no Windkessel boundary condition and no ``wmake`` for ``codedFixedValue``, hence
  this explicit, staggered coupling; with the exponential update it is stable for the window lengths used here, and
  :meth:`CoupledRun.check` reports how far the outlet pressures are from the Windkessels driven by the 3-D flows.

Blood is Newtonian by default (``rho`` 1060 kg/m^3, ``mu`` 3.5 mPa s, round values); ``viscosity="carreau"`` uses
OpenFOAM's BirdCarreau model with the Cho and Kensey (Biorheology 28:241-262, 1991) blood coefficients.

classes.name: CoupledRun
classes.doc:
Windkessel-coupled pimpleFoam run of a case written by :func:`setup_case`.

The coupling is explicit: each window runs with the outlet pressures of the previous one. It is stable only while
the window is short against the inertia of the rigid 3-D domain (gain ~ Rp * dt_couple / L < 1): on the library's
aortic arch, dt_couple = 0.01 s made the outlet pressures flip sign and grow every window, 0.001 s does not.

methods.sig: (t_end: float, verbose: bool = False) -> list[dict[str, Any]]

methods.name: check
methods.doc:
Over the last full period: mass imbalance, cycle-mean flows and pressures, and how far each outlet's 3-D
pressure is from its Windkessel (staggering of the explicit coupling).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.hemodynamics.windkessel
children.doc:
Three-element Windkessel (RCR) outlets: the lumped model of the arterial tree downstream of a 3-D vessel.

``P = Rp Q + Pc``, ``C dPc/dt = Q - (Pc - P_venous) / Rd`` (Westerhof, Lankhaar and Westerhof, Med Biol Eng Comput
47:131-141, 2009): proximal (characteristic) resistance ``Rp``, compliance ``C``, distal resistance ``Rd``. SI units:
Q in m^3/s, P in Pa, R in Pa s / m^3, C in m^3 / Pa.

* :class:`Windkessel` integrates the model for any flow history (exact exponential update for piecewise-constant
  Q, so a coupling step of any length is stable) and gives its input impedance
  ``Z(w) = Rp + Rd / (1 + i w Rd C)``, the analytic check of the integrator;
* :func:`split_rcr` sizes one RCR per outlet from a target mean pressure, mean flow, flow fractions, a proximal
  share of the resistance and a total compliance (the usual way RCR outlets are tuned when no patient data are
  available: Q_i fraction by Murray's law ``d^3``, ``R_T,i = P_mean / Q_i``, ``C_i`` proportional to ``Q_i``);
* :func:`explicit_coupling_gain` is the stability number of an explicit (lagged-pressure) coupling of an RCR to a
  rigid 3-D vessel, ``g = Rp dt / L``: with the outlet pressure held for a window ``dt``, an error dQ in the outlet
  flow comes back as (1 - g) dQ one window later, so the coupling oscillates for g > 1 and diverges for g > 2;
* :func:`half_sine_inflow` is a simple cardiac inflow: a half-sine ejection of ``stroke_volume`` during
  ``systole`` of each period and no flow in diastole.

methods.name: step
methods.doc: Advance ``dt`` with the flow ``Q`` held constant; returns the outlet pressure at the end.

methods.name: simulate
methods.sig: (t: np.ndarray, Q: np.ndarray, Pc0: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: Outlet pressure for a sampled flow (piecewise-constant between samples).

methods.sig: (t: np.ndarray, Q: np.ndarray, cycles: int = 20) -> float
methods.doc: ``Pc`` at the start of a cycle once the response is periodic (repeats the cycle ``cycles`` times).

functions.name: split_rcr
functions.sig: (diameters: Mapping[str, float], *, P_mean: float = 93 * MMHG, Q_mean: float = 7e-05, proximal_fraction: float = 0.09, C_total: float = 1e-08, fractions: Mapping[str, float] | None = None) -> dict[str, Windkessel]
functions.doc:
One :class:`Windkessel` per outlet. Flow fractions default to Murray's law (``d^3``); every outlet sees the
same mean pressure ``P_mean`` at its mean flow, ``Rp = proximal_fraction R_T``, and the compliance is shared in
proportion to the flow. The defaults (93 mmHg, 70 mL/s, 9 %, 1e-8 m^3/Pa ~ 1.3 mL/mmHg) are round adult values
chosen for a demonstration, not patient data.

functions.name: half_sine_inflow
functions.sig: (t, *, stroke_volume: float = 7e-05, period: float = 1.0, systole: float = 0.3) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Flow (m^3/s): ``Qmax sin(pi tau / systole)`` for ``tau = t mod period < systole``, else 0, with
``Qmax = pi stroke_volume / (2 systole)`` so each beat ejects ``stroke_volume``.

functions.name: check_against_impedance
functions.sig: (wk: Windkessel, omega: float, amplitude: float, n_per_period: int = 2000, periods: int = 40) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Drive the integrator with ``Q = amplitude sin(w t)`` and compare the periodic pressure amplitude and phase
with ``|Z(w)|`` and ``arg Z(w)``. Returns the relative amplitude error and the phase error (rad).

functions.name: outlet_flows
functions.sig: (Q_in: float, resistances: Sequence[float]) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Steady flow split of parallel resistances (the 0-D limit used to check a 3-D coupled run).

functions.name: vessel_inertance
functions.sig: (length: float, diameter: float, rho: float = 1060.0) -> float
functions.doc: Inertance ``L = rho l / A`` of a rigid tube [Pa s^2 / m^3]: the pressure drop per unit flow acceleration.

functions.name: explicit_coupling_gain
functions.sig: (wk: Windkessel, inertance: float, dt: float) -> float
functions.doc:
``g = Rp dt / L`` of a coupling that holds the Windkessel pressure for ``dt`` while the 3-D vessel (inertance
``L`` between its inlet and this outlet) integrates; stable without oscillation for g < 1, divergent for g > 2.
An estimate: the 3-D domain is reduced to one inertance, so keep a margin.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.immersed.compare
children.doc:
Immersed against conforming FEM on the same parts, at equal accuracy.

For each part (a sphere and a finite cylinder with convection in closed form, and a manufactured temperature on a
sphere) the immersed solver (Q1, Q2 on a background grid) and conforming tetrahedra (P1, P2 on a gmsh mesh, P2
nodes on the CAD surface; the same Python assembly and linear solver; and CalculiX on the identical P2 mesh) are run
over a sequence of resolutions. Every run records the unknowns, the error against the exact field and the wall time
by phase: the geometry phase (cut-cell quadrature for immersed, meshing for conforming), assembly and solve. The
equal-accuracy table interpolates, per method, the unknowns and the time needed to reach a target error (log-log,
between measured runs only: no extrapolation).

    from pinneapple_simulation.immersed import compare
    rows = compare.sweep(compare.parts()["sphere"], quick=True)
    compare.equal_accuracy(rows, targets=[1e-3, 1e-4])

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.immersed.elasticity
children.doc:
Linear elasticity on an immersed discretisation: -div sigma(u) = f in the part, sigma = lambda tr(eps) I + 2 mu eps,
with prescribed displacements (Nitsche, all or some components), tractions and pressures on its surface.

Weak form (Nitsche for the displacement set Gamma_D, components selected by the projection P):

    int sigma(u) : eps(v) - int_GD (P sigma(u) n) . v - int_GD (P sigma(v) n) . u + int_GD gamma P u . v + s(u, v)
      = int f . v + int_GN t . v - int_GD (P sigma(v) n) . g + int_GD gamma P g . v

``s`` is the same small-cut stabilisation as for heat (ghost penalty on every displacement component scaled by
2 mu + lambda, or the finite cell method's fictitious material). Unknowns are interleaved by node (u_x, u_y, u_z).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.immersed.geometry
children.doc:
Geometry for immersed analysis: anything that answers "how far inside or outside is this point".

Every geometry is a level set ``phi(X)`` (negative inside, positive outside, zero on the surface) with a bounding box
and a Lipschitz bound (1 for a signed distance). The solver never meshes it: the cut-cell quadrature only evaluates
``phi`` on a background grid and its subcells.

- :class:`SDFGeometry` wraps any vectorised signed distance (the primitives below, their CSG, the SDFs of
  ``pinneapple_design.geometry.gen.sdf_shapes`` or any callable).
- :class:`VoxelGeometry` turns a voxel mask (CT scan, topology optimisation, a rasterised part) into a signed distance
  by Euclidean distance transforms, interpolated trilinearly.
- :class:`STLGeometry` takes a triangle surface: the inside test is the generalised winding number (Jacobson et al.,
  SIGGRAPH 2013; robust to small holes and flipped facets), evaluated with a dipole tree (Barill et al., SIGGRAPH
  2018), and the distance is the exact point-triangle distance to the nearest candidates.

classes.name: Geometry
classes.doc: A level set with a bounding box. Subclasses implement :meth:`phi`.

classes.name: SDFGeometry
classes.doc: Any vectorised level set ``fn(X) -> (n,)`` with its bounding box ``(lo, hi)``.

classes.name: VoxelGeometry
classes.doc:
A voxel mask (True = material) with the position of the corner of voxel 0 and the voxel size.

The signed distance is the Euclidean distance transform of the material and of the void, measured between voxel
centres and shifted by half a voxel so the zero level runs through the voxel faces; between centres it is
interpolated (multi)linearly. The surface is therefore the staircase of the voxels smoothed over one voxel.

methods.name: from_geometry
methods.sig: (geom: Geometry, spacing: float, margin: int = 1) -> VoxelGeometry
methods.doc: Rasterise another geometry (voxel centres inside it): a test and demo source of voxel data.

classes.name: STLGeometry
classes.doc:
A closed (or nearly closed) triangle surface. Inside = generalised winding number above 1/2.

``sample_spacing`` controls the surface samples that index the triangles for the distance query: the distance is
exact within ``near`` of the surface (where the cut cells are) and a lower bound farther away, which is all the
cut-cell classification needs. ``sign``: ``"winding"`` evaluates the winding number at every point;
``"auto"`` (default) does so far from the surface and for any surface that is not watertight and consistently
oriented, and inside the near band of a watertight one takes the sign of the angle-weighted pseudonormal of the
closest feature (Baerentzen & Aanaes, IEEE TVCG 2005), which is exact there and much cheaper.

methods.name: closest
methods.sig: (X: np.ndarray, k: int = 16) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
methods.doc:
Unsigned distance (exact within ``near``, a lower bound beyond), and for the near points the closest
triangle, point and feature (-1 where not computed).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.immersed.heat
children.doc:
Steady heat conduction on an immersed discretisation: -div(k grad T) = f in the part, with prescribed
temperatures (Nitsche), heat fluxes and convection on its surface.

Weak form on the active cells (Nitsche, Comput. Methods Appl. Mech. Eng. 1971; Hansbo & Hansbo 2002 for cut
elements):

    int k grad T . grad v - int_GD k (dT/dn v + dv/dn T) + int_GD gamma T v + int_GR h T v + s(T, v)
      = int f v - int_GD k dv/dn g + int_GD gamma g v + int_GR h T_inf v + int_GN q v

with ``s`` the small-cut stabilisation: ``"ghost"`` (ghost penalty on the faces of cut cells, Burman 2010; the Nitsche
penalty is then ``beta k / h``), ``"fcm"`` (the finite cell method's fictitious material of conductivity
``alpha k`` filling each cut cell, Parvizian, Duester & Rank 2007; the Nitsche penalty per cut cell from a local
eigenvalue problem, Embar, Dolbow & Harari 2010) or ``"none"``.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.immersed.quadrature
children.doc:
Cut-cell quadrature by adaptive octree subdivision (quadtree in 2-D).

Every background cell is classified from the level set at its corners and centre (a box whose centre is farther from
the surface than its half-diagonal, times the Lipschitz bound, cannot be cut). Cut cells are split into 2^d children,
recursively, down to ``depth`` levels. Children that are inside get a tensor Gauss rule; the leaves still cut at the
last level are split into d! Kuhn simplices and each simplex is clipped by the level set (Parvizian, Duester & Rank,
Comput. Mech. 2007, octree integration; simplex clipping as in marching tetrahedra). The surface points on the
simplices are found by a few regula-falsi steps on the true level set, so the clipped surface interpolates the real
one: the geometric error is O((h / 2^depth)^2). The same clipping yields the boundary facets, with their normals, for
the surface quadrature of Nitsche, Neumann and Robin terms.

methods.sig: (parts: list[Points], d: int, surface: bool = False) -> Points

classes.doc: Volume quadrature of the cut cells, the list of the cells entirely inside, and the boundary quadrature.

methods.doc: Cut cells and the fraction of each one that is inside the part.

methods.doc: Tensor Gauss points of the cells entirely inside.

classes.sig: (grid: BackgroundGrid, cells: np.ndarray, m: int)
classes.doc:
Moment fitting: everything integrated over the inside part of a cut cell is compressed onto the m^d Gauss
points of the whole cell, with the weights w_g = int l_g (l_g the Lagrange polynomials of the Gauss points).
The compressed rule integrates every polynomial of degree m - 1 per axis exactly as the fine rule does
(stiffness and mass of Q_p need m = 2p + 1); its points can lie outside the part and its weights can be
negative (Mueller, Kummer & Oberlack, IJNME 2013).

degree-2 rule (dim + 1 points, 2 on a segment); ``n`` < 0: the centroid.

``depth``: subdivision levels of cut cells (the leaves are h / 2^depth); ``n_gauss``: Gauss points per axis on
the cells entirely inside (default order + 1); ``n_simplex``: rule on the clipped simplices and facets (0 = the
symmetric degree-2 rules, n >= 1 = collapsed Gauss with n points per direction); ``n_facet``: the same for the
boundary facets (default 0: degree 2; the centroid, -1, is cheaper but costs accuracy in Q2); ``refine``: regula-falsi steps
that put the facet vertices on the true surface (0 = linear interpolation of the level set); ``fit``: compress
the volume rule of each cut cell by moment fitting onto (2 order + 1)^d points (exact for the stiffness and mass
integrands, see :class:`MomentFitter`); ``keep_fine``: also keep the fine octree points (positive weights, all inside
the part: used for error norms).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.immersed.transient
children.doc:
Transient heat conduction on an immersed discretisation: rho c dT/dt - div(k grad T) = f(X, t), by the theta
scheme (theta = 1 backward Euler, 1/2 Crank-Nicolson):

    (M / dt + theta A) T^{n+1} = (M / dt - (1 - theta) A) T^n + theta b^{n+1} + (1 - theta) b^n

A and b are the steady operator and load of :mod:`.heat` (Nitsche, flux, convection, small-cut stabilisation). The
mass matrix M is integrated with the same cut-cell rule; with the ghost penalty its small-cut conditioning is
controlled by a mass ghost term gamma_M rho c h^2 (the gradient ghost faces scaled by h^2), with the finite cell
method by the fictitious material. Sources and boundary data may depend on time: pass ``source(X, t)`` and
``bcs(t)`` (a function returning the list of conditions); constant data are assembled once.

``offset`` x h past a grid line into the next column of cells, which therefore hold slivers of the part. For

functions.doc:
A sum of plane waves u = sum_j A_j sin(k_j . x + phi_j) on a disk / sphere (or torus in 3-D), with the body
force f = sum_j [(lam + mu) k_j (k_j . A_j) + mu |k_j|^2 A_j] sin(...) that makes it exact, and the displacement

functions.sig: (a: float = 0.3, b: float = 0.6, p: float = 1.0, E: float = 1.0, nu: float = 0.3) -> ElasticCase
functions.doc:
Thick-walled sphere under internal pressure p (Lamé): u = (A + B / r^3) x with
A = p a^3 (1 - 2 nu) / (E (b^3 - a^3)), B = p a^3 b^3 (1 + nu) / (2 E (b^3 - a^3)) (Timoshenko & Goodier,
Theory of Elasticity, 3rd ed., section 141). Pressure on the inner surface; the exact displacement is imposed on
the outer one (removes the rigid modes and tests Nitsche on a curved surface).

children.doc:
Immersed (finite cell / CutFEM) analysis on raw geometry: no conforming mesh.

A part given as a signed distance (any SDF, CSG of SDFs), a voxel mask or an STL surface (generalised winding number)
is put in a uniform background grid of Q1 or Q2 elements; the cells it cuts are integrated by adaptive octree
quadrature compressed by moment fitting, small cuts are stabilised (ghost penalty or the finite cell method's
fictitious material, with the condition number reported), and boundary conditions on the curved surface are imposed
weakly: Nitsche's method for temperatures, surface quadrature for heat fluxes and convection.

    from pinneapple_simulation import immersed as im
    part = im.cylinder((0, 0, 0), 0.02, 0.1) - im.cylinder((0, 0, 0), 0.008, 0.12)      # or im.STLGeometry.from_file
    disc = im.Discretization(part, h=0.004, order=2)
    sol = im.solve_heat(disc, conductivity=200.0, source=0.0,
                        bcs=[im.Dirichlet(80.0, where=lambda X, n: np.hypot(X[:, 0], X[:, 1]) < 0.01),
                             im.Convection(h=25.0, T_inf=20.0)])
    sol(points), sol.balance, sol.info

Linear elasticity on the same discretisation: :func:`solve_elasticity` (Nitsche displacements, tractions, pressures
and total forces). Verification (manufactured solutions on curved domains, sphere, cylinder and Lame sphere in closed
form, conditioning of small cuts): :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.immersed.verification`; STL parts against conforming
FEM: :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.immersed.parts`.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.launch
pinneapple_simulation.launch.ascent
children.doc:
The three-degree-of-freedom ascent of a launch vehicle: position, velocity and mass in an Earth-centred inertial
frame, driven by thrust along a commanded direction, gravity (with J2 optionally), drag against the 1976 standard
atmosphere, and the Earth's rotation under the pad.

The flight has three parts, each with its own guidance:

* **The pitch program** (stages one and two). A vertical rise, then the thrust pitched above the local horizon along
  a schedule in *altitude*: the pitch falls from 90 deg at 1.5 km to ``pitch_end_deg`` at ``pitch_end_altitude_km``
  and stays there, following the local vertical and the azimuth of the orbit plane. With the exponent < 1 the vehicle
  pulls over gently where the dynamic pressure is highest and faster once the air is thin, which keeps the peak
  dynamic pressure and the gravity losses where a launcher wants them.
* **The coast to apogee.** The second stage is cut off when its tanks run dry, leaving a transfer orbit whose apogee
  is the target altitude; the vehicle coasts ballistically to that apogee (no thrust, gravity and drag only).
* **The circularisation** (the kick stage). At apogee the last stage burns along the velocity-to-be-gained,
  ``v_circular(r_target) - v``, until the velocity of the circular orbit at the target altitude is reached: a short
  prograde burn, the way a small launcher inserts a payload

Every loss is integrated over the whole flight, so the velocity bookkeeping closes:

    dv_thrust - dv_gravity - dv_drag - dv_steering = |v_cutoff| - |v_liftoff|

    from pinneapple_simulation.launch.ascent import Site, Target, simulate_ascent
    from pinneapple_simulation.launch.vehicle import small_launcher
    hist = simulate_ascent(small_launcher(), Site("Tanegashima", 30.4, 130.97), Target(500.0))
    hist.final_orbit()          # a, e, i, perigee, apogee, period of the inserted orbit
    hist.losses                 # the measured gravity, drag and steering losses [m/s]

The orbit is osculating and two-body: the model has no third-body, no solar pressure and no oblateness of the
inserted orbit (J2, when enabled, acts on the trajectory, and the check in :mod:`.verification` accounts for it).

functions.sig: (lat_deg: float, inclination_deg: float, eastward: bool = True)
functions.doc:
Azimuth [deg from north] of the launch that inserts into ``inclination_deg`` from ``lat_deg``.

``sin(azimuth) = cos(inclination) / cos(latitude)``; a due-east launch (90 deg) gives an inclination equal to the
latitude, which is what Tanegashima does for its 30 deg missions, and an inclination above 90 deg (retrograde)
gives an azimuth past 180 deg, towards the south. ``eastward=False`` mirrors it to the western azimuth.

functions.doc:
Fly ``vehicle`` from ``site`` to ``target`` and return the recorded :class:`AscentHistory`.

``dt`` is the integration step (RK4), ``record_dt`` the sampling of the returned arrays, ``coast_s`` the time
flown ballistically after cut-off (0 stops the run at the engine cut-off). The feedback guidance is evaluated at
every integrator substep, so the trajectory is the closed loop, not a pre-computed pitch program.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.launch.atmosphere
children.doc:
The US Standard Atmosphere 1976 from the ground to 1000 km: temperature, pressure, density and speed of sound,
the model every ascent calculation below drags against.

Up to 84.852 km (geopotential) the atmosphere is the seven-layer table of NASA-TM-X-74335 (the 1976 standard): a
base geopotential altitude, a lapse rate, a base temperature and a base pressure per layer, with

    T(H) = T_b + L (H - H_b)
    p(H) = p_b (T_b / T) ** (g0 M / (R* L))      (L != 0)
    p(H) = p_b exp(-g0 M (H - H_b) / (R* T_b))   (L == 0)
    rho  = p M / (R* T),   a = sqrt(gamma R* T / M)

and the geopotential altitude H = R0 h / (R0 + h) over the geometric altitude h (R0 = 6356.766 km, the effective
radius of the 1976 standard). Above 84.852 km the same document's upper table (86 km to 1000 km) is used with the
density interpolated linearly in ln(rho) in geopotential altitude, which is what an ascent needs there: the drag at
100 km is already a thousandth of the dynamic pressure at 50 km.

    from pinneapple_simulation.launch import atmosphere
    atmosphere.state(5000.0)["rho"]          # density [kg/m^3] at 5 km
    atmosphere.speed_of_sound(11000.0)       # [m/s] at the tropopause

The model is dry and mid-latitude, no wind, no day-night or latitude variation: an ascent through it is reproducible
to the last digit, which is what a verification needs.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.launch.sizing
children.doc:
Sizing the stages: how much propellant each one needs for its share of the velocity, and how much thrust it needs
to leave the pad.

The inverse of the Tsiolkovsky relation, stage by stage from the payload down:

    R    = exp(dv / (Isp g0))                       (wet + above) / (dry + above)
    wet  = m_above (R - 1) / (1 - R eps)            m_dry = eps wet,   m_prop = wet - m_dry

with ``eps`` the structural coefficient (dry mass over wet mass of that stage) and ``m_above`` everything carried on
top of it at lift-off. A stage that is too small for its share (``exp(-dv / c) <= eps``) cannot be built: the split
is infeasible and the function says so instead of returning a negative tank.

    from pinneapple_simulation.launch.sizing import size_vehicle
    veh = size_vehicle(200.0, delta_v=(3500.0, 4100.0, 700.0))
    veh.liftoff_mass_kg, veh.delta_v_vac_m_s

The velocity split here is the one the ascent measures, not a guess: :func:`close` iterates the split against the
simulation (the gravity, drag and steering losses the flight actually pays) until the design inserts on the target.

functions.sig: (target_altitude_km: float, site_lat_deg: float, mu: float = 398600441800000.0, radius: float = 6371000.0, omega: float = 7.292115e-05, losses_m_s: float = 1900.0) -> dict
functions.doc:
The velocity budget the ascent has to find: the orbital speed less the help of the Earth's rotation, plus the
gravity, drag and steering losses (``losses_m_s`` defaults to the 1.9 km/s this model measures).

functions.name: size_vehicle
functions.sig: (payload_kg: float, delta_v = (3500.0, 4100.0, 700.0), *, isp_vac = DEFAULTS['isp_vac'], isp_sl = DEFAULTS['isp_sl'], eps = DEFAULTS['eps'], tw_liftoff: float = DEFAULTS['tw_liftoff'], diameter = DEFAULTS['diameter'], fairing_kg: float = DEFAULTS['fairing_kg'], fairing_jettison_altitude_km: float = DEFAULTS['fairing_jettison_altitude_km'], name: str = 'Concept-200') -> LaunchVehicle
functions.doc: A vehicle whose three stages carry ``delta_v`` [m/s], sized from the payload up.

functions.name: close
functions.sig: (site, target, *, payload_kg: float = 200.0, dt: float = 0.2, iterations: int = 6, kick_m_s: float = 950.0, pitch_end_altitude_km: float = 300.0, pitch_exponent: float = 0.6, verbose: bool = False)
functions.doc:
Close the velocity budget on the simulation and return ``(vehicle, history, report)``.

One knob is solved: the total ideal velocity the three stages carry. Each iteration flies the vehicle, reads the
apogee the second stage leaves (the transfer the kick stage circularises from) and the orbit the kick stage
reaches, and scales the budget by what the transfer was short or long. The kick stage carries a fixed ``kick_m_s``
(it only has to circularise at apogee) and the rest is split 40 % / 60 % between the first two stages: the first
leaves the dense air, the second builds the transfer.
