children.name: pinneapple_simulation.launch.vehicle
children.doc:
A launch vehicle as the ascent model needs it: stages with their masses, their vacuum and sea-level thrust and
specific impulse, their drag area and a Mach-dependent drag coefficient.

A stage is jettisoned when its propellant is spent; what remains is the mass of the stages above it, the payload and
the fairing (dropped at ``fairing_jettison_altitude_km``). Thrust and mass flow follow the ambient pressure:

    T(p) = T_vac - (T_vac - T_sl) p / p_sl          m_dot = T / (Isp g0)
    Isp(p) = T(p) / (m_dot g0)

so a stage that leaves the ground with a sea-level specific impulse finishes its burn with the vacuum one, and the
ideal velocity of the stage is the Tsiolkovsky one at the vacuum impulse for the whole burn (it is an upper bound;
the ascent integrates the real thing).

    from pinneapple_simulation.launch import vehicle
    veh = vehicle.small_launcher()          # the concept vehicle of ``examples/rocket_launch``
    veh.liftoff_mass_kg, veh.delta_v_vac_m_s, veh.stage_delta_v_m_s

Nothing here is a published vehicle: every number is an assumption of the concept study, listed in
``examples/rocket_launch/README.md`` with what it stands on. The published cross-checks in
:mod:`.verification` use closed forms, not a real launcher's flight data.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.launch.visuals
children.doc:
The flight as a display: a globe with the ascent drawn on it, a chase view of the vehicle, and a mission-control
page whose charts follow the same time cursor.

Two 3-D scenes come out of one recorded ascent, because the two views live at scales 350 000 apart (the Earth's
6 371 km against the vehicle's 18 m) and no single camera holds both without losing the depth buffer:

* ``view="globe"``: the Earth (a sphere with the Natural Earth 1:110m land mask), the vehicle as a marker a few tens
  of kilometres long, and the path flown so far, coloured by speed.
* ``view="vehicle"``: the launcher at its own scale in a body-centred chase camera, with the plume, the trail and the
  head-up numbers.

    from pinneapple_simulation.launch.visuals import flight_scene, mission_control
    scene = flight_scene(hist, view="globe")
    pp.viz.web_viewer(scene, "viewer_globe/", single_file=True)     # opens from file://
    mission_control(hist, "mission_control.html")                    # charts + map + tiles

Scene axes are the inertial frame of the ascent (z along the Earth's spin axis), so the globe does not turn under the
trajectory: the Earth's rotation is already in the recorded positions.

functions.name: land_mask
functions.sig: (cell_deg: float = 1.0)
functions.doc:
``(lat, lon, mask)`` on a regular grid: whether the centre of each cell is land, from the Natural Earth
1:110m coastlines that ship with the weather module (public domain). Cached per resolution.

functions.name: globe_surfaces
functions.sig: (radius: float = 6371.0, cell_deg: float = 1.0)
functions.doc:
The Earth as two surfaces — the ocean sphere and the land cells lifted a hair above it — at ``radius``.

``radius`` is in whatever unit the scene uses (the globe view of the examples works in kilometres).

functions.name: rocket_surfaces
functions.sig: (length: float = 18.0, diameter: float = 1.3, plume: float = 1.0)
functions.doc:
The launcher at its own scale, body frame x along the thrust axis (nose at +x), origin at the tail.

Three stacked stages, a nose cone, four fins and (``plume`` > 0) the exhaust: a display model, not the CAD — it
is the silhouette a chase camera needs, with the real length and diameter of the concept vehicle.

functions.name: marker_surfaces
functions.sig: (size: float = 120.0)
functions.doc: A chevron a launcher-sized-object cannot be at globe scale: the vehicle as a marker ``size`` long along +x.

functions.name: flight_scene
functions.sig: (hist, *, view: str = 'globe', n_frames: int = 300, earth_radius_km: float = 6371.0)
functions.doc:
The recorded ascent as a :class:`~pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.scene.Scene` with an animation.

``view="globe"``: kilometres, the Earth and the marker; ``view="vehicle"``: metres, the launcher and its plume in
a chase camera. Resample the animation with ``n_frames`` to keep the page small.

Write the mission-control page: a map of the ground track, the telemetry charts and the tiles, all on one
time cursor (scrubbing a chart seeks the map). Returns the path.

children.doc:
Ascent to orbit: a launch vehicle from a pad to a near-circular orbit, with the standard atmosphere it drags
against, a gravity-turn and velocity-to-be-gained guidance, the velocity bookkeeping that closes on the Tsiolkovsky
budget, and the checks a result needs before anyone flies it.

    from pinneapple_simulation.launch import Site, Target, simulate_ascent, small_launcher
    hist = simulate_ascent(small_launcher(), Site("Tanegashima", 30.4, 130.97), Target(500.0))
    print(hist.summary())                 # perigee, apogee, eccentricity, max Q, the losses
    print(hist.losses)                    # thrust, gravity, drag and steering [m/s], and the closure

Modules: :mod:`.atmosphere` (US Standard Atmosphere 1976), :mod:`.vehicle` (stages, thrust, impulse, drag),
:mod:`.sizing` (the design closure that sizes the stages from the measured losses and solves the pitch schedule), :mod:`.ascent` (the 3-DOF
simulation and the guidance), :mod:`.verification` (the checks), :mod:`.visuals` (the 3-D flight and the
mission-control display). Guide: ``docs/guides/launch_ascent.md``.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.meshless.domains
children.doc:
2-D domains and node sets for the meshless study.

A :class:`Domain2D` has a signed distance (negative inside, from ``pinneapple_design.geometry.csg``) and its boundary
as exact pieces (straight segments and circular arcs), so boundary nodes lie on the true boundary and the corners of a
polygon are nodes. ``nodes(h)`` returns a quasi-uniform node set: a Cartesian lattice of spacing ``h`` kept at least
``0.4 h`` inside, plus boundary nodes at spacing ``h`` along every piece (optionally jittered, for robustness checks).

An uploaded point cloud (``point_cloud_domain``) has no signed distance: it has one node set (the points given) and
the methods that need the geometry itself (embedded finite differences, refinement) are not available on it.

methods.name: perimeter
methods.doc: Total length of the boundary pieces (outer boundary and holes); 0 for a point cloud.

methods.name: estimate_nodes
methods.doc:
Node count of ``nodes(h)`` without building it: ``area / h**2 + perimeter / h`` (lattice plus boundary).
A point cloud returns its own node count.

methods.name: nodes
methods.sig: (h: float, *, jitter: float = 0.0, seed: int = 0) -> NodeSet
methods.doc:
Lattice nodes at spacing ``h`` at least ``0.4 h`` inside, boundary nodes at spacing ``h``.
``jitter``: random displacement of the interior nodes, as a fraction of ``h``.

methods.name: sample_eval
methods.doc: Evaluation points strictly inside, independent of every node set (seeded).

methods.name: outline
methods.doc: Boundary as closed polylines (for drawing).

functions.name: polygon_domain
functions.sig: (vertices: Sequence[Sequence[float]], name: str = 'polygon', holes: Sequence[tuple[tuple[float, float], float]] = ()) -> Domain2D
functions.doc: A simple polygon (vertices in order), optionally with circular holes ``((cx, cy), r)``.

functions.name: domain
functions.sig: (name: str) -> Domain2D
functions.doc: A preset: ``square``, ``lshape``, ``disk``, ``annulus``, ``plate_hole``.

functions.name: point_cloud_domain
functions.sig: (X: np.ndarray, boundary: np.ndarray, *, eval_fraction: float = 0.1, seed: int = 0, name: str = 'point cloud') -> Domain2D
functions.doc:
An uploaded point cloud: nodes ``X`` (N, 2) with a boundary flag. ``eval_fraction`` of the interior points
are held out as evaluation points (not used by any method).

functions.name: default_spacings
functions.sig: (dom: Domain2D, levels: int = 3) -> list[float]
functions.doc: The default refinement ladder of a study: ``diameter / 10 / 2**k`` for ``k < levels``, coarsest first.

functions.name: point_cloud_from_table
functions.sig: (df, name: str = 'point cloud') -> Domain2D
functions.doc:
A point-cloud domain from a table (a pandas ``DataFrame``) with columns ``x``, ``y`` and a boundary flag
(``boundary``, ``is_boundary``, ``b`` or ``on_boundary``; 1 on the boundary, 0 inside). Column names are matched
without regard to case. Raises ``ValueError`` when a column is missing.

functions.name: domain_from_spec
functions.sig: (d: dict | None, table = None, name: str = '') -> Domain2D
functions.doc:
The domain a study request describes: a point-cloud ``table`` (see :func:`point_cloud_from_table`) if given,
else ``{"polygon": [[x, y], ...], "holes": [[cx, cy, r], ...]}``, else ``{"preset": name}`` (default
``"square"``).

children.summary: 2-D domains and node sets for the meshless study.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.meshless.methods
children.doc:
Five ways to solve the same 2-D problem on the same domain.

==========  ===================================================================================================
``kansa``   global RBF collocation (Kansa 1990): multiquadric φ = sqrt(1 + (ε r)²) centred at every node; dense
``rbf_fd``  RBF-generated finite differences: polyharmonic spline r³ + polynomials up to ``degree`` on the ``n``
            nearest nodes of each node (Flyer, Fornberg, Bayona, Barnett 2016); sparse
``fd``      5-point finite differences on a Cartesian grid embedded in the domain, Shortley-Weller formula where
            the grid meets the curved boundary (the boundary intersections are the boundary nodes); sparse
``fem``     linear (P1) finite elements on the Delaunay triangulation of the nodes, cells outside removed; sparse
``pinn``    a physics-informed network trained on the same nodes within a wall-clock budget
            (``pinneapple_analysis.cost.train_within_budget``)
==========  ===================================================================================================

``discretize(method, domain, nodes)`` builds the operator (setup cost measured), ``solve(problem, disc)`` solves the
steady problem or marches the heat equation (Crank-Nicolson) and returns the nodal values, the solve time, a 1-norm
condition-number estimate of the system matrix and the noise amplification (relative change of the solution per
relative perturbation of the right-hand side). ``disc.evaluate(u, P)`` gives the solution anywhere inside, with each
method's own interpolant (global RBF, local RBF-FD interpolation, P1, the network).

functions.name: default_eps
functions.sig: (domain: Domain2D) -> float
functions.doc:
Shape parameter of the multiquadric: 3 / diameter (a fixed, not node-scaled, value: spectral convergence until
the condition number stops it).

functions.name: rbf_fd_weights
functions.sig: (X: np.ndarray, Q: np.ndarray, idx: np.ndarray, op: str = 'lap', degree: int = 4) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
RBF-FD weights (q, n) of the stencils ``idx`` (q, n) (rows of ``X``) for the operator ``op`` at the points
``Q``: ``lap`` (the Laplacian) or ``eval`` (interpolation). PHS r³ + all monomials up to ``degree``, in local
coordinates centred at the point and scaled by the stencil radius.

functions.name: fd_nodes
functions.sig: (domain: Domain2D, h: float)
functions.doc: Grid nodes inside the domain and the points where grid lines cross the boundary.

functions.name: discretize
functions.sig: (method: str, domain: Domain2D, nodes: NodeSet, **options) -> Discretization
functions.doc: Build the operator of ``method`` on ``nodes`` (FD builds its own grid nodes at the same spacing).

functions.name: solve
functions.sig: (problem: Problem, disc: Discretization, *, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Solve on the discretization; returns ``u`` (nodal values, or the network for the PINN) and the costs.

children.summary: Five ways to solve the same 2-D problem on the same domain.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.meshless.pinn
children.doc:
PINN on the meshless node set: the interior nodes are the collocation points, the boundary nodes carry the Dirichlet
condition, and training stops at a wall-clock budget (``pinneapple_analysis.cost.train_within_budget``), so the PINN
is compared with the other methods at a stated cost. ``pp.solve(..., "pinn")`` samples a box, which is why the
training step is set up here on the domain's own nodes; the network comes from the model registry and the
derivatives from the PDE compiler's autograd operators.

functions.name: train_pinn
functions.sig: (problem, disc, *, budget_s: float = 5.0, width: int = 32, depth: int = 3, lr: float = 0.002, bc_weight: float = 10.0, n_times: int = 8, seed: int = 0, **_) -> dict[str, Any]

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.meshless.problems
children.doc:
Linear 2-D problems with Dirichlet conditions, defined by expressions in ``x``, ``y`` (and ``t``).

``Problem("poisson", exact="sin(pi*x)*sin(pi*y)")`` derives the source and the boundary values from a manufactured
solution (with sympy), so every method can be scored against the exact solution. Without ``exact``, give ``source``
and ``boundary``; the study then uses a fine reference solution.

==========  =============================================  ========================================
kind        equation                                       data
==========  =============================================  ========================================
poisson     -Δu = f                                        u = g on the boundary
helmholtz   -Δu - k² u = f                                 u = g on the boundary
heat        u_t = α Δu + f  on (0, t_end]                  u = g on the boundary, u(t=0) = u0
==========  =============================================  ========================================

methods.name: c
methods.doc: Coefficient of u in the steady operator -Δu - c u (0 for Poisson, k² for Helmholtz).

children.summary: Linear 2-D problems with Dirichlet conditions, defined by expressions in x, y (and t).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.meshless.stencils
children.doc:
Stencil weights in any dimension for meshless discretisations: RBF-FD and GFDM (weighted least squares).

``stencil_weights(X, Q, idx, ops, method=...)`` returns, for every query point ``Q[i]`` and its stencil ``X[idx[i]]``,
the weights ``w`` such that ``(L u)(Q[i]) ~ sum_j w[i, j] u[idx[i, j]]`` for each operator in ``ops``:

* ``"eval"`` (interpolation), ``"d0"``, ``"d1"``, ``"d2"`` (first derivatives along each axis), ``"lap"`` (the
  Laplacian).

Methods:

``rbf_fd``
    Polyharmonic spline ``r^3`` plus all monomials up to ``degree`` in local coordinates centred at the query point
    and scaled by the stencil radius (Flyer, Fornberg, Bayona and Barnett, J. Comput. Phys. 321 (2016) 21; the 2-D
    Laplacian version is :func:`.methods.rbf_fd_weights`). Exact for the polynomials, interpolating in the stencil.
``gfdm``
    Generalised finite differences: a weighted least-squares fit of the monomials up to ``degree`` (Gaussian weights
    of the distance, scaled by the stencil radius), differentiated at the query point (Benito, Urena and Gavete,
    Appl. Math. Model. 25 (2001) 1039, doi:10.1016/S0307-904X(01)00029-4). Exact for the polynomials, not
    interpolating.

Both are exact for polynomials up to ``degree``: the consistency tests of ``tests/test_meshless_stencils.py`` check
it in 2-D and 3-D.

functions.name: monomials
functions.sig: (dim: int, degree: int) -> list[tuple[int, ...]]
functions.doc: Exponent tuples of every monomial of total degree <= ``degree`` in ``dim`` variables (constant first).

functions.name: stencil_weights
functions.sig: (X: np.ndarray, Q: np.ndarray, idx: np.ndarray, ops = ('lap',), *, method: str = 'rbf_fd', degree: int = 2, batch: int = 2000) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Weights ``{op: (q, n)}`` (see the module docstring). ``X``: (N, dim) nodes; ``Q``: (q, dim) query points;
``idx``: (q, n) stencil node indices.

children.summary: Stencil weights in any dimension for meshless discretisations: RBF-FD and GFDM (weighted least squares).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.meshless.study
children.doc:
Refinement study of meshless and mesh-based methods on one problem and one domain.

For every node spacing ``h`` and every method: the error at independent evaluation points (each method's own
interpolant) and at its nodes, against the manufactured solution or, without one, against a fine finite-element
reference (whose own error is estimated and reported); the setup and solve time; the 1-norm condition number of the
system matrix and the noise amplification. Then the observed order of convergence, the growth of the condition
number, a shape-parameter sweep for Kansa, and where each method wins (no family is assumed to be better: each
criterion names its own winner, with the numbers).

methods.name: solutions_csv
methods.doc:
The solution of every method at the evaluation points, with the reference: CSV text with the columns
``x, y, reference, <method>...`` (9 significant digits). Empty header only when no field was kept.

functions.name: meshless_study
functions.sig: (problem: Problem, dom: Domain2D, h: Sequence[float] | None = None, *, methods: Sequence[str] = ('kansa', 'rbf_fd', 'fd', 'fem', 'pinn'), options: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] | None = None, pinn_levels: str = 'finest', n_eval: int = 2000, tolerance: float = 0.001, eps_sweep: bool = True, seed: int = 0, progress: Callable[[str], None] | None = None) -> MeshlessStudy
functions.doc:
Run every method at every spacing in ``h`` (default: three halvings from diameter / 10). ``options``: per
method, e.g. ``{"kansa": {"eps": 2.0}, "rbf_fd": {"degree": 3}, "pinn": {"budget_s": 5}}``. ``pinn_levels``:
``finest`` (default, the PINN trains once) or ``all``.

children.summary: Refinement study of meshless and mesh-based methods on one problem and one domain.

children.doc:
Meshless and mesh-based solvers of the same 2-D problems, and the study that compares them.

* :mod:`.domains`   -- 2-D domains (square, disk, L-shape, annulus, plate with a hole, any polygon, an uploaded point
  cloud) with their signed distance and quasi-uniform node sets at a spacing ``h``.
* :mod:`.problems`  -- Poisson, Helmholtz and heat problems with Dirichlet conditions, from a manufactured solution
  (sympy expression) or from a source and a boundary value.
* :mod:`.methods`   -- Kansa (global RBF collocation), RBF-FD (polyharmonic splines + polynomials), finite differences
  on an embedded Cartesian grid (Shortley-Weller at the boundary), linear finite elements on the Delaunay mesh of
  the nodes, and a PINN on the same nodes.
* :mod:`.study`     -- refinement study: error, cost, condition number, noise amplification, observed order, and
  where each method wins.

    from pinneapple_simulation.meshless import Problem, domain, meshless_study
    res = meshless_study(Problem("poisson", exact="sin(pi*x)*sin(pi*y)"), domain("lshape"), h=[0.1, 0.05, 0.025])

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.multibody
pinneapple_simulation.multibody.arm
children.doc:
Fixed-base serial arms on :class:`~pinneapple_simulation.multibody.tree.MultibodyTree`: inverse and forward
dynamics, a closed-form planar two-link reference, quintic trajectories, and the energy balance of a motion.

``fixed_base_inverse_dynamics``  joint torques ``tau = M_jj qdd + h_j - Q_g,j`` with the base held still.
``fixed_base_forward``           integrate the joint equations (RK4) under given torques (base held still).
``planar_two_link_torques``      the closed-form torques of a planar two-link arm (Spong, Hutchinson & Vidyasagar,
                                 *Robot Modeling and Control*, 2006, sec. 7.3), an independent check of the tree.
``quintic``                      rest-to-rest quintic polynomial between two joint configurations.
``energy_balance``               work done by the joint torques against the change of kinetic + potential energy.

functions.sig: (tree: MultibodyTree, q, qd, qdd) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: ``(n, nj)`` joint torques along a trajectory ``q, qd, qdd`` (each ``(n, nj)``), base fixed at the origin.

functions.name: fixed_base_forward
functions.sig: (tree: MultibodyTree, q0, qd0, tau_fn, t) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: Joint angles and rates at the times ``t`` (RK4 between them) under torques ``tau_fn(t, q, qd)``.

functions.name: planar_two_link_torques
functions.sig: (m1, m2, l1, lc1, lc2, I1, I2, g, q, qd, qdd) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Closed-form torques of a planar two-link arm in a vertical plane; angles from the horizontal (``q2``
relative), ``I1``, ``I2`` about the centres of mass and normal to the plane. Shapes ``(n, 2)``.

functions.name: energy_balance

functions.doc:
``W = integral of tau . qd dt`` (trapezoid) against ``Delta(T + U)``; ``rel`` is the mismatch relative to the
largest of ``|W|`` and the peak energy swing.

functions.name: link_world_points
functions.sig: (tree: MultibodyTree, q, points: dict[str, np.ndarray]) -> dict[str, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: World positions of body-frame points ``{body name: (m, 3)}`` for each configuration in ``q (n, nj)``.

functions.name: lumped_link
functions.sig: (name: str, length: float, mass_per_m: float, point_masses = (), width: float = 0.05)

A :class:`~pinneapple_simulation.multibody.tree.Body` for a straight link along its x axis: a uniform beam
(``mass_per_m`` over ``length``, square section ``width``) plus point masses ``[(x, m), ...]`` (motors,
payload). Mass, centre of mass and inertia about it (parallel-axis theorem).

functions.name: link_root_checks
functions.sig: (tau, section, *, yield_strength: float, fatigue_strength: float | None = None, safety: float = 3.0, names = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, list[dict]]
functions.doc:
Bending stress at each link root from the joint torques ``tau (T, nj)`` (the torque a joint delivers is the
bending moment it passes into the child link), checked against ``yield / safety`` and, with
``fatigue_strength`` (fully reversed, at the design life), the stress amplitude (half the range over the
cycle) against ``fatigue_strength / safety``. Returns ``(stress (T, nj) [Pa], checks)``.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.multibody.tree
children.doc:
Floating-base multibody tree with revolute joints: kinematics, Jacobians, mass matrix, bias forces and a
linearly implicit time step.

Generalised coordinates ``q = (p_base (3), quat_base (4, w x y z), joint angles (nj))`` and velocities
``v = (v_base (3, world, of the base origin), omega_base (3, world), joint rates (nj))``. Equations of motion

    M(q) dv/dt + h(q, v) = Q_gravity + Q_external(q, v) + tau_joints

with ``M = sum_i (Jv_i^T m_i Jv_i + Jw_i^T I_i Jw_i)`` over the bodies' centres of mass and ``h`` the Coriolis and
centrifugal terms, obtained by a forward recursion of the velocity-product accelerations (accelerations of the bodies
with dv/dt = 0). :meth:`MultibodyTree.step` takes a linearly implicit Euler step: force providers return their
generalised force and its derivative with respect to v (contact damping, PD gains), so stiff terramechanics and
servo terms stay stable at millisecond steps.

Every body has a mass, a centre of mass and an inertia tensor about it in its own frame; the base is body 0.

classes.name: Body
classes.doc: A rigid body: ``mass`` [kg], ``com`` [m] and ``inertia`` (3, 3) about the com [kg m^2], both in the body frame.

classes.name: RevoluteJoint
classes.doc:
Child frame = parent frame * (translate ``origin``, rotate ``R0``) * rotation(``axis``, q). ``axis`` in the
child frame (equal to the joint frame). ``limits`` (lo, hi) [rad] act through a stiff penalty spring.

classes.name: Kinematics
classes.doc: World poses and velocities of every body for one state.

classes.name: MultibodyTree
classes.doc: Build with :meth:`add_body` (the first body is the floating base) and :meth:`add_revolute`.

methods.sig: (name, parent: int | str, child: Body, origin, axis, R0 = None, limits = None, damping: float = 0.0) -> int

methods.name: ancestors
methods.doc: Joint indices from body ``i`` up to the base.

methods.name: point_jacobian
methods.doc: (3, nv) Jacobian of the world velocity of a point fixed to ``body`` (point given in world coordinates).

methods.name: bias
methods.doc: Coriolis and centrifugal generalised forces h(q, v).

methods.name: integrate
methods.doc: Positions after a step with velocity ``v`` (exponential map for the base orientation).

methods.name: step
methods.sig: (q, v, dt, forces) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray, Kinematics]
methods.doc:
One linearly implicit Euler step. ``forces(kin, q, v)`` returns (Q (nv,), D (nv, nv)) with ``D = dQ/dv``
(and any position stiffness already folded in as ``dt K``). Returns the new (q, v) and the kinematics at the
start of the step.

methods.doc: Kinetic and gravitational potential energy [J].

children.doc:
Rigid multibody dynamics in reduced coordinates: a floating base with trees of revolute joints.

    from pinneapple_simulation.multibody import MultibodyTree, Body
    tree = MultibodyTree(gravity=(0, 0, -1.62))
    tree.add_body(Body("chassis", 300.0, inertia=np.diag([40, 50, 60])))
    tree.add_revolute("arm_FL", "chassis", Body("arm_FL", 12.0), origin=(0.5, 0.4, 0.0), axis=(1, 0, 0))
    q, v = tree.initial_state(p=(0, 0, 1))
    q, v, kin = tree.step(q, v, 1e-3, lambda kin, q, v: (np.zeros(tree.nv), np.zeros((tree.nv, tree.nv))))

Used by :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.vehicle` for wheeled rovers; validated in ``tests/test_vehicle_multibody.py`` against
free fall, a pendulum's period, energy conservation and momentum conservation of a free tree.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.multiphysics
pinneapple_simulation.multiphysics.cases
children.doc:
Coupled cases with closed-form solutions for the multiphysics workflow (#1209).

Each builder returns a :class:`CoupledCase`: the two participants (:mod:`.coupling`), the reference interface field
for the one-way solve, the quantities of interest, the interface and energy balances, and the closed-form
solution of the *coupled* problem the discrete result is checked against.

* :func:`joule_wire` (electro-thermal, two-way, nonlinear): a wire of length ``L`` carrying a current ``I``, ends
  held at ``T0``, resistivity ``rho(T) = rho0 (1 + alpha (T - T0))``. Electric participant: ``q = J^2 rho(T)``;
  thermal participant: ``-k T'' = q``. Closed form, with ``m^2 = J^2 rho0 alpha / k``:
  ``T - T0 = (cos(m (x - L/2)) / cos(m L / 2) - 1) / alpha`` and ``dV = rho0 J (2/m) tan(m L / 2)``; no steady
  state exists for ``m L >= pi`` (thermal runaway), which the builder refuses.
* :func:`bimetal_strip` (thermal-structural, one-way by nature): two bonded layers heated by ``dT``. Thermal
  participant: conduction through the thickness; structural participant: beam (laminate) theory, axial force and
  bending moment equilibrium for the mid-plane strain and the curvature. Closed form: Timoshenko (1925),
  ``kappa = 6 (a2 - a1) dT (1 + m)^2 / (h (3 (1 + m)^2 + (1 + m n) (m^2 + 1 / (m n))))``, ``m = t1/t2``,
  ``n = E1/E2``, tip deflection ``kappa L^2 / 2`` for a cantilever.
* :func:`conjugate_channel` (fluid-thermal, conjugate heat transfer): fluid in a channel (capacity rate
  ``C = m_dot c_p``, ``C T_f' = hP (T_w - T_f)``) against a wall with axial conduction heated by ``q'`` per unit
  length (``kA T_w'' - hP (T_w - T_f) + q' = 0``, insulated ends). The partition is the usual CHT one: the solid
  reads the fluid temperature (Robin), the fluid reads the wall temperature. Closed form: the exact solution of
  the linear constant-coefficient system (matrix exponential), and ``C (T_out - T_in) = q' L``.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.multiphysics.coupling
children.doc:
Steady coupling of two physics participants through named interface fields (#1209).

A :class:`Participant` owns a discrete state and exposes three functions:

* ``solve(input) -> state``: its own solver, given the other participant's interface output;
* ``residual(state, input) -> r``: its discrete equations (used by the monolithic solve);
* ``output(state) -> field``: the interface field it hands to the other participant.

Participant ``a`` reads ``b``'s output and vice versa. The strategies:

* :func:`one_way`: ``a`` sees ``b``'s reference (uncoupled) output, ``b`` sees ``a``'s result; no feedback.
* :func:`gauss_seidel`: two-way partitioned, ``y -> b.output(b.solve(a.output(a.solve(y))))`` relaxed on the field
  ``y`` that ``a`` reads, with Aitken's dynamic relaxation (Irons & Tuck 1969; Kuttler & Wall 2008, eq. 44)
  or a fixed factor. The interface residual history is returned.
* :func:`monolithic`: both residuals solved together for both states (``scipy.optimize.root``, Powell hybrid with
  a finite-difference Jacobian), started from the one-way states.

:func:`coupling_strength` measures the contraction factor of the plain (unrelaxed) Gauss-Seidel map from its first
iterations (a power-iteration estimate of the spectral radius of the interface Jacobian), and
:func:`recommend_strategy` turns it and the measured one-way error into the strategy to use.

functions.name: one_way
functions.sig: (a: Participant, b: Participant, y_ref: np.ndarray) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: ``a`` solved with ``b``'s reference output ``y_ref``; ``b`` solved with ``a``'s result.

functions.name: gauss_seidel
functions.sig: (a: Participant, b: Participant, y0: np.ndarray, *, aitken: bool = True, omega0: float = 0.5, omega: float = 1.0, tol: float = 1e-10, max_iter: int = 200) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Two-way partitioned coupling; ``tol`` on ``|r_k| / |y_k|`` (``r_k = G(y_k) - y_k``).

functions.name: monolithic
functions.sig: (a: Participant, b: Participant, sa0: np.ndarray, sb0: np.ndarray, *, tol: float = 1e-12) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Both discrete residuals solved together, started from ``(sa0, sb0)``.

functions.name: coupling_strength
functions.sig: (a: Participant, b: Participant, y0: np.ndarray, n: int = 6) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Contraction factor of the unrelaxed Gauss-Seidel map, from the ratios of its first interface corrections.

functions.name: recommend_strategy
functions.sig: (contraction: float, one_way_error: float, one_way_tolerance: float) -> tuple[str, str]
functions.doc:
``one_way`` when its measured error is within the tolerance; partitioned Gauss-Seidel with Aitken while the
plain map contracts (rho < 1); monolithic otherwise.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.multiphysics.workflow
children.doc:
The standard multiphysics-coupling workflow (#1209): one coupled case, every strategy, and the checks.

1. **Coupling strength** first: the contraction factor of the plain partitioned map (:func:`.coupling.coupling_strength`).
2. **Strategies**, all run on the same discrete case: one-way, two-way partitioned Gauss-Seidel (plain, and with
   Aitken relaxation), and monolithic (both residuals together). Each is timed.
3. **Recommendation** (:func:`.coupling.recommend_strategy`) from the measured contraction and the measured error
   of the one-way result against the two-way one, so the user sees when one-way is enough.
4. **Checks**: convergence of the coupling iteration (with the interface residual history); partitioned against
   monolithic; the interface and global energy / force balances of the case; the coupled closed-form solution.

functions.doc:
Run the protocol on ``case`` (``joule_wire``, ``bimetal_strip``, ``conjugate_channel``) with
``case_params`` passed to its builder. Returns the strategies, the recommendation, the checks and the
measured numbers. ``one_way_tolerance``: the largest relative error on the quantities of interest at which
one-way coupling is accepted.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.multirotor
pinneapple_simulation.multirotor.power
children.doc:
Electric drive of a multirotor: a brushless DC motor (Kv / Kt with copper and no-load losses) and a lithium-polymer
pack (Peukert-corrected capacity, open-circuit voltage against state of charge, internal-resistance sag).

Motor (the standard first-order DC model, e.g. Drela, *First-Order DC Electric Motor Model*, MIT 2007):
``K_t = 1 / K_v`` in SI units (``K_v`` [rad/s per V]; ``K_t = 60 / (2 pi Kv_rpm)`` [N m/A]),
``I = Q / K_t + I_0``, ``V = I R_m + omega / K_v``, ``P_elec = V I = Q omega + I^2 R_m + I_0 omega / K_v``
(shaft + copper + no-load loss: :meth:`Motor.operating_point` returns all three and their sum closes ``V I``).

Battery: ``n_series`` cells, open-circuit voltage ``V_oc(SOC)`` interpolated from ``ocv_curve`` (a stated typical
LiPo curve, 3.3 V empty to 4.2 V full; replace it with the cell's datasheet curve), terminal voltage
``V = n (V_oc(SOC) - I R_cell / n_parallel)``. Peukert: at a constant current ``I`` the delivered capacity is
``C (C / (I H))^{k-1}`` for a rating at ``H`` hours (Peukert 1897; ``k = 1`` switches it off; lithium cells are close
to 1, the default 1.05 is a stated assumption). The discharge is integrated in time with the charge drawn scaled
by ``(I H / C)^{k-1}``, which gives that capacity exactly at constant current.

classes.doc: ``kv_rpm`` [rpm/V], winding resistance ``r_ohm`` [ohm], no-load current ``i0`` [A], ``mass`` [kg].

exponent ``peukert`` at a rating of ``rating_hours`` [h], ``specific_energy`` [W h/kg] for the pack mass.

methods.doc: Pack capacity [A h].

methods.name: peukert_capacity
methods.doc: Capacity [A h] delivered at a constant ``current`` [A] (Peukert).

methods.doc: State of charge after drawing ``current`` [A] for ``dt`` [s].

methods.name: current_for_power
methods.doc:
Current [A] that delivers ``power`` [W] at the terminals: ``(V_oc - I R) I = P`` (the smaller root);
nan when the pack cannot deliver it.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.multirotor.quad
children.doc:
A quadrotor in X configuration: mass build-up, 6-DOF rigid-body dynamics with rotor lag, an LQR hover controller
with position integrators, its stability margins, and a mission flown on the battery until it is empty.

Frames: world z up (gravity ``-g e_z``), body z along the thrust. State: position, velocity (world), attitude
quaternion ``(w, x, y, z)`` body-to-world, body rates, rotor speeds. Rotor ``i`` sits at ``L (cos psi_i, sin psi_i)``
with ``psi = 45, 135, 225, 315 deg`` and spins ``s_i = +1, -1, +1, -1`` (counter-clockwise seen from above for
``+1``); its thrust ``T = c_T(J) rho n^2 D^4`` and torque ``Q = c_P(J) rho n^2 D^5 / (2 pi)`` come from a BEMT table
over the axial advance ratio ``J = V_axial / (n D)`` (:func:`.rotor.bemt`), the yaw reaction is ``-s_i Q_i``, the
rotor speed follows its command with the motor time constant ``tau_motor``. Body drag ``-1/2 rho C_d A |v - w| (v -
w)`` with the wind ``w(t)``. Edgewise (forward-flight) rotor effects are not modelled: the cruise power is that of
the axial-flow rotor (stated with the result).

LQR (:func:`pinneapple_systems.control.tuning.lqr`) on the hover linearisation ``p' = v``, ``v' = (g theta,
-g phi, dF / m)``, ``Theta' = omega``, ``omega' = J^-1 tau``, with integrators of the position error, so a steady wind
leaves no offset. Margins: each input channel of the loop is broken in turn with the others closed, the motor lag
included (:func:`loop_margins_per_channel`).

classes.name: Quad
classes.doc:
A quadrotor: ``rotor`` with its ``table`` (:func:`rotor_table`), ``motor``, ``battery``, arm length ``arm``
[m], total ``mass`` [kg] and its ``parts``, inertia ``J`` [kg m^2], body drag area ``cd_area`` [m^2].

methods.name: mixer
methods.doc: ``[F, tau_x, tau_y, tau_z] = M T`` for the four rotor thrusts (hover yaw ratio ``Q / T``).

methods.name: omega_max
methods.doc:
Rotor speed the motor reaches at ``voltage`` in hover: ``(Q / K_t + I_0) R + K_t omega = V`` with
``Q = k_Q omega^2``.

classes.name: Segment
classes.doc:
A mission leg: hold ``target`` (world position [m]) for ``duration`` [s], reached along a straight line at
``speed`` [m/s] (the reference moves, the controller tracks it).

functions.sig: (rotor: Rotor, rpm: float, j_max: float = 0.6, n: int = 13, rho: float = RHO_SEA_LEVEL) -> dict
functions.doc: Propeller ``c_T`` and ``c_P`` against the axial advance ratio ``J`` at ``rpm`` (BEMT).

functions.name: hover_power
functions.sig: (q: Quad, soc: float = 0.8) -> dict
functions.doc:
Electrical hover power [W] at ``soc``: rotor speed for ``m g / 4``, the motor's current and voltage, the ESC
efficiency and the avionics; the battery current and the thrust-to-weight at full voltage.

functions.name: lqr_hover
functions.sig: (q: Quad, *, q_pos: float = 4.0, q_vel: float = 1.0, q_ang: float = 4.0, q_rate: float = 2.0, q_int: float = 0.5, r_force: float = 0.5, r_torque: float = 3000.0) -> dict
functions.doc:
LQR gains on the 15-state hover model (position, velocity, roll-pitch-yaw, body rates, position-error
integrals) with inputs ``[dF, tau_x, tau_y, tau_z]`` (diagonal weights; the defaults were chosen on the default
design for >= 45 deg phase margin per channel with a 30 ms motor lag and a 1 m step overshoot under 30 %).

functions.name: loop_margins_per_channel
functions.sig: (ctrl: Mapping[str, Any], tau_motor: float) -> list[dict]
functions.doc:
Gain and phase margins at each input channel, the loop broken there with the other channels closed and the
motor lag ``1 / (tau s + 1)`` in every channel: ``L_j(s) = K_j (sI - A_j)^-1 B_j / (tau s + 1)``.

functions.name: simulate
functions.sig: (q: Quad, ctrl: Mapping[str, Any], *, t_end: float, dt: float = 0.01, reference: Callable[[float], np.ndarray] | None = None, wind: Callable[[float], np.ndarray] | None = None, battery: bool = False, soc0: float = 1.0, record_every: int = 5, stop_on_empty: bool = True) -> dict
functions.doc:
Integrate the 6-DOF quadrotor (RK4 on the rigid body, exact first-order rotor lag) under the LQR. With
``battery`` the rotor speeds are limited by the pack's terminal voltage and the state of charge is drawn down;
the run stops when the pack is empty (cut-off voltage or reserve). Returns the time history and the energy
drawn.

functions.name: fly_mission
functions.sig: (q: Quad, ctrl: Mapping[str, Any], segments: Sequence[Segment], *, repeat: bool = True, dt: float = 0.02, t_max: float = 7200.0, wind = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
Fly ``segments`` (repeated while ``repeat``) on the battery from full until it is empty: the endurance is the
time the run lasted. The reference moves to each target at the segment's speed, then holds it.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.multirotor.rotor
children.doc:
Rotor aerodynamics of a multirotor: momentum theory and blade-element momentum theory (BEMT) in hover and axial
flight, with the Prandtl tip loss.

Conventions (Leishman, *Principles of Helicopter Aerodynamics*, 2nd ed., 2006, ch. 2-3): rotor coefficients
``C_T = T / (rho A (Omega R)^2)``, ``C_P = C_Q = P / (rho A (Omega R)^3)``, inflow ratio ``lambda = (V_c + v_i) /
(Omega R)``, solidity ``sigma = N c / (pi R)``, figure of merit ``FM = C_T^{3/2} / (sqrt(2) C_P)``. Propeller
coefficients (the UIUC / APC convention) ``c_T = T / (rho n^2 D^4) = C_T pi^3 / 4`` and
``c_P = P / (rho n^3 D^5) = C_P pi^4 / 4`` with ``n`` in rev/s.

The BEMT balances, on each annulus, the momentum thrust ``dC_T = 4 F lambda (lambda - lambda_c) r dr`` against the
blade-element thrust ``dC_T = (sigma / 2) (U / Omega R)^2 (c_l cos phi - c_d sin phi) dr`` (exact inflow angle
``phi = atan(lambda / r)``) and solves for ``lambda`` by bracketing; ``small_angle=True`` uses ``cos phi = 1``,
``sin phi = phi`` and ``U = Omega r``, the form in which an ideally twisted rotor without tip loss and profile drag
has uniform inflow and exactly the momentum-theory induced power ``C_P = C_T^{3/2} / sqrt(2)`` (the closed-form check
of :func:`ideal_twist_check`).

classes.name: Airfoil
classes.doc:
A linear lift curve with a stall clip and a parabolic drag polar: ``c_l = a (alpha - alpha_0)`` within
``[cl_min, cl_max]``, ``c_d = cd0 + cd2 (c_l - cl_cd_min)^2`` (stated defaults: a thin cambered section at low
Reynolds number, ``a = 5.7 /rad``, ``alpha_0 = -4 deg``, ``c_d0 = 0.012``; change them for a measured polar).

methods.name: cd0_at
methods.doc:
Profile drag at zero lift; with ``re_ref > 0`` scaled as ``cd0 (Re / Re_ref)^re_exponent`` (the laminar
skin-friction trend that dominates low-Reynolds propellers).

classes.name: Rotor
classes.doc:
A rotor: tip ``radius`` [m], ``blades``, chord ``c/R`` and pitch ``beta`` [deg] at stations ``r/R`` (the
UIUC geometry-file convention), ``root`` cut-out ``r/R``.

methods.name: stations
methods.doc: Mid-points ``r``, widths ``dr``, chord ``c/R`` and pitch [rad] of ``n`` annuli from the root to the tip.

methods.name: ideal
methods.sig: (radius: float, blades: int, chord_over_r: float, theta_tip_deg: float, root: float = 0.1, airfoil: Airfoil | None = None) -> Rotor
methods.doc: Constant chord with the ideal twist ``theta = theta_tip / r`` (uniform inflow in hover, Leishman 3.3.3).

functions.name: induced_velocity
functions.sig: (thrust: float, radius: float, rho: float = RHO_SEA_LEVEL) -> float
functions.doc: Momentum-theory hover induced velocity ``v_h = sqrt(T / (2 rho A))`` [m/s].

functions.name: momentum_hover_power
functions.sig: (thrust: float, radius: float, rho: float = RHO_SEA_LEVEL) -> float
functions.doc: Ideal hover power ``T^{3/2} / sqrt(2 rho A)`` [W] (momentum theory, uniform inflow).

functions.name: bemt
functions.sig: (rotor: Rotor, omega: float, v_climb: float = 0.0, rho: float = RHO_SEA_LEVEL, *, n: int = 40, tip_loss: bool = True, profile_drag: bool = True, small_angle: bool = False) -> dict
functions.doc:
Thrust [N], torque [N m], power [W], ``C_T``, ``C_P``, ``FM`` and the propeller ``c_T``, ``c_P`` of
``rotor`` at ``omega`` [rad/s] and axial speed ``v_climb`` [m/s], with the spanwise inflow, angle of attack and
lift coefficient.

functions.name: prop_coefficients
functions.sig: (rotor: Rotor, rpms: Sequence[float], rho: float = RHO_SEA_LEVEL, **kw) -> dict
functions.doc: Static propeller ``c_T`` and ``c_P`` (UIUC convention) at each RPM.

functions.name: ideal_twist_check
functions.sig: (radius: float = 0.127, blades: int = 2, chord_over_r: float = 0.1, theta_tip_deg: float = 8.0, rpm: float = 6000.0, rho: float = RHO_SEA_LEVEL) -> dict
functions.doc:
The closed-form check of the BEMT: an ideally twisted rotor without tip loss and profile drag (small angles)
has uniform inflow, so its power equals the momentum-theory ideal ``T^{3/2} / sqrt(2 rho A)``. Returns the
relative power difference and the spread of the inflow.

functions.name: apc_10x4_7
functions.sig: (airfoil: Airfoil | None = None, scale: float = 1.0) -> Rotor
functions.doc:
The APC Slow Flyer 10 x 4.7 (D = 10 in) as a :class:`Rotor`; ``scale`` scales the diameter (same c/R and
pitch angles: a geometrically similar propeller).

functions.sig: (rotor: Rotor, rpm, cT, cP, *, train = None, re_ref: float = 100000.0) -> dict
functions.doc:
Fit the polar (lift slope, zero-lift angle, ``c_d0`` and the Reynolds exponents of lift and drag at
``re_ref``) to measured static ``c_T``, ``c_P`` on the ``train`` rows (relative least squares) and report the
errors on the held-out rows before (the rotor's own polar) and after.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.multirotor.workflow
children.doc:
The standard multirotor workflow (#1201): rotor -> motor and battery -> airframe and sizing -> 6-DOF control ->
the designed drone flown on a mission until its battery is empty.

1. **Rotor**: BEMT (:mod:`.rotor`) checked against momentum theory (an ideally twisted rotor without losses has
   exactly the ideal induced power) and against the published static ``c_T``, ``c_P`` of the APC Slow Flyer
   10 x 4.7 (UIUC database). The assumed polar is reported as it is; the polar is then calibrated on the even rows
   and its error measured on the odd (held-out) rows, and on the high-RPM half after a fit on the low half.
2. **Motor and battery** (:mod:`.power`): ``K_v`` / ``K_t`` with copper and no-load losses (the power split closes
   ``V I``), Peukert-corrected LiPo pack with voltage sag.
3. **Sizing**: propeller diameter (the APC geometry scaled), cells in series and capacity on a grid; for each, the
   motor ``K_v`` that reaches the thrust-to-weight target at 95 % of the loaded pack voltage, the arm length from the
   propeller clearance, and the mass build-up (:func:`build_quad`, stated coefficients in ``MASS_MODEL``); the
   lightest design whose estimated hover endurance meets the target.
4. **Control** (:mod:`.quad`): LQR on the hover linearisation with position integrators; checks: every closed-loop
   pole in the left half plane, per-channel gain and phase margins with the motor lag, a 1 m step (overshoot,
   settling) and a 3 m/s wind gust (peak excursion, recovery).
5. **Re-verification**: the drone flies hover -> climb -> cruise -> return legs repeatedly on the battery until it
   is empty; the endurance is the time the flight lasted (measured), compared with the sizing estimate and with the
   momentum-theory ideal hover power over the figure of merit.

**Published endurance**: :func:`published_endurance_check` builds a quad with the DJI Phantom 4's published take-off
mass and battery (``PHANTOM4``, each value with its source) on the scaled APC propeller (the Phantom's own propeller
geometry is not public here: an assumption), hovers it until the pack is empty and compares with the published
maximum flight time within ``PHANTOM4_BAND``.

functions.name: rotor_verification
functions.sig: (airfoil: Airfoil | None = None) -> dict

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.naval.submarine
children.doc:
Depth-keeping of a submerged submarine: hydrostatic instability, the trim tank and the choice of what the
controller commands.

Buoyancy at depth ``z`` (positive down) with a compressible hull in compressible seawater:

    B(z) = rho0 (1 + kw z) * V0 (1 - kh z) * g

The hull compressibility ``kh`` is usually larger than the water compressibility ``kw``. When it is,
``dB/dz < 0``: going deeper loses buoyancy, and the depth equilibrium is statically unstable. The small-signal
model is ``m_eff z'' = -B'(z) z + g u``, with ``u`` the extra mass in the trim tank. It has a real pole at
``+sqrt(-B'(z) / m_eff)``.

Vertical motion uses the net downward force ``(m g - B(z) - Cd |w| w)`` over ``(1 + ca) m``:
* ``m`` is the dry mass plus the trim-tank mass plus a disturbance mass;
* ``ca`` is the added-mass coefficient;
* ``Cd`` is a quadratic drag coefficient in N s^2/m^2.

As in many depth-keeping studies, the momentum of the water pumped in or out is neglected. The trim tank is
driven by a pump with a flow limit, and the tank has a capacity.

:func:`architectures` builds the two command choices:
* **PID → target tank mass:** the pump is a rate-limited servo that moves the tank towards the target.
* **PID → pump flow:** the command is a rate, so the actuator integrates.
:func:`depth_study` simulates both, linearises both closed loops (:func:`pinneapple_systems.control.loop_eigenvalues`)
and explains the difference. With the derivative on the measured vertical speed, the target-mass loop has the
characteristic polynomial ``m s^3 + g Kd s^2 + (k + g Kp) s + g Ki``. Commanding the flow gives
``m s^4 + c s^3 + (k + g Kd) s^2 + g Kp s + g Ki``. With no linear damping at rest (``c = 0``, quadratic drag), the
``s^3`` coefficient is zero, so by the Routh criterion no PID gains can stabilise it.

:data:`ILLUSTRATIVE` holds the parameters of a public illustrative example (not a real boat). With them,
:func:`depth_study` reproduces that example: without control the depth runs away to the 600 m limit, and with the
PID commanding the target mass it holds depth.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.beam_bvp_fdm
children.doc:
Euler-Bernoulli beam deflection: 4th-order finite-difference solve of the
beam BVP

    EI * d^4w/dz^4 = q(z),   z in [0, L]

for a uniform distributed load q, under one of three classical boundary
condition sets (simply-supported, cantilever, fixed-fixed), plus the
standard post-processing (moment, shear, bending/shear/von-Mises stress) for
a few common cross-sections. This is the classical numerical counterpart to
a PINN-based Euler-Bernoulli residual (e.g. this package's
`euler_bernoulli_beam` PDE compiler kind) -- same governing equation, solved
by direct sparse linear algebra on a fixed grid instead of by training a
network, useful as a fast reference/ground-truth or wherever no training is
wanted.

t_m  : section width at the neutral axis [m]
A_m2 : total cross-sectional area [m^2]

functions.name: second_derivative
functions.sig: (f: np.ndarray, dz: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Second derivative of `f`, second-order accurate everywhere including
the two boundary points (3-point central stencil in the interior, a
3-point one-sided stencil at each edge).

Used to get the bending moment (EI * d2w/dz2) directly from the
deflection, instead of differentiating twice with `np.gradient` (i.e.
slope = gradient(w), then moment = gradient(slope)): that two-step path
compounds np.gradient's first-order-accurate edge formula twice at the
boundary points, which -- for the fixed/simply-supported ends that are
exactly where bending stress peaks -- silently halves the reported
moment there (verified against the closed-form Euler-Bernoulli
solution: the error sits at -50% and does not shrink as the grid is
refined, i.e. it isn't ordinary truncation error). A single proper
second-derivative stencil doesn't have that failure mode.

Solve the 1D Euler-Bernoulli beam BVP EI*w''''=q under a uniform
distributed load q_N_per_m, for one of the three BC_* boundary
condition sets. `section` (default: an 0.10x0.10 m rectangular section)
supplies the cross-section geometry used for the returned stresses --
pass a `SectionProps` built to match I_m4 for a physically consistent
stress calculation (a mismatched section only affects the stress
outputs, not the deflection/moment/shear, which depend on I_m4 alone).

Returns a dict: z, deflection_m, moment_Nm, shear_N, slope_rad,
sigma_b_Pa, tau_Pa, sigma_vm_Pa, strain_b, failed, utilization, L,
yield_Pa. `failed`/`utilization` are all-zero when yield_Pa<=0 (check
disabled).

children.doc:
Euler-Bernoulli beam by Hermite finite elements: static deflection and natural modes.

Two degrees of freedom per node (deflection w, rotation theta), cubic Hermite shape functions, consistent mass
matrix (Przemieniecki, *Theory of Matrix Structural Analysis*, 1968, ch. 5 and 11). Supports: "pinned"
(simply supported), "fixed" (clamped) or "free" at each end. Converges to the exact Euler-Bernoulli answers: the
simply supported first mode ``f1 = pi / (2 L^2) sqrt(EI / m)`` and mid-span deflection ``5 q L^4 / (384 EI)``.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.bekker_wong
children.doc:
Bekker-Wong numerical solver for rigid-wheel / deformable-soil interaction.

Model (Wong & Reece 1967; Wong 1978)
-----------------------------------
Contact arc: entry angle theta_f = arccos(1 - z/R), rear angle theta_r = -rear_angle_ratio*theta_f,
maximum-stress angle theta_m = (a0 + a1*s)*theta_f.

    sigma(theta) = (k_c/b + k_phi) * (R (cos theta* - cos theta_f))^n
        theta* = theta                                                    (front region, theta >= theta_m)
        theta* = theta_f - (theta - theta_r)/(theta_m - theta_r)*(theta_f - theta_m)   (rear region)
    j(theta)     = R [(theta_f - theta) - (1 - s)(sin theta_f - sin theta)]
    tau(theta)   = sign(j) (c + sigma tan phi)(1 - exp(-|j|/K))               (Janosi-Hanamoto)

    F_x = R b int (tau cos - sigma sin),  F_z = R b int (sigma cos + tau sin),  M_y = R^2 b int tau

Robustness features (vs. the first version of this module)
-----------------------------------------------------------
* Input validation (0 < z < R, -1 <= s < 1, positive soil/wheel parameters) -- raises instead
  of silently returning garbage.
* ``forces`` passes the integrand's kinks (theta_m, 0) as ``quad`` break points and exposes the
  quadrature error estimate.
* ``forces_batch`` / :func:`bekker_wong_forces_torch`: vectorised piecewise Gauss-Legendre
  quadrature (numpy or differentiable torch, per-sample soil parameters allowed), verified
  against adaptive ``quad``; ~10^4x faster for batches.
* ``sinkage_from_load`` brackets and solves F_z(z) = W with Brent's method (F_z is monotone in z
  on the checked domain) instead of an unguarded secant iteration.
* ``generate_dataset`` never writes fabricated zeros for failed evaluations; it raises (strict)
  or drops the point and reports how many were dropped.
* Shear stress is sign-aware, so braking (s < 0) no longer produces an exponentially growing
  tau for negative shear displacement.

References
----------
- Bekker, M.G. (1969). Introduction to Terrain-Vehicle Systems. U Michigan Press.
- Wong, J.Y. (1978). Theory of Ground Vehicles. Wiley.
- Wong, J.Y., Reece, A.R. (1967). Prediction of rigid wheel performance based on the analysis of
  soil-wheel stresses. J. Terramechanics 4(1).

Full CAD-to-CFD pipeline: STEP/STL → mesh → Navier-Stokes solve.

Integrates with the existing OpenFOAM / FEniCS bridges in
``pinneapple_solvers`` and adds a pure-Python / NumPy mesh-native
incompressible NS solver for rapid prototyping and PINN data generation.

External dependencies (optional, gracefully handled)
-----------------------------------------------------
- ``gmsh``   – mesh generation from STEP / STL files.
- ``scipy``  – sparse direct / iterative linear solver for the FEM NS system.

If ``gmsh`` is not installed, :class:`CFDMesh` falls back to generating a
simple structured rectangular mesh.  If ``scipy`` is not installed,
:class:`NSFlowSolver` uses a simplified iterative Picard loop with PyTorch.

Usage::

    pipeline = CADToCFDPipeline(nu=1e-3)
    pipeline.load_geometry("airfoil.step")
    pipeline.mesh(max_edge_length=0.02)
    pipeline.set_bcs(inlet_velocity=(1.0, 0.0))
    results = pipeline.solve()
    train_data = pipeline.to_pinn_data()

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.compressible_fv
children.doc:
Compressible Navier-Stokes / Euler finite-volume solver (2-D and 3-D Cartesian), PyTorch.

Scheme
------
* Conservative variables U = (rho, rho*u_d..., E) on a uniform Cartesian grid, two ghost layers.
* MUSCL reconstruction of primitive variables (rho, u_d..., p) with a minmod or van Leer limiter.
* HLLC approximate Riemann solver (Toro, *Riemann Solvers and Numerical Methods for Fluid Dynamics*, ch. 10)
  with Davis wave-speed estimates.
* Viscous fluxes: Newtonian stress with Stokes' hypothesis, Fourier conduction (constant Prandtl number),
  power-law viscosity mu = mu_ref * T^omega; normal derivatives compact at faces, tangential derivatives
  averaged from the two adjacent cells.
* SSP-RK2 (Heun) time integration, CFL + viscous time-step limit.

Non-dimensionalisation: reference density, reference sound speed and a length H. With p = rho*T/gamma the
reference state has rho = 1, T = 1, p = 1/gamma, c = 1; mu_ref = (rho u H / Re) for a chosen Mach.

Boundary conditions (per face): "supersonic_inflow" (Dirichlet on every primitive), "pressure_outlet"
(extrapolate rho and velocity, impose static pressure -- the fixed-pressure outlet), "extrapolate",
"wall" (no-slip, adiabatic), "slip" (inviscid wall / symmetry), "periodic".

Delegates to :func:`pinneapple_physics.pde_environment.presets.astrophysics.sod_exact_solution`, which covers
every wave pattern (shock or rarefaction on either side).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.crash_cases
children.doc:
The pole-impact case of a bumper beam on its two crash boxes — a crash-test coupon the solver can afford.

The case is the component-scale half of a crash programme: a DP1000 bumper beam held by two DP600 crash boxes,
driven into a rigid pole, exactly the object of the pole-impact benchmark (design vector -> crashworthiness
quantities, and the displacement sequence of every node). It is built on a **fixed hexahedral mesh** so that every
design shares the same node set — what a field surrogate (and a spatial comparison between designs) needs — and the
design variables act through the material and the obstacle:

- ``velocity``          impact speed [m/s];
- ``box_thickness``     crash-box wall thickness, through its flow stress and mass (see the note below);
- ``beam_thickness``    bumper-beam thickness, the same way;
- ``dp600_yield``       initial yield stress of the crash boxes [Pa];
- ``dp1000_yield``      initial yield stress of the bumper beam [Pa];
- ``pole_radius``       radius of the rigid pole [m];
- ``pole_offset``       lateral offset of the pole from the assembly centre line [m].

Note on thickness on a fixed mesh: the mesh keeps the walls at the reference thickness ``t_ref`` and a design
``t`` scales the flow stress and the density of the part by ``t / t_ref`` (the axial crush force of a thin-walled
column grows with the wall thickness, and so does its mass). Bending stiffness would scale as ``t^3`` and is
therefore under-represented; the quantities this case reports (peak wall force, energy absorbed, pulse duration) are
axial-crush dominated. Say so when reporting a sweep: this is a coupon, not a full vehicle.

    from pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.crash_cases import DESIGN_BOUNDS, bumper_beam_assembly, pole_impact

    assembly = bumper_beam_assembly()                      # reference design, fixed mesh, 3 parts
    res = pole_impact({"velocity": 16.0, "box_thickness": 0.002}, end_time=6e-4)
    print(res.qoi(), res.displacement.shape)

The flow stress and the density scale with ``thickness / t_ref`` (axial crush force and mass of a thin-walled

Build the fixed-mesh assembly (see the module docstring). Every design shares this mesh and these nodes.

Geometry (metres, x is the impact direction, z up, y across): two square crash boxes with their rear face at
``x = 0`` (held), walls one cell thick, spanning ``x`` up to :data:`BOX_LENGTH`; the bumper beam as a slab on
their front face, two cells thick, spanning the box spacing in ``y``. The pole stands :data:`GAP` ahead of it.

``n_parts`` splits the three structural groups into finer semantic parts (3: beam + two boxes; 6: each group in
two halves; 12: the beam in three segments and each box in two), so a part-aware surrogate can be exercised at
several hierarchy depths on the same mesh.

functions.sig: (design: dict | None = None, *, end_time: float = 0.0015, frames: int = 21, n_parts: int = 3, cfl: float = 0.9, record_velocity: bool = False, material_override: dict | None = None) -> CrashResult

Run one design of the coupon (see the module docstring) and return the full result.

``design`` is a partial or complete design vector (missing keys take :data:`DESIGN_DEFAULTS`). The coupon is the
sled view of the pole impact: the rear face of the crash boxes is held (the body it is bolted to) and the rigid
pole travels at the impact velocity into it, so the crush is driven by the pole's travel and the impact starts
at ``GAP / velocity`` in every design of the sweep.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.crash_fem
children.doc:
Explicit structural crash dynamics on 8-node hexahedra (pole impact, barrier impact, axial crush).

Written from the published methods — no code from OpenRadioss, LS-DYNA or CalculiX is used:

- central-difference explicit time integration with lumped mass, the scheme every explicit crash code runs, at the
  critical time step of the mesh (``dt = cfl * h / c_d``, ``c_d`` the dilatational wave speed of the element);
- 2 x 2 x 2 Gauss integration instead of one-point integration with hourglass control: the eight integration points
  supply the anti-hourglass stiffness themselves, so the element has nothing to tune and cannot hourglass;
- **corotational kinematics**: every element carries the rotation ``R`` of the polar decomposition of its centre
  deformation gradient; the previous stress and strain are rotated with ``R_new R_old^T`` and the strain measure is
  taken in the rotated frame (``eps = 0.5 (R^T F + F^T R) - I``), so a part can fold and rotate without the
  small-strain measure invalidating the result — which is what a crash simulation is made of;
- J2 (von Mises) plasticity with linear isotropic hardening, radial return at every integration point, element
  erosion at a critical equivalent plastic strain (and on element inversion), with the eroded element's mass removed
  from its nodes;
- penalty contact against a **rigid obstacle**: a moving wall (the barrier of a full-frontal impact) or a moving
  cylinder (the pole of a pole impact), with Coulomb friction, the elastic contact energy kept and the reaction
  force recorded;
- the energies (kinetic, internal, plastic work, contact) and the crashworthiness quantities a design sweep ranks by:
  peak wall force, peak deceleration, peak internal energy, peak plastic work, kinetic-energy absorption
  ``eta = 1 - E_kin(T) / E_kin(0)`` and the impact duration above a threshold of the peak force.

Envelope: the corotational strain measure holds for moderate stretches (elastic strains are small, plastic ones may
be large, but no single element should be stretched by more than a few tens of percent); the material is isotropic
hardening without damage, and erosion stands in for failure. Elements that would break that envelope (relative
length change above ``ENVELOPE``) set ``CrashResult.out_of_envelope`` — the run still returns, but its numbers are
outside the verified range of this model.

    from pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.crash_fem import Material, RigidPole, CrashSolver
    from pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.solid_fem import box_mesh

    mesh = box_mesh(0.30, 0.06, 0.04, 30, 6, 4)                     # a 300 mm bar, 5 mm elements
    mat = Material(rho=7.8e3, E=2.1e11, nu=0.3, yield_stress=6.0e8, hardening=4.0e8, erosion_strain=0.4)
    pole = RigidPole(radius=0.10, x0=0.32)                          # rigid cylinder just ahead of the bar
    solver = CrashSolver(mesh, material=mat, contact=pole, initial_velocity=(30.0, 0.0, 0.0), end_time=0.02)
    res = solver.run()
    print(res.qoi())                                                # peak_wall_force, ke_absorption, ...

classes.doc:
Isotropic-hardening J2 material — the phenomenological model of a crash alloy (DP600, DP1000, mild steel).

``yield_stress`` is the initial yield stress, ``hardening`` the slope of the yield stress against the equivalent
plastic strain (linear isotropic hardening; 0 is perfectly plastic), ``erosion_strain`` the equivalent plastic
strain at which the element is removed (0 keeps every element).

classes.sig: (mesh: HexMesh, *, material: Material | dict[int, Material], parts = None, contact: RigidPole | RigidWall | None = None, fixed = None, initial_velocity = 0.0, cfl: float = 0.9, penalty: float = 1.0, friction: float = 0.0, end_time: float | None = None, frames: int = 41, record_velocity: bool = True, dt: float | None = None)

Parameters

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.cylinder_wake
children.doc:
Confined cylinder wake with the D2Q9 lattice-Boltzmann solver: one run, its verification and the zoo dataset
``cylinder_wake_lbm``.

A cylinder of diameter ``D`` lattice cells sits 3 D downstream of a uniform (plug) inlet in a channel of height
``height`` D and length ``length`` D (blockage D/H = 1/height), with no-slip walls (bounce-back) and a pressure
outlet. :func:`simulate` runs ``conv_time`` convective units (t U / D) and keeps the last ``keep_time``: vorticity
snapshots normalised by U/D, the transverse-velocity probe 2 D behind the cylinder, the wake regime (steady or
shedding) and the Strouhal number (Hann-windowed, peak-refined spectrum of the probe).

* :func:`verify`: the developed channel profile against plane Poiseuille flow (low Re, two grids), and a resolution
  study at Re 100 (D = 20, 30, 40 at the same physical time and sampling);
* :data:`PLAN` / :func:`generate`: the dataset, Re 20..100 without a turbulence model, written as
  ``<split>[-NN].npz`` + ``meta.json`` (split by Reynolds number).

functions.name: probe_strouhal
functions.sig: (signal: np.ndarray, dt: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Strouhal number of a probe record sampled every ``dt`` convective units: strongest peak of the
Hann-windowed, 4x zero-padded spectrum with Gaussian peak interpolation (a fraction of a bin).

functions.name: simulate
functions.sig: (Re: float, D: int = SETUP['D'], height: int = SETUP['height'], length: int = SETUP['length'], u_in: float = SETUP['u_in'], conv_time: float = SETUP['conv_time'], keep_time: float | None = SETUP['keep_time'], save_dt: float = SETUP['save_dt'], Cs: float = SETUP['Cs']) -> dict
functions.doc:
One run. Returns the setup, the convective times ``t`` and vorticity frames ``vorticity`` (n, nx, ny) of the
last ``keep_time`` convective units (``None``: the second half of the run), the probe ``probe_uy`` (/U) over
the same times, ``wake_amplitude`` (its rms), ``amplitude_growth`` (probe rms of the last quarter of the window
over the first: ~1 for a saturated wake), ``regime`` and ``strouhal`` (0 for a steady wake), and the ``solid``
mask.

functions.name: verify
functions.sig: (Ds = (20, 30, 40), Re: float = 100.0, channel_Re: float = 2.0) -> dict
functions.doc:
Developed channel profile (plane Poiseuille; at ``channel_Re`` on D the entrance length is ~2.5 D, so the
profile is developed 9 D downstream) on the dataset grid and a 2x coarser one, and the resolution study of the
wake at ``Re``. At the dataset's Reynolds numbers the 12 D channel is far shorter than the entrance length, so
the cylinder sees a nearly uniform inflow with thin wall boundary layers.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.dfsph
children.doc:
DFSPH: Divergence-Free SPH (Bender & Koschier 2015 / 2017).

DFSPH enforces two constraints per time step:
  1. Divergence-Free  : ∇·v = 0  (velocity divergence solver — inner loop)
  2. Constant Density : ρ = ρ₀   (density solver — outer loop, optional)

Algorithm per step:
  1. Find neighbors, compute densities.
  2. Compute non-pressure forces (viscosity, gravity).
  3. Divergence-free pressure solve → adjust velocity so ∇·v ≈ 0.
  4. Advect positions.
  5. Density-correction pressure solve → adjust velocity so ρ ≈ ρ₀.
  6. Enforce boundary repulsion.

References
----------
Bender & Koschier (2015), SCA — DFSPH.
Bender & Koschier (2017), IEEE TVCG — improved formulation.

Divergence-Free SPH (DFSPH) solver.

mu              : dynamic viscosity
gravity         : body acceleration list  e.g. [0.0, -9.81]
boundary_lo/hi  : domain extents for wall repulsion
div_max_iters   : divergence-free inner loop iterations
dens_max_iters  : density-correction inner loop iterations

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.discrete_time_pinn
children.doc:
Discrete-time physics-informed neural network (PINN), per Raissi,
Perdikaris & Karniadakis, "Physics Informed Deep Learning (Part II):
Data-driven Discovery of Nonlinear Partial Differential Equations"
(arXiv:1711.10566), Section 2 ("Discrete Time Models"), specialized here to
the pure forward-solve (not data-driven-discovery) setting for `burgers_1d`
and `allen_cahn_1d`.

Unlike every other PINN in this package (and unlike `xtfc_ivp.py`/
`xtfc_pde.py`, which are gradient-free), this module DOES use ordinary
gradient-based training -- but with a distinctive architecture and time
discretization that is algorithmically unrelated to the usual "continuous
time" PINN (a network of (x,t) -> u trained on scattered space-time
collocation points): here, a SINGLE network of x -> (q+1) values represents
an entire q-STAGE IMPLICIT RUNGE-KUTTA STEP from a known time t_n to
t_{n+1} = t_n + dt, where dt can be a SUBSTANTIAL fraction of the whole time
horizon (the original paper's Burgers example takes ONE step of dt=0.8 using
q=500 stages) -- the high stage-count IRK method supplies enough temporal
accuracy (local truncation error is formally O(dt^(2q+1)) for the q-stage
Gauss-Legendre family; see `irk_gauss_legendre.py`) to make a single giant
step numerically meaningful, in exchange for a much harder per-step training
problem than an explicit few-step scheme would pose.

Method summary
--------------
1. IRK tableau: the exact q-stage Gauss-Legendre (A, b, c) tableau from
   `irk_gauss_legendre.get_irk_tableau(q)` -- imported and reused verbatim,
   NOT rederived here (this module owns none of the tableau algebra).
2. Network (`DiscreteTimeRKNet`): a plain x -> R^(q+1) MLP. Column i (i=0..
   q-1) is the network's prediction of the solution at the i-th INTERMEDIATE
   RK stage time t_n + c_i*dt; column q is its prediction at the FINAL time
   t_n + dt. (Raissi et al.'s own notation: U^n_i for the stage predictions,
   U^{n+1} for the final one.)
3. Stage derivatives via forward-mode AD (`stage_derivatives`): because the
   network is applied POINTWISE to a batch of scalar x's (batch dimension is
   independent samples, not a computation graph coupling them), the
   per-sample derivative d(output_k)/dx for EVERY one of the q+1 outputs at
   EVERY batch point is obtainable from a SINGLE `torch.func.jvp` call with
   tangent = ones_like(x) (since d(f(x))/dx * 1 = f'(x) elementwise) -- far
   cheaper than q+1 separate reverse-mode passes or per-output autograd.grad
   calls. The second (viscous/diffusive) derivative is obtained the same way
   by taking the jvp of the jvp itself (forward-over-forward AD), still just
   two total forward evaluations of the network's computation graph.
4. RK residual (`discrete_time_rk_residual`): given the nonlinear spatial
   operator N[u] (e.g. Burgers' -u*u_x + nu*u_xx, or Allen-Cahn's
   eps^2*u_xx + 5u - 5u^3) evaluated at every stage's (value, first, second
   x-derivative) triple, the implicit-RK consistency equations (paper's
   Eqs. 2.4-2.6, adapted to a pure forward solve: `u_n_data` plays the role
   of the paper's known snapshot at t_n) are:

       U_i     - dt * sum_j A[i,j] * N[U_j]  ==  u_n_data,   i = 1..q
       U_{q+1} - dt * sum_j b_j   * N[U_j]   ==  u_n_data

   i.e. running the SAME IRK scheme backward from any stage (or from the
   final time) to t_n must reproduce the known data at t_n -- this is the
   trick that lets a single network encode the whole implicit step without
   ever needing labeled data at any intermediate or final time. Boundary
   conditions (time-invariant Dirichlet data here) are enforced as an
   ordinary MSE penalty at x0/x1 applied to ALL q+1 columns (the BC holds at
   every one of the q+1 times spanned by the step).
5. `train_discrete_time`: an L-BFGS driver (matching the original paper's
   optimizer choice -- these problems are small, smooth least-squares-like
   fits that L-BFGS converges on much faster than SGD/Adam) minimizing the
   sum of the interior RK-residual MSE and the boundary MSE.

Caveats (explicit, not glossed over)
-------------------------------------
- This is a genuine gradient-trained network (autograd/backprop), unlike
  every other X-TFC-family module in this package -- intentionally so, since
  discrete-time collocation in x alone (no t input) has no fixed-ELM
  analogue as directly applicable as the continuous-time TFC construction in
  `xtfc_pde.py`.
- q here defaults much smaller than the original paper's q=500 (which needed
  a full-batch L-BFGS run of order minutes) so this module's own tests run in
  seconds; `train_discrete_time`'s `q` argument can be raised freely for a
  more paper-faithful (and slower) reproduction.
- Only a SINGLE discrete step (t_n -> t_n+dt) is implemented per
  `train_discrete_time` call -- chaining multiple discrete-time steps (each
  using the previous step's converged U_{q+1} as the next step's u_n_data,
  the way the paper does for e.g. Allen-Cahn) is left to the caller by simply
  calling `train_discrete_time` again with the previous call's output.

functions.name: stage_derivatives
functions.sig: (model: nn.Module, x: torch.Tensor) -> 'tuple[torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor, torch.Tensor]'
functions.doc:
U(x), U_x(x), U_xx(x), each (N, q+1), via forward-mode AD.

x: (N, 1). Uses `torch.func.jvp` with tangent=ones_like(x): since the
network is applied pointwise (batch dim is independent samples, not a
coupled computation), d(f(x))/dx * 1 = f'(x) for every sample and every
output column SIMULTANEOUSLY from one jvp call -- and the second
derivative from one more (forward-over-forward), rather than q+1
reverse-mode passes. `model` is called directly (not via
`torch.func.functional_call`): jvp only pushes a tangent through the
INPUT here, so treating the model's parameters as fixed constants during
the push-forward is exactly the semantics wanted (we are differentiating
U(x) w.r.t. x for fixed weights, not w.r.t. the weights).

Stage and final-time IRK consistency residuals (module docstring
point 4). Returns (res_stage, res_final), shapes (N, q) and (N, 1).

x: (N, 1) interior collocation points.

    step's converged final-time output).
dt: step size t_{n+1} - t_n.
A, b: IRK tableau (q,q) and (q,), e.g. from `get_irk_tableau(q)`, as
    torch tensors matching `x`'s dtype/device.

    once (each argument (N, q)); returns (N, q).

functions.doc:
Train a `DiscreteTimeRKNet` for one implicit-RK step of `pde` in
{"burgers_1d", "allen_cahn_1d"}, from known data (x_n, u_n) at t_n to
t_n + dt, via L-BFGS (module docstring point 5).

pde: selects the nonlinear operator N[u] and the (time-invariant
    Dirichlet) boundary value from `_PDE_PRESETS`.
x_n, u_n: (N,) known solution samples at t_n (e.g. the problem's initial
    condition, or a previous `train_discrete_time` call's
    `predict_final` output for a chained multi-step run).
dt: step size (t_n -> t_n+dt); may be a large fraction of the whole
    horizon given a large enough `q` (see module docstring).
q: number of IRK stages (Gauss-Legendre order 2q). Paper-scale examples
    use q up to ~500; kept smaller by default here for test speed.
x_span: domain for boundary points; defaults to the preset's standard
    domain when omitted.

    standard benchmark value when omitted.

bc_weight: loss weight on the boundary MSE term relative to the interior
    RK-residual MSE.

seed: torch RNG seed for network initialization.

`predict_final`/`predict_stage` convenience methods).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.numerical_solvers.eddy_current_fdm
children.doc:
2D axisymmetric magnetostatic / eddy-current FDM solver.

Governing equation (azimuthal magnetic vector potential A_theta, single
angular frequency omega, quasi-static / low-frequency eddy-current
approximation):

    d2A/dr2 + (1/r) dA/dr - A/r2 + d2A/dz2 - i*omega*mu*sigma*A = -mu*J_source

Solved via a sparse COMPLEX linear system (scipy.sparse + spsolve) on a
rectangular (r, z) grid, r in [r_min, r_max], z in [z_min, z_max], with
Dirichlet A=0 on the outer domain boundary by default. This is the standard
axisymmetric formulation used throughout applied electromagnetics for any
problem with rotational symmetry about the z-axis: induction heating,
transformers/inductors, magnetic bearings, eddy-current braking, non-
destructive eddy-current inspection, or any other axisymmetric conductor in
a time-harmonic magnetic field -- the equation and discretization are
generic; the material maps (mu, sigma) and source current density are
caller-supplied, not hardcoded to any one application's geometry.

At omega=0 (mu*sigma term vanishes) this reduces to the axisymmetric
magnetostatic (Poisson-like) equation for a DC current distribution.

classes.name: EddyCurrentFDMSolver
classes.sig: (nr: int = 60, nz: int = 120)
classes.doc:
Thin `SolverBase`/registry wrapper. The functional API
(`solve_axisymmetric_eddy_current`, `build_axisymmetric_helmholtz_system`,
`annular_current_source`) is the primary entry point and can be used
directly without this wrapper.

methods.name: forward
methods.sig: (r_bounds: tuple[float, float], z_bounds: tuple[float, float], omega: float, mu: np.ndarray, sigma: np.ndarray, source_current_density: np.ndarray) -> SolverOutput

functions.name: build_axisymmetric_helmholtz_system
functions.sig: (r: np.ndarray, z: np.ndarray, k2: np.ndarray, rhs_2d: np.ndarray)
functions.doc:
Assemble the sparse complex system M @ a = b for the axisymmetric
operator

    L[A] - k2(r,z)*A = rhs(r,z)

where L[A] = d2A/dr2 + (1/r)dA/dr - A/r2 + d2A/dz2 (the axisymmetric
vector-Laplacian-like operator acting on a single scalar component
A_theta), via a standard 5-point finite-difference stencil at interior
points and Dirichlet A=0 at all boundary points.

r, z: 1D coordinate arrays (uniform spacing assumed within each axis).
k2: (len(r), len(z)) complex array -- e.g. k2 = 1j*omega*mu*sigma for the
    eddy-current equation, or k2 = 0 for pure magnetostatics.
rhs_2d: (len(r), len(z)) complex array -- e.g. rhs = -mu*J_source.

Returns (M_csr, b_dense) with flat node ordering n = i*nz + j.

functions.name: annular_current_source
functions.sig: (r: np.ndarray, z: np.ndarray, r_center: float, z_center: float, width_z: float, width_r: float, n_turns: float, current_amp: float) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Uniform azimuthal current density J_theta (A/m^2) in a rectangular
annular band centered at (r_center, z_center) -- the standard
lumped-coil approximation for an axisymmetric current loop / solenoid
turn, used to drive the eddy-current or magnetostatic equation above.
The band is ``|z - z_center| <= width_z / 2`` and ``|r - r_center| <= width_r``
(``width_r`` is the radial half-width).

The density is normalised on the grid so that the discrete total current
``sum(J * dr * dz)`` over the band nodes equals ``n_turns * current_amp``
exactly, whatever the alignment of the band with the grid (a band narrower
than one cell falls back to the nearest node). Normalising by the nominal
band area instead made the injected current depend on that alignment (0.75
of N I on a grid where the band covers 4 x 5 nodes), which is what the
validation gallery saw as a coil field of a fraction of the loop formula.
Returns a (len(r), len(z)) real array.

functions.name: solve_axisymmetric_eddy_current
functions.sig: (r: np.ndarray, z: np.ndarray, omega: float, mu: np.ndarray, sigma: np.ndarray, source_current_density: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Solve for the azimuthal vector potential A_theta(r,z) at angular
frequency `omega` (rad/s), given material maps mu(r,z) [H/m] and
sigma(r,z) [S/m] and a source current density J_source(r,z) [A/m^2],
all as (len(r), len(z)) arrays matching the r,z grids. `omega=0` solves
the magnetostatic limit (no eddy currents).

Returns A, shape (len(r), len(z)), complex (purely real when omega=0).

functions.name: eddy_current_density
functions.sig: (A: np.ndarray, omega: float, sigma: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Induced eddy-current density J_theta = -i*omega*sigma*A, given the
solved vector potential A and the same sigma(r,z) map used to solve it.

The system above, ``L[A] - i omega mu sigma A = -mu J_source``, is Ampere's law
``L[A] = -mu (J_source + J_eddy)`` with ``J_eddy = sigma E`` and ``E = -i omega A``:
the phasor convention ``exp(+i omega t)``. (Before this was fixed the function
returned ``+i omega sigma A``, the eddy current with the wrong sign.)

functions.name: axial_flux_density
functions.sig: (A: np.ndarray, r: np.ndarray, z: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
B_z(r,z) = (1/r) d(r*A)/dr = A/r + dA/dr, computed via central differences (the
axisymmetric curl relating A_theta to the axial field component). Complex A gives the
complex phasor B_z (in-phase and quadrature parts); A = B0 r / 2 gives B_z = B0, on the axis too.
