children.name: pinneapple_simulation.robot_sim.sim
children.doc:
PINNeAPPle Robot Sim: robots simulated with NVIDIA Newton (CPU or GPU through Warp), recorded with the
quantities PINNeAPPle checks (joint torques, energy, body poses, IMU), and an Isaac Sim backend with the same
interface for machines that have it.

    sim = RobotSim.from_spec(spec)                     # or from_urdf(path) / from_usd(path) / from_mjcf(path)
    run = sim.run(t_end=0.8, dt=5e-4, q0=q0, controller=pd_tracking(ref, kp, kd, feedforward=tau_fn))
    run.q, run.qd, run.tau, run.energy(), run.imu("link2")

Controllers are plain functions ``controller(t, q, qd) -> tau`` (joint torques before the actuator limits); the
recorded ``tau`` is what the actuators delivered (clipped to each joint's effort limit, and the clipping is counted
in ``run.saturated``). Helpers: :func:`torque_trajectory`, :func:`pd_tracking`. The solver is Newton's
``SolverFeatherstone`` (reduced coordinates; semi-implicit, first order in ``dt``: halve ``dt`` and the error of a
smooth motion halves, which :func:`convergence_order` measures).

methods.name: energy
methods.doc: Kinetic, potential and total mechanical energy of every body over time [J].

methods.name: actuator_work
methods.doc: Cumulative work of the joint torques [J] (torque held over each step, rate at the step's midpoint).

methods.name: imu
methods.doc:
Simulated IMU at a body's centre of mass: specific force (acceleration minus gravity) and angular rate,
both in the body frame, by central differences of the recorded velocities.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.rover
pinneapple_simulation.rover.autolab
pinneapple_simulation.rover.autolab.estimation
children.doc:
What the rover measures, and what it infers about the soil from it.

Measurements (:func:`measure`): from a :class:`~pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.VehicleRun`, per wheel and sample, the
normal load (suspension), slip (visual odometry against wheel odometry), sinkage (wheel camera) and motor torque
(motor current), each with Gaussian sensor noise (:class:`Sensors`; the noise levels are stated assumptions, not
datasheet values). Only the front wheels are used: they run on undisturbed soil (the rear wheels run in the ruts of
the front ones, which the steady single-pass model below does not describe).

Inference (:class:`SoilBelief`): a Gaussian belief over ``theta = (log10 k_phi, n0, n1, phi_deg)`` per mapped soil
unit, started from the soil the orbital map assigns to the unit, updated with an iterated extended Kalman filter
(static parameters, no process noise). The observation model is the steady Wong-Reece wheel: for the measured load
and slip it predicts the sinkage and the soil torque. Cohesion, the shear modulus K and k_c stay at the prior soil's
values (not identifiable from these signals at these loads). ``samples()`` draws soils from the belief for the
planner's risk estimate.

classes.name: Sensors
classes.doc: Noise levels (one standard deviation) of the rover's measurements; stated assumptions.

classes.name: SoilBelief
classes.sig: (prior_soils: list[Soil], wheel: Wheel, g: float = 1.62, prior_sd = PRIOR_SD, obs_sd_sinkage: float = 0.008, obs_sd_torque = (2.0, 0.1), input_sd = (0.008, 0.05), n_gl: int = 12)
classes.doc:
Gaussian beliefs over the soil parameters of each mapped unit (see the module docstring).

``obs_sd_sinkage`` and ``obs_sd_torque`` (abs, rel) are the observation noise of the filter: sensor noise plus an
allowance for what the steady single-wheel model leaves out of the multibody rover (dynamics, slip lag, load
transfer); ``input_sd`` the noise of the measured slip and (relative) load, carried through the model; stated
choices (match them to :class:`Sensors`).

methods.name: predict
methods.sig: (unit: int, theta, load, slip, slip_sink = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc:
Predicted (sinkage [m], torque [N m]) stacked as one vector [z..., tau...]; ``slip_sink`` is the slip
that sets the sinkage exponent (default: ``slip``).

methods.name: update
methods.sig: (unit: int, load, slip, sinkage, torque, t: float = 0.0, iters: int = 10, slip_sink = None) -> UnitBelief
methods.doc: Iterated EKF update of one unit with a batch of measurements.

methods.name: assimilate
methods.sig: (meas: dict, batch: int = 8, units = None, calibrate: bool = True) -> None
methods.doc: Feed measurements in time order, ``batch`` rows per update, to the unit each row was taken on.

methods.name: chi2
methods.sig: (unit: int, meas: dict, rows) -> tuple[float, int]
methods.doc:
Chi-square of the residuals of ``rows`` under the current mean (with the filter's covariance), and the
degrees of freedom (observations minus parameters).

methods.name: samples
methods.sig: (unit: int, n: int = 24, seed: int = 0) -> list[Soil]
methods.doc: Soils drawn from the belief of ``unit`` (the mean first).

methods.name: recovery
methods.doc:
Error of the belief against a known true soil: per parameter the error, the posterior sd and the error in

Noisy measurements from a vehicle run (front wheels by default), one row per wheel and kept sample.

Slip is measured at every output sample with noise ``sensors.slip_sd`` and averaged over a centred window of
``slip_window`` seconds (the rover processes its log after the fact; a trailing window would delay the slip and
bias the soil estimate); the slip that sets the sinkage exponent is that measured
slip lagged over ``sink_length`` metres of rim travel, the same first-order lag the multibody simulator uses (a
model setting, see :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.sim`). Keeps rows every ``every`` outputs where the
wheel touches the soil, turns, and slips at most ``max_slip`` (beyond it the wheel is digging in, a transient the
steady model does not describe). Returns arrays ``t, x, y, wheel, unit, load, slip, slip_sink, sinkage,
torque`` and the noise-free values (``*_true``).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.rover.autolab.mission
children.doc:
A mission in plain language -> the rover's lab loop, through a fixed set of tools.

Stages (the Autonomous Physics Lab loop): **mission** (parse the request) -> **plan** (which tools, in which order)
-> **build** (site, rover, beliefs from the orbital map) -> **simulate** (drive the planned route with the multibody
rover on the true terrain) -> **learn** (measurements -> soil belief) -> **optimize** (replan on the new belief) ->
**verify** (trust report against the physics and, on a synthetic site, the known truth) -> **deliver** (report).

The request is turned into a :class:`MissionSpec` by a parser with the ``extract(text, schema) -> dict`` interface of
:class:`pinneapple_design.intent.parse.CallLLM`: pass ``llm=CallLLM(...)`` to use a language model (its answer is
checked against the text: every value needs a quote found in the request), otherwise :class:`RuleParser` does it
deterministically. Either way the agent only calls the tools of :data:`TOOLS`, with arguments it validated.

    from pinneapple_simulation.rover.autolab import demo_site, RoverMission
    m = RoverMission(demo_site(), "Drive the rover to (37, 15) without getting stuck, slip at most 40 %, "
                                  "minimum energy")
    result = m.run(out_dir="out")        # result.report (TrustReport), result.routes, result.log

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.rover.autolab.planner
children.doc:
Risk-aware route planning on a site from what the rover believes about its soils.

For every soil unit the planner draws soils from the rover's belief (:class:`~.estimation.SoilBelief`), computes for
each the quasi-static operating point on every grade (:func:`~.wheel_models.grade_table`) and so knows, per unit and
grade, the expected drive energy per metre and the *risk*: the share of belief samples in which the rover cannot
climb that grade at a slip at or below the mission's slip limit. Routes are shortest paths (Dijkstra, 8-connected
grid) with edge cost ``length * (energy per metre + risk_weight * risk)`` (``objective="distance"``: length times
``1 + risk_weight / 200 * risk``); edges whose risk exceeds ``risk_max`` are removed. The grade of an edge is the
height difference along it. Risk: the soil is sampled at both ends, the midpoint and ``half_width`` (half the track
plus a margin) to either side, the worst counting. Slip and energy: the mean of the left and right wheels
(``half_track`` to either side). Cross-slope is not part of the model.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.rover.autolab.site
children.doc:
A synthetic planetary site whose truth is known: relief, soils, and what an orbiter would have said about them.

The site is a height function (planar tilt + Gaussian mounds) and a map of soil *units*. Each unit has a true soil
(hidden from the rover, used only by the simulator and to score what the rover learns) and an orbital class: the
soil an orbital map would assign to that unit before any wheel touched it. A unit whose orbital class is wrong (soft
sand mapped as compact regolith) is how a first route can fail.

    from pinneapple_simulation.rover.autolab import demo_site
    site = demo_site()
    site.unit_at(x, y)              # unit index per point (truth map; units are what the orbiter also sees)
    site.true_soil(k)               # hidden truth, for the simulator and for scoring
    site.prior_soil(k)              # what the orbital map assumes
    site.deformable_terrain(cell)   # DeformableTerrain for pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.VehicleSimulator

All numbers of :func:`demo_site` (positions, sizes, the soft-sand parameters) are choices made for this synthetic
site, not measurements of a real one; the compact regolith and the firm gravelly ground use library soils with
their recorded provenance (``GRC-1`` and ``JSC-1A`` in :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.soils`).

classes.doc: Gaussian hill ``height * exp(-((x-x0)^2/sx^2 + (y-y0)^2/sy^2) / 2)`` [m].

a ``cell`` grid) for the multibody simulator.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.rover.autolab.verify
children.doc:
Trust report of a rover mission: did it work, does the physics hold, and can the learned soil be believed.

Checks (``pinneapple_analysis.trust.Check``; values are measured in this mission's simulations):

* ``goal_reached`` (critical) and ``slip_within_limit`` (critical): the final run reached the goal with the 2-s mean
  front-wheel slip at or below the mission limit everywhere.
* ``energy_covers_climb``: the measured drive energy of the final run is at least ``m g`` times the total climb along
  it (the wheels do not regenerate and the kinetic energy at walking speed is negligible, so less would break energy
  conservation).
* ``time_step_converged``: the first seconds of the final route rerun at half the time step give the same mean
  slip and sinkage (relative change at most 5 %).
* ``planner_vs_multibody_energy`` / ``planner_vs_multibody_slip``: the planner's quasi-static prediction of the
  final route against the multibody measurement.
* ``replanned_route_risk``: the final route's risk under the learned belief is at most ``risk_max``;
  ``failed_route_risk_learned``: the first route's risk under the learned belief exceeds it (the update explains
  the failure).
* ``learned_soil_predictive``: held-out measurements of the stall unit are predicted within 20 % (sinkage RMSE /
  RMS sinkage).
* ``learned_soil_calibrated`` and ``learned_soil_closer_to_truth``: only on a synthetic site -- the error against the
  known true soil is within 3 posterior standard deviations for every parameter, and smaller than the prior's for
  k_phi and phi.
* ``models_used_in_validity``: the planner used the analytic law; the zoo surrogate's share of operating points
  outside its validity box is reported in ``details``.

The traction monitor's quantity: front-wheel mean slip averaged over the last ``window_s`` seconds (per output

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.rover.autolab.wheel_models
children.doc:
Wheel-soil laws at the operating point a rover needs, and the three ways to get them.

The planner needs, per soil and grade, the slip a wheel must run at to climb (and whether any slip below the
limit suffices), its sinkage, the motor torque and the drive energy per metre. :func:`grade_table` computes these
from the Wong-Reece model (quasi-static rover: ``n`` equally loaded wheels, load ``m g cos(a) / n``, drawbar pull
``m g sin(a) / n``; no load transfer, no cross-slope, no acceleration).

Three approximations of the same wheel-soil law are compared by :func:`compare_contact_models`:

* ``analytic`` -- :class:`~pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.WongReeceModel` with the soil the rover believes in;
* ``surrogate`` -- any ``predict(slip, sinkage) -> (Fx, Fz, My)`` model, e.g. the model-zoo network
  ``rover_contact_grc1_viper`` (trained on GRC-1 only; its validity box is checked per point);
* ``measured`` -- operating points recorded by the simulated rover (the multibody simulation on the true soil, with
  sensor noise), the reference both are scored against.

classes.doc: Operating points of a quasi-static rover on one soil, per grade [deg] (arrays over ``grades``).

methods.doc: Interpolate a quantity at grades (nan where the rover cannot climb).

functions.doc: Slip, sinkage, torque and energy per metre a ``mass`` kg rover on ``n_wheels`` needs on each grade.

functions.doc:

forces there. Returns dict like :meth:`WongReeceModel.steady_state`.

functions.doc:
Score the analytic law (believed soil) and a surrogate against measured operating points.

``measured``: arrays ``load`` [N], ``slip`` [-], ``sinkage`` [m], ``torque`` [N m] (one entry per sample).
Each model predicts sinkage and torque from the measured load and slip. Returns RMSE and bias per model and,
for the surrogate, the share of the measured operating points (measured slip and sinkage) outside its validity
box (``in_range(slip, z)``); a surrogate trained on another soil is outside its validity whatever the box says.

children.doc:
PINNeAPPle Autonomous Physics Lab, rover demo: *the rover that learns the planet*.

A mission in plain language ("drive to (37, 15) without getting stuck, slip at most 40 %, minimum energy") runs the
lab loop on a synthetic site whose truth is known: plan a route on the orbital map's soils, drive it with the
multibody VIPER on the true terrain (Wong-Reece wheels, several soils), stop when the measured slip exceeds the
limit, learn the soil from what the wheels measured (iterated EKF on sinkage and torque), replan on the learned
belief with its uncertainty, drive again, and verify everything in a trust report (including the error of the
recovered soil against the known truth).

    from pinneapple_simulation.rover.autolab import RoverMission, demo_site
    res = RoverMission(demo_site(), "Drive the rover to (37, 15) without getting stuck, slip at most 40 %, "
                                    "minimum energy").run(out_dir="out")
    res.report.decisao, [r.meta["ended"] for r in res.runs]

Modules: :mod:`.site` (synthetic site with hidden truth), :mod:`.wheel_models` (operating points per grade; analytic
vs surrogate vs measured), :mod:`.estimation` (sensors, soil belief), :mod:`.planner` (risk-aware routes),
:mod:`.mission` (parser, tools, the loop), :mod:`.verify` (trust report), :mod:`.report`, :mod:`.visuals`
(matplotlib), :mod:`.render` (Blender Cycles). Guide: ``docs/guides/rover_learns_the_planet.md``.
children.summary: PINNeAPPle Autonomous Physics Lab, rover demo: *the rover that learns the planet*.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.rover.checks
children.doc:
Verification of the rover model against closed forms, the standalone solver and its own balance laws.

* :func:`single_wheel_check` -- every wheel of a full-model state against the standalone ``BekkerWongSolver``
  (adaptive ``quad``): sinkage for the wheel's load and slip, then F_x and M_y at that sinkage.
* :func:`static_sinkage_check` -- the rover at rest on level ground on a pressure-only soil (no shear, front contact
  only) against Bekker's closed form for a rigid wheel, ``W = (3 - n) b k sqrt(D) z^((2n+1)/2) / 3``
  (Bekker 1969), and against the exact integral of the same pressure law.
* :func:`balance_check` -- independent recomputation of the force and moment balance of a state.
* :func:`surrogate_vs_numerical` -- a surrogate against the numerical law at the (slip, sinkage, soil) inputs
  met along a trajectory, with the share of inputs outside the training box.
* :func:`dp_grade_estimate` -- the maximum grade from "drawbar pull = grade resistance" for one wheel carrying
  ``m g cos(a) / 6`` at the limit slip, to compare with :meth:`RoverSimulator.max_slope`.

functions.sig: (soil: SoilParams) -> SoilParams
functions.doc:
The soil's pressure-sinkage law with shear switched off (c = 0, K very large) and the stress peak at the
bottom of the wheel (a0 = a1 = 0); use with ``rear_angle_ratio=0`` for front-only contact.

functions.doc: Bekker's closed form for the static sinkage of a rigid wheel: z = [3 W / ((3 - n) b k sqrt(D))]^(2/(2n+1)).

functions.doc:
Net force (including gravity, the lateral reaction, the tow load and the d'Alembert force) and net moment
about the centre of mass, recomputed from the stored wheel forces; scaled by m g and m g L.

functions.sig: (states, surrogate, numerical, soils: list[SoilParams]) -> dict
functions.doc: Errors of ``surrogate`` against ``numerical`` at every loaded (slip, sinkage) of the given states.

functions.sig: (rover: RoverParams, soil: SoilParams, s_limit: float, g: float = 1.62, rear_angle_ratio: float = 1.0 / 3.0, tol: float = 0.01) -> dict

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.rover.contact
children.doc:
Wheel-soil force laws for the rover: (slip, sinkage, soil) -> (F_x, F_z, M_y) per wheel.

* :class:`BekkerWongContact` -- the library's Bekker-Wong solver (``numerical_solvers.bekker_wong``): vectorised
  piecewise Gauss-Legendre quadrature (default, the reference) or adaptive ``quad`` (``method="quad"``, slow, for
  checks). Per-wheel soils are supported, so wheels on different regions use their own parameters.
* :class:`SurrogateContact` -- any fast surrogate of the same law trained for one soil and one wheel, e.g. the
  TorchScript PINN exported by ``examples/use_cases/terramechanics/terramechanics_rover_pinn.py``. Every call
  records which inputs fall outside the training box, so a run can report how much of it was extrapolated.

Forces are in the wheel's contact frame: F_x along the terrain in the travel direction (drawbar pull), F_z along

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.rover.dynamics
children.doc:
Rocker-bogie rover on lunar terrain with Bekker-Wong wheel forces.

Model
-----
* Rigid body (all mass in the body, links and wheels massless) carried by two rockers through frictionless pivots
  and a differential (right rocker angle = - left rocker angle), each rocker carrying a bogie; six driven wheels.
* Wheel-soil forces from Bekker-Wong (:mod:`.contact`): each wheel's sinkage is its penetration into the terrain
  (``R`` minus the distance from the axle to the local surface), its slip comes from the commanded wheel speed and
  the wheel-centre velocity along the terrain, and the force (F_x along the terrain, F_z along the normal) acts at
  the axle together with the soil torque -M_y about it.
* Quasi-static in heave, pitch, roll and suspension: at every step the unknowns
  ``(z, pitch, roll, rocker, bogie_L, bogie_R)`` satisfy the normal-force balance, the roll and pitch moment balance
  about the centre of mass, the moment balance of each bogie about its pivot and the differential condition (equal
  pivot moments on both rockers). The longitudinal direction is integrated with a backward-Euler step.
* Lateral forces are not given by Bekker-Wong; a lateral reaction proportional to the wheel loads closes the
  lateral force balance and the rover follows its straight path (no side slip, no yaw dynamics).

Drive modes
-----------
``speed``: the rover holds the speed ``v``; the common wheel speed (equivalently the commanded slip ``s_cmd``,
omega = v / (R (1 - s_cmd))) is an unknown fixed by the longitudinal balance. No solution with
``s_cmd <= s_limit`` means traction failure (the rover cannot hold the speed).
``slip``: the rover holds ``v`` and the wheels turn at omega = v / (R (1 - s_cmd)) for a given ``s_cmd``; the
external pull (drawbar pull of the whole rover) is what is left of the longitudinal balance -- a drawbar-pull test.

>>> traj.energy_per_metre()

Parametric six-wheel rocker-bogie rover: parameters, kinematics and meshes (glTF / STL export).

Every default is generic (not taken from a real rover). The wheel (R = 0.125 m, b = 0.06 m), the six driven wheels
and the 40 kg mass are the values of the terramechanics use case (``WheelParams``), so the PINN surrogate trained
there applies to this rover unchanged.

Body frame: origin on the rocker pivot axis midway between the two pivots, x forward, y left, z up.
Per side the rocker carries the front wheel and, at its rear end, the bogie pivot; the bogie carries the middle and
rear wheels. A differential makes the right rocker angle the negative of the left one (relative to the body).
With the default proportions (front arm = 2 x rear arm, bogie pivot midway between its wheels, centre of mass
above the rocker pivots) the six wheels carry equal loads on level ground and the wheels are equally spaced.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.rover.terrain
children.doc:
Lunar terrain for rover simulation: a height function with a planar slope, craters and rocks, plus soil regions.

Coordinates are metres, z up. The height is an analytic function ``h(x, y)`` (so contact geometry is exact and needs
no mesh); :meth:`LunarTerrain.grid` samples it for plots and :meth:`LunarTerrain.mesh` for the 3D viewer.

Crater shape
------------
Bowl ``h = h_rim + d (rho^2 - 1)`` inside the rim (``rho = r / (D/2)``) and an ejecta flank ``h = h_rim rho^-3``
outside it, joined by a smooth minimum so the crest is rounded over ``crest_width``.

* Depth: the default depth/diameter ratio is 0.2, the value Pike (1977) reports for fresh simple lunar craters
  (D below about 15 km): Pike, R.J. (1977), "Apparent depth/apparent diameter relation for lunar craters",
  Proc. Lunar Sci. Conf. 8th, 3427-3436. Craters a few metres across are mostly degraded and shallower; pass
  ``depth_ratio`` for those (no published small-crater ratio is built in).
* Flank: the ``rho^-3`` decay is the radial decay of ejecta thickness of McGetchin, Settle & Head (1973),
  "Radial thickness variation in impact crater ejecta: implications for lunar basin deposits",
  Earth Planet. Sci. Lett. 20, 226-236 (thickness proportional to (r/R)^-3).
* Rim height: a required input (``rim_ratio`` = h_rim / D). No published value is built in.

Rocks are smooth bumps ``H (1 - (r/a)^2)^2``. They are geometry only: a wheel on a rock still gets the regolith
law of the region (no rigid rock contact), so runs over rocks are qualitative.

``slope_deg``: planar grade rising along ``slope_dir_deg`` (0 = +x). ``ramp``: optional (x0, x1, a0_deg, a1_deg),
a grade along x that grows linearly from a0 at x0 to a1 at x1 (constant outside), for climb-until-failure runs.
The default soil is GRC-1 (``SoilParams()``, the values of the terramechanics use case); ``regions`` override it.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics
pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.mobility
children.doc:
Wheel mobility screening with the ``bekker_wong_surrogate_2d`` PINN: train it, find the sinkage that carries a
given load, read drawbar pull against slip, and re-check each physics constraint on its own.

The preset trains (slip, sinkage) -> (Fx drawbar pull, Fz normal force, My torque) for a rigid wheel under
constraints that are inequalities, not a PDE residual:

* R1 ``Fx(slip = 0) = 0`` (an initial condition),
* R2 the Mohr-Coulomb traction limit ``Fx <= c A + Fz tan(phi)`` with the rigid-wheel contact area
  ``A = b R theta1``, ``theta1 = arccos(1 - z / R)`` (Bekker 1956/1969; Wong & Reece 1967),
* R3 ``dFx/ds >= 0`` for slip <= 0.4,
* R4 ``My >= R Fx``.

:func:`mohr_coulomb_traction_limit` is that R2 bound in closed form, written independently of the compiled
residual; ``tests/test_terramechanics_mobility.py`` checks that the two agree (the source app's
``verify_analytical_crosscheck.py``). :func:`analyze_wheel_surrogate` reports R1-R4 per slip point next to the
guardrail, because the guardrail's ``pde_residual`` (a) pools R2-R5 into one mean, so one violated constraint is
diluted by the others, and (b) never evaluates conditions given as ``InitialCondition`` (R1). A pooled residual
of 0.0 can therefore sit next to a surrogate that collapsed to Fx ~ 0 (the constraints bound relations between
Fx, Fz and My but never anchor Fz's scale): read ``max_drawbar_pull_N`` and ``sinkage_solve_reliable`` too.

The sinkage for a target load is found on a dense grid of the surrogate's own Fz(slip, sinkage), so it inherits
the surrogate's error (reported per row as ``sinkage_solve_error_N``). Rigid wheel, 2-D, single wheel.

Moved here from the PINNeAPPle-apps ``rover_mobility_analysis`` product.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.soils
children.doc:
Soil database for wheel-soil models: Bekker, Janosi-Hanamoto, Wong-Reece, slip-sinkage and unloading parameters.

Every entry carries, per parameter, where the number comes from and how far it was checked (``Soil.sources``):

* ``"secondary"`` -- the value as another publication or open dataset reports it, with the original citation; it
  was not checked against the original table here (the original was not readable from this build environment).
* ``"estimate"`` -- no published value was found; the number is a stated engineering estimate and the reason is
  given. Change it with ``dataclasses.replace(soil, ...)`` when you have a measurement.

Units: c [Pa], phi [deg], K and K_y [m], Bekker k_c [N/m^(n+1)], k_phi [N/m^(n+2)], rho [kg/m^3], k_u0 [N/m^3],
A_u [N/m^4]. The databases quoted in kN units are converted (x 1000).

Entries: ``"GRC-1"`` (NASA Glenn lunar terramechanics simulant), ``"JSC-1A"`` (lunar mare simulant),
``"Ding2011-TYII"`` (the planetary simulant of the Ding et al. 2011 single-wheel tests, used for validation),
``"FJS-1/Hurrell2025"`` (the FJS-1 state of the Rashid-1 wheel tests) and ``"KLS-1"`` (Wang & Han 2016 tests), both used
for validation, and
``"Apollo-lunar"`` (the values the library used before for "GRC-1", kept for reproducibility). See
``docs/core_concepts/lunar_rover_terramechanics.md`` for the full reference list.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.surrogate
children.doc:
PINN surrogate of a wheel-soil contact model: (slip, sinkage) -> (drawbar pull, normal load, soil torque).

    from pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics import WongReeceModel, get_soil
    from pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.surrogate import train_contact_surrogate
    sur, report = train_contact_surrogate(WongReeceModel(get_soil("GRC-1"), wheel), sinkage_range=(0.002, 0.06))
    report["test"]["Fx"]["rmse_N"], sur.predict(slip, z)           # held-out error, fast evaluation
    sur.save("outputs/viper_contact")                              # TorchScript + JSON (SurrogateContact format)

Training data: the reference model on a grid + Latin hypercube over the slip x sinkage box. A disjoint Latin
hypercube (different seed, never seen in training) is the held-out test set; its errors are the ones to report.

Physics terms (soft, one-sided, evaluated with autograd at random collocation points):

* ``dFz/dz >= 0`` (more sinkage carries more load),
* ``dFx/ds >= 0`` up to ``monotone_slip`` (drawbar pull grows with slip before its peak),
* Mohr-Coulomb traction limit ``Fx <= c A + Fz tan(phi)`` with ``A = b R theta_f``,
* torque coupling ``My >= R Fx``.

Each is first checked on the reference model over the training box; a constraint the reference itself violates there
is dropped (and listed in the report) -- a surrogate must not be pushed away from its own reference.

Deformable terrain for wheel-soil simulation: plastic sinkage memory (ruts, multi-pass), grouser imprints, contact
stress maps and rigid rocks.

The undisturbed surface is ``base.height(x, y)`` (any object with that method, e.g. the rover module's
``LunarTerrain``) plus an optional small-scale relief grid. On top of it a regular grid keeps, per cell:

* ``z_max`` -- the deepest sinkage below the undisturbed surface the soil has carried (Wong's repetitive loading:
  the soil remembers it; a later wheel reloads it elastically up to that depth, see :mod:`.wong_reece`). The visible
  rut is ``z_max`` minus the elastic rebound.
* ``imprint`` -- grouser marks stamped where a grouser left the soil (visual layer: depth of the lug trench).
* ``wall`` / ``berm`` -- the rut walls slumped to the angle of repose and the soil displaced to both sides of the
  rut (visual layers: depth and height [m]). Together with ``z_max`` they give the rut its cross-section: a flat
  floor as wide as the wheel, walls at the angle of repose and rounded berms beyond them.
* ``j_mem`` -- the shear displacement the last wheel left in the soil [m] (multi-pass shear, see :mod:`.wong_reece`).
* ``sigma`` / ``tau`` -- the largest normal and shear stress the cell has seen [Pa], for contact colour maps.

Rocks (:class:`RigidRock`) are rigid half-buried ellipsoids: wheels touching them get a penalty contact, not soil
forces. Their surface is :meth:`RigidRock.height`.

classes.name: RigidRock
classes.doc: Ellipsoid centred at (x, y, soil height - ``burial`` c), semi-axes (a, b, c) [m], rotated by ``yaw`` [rad].

methods.name: height
methods.doc: Top surface of the rock [m], -inf outside its footprint.

methods.name: penetration
methods.doc: Approximate penetration depth (>0 inside) and outward normal for points (N, 3).

methods.name: mesh
methods.doc:
A rough rock surface (the ellipsoid displaced by smooth random lumps of relative size ``roughness``),
clipped to above the soil. Visual only.

classes.name: DeformableTerrain
classes.sig: (base, x_range, y_range, cell: float = 0.01, rebound = None, relief: float = 0.0, relief_seed: int = 0, berm: float = 0.3, wall_angle_deg: float = 38.0)
classes.doc:
Grid memory over ``x_range`` x ``y_range`` with spacing ``cell`` on top of ``base``.

``rebound(z_max)`` gives the elastic rebound of the soil (use ``WongReeceModel.rebound``); ``relief`` [m] is the RMS
of a fractal small-scale relief added to the base (0 = none). ``berm`` is the share of the rut cross-section
pushed sideways into the two berms (the rest is compaction); ``wall_angle_deg`` is the slope of the rut walls
(the angle of repose of the regolith, about 35-40 deg for lunar simulants). Both are visual only.

methods.name: height0
methods.doc: Undisturbed soil surface (base + relief) [m], bilinear on the grid (the base function outside it).

methods.name: surface
methods.doc:
Visible soil surface: undisturbed surface minus the rut (floor and walls) and the grouser imprints, plus
the berms (no rocks) [m].

methods.name: precompaction
methods.doc: Largest remembered sinkage over a segment across the track at points ``P`` (N, 2) [m].

methods.name: prior_shear
methods.doc: Shear displacement left in the soil at points ``P`` (N, 2), averaged across the track [m].

methods.name: record_wheel
methods.sig: (cx, cy, fwd, radius: float, width: float, sinkage: float, sigma_max: float = 0.0, tau_max: float = 0.0, j_exit: float | None = None)
methods.doc:
Write the plastic trace of a wheel whose lowest rim point is ``sinkage`` below the undisturbed surface at
(cx, cy): every cell under the rim gets ``z_max = max(z_max, rim depth)``, plus side berms; the cells behind
the bottom point keep the shear displacement ``j_exit`` the wheel leaves.

methods.name: stamp_grouser
methods.sig: (gx, gy, fwd, width: float, depth: float, thickness: float, shape: str = 'straight', chevron_angle_deg: float = 0.0)
methods.doc:
A grouser mark centred at (gx, gy): a trench ``depth`` deep and ``thickness`` wide across a track of
``width`` (a V for chevrons, its apex towards ``fwd``).

methods.name: mesh
methods.doc:
Triangulated visible surface on the grid (every ``step`` cells): vertices, faces and per-vertex fields
``rut_depth`` [mm], ``normal_stress`` [kPa], ``shear_stress`` [kPa].

methods.name: copy_empty
methods.doc: Same base, grid, relief and rocks, with no ruts or marks (to replay recorded terrain events).

functions.name: fractal_relief
functions.sig: (shape, cell: float, amplitude: float, seed: int = 0, beta: float = 2.2, min_wavelength: float = 0.05) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Gaussian random surface with a power-law spectrum (exponent ``beta``) of RMS ``amplitude`` [m], sampled on a
grid of ``shape`` with spacing ``cell``; wavelengths below ``min_wavelength`` are removed.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.testbed
children.doc:
Single-wheel testbed: drawbar pull, torque and sinkage versus slip at a fixed vertical load, and comparison with
published measurements.

    from pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics import testbed
    data = testbed.load_dataset("ding2011", "grousered")         # bundled points, see data/single_wheel_tests.csv
    rep = testbed.validate(data)                                   # model with the cited soil, errors per quantity
    cal = testbed.calibrate_holdout(data)                          # slip-sinkage fit on a training subset only
    cal["test_before"], cal["test_after"]                          # errors on the held-out points
    testbed.plot_validation([rep], "validation.png", calibrated=[cal])

Slip-sinkage calibration (:func:`calibrate_holdout`): the sinkage exponent of the Bekker pressure-sinkage law grows
with slip, ``n = n0 + n1 |s|`` (Ding et al. 2010, 2011: the slip-sinkage model they identified from single-wheel tests
on lunar simulant). ``n0`` and ``n1`` (and the shear modulus ``K``) are fitted by least squares to the sinkage and
drawbar pull of a *training* subset of the published points (every other point by slip, see :func:`holdout_split`);
the remaining points are held out and the errors on them are reported with the cited soil (before) and the fitted
soil (after). The published points are never changed.

The model side is :meth:`WongReeceModel.steady_state` (sinkage from the load balance, then forces). A testbed runs on
Earth, so the bundled cases use g = 9.81 m/s^2 (it only enters the bulldozing term; the load is prescribed).

classes.name: TestbedData
classes.doc: Measured single-wheel points of one wheel on one soil at one load.

functions.name: list_datasets
functions.sig: () -> list[tuple[str, str]]

functions.name: load_dataset
functions.sig: (dataset: str, wheel: str, lambda_grouser: float = 1.0) -> TestbedData
functions.doc:
Bundled points of ``dataset`` ("ding2011", "hurrell2025", "wanghan2016") for ``wheel`` ("smooth" or
"grousered"), sorted by slip; the soil comes from the database entry named in the file.

functions.name: run_testbed
functions.sig: (model: WongReeceModel, load: float, slips) -> dict
functions.doc: Model drawbar pull [N], torque [N m], sinkage [m] and DP/W versus slip at a fixed load [N].

functions.name: validate
functions.sig: (data: TestbedData, soil: Soil | None = None, g: float = 9.81, **model_kw) -> ValidationReport
functions.doc:
Run the testbed at the measured slips with ``soil`` (default: the dataset's cited soil) and report the errors:
drawbar pull and torque RMSE [N, N m] and RMSE relative to the load / load x radius; sinkage RMSE [m] and
relative to the largest measured sinkage.

functions.name: holdout_split
functions.sig: (data: TestbedData, every: int = 2, offset: int = 0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Boolean training mask over the points of ``data`` (sorted by slip): every ``every``-th point starting at
``offset`` is used for fitting, the others are held out. The default (0, 2, 4 ...) keeps the lowest slip in the
training set, so the static sinkage is constrained, and holds out points across the whole slip range.

functions.name: calibrate
functions.sig: (data: TestbedData, params = ('n0', 'n1', 'K'), bounds = None, g: float = 9.81, train = None) -> dict
functions.doc:
Least-squares fit of soil ``params`` to the drawbar pull and sinkage of ``data`` (scaled by the load and the
largest measured sinkage). ``train`` (boolean mask) restricts the fit to those points; by default all points are
used, which is a fit, not a validation. Returns the fitted soil, its parameters and the report on all points.

functions.name: calibrate_holdout
functions.sig: (data: TestbedData, params = ('n0', 'n1', 'K'), every: int = 2, offset: int = 0, g: float = 9.81) -> dict
functions.doc:
Slip-sinkage calibration with held-out points: fit ``params`` (default: the slip-dependent sinkage exponent
``n = n0 + n1 |s|`` of Ding et al. 2010/2011 and the shear modulus K) on :func:`holdout_split` training points
only, then report the errors on the training and held-out points with the cited soil (``*_before``) and the
fitted soil (``*_after``).

functions.name: plot_validation
functions.sig: (reports, path: str, title: str = '', calibrated = None) -> str
functions.doc:
Drawbar pull / load and sinkage versus slip: measured points and model curves, one colour per report.

With ``calibrated`` (results of :func:`calibrate_holdout`, one per report, same order) the solid lines are the
calibrated model, the dashed lines the cited soil; filled points were used for fitting, open points are held
out, and the legend gives the held-out RMSE before and after.

classes.name: Grousers

Grousers (lugs) on a rigid wheel.

``count`` lugs of ``height`` [m] and ``thickness`` [m] around the rim. ``shape`` is ``"straight"`` (lugs across the
tread) or ``"chevron"`` (two half-lugs meeting at the tread centre line, swept by ``chevron_angle_deg`` from the

Ding et al. (2011), see :mod:`.wong_reece`.

methods.name: pitch_angle
methods.doc: Angle between neighbouring grousers [rad].

classes.name: Wheel

A rigid wheel: ``radius`` to the rim surface (grousers excluded) and ``width`` [m]; ``mass`` [kg] and
``spin_inertia`` [kg m^2] about the axle (None = thin rim, ``m R^2``, an upper bound for a spoked wheel).

methods.name: shear_radius
methods.doc: Equivalent shear radius ``R + lambda h`` (Ding et al. 2011); the rim radius without grousers.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.wong_reece
children.doc:
Wong-Reece rigid-wheel / deformable-soil model with slip-sinkage, grousers, multi-pass, bulldozing and lateral force.

Every quantity is vectorised over wheels / operating points (numpy, piecewise Gauss-Legendre quadrature on the contact
arc). Angles are measured from the vertical through the axle, positive towards the front; the soil surface ahead of
the wheel is the reference for the sinkage.

Stresses on the contact arc (Wong & Reece 1967; Wong 2008)
----------------------------------------------------------
Entry angle ``theta_f = acos(1 - z / R)``, exit angle ``theta_r = -c3 theta_f`` and angle of the maximum normal stress
``theta_m = (a0 + a1 s) theta_f``. The depth of the rim below the soil surface is ``h(theta) = R (cos theta* -
cos theta_f)`` with ``theta* = theta`` ahead of ``theta_m`` and, behind it, the Wong-Reece mapping of the rear arc onto
the front arc ``theta* = theta_f - (theta - theta_r) / (theta_m - theta_r) (theta_f - theta_m)``.

* Normal stress, Bekker pressure-sinkage: ``sigma = (k_c / b + k_phi) h^n``.
* Slip-sinkage: the exponent grows with slip, ``n = n0 + n1 |s|`` (Ding et al. 2010, 2011; calibrated with held-out points in
  :func:`.testbed.calibrate_holdout`).
* Shear, Janosi-Hanamoto with Mohr-Coulomb strength: ``tau_x = (c + sigma tan phi) (1 - exp(-j_x / K))`` with the
  shear displacement ``j_x = R_s [(theta_f - theta) - (1 - s)(sin theta_f - sin theta)]``.
* Grousers: shear displacement on the equivalent radius ``R_s = R + lambda h_g`` (Ding et al. 2011).
* Lateral shear on a wheel with slip angle beta (Ishigami et al. 2007): ``j_y = R (1 - s)(theta_f - theta) tan beta``,
  ``tau_y = (c + sigma tan phi)(1 - exp(-j_y / K_y))``.

Forces (wheel frame: x forward along the soil surface, z along its normal, y along the axle)::

    F_x = R b int (tau_x cos - sigma sin)            drawbar pull
    F_z = R b int (sigma cos + tau_x sin)            load carried
    M_y = R R_s b int tau_x                          soil torque the drive must supply
    F_y = -sign(beta) [R b int |tau_y| + R_b]        lateral force, opposing the side slip

Bulldozing (Bekker 1969; Wong 2008): passive earth pressure on the soil wedge pushed by the wheel,
``R_b = b (0.67 c z K_pc + 0.5 z^2 gamma K_pgamma)`` with ``K_pc = (N_c - tan phi) cos^2 phi``,
``K_pgamma = (2 N_gamma / tan phi + 1) cos^2 phi`` and Terzaghi's bearing capacity factors. On the side face it uses
the side area (contact length instead of width); ahead of the wheel it is optional (``bulldozing="both"``) because the
``sigma sin`` term of Wong-Reece already holds the compaction resistance.

Multi-pass (repetitive loading, Wong 2008)
------------------------------------------
``precompaction`` is the deepest sinkage the soil ahead of the wheel has already carried (``z_u``, e.g. the rut of a
wheel in front). The soil rebounds elastically by ``p_u / k_u`` with ``p_u = k z_u^n`` and the unloading-reloading
modulus ``k_u = k_u0 + A_u z_u``; reloading follows ``p = k_u h`` until ``p_u`` and the virgin curve beyond it. The
sinkage passed in is then measured from the original (undisturbed) surface. As in Wong's multi-pass treatment of
consecutive wheels in one track, the shear displacement the soil already carries (``prior_shear``, left by the wheel
in front at its exit angle, :attr:`ContactResult.j_exit`) is added to the shear displacement of the following wheel,
so a wheel in a rut mobilises the soil strength over a shorter arc.

References are listed in :mod:`.soils` and ``docs/core_concepts/lunar_rover_terramechanics.md``.

classes.name: ContactResult
classes.doc: Forces per operating point (all arrays of shape (N,)), plus the stresses on the arc when requested.

classes.name: WongReeceModel
classes.sig: (soil: Soil, wheel: Wheel, g: float = 1.62, bulldozing: str = 'lateral', n_gl: int = 24, slip_sinkage: str = 'drive')
classes.doc:
Wong-Reece wheel on one soil.

>>> from pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics import WongReeceModel, Wheel, get_soil
>>> m = WongReeceModel(get_soil("GRC-1"), Wheel(radius=0.25, width=0.2))
>>> r = m.forces(slip=[0.1, 0.3], sinkage=[0.01, 0.02])
>>> r.Fx, r.Fz, r.My

``bulldozing``: "lateral" (default, side face only), "both", or "none". ``n_gl``: Gauss-Legendre nodes on each of
the three smooth pieces of the arc. ``slip_sinkage``: which slips raise the sinkage exponent ``n = n0 + n1 s``:
"drive" (default, driving slip s > 0 only -- the range Ding et al. identified it on), "both" (``n1 |s|``, skid
too) or "none".

methods.name: physics_config
methods.doc:
Everything that sets this model's forces, as plain data: the soil (name and every parameter), the wheel,
gravity and the model options. A surrogate trained on the model records it (e.g. in a zoo model card), so a
later change of the library's physics can be detected with :func:`physics_mismatch`.

methods.name: from_physics_config
methods.doc: The model a :meth:`physics_config` describes (e.g. the one recorded in a zoo model card).

methods.name: sinkage_exponent
methods.doc:
Exponent of the pressure-sinkage law at ``slip``: ``n0 + n1 s`` (Ding et al. 2010, 2011), see
``slip_sinkage``.

methods.name: normal_stress
methods.doc: Normal stress [Pa] at depth ``h`` below the current surface, exponent ``n``, prior sinkage ``zu``.

methods.name: rebound
methods.doc: Elastic rebound [m] of soil unloaded from sinkage ``zu`` (depth of a rut = ``zu - rebound``).

methods.name: forces
methods.sig: (slip, sinkage, slip_angle = 0.0, precompaction = 0.0, prior_shear = 0.0, *, stresses: bool = False, sinkage_slip = None) -> ContactResult
methods.doc:
Forces for arrays of slip [-], sinkage below the original surface [m], slip angle [rad], prior sinkage [m]
and prior shear displacement [m] of the soil ahead (all broadcast to one shape). ``sinkage_slip`` (default:
``slip``) is the slip that sets the sinkage exponent, e.g. a slip gated by the wheel speed in a dynamic
simulation, where the slip ratio of a nearly stopped wheel is not meaningful.

methods.name: sinkage_for_load
methods.sig: (load, slip, slip_angle = 0.0, precompaction = 0.0, prior_shear = 0.0, z_max: float | None = None, iters: int = 60, sinkage_slip = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc:
Sinkage [m] with ``F_z(slip, z) = load`` (vectorised bisection; F_z grows with z on the bracket).
``sinkage_slip`` as in :meth:`forces` (default: ``slip``).

methods.name: steady_state
methods.sig: (load, slip, slip_angle = 0.0, precompaction = 0.0, prior_shear = 0.0, sinkage_slip = None) -> dict
methods.doc:
Single-wheel testbed operating point: sinkage for the load, then drawbar pull, torque and lateral force.
``sinkage_slip``: the slip that sets the sinkage exponent if it differs from ``slip`` (e.g. a lagged slip).

functions.name: bearing_capacity_factors
functions.sig: (phi_deg) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Terzaghi's general-shear bearing capacity factors (N_c, N_gamma) in the closed forms used by Wong (2008):
``N_q = exp((3 pi / 2 - phi) tan phi) / (2 cos^2(pi / 4 + phi / 2))``, ``N_c = (N_q - 1) / tan phi`` and the
common approximation ``N_gamma = 2 (N_q + 1) tan phi`` (Vesic).

functions.name: bulldozing_resistance
functions.sig: (soil: Soil, depth, width, g: float)
functions.doc: Bulldozing resistance [N] of a soil wedge of ``depth`` pushed by a face of ``width`` (Bekker 1969, Wong 2008).

functions.name: slip_ratio
functions.sig: (v_long, omega, radius, v_eps: float = 0.001)
functions.doc:
Longitudinal slip from the wheel-centre speed along the surface and the wheel speed (driving
``1 - v / (R omega)``, braking ``R omega / v - 1``), regularised near standstill by ``v_eps`` [m/s].

functions.name: slip_angle
functions.sig: (v_long, v_lat, v_eps: float = 0.001)
functions.doc: Slip angle [rad] of a wheel from its centre velocity components along and across its heading.

functions.name: physics_mismatch
functions.sig: (recorded: dict | None, current: dict, rtol: float = 1e-09) -> list[str]
functions.doc:
Keys (dotted paths) where a recorded :meth:`WongReeceModel.physics_config` differs from ``current``; a key the
recorded configuration lacks counts as a difference ("not recorded"). Empty list: same physics.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.workflow
children.doc:
The standard terramechanics workflow (#1199): soil parameters -> single-wheel performance -> wheel design ->
re-verification, each step with its checks.

1. **Soil.** A database soil (:mod:`.soils`, every parameter with its source), or the soil identified from plate
   (bevameter) and shear-box tests through the inverse workflow
   (:func:`pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.workflow.inverse_workflow`): Bekker ``p = (k_c / b + k_phi) z^n``
   from plates of at least two widths (one width cannot separate ``k_c`` from ``k_phi``, and the identifiability
   step says so), Mohr-Coulomb with Janosi-Hanamoto ``tau = (c + sigma tan phi)(1 - exp(-j / K))`` from the shear
   curves. Without measurements, ``identify="synthetic"`` runs the same identification on tests generated from the
   database soil with the stated noise and checks that the intervals hold the soil that made them.
2. **Single-wheel performance** (:meth:`.wong_reece.WongReeceModel.steady_state`): sinkage from the load balance,
   drawbar pull, driving torque and DP/W against slip, with the Wong-Reece stress distribution (Bekker normal
   stress, Janosi-Hanamoto shear, the maximum-stress angle ``theta_m = (a0 + a1 s) theta_f``, slip-sinkage
   ``n = n0 + n1 s``). Checks: the vertical load balance, the quadrature converged (24 against 96 nodes) and DP rising
   with slip over the operating range.
3. **Wheel design**: rim radius, width and grouser height for a required drawbar pull at a slip limit, a sinkage
   limit and an optional torque limit, at minimum wheel mass (a rim, side discs and grousers of one material:
   :func:`wheel_mass`) or minimum torque at the required pull: a grid over the box, then SLSQP from the best
   feasible point.
4. **Re-verification**: the design re-run with the full model (96 quadrature nodes per arc piece, 80 bisection
   steps), its margins restated, the driving slip at the required pull found, and
   :func:`~pinneapple_analysis.verification.architecture_recommendation.recommend_architecture` asked whether a
   contact surrogate pays off; when it does, the zoo PINN is used only if it was trained on the same physics
   (:func:`.wong_reece.physics_mismatch`), otherwise the step says why it was not run.

**Verification against published tests**: :mod:`.testbed` runs the model on the bundled single-wheel points of
Ding et al. (2011) (smooth and grousered wheel, 80 N, planetary soil simulant, the cited soil), and the errors are
checked against the band stated in ``PUBLISHED_BAND``. The Wong & Reece (1967) test data are not bundled (the
original tables could not be read from the build environment); the Ding et al. points are the published
single-wheel case used here.

functions.name: bekker_pressure
functions.sig: (width: float, sinkage: float, k_c: float, k_phi: float, n: float) -> float
functions.doc: Bekker plate pressure [Pa] ``(k_c / b + k_phi) z^n`` of a plate of width ``b`` [m] at sinkage ``z`` [m].

functions.name: janosi_shear
functions.sig: (normal_stress: float, displacement: float, c: float, phi_deg: float, K: float) -> float
functions.doc: Janosi-Hanamoto shear stress [Pa] ``(c + sigma tan phi)(1 - exp(-j / K))`` at displacement ``j`` [m].

functions.name: synthetic_soil_tests
functions.sig: (soil: Soil, widths: Sequence[float] = (0.03, 0.06, 0.12), z_max: float = 0.04, normal_stresses: Sequence[float] = (5000.0, 10000.0, 20000.0), j_max: float = 0.06, n_points: int = 8, noise: float = 0.02, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Plate and shear-box tests of ``soil`` with a relative Gaussian noise ``noise`` (the measurements an
identification is checked on): ``{"plates": {"width", "sinkage", "pressure", "sigma"}, "shear": {...}}``.

functions.name: identify_soil
functions.sig: (plates: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, shear: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, *, base: Soil | str = 'Ding2011-TYII', bootstrap: int = 20, n_recovery: int = 8, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Bekker (``k_c``, ``k_phi``, ``n``) from plate tests and Mohr-Coulomb / Janosi (``c``, ``phi``, ``K``) from
shear-box tests through :func:`~pinneapple_analysis.inverse_problems.workflow.inverse_workflow` (identifiability
first, then estimation with intervals, held-out rows and a synthetic recovery). The parameters not measured
keep the ``base`` soil's values. Returns ``{"soil", "pressure", "shear", "checks"}``.

functions.name: wheel_curves
functions.sig: (soil: Soil, wheel: Wheel, load: float, g: float, slips: Sequence[float], *, n_gl: int = 24) -> dict[str, list[float]]
functions.doc: Sinkage [m], drawbar pull [N], torque [N m], DP/W and the load the stresses carry [N] against slip.

functions.name: wheel_mass
functions.sig: (radius: float, width: float, grouser_height: float = 0.0, grouser_count: int = 0, **material) -> float
functions.doc:
Mass [kg] of a rigid wheel: a cylindrical rim ``2 pi R b t_rim``, two side discs ``pi R^2 t_side`` filled to
``side_fill`` (spokes), ``grouser_count`` lugs ``h b t_g`` and a hub, all of density ``density``
(:data:`DEFAULT_MATERIAL`: aluminium, 2 mm rim and sides, 30 % filled sides, 4 mm lugs, 0.3 kg hub; a stated
assumption, change it with keywords).

functions.name: design_wheel
functions.sig: (soil: Soil, *, load: float, g: float, required_pull: float, max_slip: float = 0.3, max_sinkage: float = 0.05, max_torque: float | None = None, grouser_count: int = 24, bounds: Mapping[str, Sequence[float]] | None = None, objective: str = 'mass', grid: int = 7, n_gl: int = 16, material: Mapping[str, float] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Rim radius, width and grouser height with ``DP(max_slip) >= required_pull``, sinkage at ``max_slip`` below
``max_sinkage`` and (when given) torque below ``max_torque``, at minimum ``objective`` ("mass" or "torque", the
torque at ``max_slip``). A ``grid``-per-variable search of the box, then SLSQP from the best feasible point.

functions.name: terramechanics_workflow

Terramechanics for planetary rover wheels: soils with provenance, the Wong-Reece wheel model and its extensions,
deformable terrain with ruts, a single-wheel testbed with published data, and PINN contact surrogates.

    from pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics import WongReeceModel, Wheel, Grousers, get_soil
    wheel = Wheel(radius=0.25, width=0.20, grousers=Grousers(count=24, height=0.025))
    model = WongReeceModel(get_soil("GRC-1"), wheel, g=1.62)

(deformable heightmap with ruts and grouser imprints), :mod:`.testbed` (single-wheel validation),
:mod:`.surrogate` (PINN training for the wheel-soil contact), :mod:`.mobility` (screening with the
``bekker_wong_surrogate_2d`` PINN: drawbar pull against slip, constraints R1-R4 checked one by one). See ``docs/core_concepts/lunar_rover_terramechanics.md``.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.ugs
pinneapple_simulation.ugs.benchmark
children.doc:
The UGS benchmark: scenarios generated by the reference simulator, a tank baseline, and the metrics.

The benchmark of the programme (#1085) asks for a scenario dataset, several surrogates trained at an equal
budget, and a speed-up that counts data generation and training. What this module delivers is the part that
does not depend on a surrogate existing: the synthetic model, the scenario dataset generated by the reference
simulator, a **tank (material balance) baseline**, the *ruler* -- relative L2 and R-squared of the pressure
field, bottom-hole-pressure error at the wells, deliverability error per day, inference time per scenario and
the break-even number of evaluations -- and the conservation check a predicted field has to pass.

**The neural surrogate is not here.** The neural-operator work is #1084 (three-dimensional and space-time FNO,
factorised spectral weights, Sobolev H1 loss) and this pass did not do it, so
:func:`run_benchmark` reports ``surrogate: {"present": False}`` with the reason rather than a number it does
not have. What the surrogate has to beat is measured and reported.

The synthetic model
-------------------
A 25 x 25 areal grid of 40 m cells (1000 m across), 10 m thick, with a log-normal permeability field of
correlation length 200 m and a porosity field correlated with it; nine wells on a 3 x 3 pattern. Scenarios are
a season -- injection at a bottom-hole pressure, a shut-in, withdrawal at a bottom-hole pressure -- sampled by
Latin hypercube over the pressure levels, a spatial gradient of the withdrawal pressure, the number of wells
shut in and the two durations. The ``extrapolation`` split holds the cases a surrogate must not be trusted on:
withdrawal pressures below the training range (the rates beyond it) and wells shut that were always open.

The tank baseline
-----------------
Zero-dimensional, and the first thing a reservoir engineer computes: the average pressure from the material
balance, ``GIP(p) = GIP(p_0) - produced``, with each well's rate from Peaceman's inflow against that average
pressure, ``q = WI (1/Bg)/mu (p_bhp - p)``. It has no spatial structure and no interference between wells,
which is exactly what the metrics then measure.

classes.name: UGSModel
classes.doc: Everything the simulator needs, in one object the scenarios and the baseline share.

classes.name: Scenario
classes.doc: One season: a schedule, the split it belongs to, and why it is where it is.

classes.name: ScenarioDataset
classes.doc: Scenarios and what the reference simulator returned for each of them.

classes.name: TankBaseline
classes.sig: (model: UGSModel)
classes.doc:
The zero-dimensional material-balance model: one average pressure, Peaceman inflow per well.

At every step each well's rate is ``q = WI (1/Bg)/mu (p_bhp - p_average)`` (or the scheduled rate, for a
well on rate control), clipped by the well's limits, and the average pressure follows from the material
balance ``GIP(p) = GIP(p_previous) - produced``. The predicted pressure field is that average, everywhere:
the model has no spatial structure, which is what the field metrics measure. Because the pressure follows
from the gas in place, the prediction conserves mass by construction -- and that is checked, not assumed.

methods.name: predict
methods.doc: Predict every scenario. Returns the pressure ``(n_scen, n_t, n_cells)`` and the well histories.

Latin-hypercube scenarios over four season parameters, plus three extrapolation cases.

The sampled parameters are the injection bottom-hole pressure, the withdrawal bottom-hole pressure, a
spatial gradient of the withdrawal pressure across the field, and the number of wells shut in for the
season. The three period durations are fixed (:data:`DAYS_INJECTION`, :data:`DAYS_SHUT_IN`,
:data:`DAYS_WITHDRAWAL`) so that every scenario shares one time axis, which is what a surrogate dataset
needs; they stay parameters of the simulator and of the deliverability optimiser. Each scenario is named
``S00``.. and split 60 / 20 / 20 into train, validation and test by its position.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.ugs.grid
children.doc:
Grids for the underground-storage simulator: a structured cartesian grid and a 1-D radial one.

Both grids hand the simulator the same three things, and nothing else:

* ``volumes`` -- the bulk volume of every cell [m3];
* ``phi0`` -- the porosity at the reference pressure [-];
* ``connections`` -- ``(a, b, T)`` for every pair of neighbouring cells, with the transmissibility
  ``T = A k_h / d`` [m3] (the harmonic mean of the two permeabilities, over the centre-to-centre distance,
  times the face area). A radial grid uses the exact steady radial transmissibility
  ``T = 2 pi k h / ln(r2/r1)``, which is what makes a logarithmically spaced radial grid the right tool for a
  line-source verification;
* ``well_index(cell, r_w, skin)`` -- Peaceman's well index [m3] for a well completed in one cell.

Boundaries are closed (no flow) unless a pressure is set on a face with :meth:`Grid.set_boundary_pressure`,
which adds ``T (p_boundary - p_cell)`` to the mass balance of the cells named -- the constant-pressure outer
boundary an aquifer is usually lumped into.

Heterogeneity comes from :func:`gaussian_field`, a log-normal permeability with a correlation length (a
FFT-filtered white field), the cheap stand-in for an SPE10-class realisation: same statistics, seconds instead
of a download.

classes.name: Grid
classes.sig: () -> None
classes.doc: What the simulator is allowed to assume about a grid.

methods.name: set_boundary_pressure
methods.doc: Hold the cells named against a fixed pressure through ``transmissibility`` [m3].

methods.name: pore_volume
methods.doc: Total pore volume [m3] at ``phi0``.

methods.name: well_index
methods.sig: (cell: int, r_w: float, skin: float = 0.0) -> float

classes.name: CartesianGrid
classes.sig: (shape, spacing, *, permeability = 1e-14, porosity = 0.2)
classes.doc:
A structured cell-centred grid in one, two or three dimensions.

``shape`` and ``spacing`` are given with one, two or three entries; a one-dimensional grid is
``(n,), (dx,)`` and its section is ``dy = dz = 1 m``, since only the product of the two matters for a
1-D problem. ``permeability`` is a scalar, a field of ``shape`` (isotropic) or a tuple of three fields
``(kx, ky, kz)``; ``porosity`` a scalar or a field of ``shape``.

methods.name: well_index
methods.sig: (cell: int, r_w: float, skin: float = 0.0) -> float
methods.doc: Peaceman's well index [m3].

classes.name: RadialGrid
classes.sig: (n_r: int = 40, *, r_w: float = 0.1, r_out: float = 10000.0, height: float = 10.0, permeability = 1e-13, porosity = 0.2, geometric: bool = True)
classes.doc:
A one-dimensional radial grid: ``n_r`` annular cells from the well radius to ``r_out``.

Faces are geometric from ``r_w`` to ``r_out`` when ``geometric`` (the usual choice for a well test: the
cells are small where the gradient is) and uniform otherwise. The transmissibility between two annuli is the
exact steady radial one, ``2 pi k h / ln(r2/r1)``, so the only spatial discretisation left is the storage
term and the well model.

methods.name: well_index
methods.sig: (cell: int, r_w: float, skin: float = 0.0) -> float
methods.doc: ``2 pi k h / (ln(r_eq/r_w) + s)`` with ``r_eq`` the volume-equivalent radius of the first cell.

functions.name: gaussian_field
functions.sig: (shape, spacing, corr_length: float, sigma: float = 1.0, seed: int = 0)
functions.doc:
Log-normal field [dimensionless multiplier] with a gaussian covariance of length ``corr_length``.

White noise filtered by a gaussian kernel in Fourier space, then exponentiated: ``exp(sigma g - sigma^2/2)``,
whose mean is 1 whatever ``sigma`` is. ``spacing`` is the cell size along each axis, so ``corr_length`` is
in metres. One cell of the field is one cell of the grid it is laid on.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.ugs.optimization
children.doc:
Operations optimisation: the peak daily deliverability of a storage season, searched on the reference model.

The problem (#1086)
-------------------
Over a withdrawal season, choose which wells deliver and how much, to maximise the **peak daily deliverability**
subject to a minimum bottom-hole pressure per well, a reservoir pressure floor, a maximum rate per well, a
surface capacity, and an end-of-season inventory.

The decision that is not obvious is *which wells to spend*. Peak deliverability on the peak day comes from every
well at its minimum bottom-hole pressure, so it depends on how much pressure each well still has around it: a
well that has produced a lot before the peak arrives with a depleted near-well region and delivers less. The
season therefore has a real trade-off -- the gas that must be produced before the peak should come from the
wells that matter least on the peak day -- and the answer is not uniform allocation unless the field happens to
be symmetric.

What is searched
----------------
The season is three periods: ``pre`` days at a fixed total rate, one **peak** day with every well on
bottom-hole-pressure control at the floor, and ``post`` days at a fixed total rate. The pre- and post-peak
rates are split by a weight vector on the simplex, and that vector is the decision. Every candidate is run on
the reference simulator of :mod:`pinneapple_simulation.ugs.simulator`, so **every recommendation is verified by
construction** -- there is no surrogate in the loop yet, and the docstrings and the returned record say so
instead of quoting a surrogate-predicted gain.

:func:`optimise_peak_deliverability` samples the simplex with a Latin hypercube, takes the best candidates and
refines them by moving weight between pairs of wells, and reports the verified gain over uniform allocation,
the constraint margins and -- computed, not quoted -- how many extra wells would buy the same gain.

classes.name: DeliverabilityProblem
classes.doc:
The season and its constraints. Rates are m3 at standard conditions per second unless the name says day.

``capacity`` is the surface (compressor or line) limit for the whole field; ``p_floor`` the average
reservoir pressure the season must not go below; the rest are the wells' own limits.

methods.name: wells
methods.doc: The model's wells with the problem's own limits applied.

classes.name: SeasonResult
classes.doc: One allocation, run to the end of the season on the reference simulator.

functions.name: equal_allocation
functions.sig: (n: int) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: The baseline every operator starts from: the same share for every well.

functions.name: greedy_allocation
functions.sig: (problem: DeliverabilityProblem, *, rounds: int = 4, config: SimConfig | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Spend the pre-peak gas on the wells that deliver least on the peak day, one round at a time.

Each round doubles the weight of the half of the wells with the smallest peak-day rate, which is the
physical intuition written as an algorithm. It is a starting point for the search, not the answer: the
search either improves on it or reports it unchanged.

functions.name: evaluate_allocation
functions.sig: (problem: DeliverabilityProblem, weights, *, config: SimConfig | None = None, wells: list[Well] | None = None) -> SeasonResult
functions.doc: Run one allocation through the whole season and read the peak day off the reference simulator.

functions.name: optimise_peak_deliverability
functions.sig: (problem: DeliverabilityProblem, *, n_samples: int = 16, seed: int = 0, refine_rounds: int = 2, config: SimConfig | None = None, capital_search: int = 4) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Search the allocation that maximises the verified peak deliverability.

Latin hypercube over the simplex, then pairwise mass transfer in shrinking steps, each candidate run on the
reference simulator; ``refine_rounds`` sets the evaluation budget of that refinement at
``n_samples + 4 n wells refine_rounds`` runs. Returns the verified optimum, the uniform baseline, the gain,
the constraint margins and the number of extra wells that would buy the same gain.

functions.name: uniform_baseline
functions.sig: (problem: DeliverabilityProblem, *, config: SimConfig | None = None) -> SeasonResult
functions.doc: The baseline schedule: the same share for every well, run on the reference simulator.

children.summary: Operations optimisation: the peak daily deliverability of a storage season, searched on the reference model.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.ugs.pvt
children.doc:
Gas PVT for underground storage: z-factor, viscosity and formation volume factor.

Units are SI throughout: pressure in Pa, temperature in K, viscosity in Pa s, density in kg/m3, and the gas
formation volume factor ``Bg`` in m3 of reservoir volume per m3 at the standard conditions the class declares
(101325 Pa and 288.71 K by default -- the ``sm3`` of a European gas storage). Every rate in this package is a
volume *at those standard conditions* per second, which is the volume an operator reports.

Correlations
------------
* pseudo-critical properties from the gas specific gravity, Sutton (1985), SPE 14265::

      T_pc [R] = 120.1 + 425.9 sg,        p_pc [psia] = 677.0 + 15.0 sg - 37.5 sg^2

* z-factor, either :func:`papay_z` (explicit, Papay 1968) or :func:`hall_yarborough_z` (implicit in the
  reduced density, Hall & Yarborough 1973, Oil & Gas J., 82; valid over 1.1 <= T_pr <= 3.0);
* viscosity, :func:`lee_gonzalez_eakin_mu` (Lee, Gonzalez & Eakin 1966, JPT 18:997).

The simulator solves for the pressure itself, fully implicit, so no pseudo-pressure is needed: it linearises
the diffusivity equation for hand analysis, not for a Newton solve. :meth:`Gas.c_g` is the isothermal gas
compressibility ``1/p - (1/z) dz/dp``, used where a total compressibility has to be quoted.

The derivatives the Newton loop needs (:meth:`Gas.dindex_dp`, :meth:`Gas.dmu_dp`) are central differences of
the correlations on a relative step of ``h``; the correlations are tabulated fits, so an analytic derivative
would carry the fit's constants but not more accuracy than the difference.

classes.name: Gas
classes.doc:
A dry natural gas described by its specific gravity and a z-correlation.

``T`` is the reservoir temperature, held constant (no thermal model). ``index`` is ``1/Bg``, the surface
volume that one cubic metre of reservoir pore space holds, and it is what the accumulation term of the
material balance integrates.

methods.name: critical
methods.doc: Pseudo-critical pressure [Pa] and temperature [K].

methods.name: z
methods.doc: Gas deviation factor [-].

methods.name: mu
methods.doc: Gas viscosity [Pa s].

methods.name: Bg
methods.doc: Formation volume factor [m3 reservoir per m3 at standard conditions].

methods.name: rho
methods.doc: Density [kg/m3].

methods.name: index
methods.doc: ``1/Bg``: surface m3 per reservoir m3, the density the material balance integrates.

methods.name: dindex_dp
methods.doc: Derivative of :meth:`index` with respect to the pressure [1/Pa].

methods.name: dmu_dp
methods.doc: Derivative of :meth:`mu` with respect to the pressure [Pa s / Pa].

methods.name: c_g
methods.doc: Isothermal gas compressibility ``1/p - (1/z) dz/dp`` [1/Pa].

classes.name: SlightlyCompressible
classes.doc:
The slightly compressible limit: a fluid of constant density (``Bg = 1``) and constant viscosity.

One reservoir cubic metre is then one surface cubic metre and all the storage comes from the rock, so the
flow equation linearises to ``dphi/dt p = eta lap(p)`` with ``eta = k / (phi mu ct)``. This is the fluid
the line-source (Theis) verification is written for, and it is the same limit in which a reservoir
engineer quotes a diffusivity.

classes.name: Rock
classes.doc: Pore compressibility: ``phi(p) = phi0 (1 + cr (p - p_ref))``, clipped to ``phi_min``.

functions.name: pseudo_critical_sutton
functions.sig: (sg: float) -> tuple[float, float]
functions.doc: Pseudo-critical pressure [Pa] and temperature [K] of a natural gas of specific gravity ``sg`` (Sutton 1985).

functions.name: papay_z
functions.sig: (p, T: float, ppc: float, tpc: float)
functions.doc: Papay's explicit z-factor correlation (pseudoreduced pressure and temperature).

functions.name: hall_yarborough_z
functions.sig: (p, T: float, ppc: float, tpc: float, *, tol: float = 1e-12, max_iters: int = 100)
functions.doc:
Hall & Yarborough's z-factor, solved for the reduced density ``Y`` by Newton.

``F(Y) = -A + (Y + Y^2 + Y^3 - Y^4)/(1-Y)^3 - (14.76 t - 9.76 t^2 + 4.58 t^3) Y^2
+ (90.7 t - 242.2 t^2 + 42.4 t^3) Y^(2.18 + 2.82 t)``, ``A = 0.06125 p_pr t exp(-1.2 (1-t)^2)``,
``t = 1/T_pr``, and ``z = A / Y``. Raises ``ValueError`` when Newton does not converge, rather than
returning a plausible-looking number.

functions.name: lee_gonzalez_eakin_mu
functions.sig: (p, T: float, mw: float, z)
functions.doc:
Gas viscosity [Pa s] by Lee, Gonzalez & Eakin (1966).

``mu = 1e-4 K exp(X rho^Y)`` cP with ``rho`` in g/cm3, ``T`` in R and ``M`` in g/mol::

    K = (9.4 + 0.02 M) T^1.5 / (209 + 19 M + T),   X = 3.5 + 986/T + 0.01 M,   Y = 2.4 - 0.2 X

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.ugs.simulator
children.doc:
The reference simulator for underground gas storage: single-phase real gas in a porous medium, with wells.

The model
---------
One equation for the pressure, written as a material balance in surface volumes::

    d/dt [ phi(p) / Bg(p) ] = div[ (1/Bg) (k/mu(p)) grad p ] + q_wells

``Bg`` is the gas formation volume factor (reservoir m3 per m3 at standard conditions), so the accumulator
``phi/Bg`` is the surface volume that one cubic metre of bulk rock holds, the flux is a surface volume per
second, and every rate the simulator reports is in m3 at standard conditions -- the unit an operator books.

Space is discretised with a two-point flux approximation: the flux across a face is
``T (1/Bg)/mu (p_b - p_a)`` with ``T`` the harmonic transmissibility from the grid and the density-mobility
group taken from the upstream cell, which keeps the scheme monotone for a strongly pressure-dependent
``1/Bg``. Time is fully implicit (backward Euler) and every step is solved by Newton with an analytic
Jacobian and a sparse direct solve, with a backtracking line search that keeps the pressure positive.

Wells
-----
A well is a source/sink in one cell, ``q = WI (1/Bg)/mu (p_bhp - p)``, resolved by the active set of
:func:`pinneapple_simulation.ugs.wells.operating_point`: a rate target that would need a bottom-hole pressure
outside the well's limits switches to that pressure, and a rate above the well's limit is capped.

Diagnostics
-----------
Every run reports, at every time step, the pressure field, the pore-volume-weighted average pressure, the gas
in place, the rate and the bottom-hole pressure of every well, the daily deliverability and a **measured
mass-balance error**: the gas in place at the end minus the gas in place at the start minus what the wells
moved, divided by the gas in place the run started with. The well terms enter the residual at the new time
level, so that number is the solver's own tolerance, not an estimate. Non-convergence is reported, never
dressed: :attr:`SimulationResult.converged` is ``False`` and :attr:`SimulationResult.reason` says at which
time and after how many Newton iterations the step stopped.

Units: pressure Pa, length m, permeability m2, viscosity Pa s, rate m3 at standard conditions per second
(m3/day in the reports).

``p0`` is the initial pressure, a scalar or a value per cell. The wells' indices come from the grid unless

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.ugs.verification
children.doc:
Verification of the underground-storage simulator: four analytic references and two observed orders.

Every case is a number, not a claim, and each compares the simulator with something that was derived without it:

* :func:`theis_line_source` -- the drawdown around a well at constant rate in an infinite homogeneous reservoir,
  against the exponential-integral solution of Theis (1935), in the slightly compressible limit. The reservoir
  is a logarithmically spaced radial grid large enough that the pressure disturbance has not reached the outer
  boundary by the last time reported (the code returns that ratio, ``r_investigated / r_out``, so the reader
  can check the infinite-acting assumption instead of trusting it);
* :func:`pseudo_steady_state` -- in a closed reservoir the average pressure falls linearly once the whole
  volume drains, at ``q / (V phi ct)``; both the linearity and the slope are measured;
* :func:`material_balance` -- ``p/z`` against cumulative production is a straight line whose slope gives the
  gas in place (the oldest plot in reservoir engineering); the gas in place it implies is compared with the
  one the simulator integrates;
* :func:`mass_conservation` -- the accumulated mass-balance error of the cases above, which is the solver's
  own tolerance because the well terms enter the residual implicitly;
* :func:`time_convergence` and :func:`grid_convergence` -- the observed order of accuracy from a
  three-resolution refinement, using :func:`pinneapple_analysis.verification.convergence.mesh_independence_study`
  (Roache 1994 / Celik et al. 2008), on the error against the line-source solution.

    from pinneapple_simulation.ugs import verification
    report = verification.run()          # dict, ~15 s
    report = verification.run(quick=True)   # the same cases at a size a test can afford, ~2 s

The output of a run is a dict of dicts; :func:`summary` prints it as the paragraph a report quotes.

functions.name: theis_drawdown
functions.sig: (radius, t_seconds: float, case: dict[str, float] | None = None)
functions.doc: Exact Theis drawdown [Pa] at ``radius`` and time: ``q mu / (4 pi k h) E1(r^2 / (4 eta t))``.

functions.sig: (n_r: int = 60, dt_days: float = 0.25, days: float = 2.0, case: dict[str, float] | None = None) -> dict[str, Any]
