children.name: pinneapple_simulation.ugs.wells
children.doc:
Wells and schedules for the underground-storage simulator.

A :class:`Well` is a completion in one grid cell, with a Peaceman index taken from the grid (or given), a
minimum and a maximum bottom-hole pressure and a maximum rate. A :class:`Period` says how each well is to be
operated during a stretch of the schedule -- a rate target with a bottom-hole-pressure limit, or a
bottom-hole pressure -- and a :class:`Schedule` is a list of them. A well the period does not name is shut in,
which is what makes a season (injection, shut-in, withdrawal) a few lines.

:func:`operating_point` resolves one well against one cell pressure by the active-set rule every commercial
simulator uses: the target is honoured unless it needs a bottom-hole pressure outside ``[bhp_min, bhp_max]``,
or a rate above ``rate_max``, in which case the binding limit takes over. The derivative it returns is the one
the implicit Jacobian needs, taken on the same branch.

classes.name: Well
classes.doc:
One completion in one grid cell.

``bhp_min`` and ``bhp_max`` bound the bottom-hole pressure the well may be operated at [Pa]; ``rate_max``
is the surface rate limit [m3 standard per second], the erosion and sand-control limit of the operating
issue. ``wi`` overrides the index the grid computes, for a well whose completion is not a plain Peaceman
block.

classes.name: Control
classes.doc:
How one well is operated during one period.

``mode`` is ``"rate"`` (``value`` in m3 standard per second, positive for injection) or ``"bhp"``
(``value`` in Pa). Both are targets: the well's own limits still apply.

classes.name: Period
classes.doc: ``days`` of a schedule with one control per well; a well left out is shut in.

classes.name: Schedule
classes.doc: A list of periods, run in order.

methods.name: controls_at
methods.doc: The controls in force on ``day`` (0 <= day < ``days``).

methods.name: steps
methods.doc: ``(dt, period index)`` for every time step, split at the period boundaries.

functions.name: operating_point
functions.sig: (well: Well, control: Control | None, p_cell: float, mobility: float, dmobility_dp: float, wi: float) -> tuple[float, float, float]
functions.doc:
Resolve a well's rate, bottom-hole pressure and ``dq/dp_cell`` at a cell pressure.

``mobility`` is ``(1/Bg)/mu`` at the cell and ``wi`` the well index [m3]. Returns ``(q, bhp, dq_dp)`` with
``q`` in m3 standard per second, positive for injection. A well with no control is shut in and returns
zeros.

children.summary: Wells and schedules for the underground-storage simulator.

children.doc:
Underground gas storage: a reference simulator, its verification, a benchmark and a deliverability optimiser.

The programme follows the UGS line of work that replaces a reservoir simulator with a neural operator
(Sirota et al., arXiv 2509.21485) -- on public and synthetic models, with our own numbers:

* :mod:`.pvt` -- the gas: z-factor (Papay, Hall-Yarborough), viscosity (Lee-Gonzalez-Eakin), formation volume
  factor and density;
* :mod:`.grid` -- a structured cartesian grid in one to three dimensions with heterogeneous permeability and
  porosity, and a one-dimensional radial grid for well tests;
* :mod:`.wells` -- completions with a Peaceman index, rate or bottom-hole-pressure control with limits, and
  injection/withdrawal schedules;
* :mod:`.simulator` -- the reference model: single-phase real gas, two-point flux in space, backward Euler in
  time, Newton with an analytic Jacobian, and the diagnostics an engineer reads first (average pressure, rate
  and bottom-hole pressure per well, gas in place, daily deliverability, measured mass-balance error);
* :mod:`.verification` -- the analytic references: the Theis line source, the pseudo-steady-state decline, the
  p/z material-balance line and the observed orders of accuracy;
* :mod:`.benchmark` -- synthetic scenarios generated by the simulator, a tank (material balance) baseline, the
  metrics, and what is still missing (the trained surrogate);
* :mod:`.optimization` -- peak daily deliverability under pressure, rate and inventory constraints, searched on
  the reference simulator and therefore verified by construction.

Quick start::

    from pinneapple_simulation.ugs import (
        CartesianGrid, Gas, Rock, Schedule, Period, Control, UGSSimulator, Well)

    grid = CartesianGrid((21, 21), (40.0, 40.0), permeability=1e-13, porosity=0.2)
    well = Well("P1", cell=0, bhp_min=5e6)
    sim = UGSSimulator(grid, Gas(T=320.0), Rock(cr=1e-9, p_ref=1.2e7), [well], p0=1.2e7)
    plan = Schedule((Period(30.0, {"P1": Control("rate", -0.2)}),))
    result = sim.run(plan)
    print(result.summary())

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.dashboard
children.doc:
The animation-centred dashboard of a vehicle run (built on :mod:`pinneapple_tools.visualization.dashboard`).

    from pinneapple_simulation.vehicle import dashboard as vdash
    frames, ks = vdash.render_frames(run, terrain, n=150)                   # rendered animation (planetary renderer)
    db = vdash.vehicle_dashboard(run, frames, ks, model=WongReeceModel(...), surrogate=sur, scene3d=True,
                                 terrain=terrain)
    db.to_html("rover.html"); db.to_png("rover.png"); db.to_video(gif="rover.gif", mp4="rover.mp4")

Charts (units on every axis):

* left -- drawbar pull, driving torque and sinkage versus slip: the single-wheel testbed curve at the static wheel
  load (``model.steady_state``) and each wheel's operating point moving with the cursor;
* right -- speed (and the command), slip per wheel, the PINN against the Wong-Reece reference for one wheel;
* bottom -- per-wheel sinkage and normal load along the traverse, the PINN error for every wheel.

Tiles: distance, mean slip, max sinkage and drive energy so far, PINN error so far. The parameter panel lists the
vehicle, the soil, the command and the surrogate's held-out error.

("normal_stress", "shear_stress", "sinkage") adds the colour map as an overlay on the ruts and wheels
(``overlay=False``: on the wheels only); ``field_alpha`` / ``field_glow`` set its opacity on the relief
(e.g. 0.6 / 0.1: semi-transparent, the rut geometry and the Sun shading stay visible), ``field_saturation``
mutes its colours. Without ``clim`` the colour range spans ``clim_percentiles`` of the stress the ruts carry

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.mission_design
children.doc:
The standard rover workflow (#1200): planet, terrain and mission -> mobility, power and thermal -> rover design ->
the traverse simulated on the mission profile.

* **Mobility** (Wong-Reece wheels, :class:`~pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.WongReeceModel`): the grade the
  rover climbs at its slip limit (``n DP(s_max, m g cos a / n) = m g sin a``, bisection), the step a front wheel
  climbs when the other wheels push it (quasi-static, :func:`step_climb_force`), static tip-over angles from the track,
  wheelbase and centre-of-mass height, static sinkage.
* **Power**: the electrical drive power at the mission speed on each slope (wheel torque at the slip that gives the
  needed drawbar pull, ``omega = v / (R (1 - s))``, over the drive efficiency), the hotel load, a solar array sized for
  the energy of a sol with a sinusoidal day profile (``E = A eta S tau t_day 2 / pi``, peak ``A eta S tau``) and a
  battery sized for the night.
* **Thermal**: a survival heater for the warm box, ``Q = eps_eff sigma A (T_in^4 - T_sink^4)`` less the internal
  dissipation, drawn from the battery at night.
* **Design**: wheel radius and width at minimum total mass (structure fraction, wheels, drive motors sized by peak
  torque, array, battery, insulation, avionics, payload; a fixed point because the loads scale with the mass), within
  the grade, step, stability, sinkage, power and thermal margins.
* **Re-verification**: :func:`traverse` time-steps the mission (sun, drive window, slope profile, wheel slip and
  power, battery state of charge) and reports the distance reached, the lowest state of charge, the largest slip and
  the energy closure.

**Published rover**: :func:`published_rover_check` runs the power and mobility model with Sojourner's published mass,
wheels, speed and array (``SOJOURNER``, each value with the source it was read from) and compares the peak array power
with the reported 16 W within ``SOJOURNER_BAND``. Every planet, mass-model and thermal default that is not from a
publication is marked "assumption" in ``ASSUMPTIONS``.

functions.name: step_climb_force
functions.sig: (h: float, radius: float, load: float, mu: float) -> float
functions.doc:
Horizontal push [N] a driven wheel of ``radius`` carrying ``load`` needs to lift onto a step of height ``h``
(quasi-static, ground reaction gone, friction ``mu`` at the step edge driven by the wheel's own torque).
Contact at the edge at angle ``a`` from the vertical (``cos a = 1 - h / R``): ``N = W / (cos a + mu sin a)``,
``P = N (sin a - mu cos a)``; for ``h >= R`` the wheel climbs the face: ``P = W / mu``. 0 when the wheel climbs
on its own torque.

functions.name: max_step_height
functions.sig: (radius: float, load: float, push: float, mu: float, cap: float) -> float
functions.doc: Largest step [m] (up to ``cap``) for which :func:`step_climb_force` is within ``push`` [N] (bisection).

functions.name: tip_over_angles
functions.sig: (track: float, wheelbase: float, cg_height: float) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc: Static tip-over slope [deg]: lateral ``atan(track / 2 / h)`` and longitudinal ``atan(wheelbase / 2 / h)``.

functions.name: grade_capability
functions.sig: (model, mass: float, g: float, n_wheels: int, max_slip: float, step_deg: float = 0.25) -> float
functions.doc:
Steepest grade [deg] the rover climbs at slip ``max_slip``: ``n DP = m g sin a`` with wheel load
``m g cos a / n`` (one vectorised solve on a ``step_deg`` grid of grades, then linear interpolation of the
crossing).

functions.name: drive_power
functions.sig: (model, mass: float, g: float, n_wheels: int, slope_deg: float, speed: float, efficiency: float, max_slip: float = 0.6) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Electrical drive power [W] at ``speed`` up ``slope_deg``: the slip where each wheel's drawbar pull is
``m g sin a / n`` (on the flat: zero, the wheel only overcomes its own compaction), the wheel torque there and
``omega = v / (R (1 - s))``. Down a slope the flat-ground power is used (no regeneration: conservative). The slip
is interpolated on a 61-point slip curve (one vectorised solve).

functions.name: solar_array
functions.sig: (area: float, efficiency: float, planet: Mapping[str, Any]) -> dict[str, float]
functions.doc:
Noon peak power ``A eta S tau`` [W] and energy per day [W h] of a horizontal array with a sinusoidal day
(mean over the daylight = peak x 2 / pi).

functions.name: heater_power
functions.sig: (area: float, eps_eff: float, t_inside: float, t_sink: float, internal_W: float) -> float
functions.doc: Survival heater [W]: radiated loss ``eps_eff sigma A (T_in^4 - T_sink^4)`` less the internal dissipation.

Time-step the mission: the sun (sinusoidal over the daylight), a drive window of ``drive_hours`` centred on
noon, a slope profile (``segment_m`` segments, slopes uniform in +-``max_slope_deg``, seeded), the wheel slip and

``battery_dod`` floor). Stops when the distance is reached or after ``max_sols``.

Sojourner's published mass, wheels, speed and array through the power and mobility model: the peak array power
against the reported 16 W (band ``SOJOURNER_BAND``) and the drive power at the reported 1 cm/s against it.

functions.sig: (*, planet: str = 'mars', soil: str | None = None, mission: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, n_wheels: int = 6, suspension: str = 'rocker-bogie', max_slip: float = 0.3, radius_bounds = (0.05, 0.2), width_bounds = (0.04, 0.15), grid: int = 6, cell_efficiency: float = 0.28, stability_factor: float = 1.5, assumptions: Mapping[str, Any] | None = None, seed: int = 0) -> dict[str, Any]

Size the lightest rover (wheel radius and width on a ``grid`` x ``grid`` box, array and battery sized inside)

sinkage limit and the power and thermal margins; then simulate the traverse and check the published rover.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.sim
children.doc:
Time-domain simulation of a wheeled vehicle on deformable terrain: multibody dynamics + Wong-Reece wheels.

Per step (``dt``, linearly implicit Euler, :meth:`MultibodyTree.step`):

1. Wheel geometry on the undisturbed surface: lowest rim point, terrain normal in the wheel plane, rolling
   direction, sinkage below the undisturbed surface; the soil memory ahead of the wheel gives its prior sinkage
   (multi-pass).
2. Slip from the wheel's angular velocity and its centre velocity, slip angle from the lateral velocity. The slip
   that sets the slip-sinkage exponent is the slip lagged over ``sink_length`` metres of rim travel: slip-sinkage
   builds up as the wheel turns and digs, a stopped wheel neither builds nor loses it, and the slip ratio of a
   nearly stopped wheel (a ratio of noise) cannot feed back into the sinkage (a model setting).
3. Wong-Reece forces (:class:`~pinneapple_simulation.terramechanics.WongReeceModel`): drawbar pull and normal force in
   the wheel plane, lateral force along the axle, soil torque about it; their derivatives with respect to the wheel
   velocities enter the implicit step, so millisecond steps stay stable while the wheels slip.
4. Vertical soil damping ``c = zeta 2 sqrt(k m)`` (``k = dF_z/dz``, ``m`` the vehicle mass per wheel) -- granular soil
   dissipates the energy of a bouncing wheel; the Wong-Reece laws are quasi-static and have none. ``zeta``
   (``soil_damping``) is a model setting, not a measured soil property (Chrono's SCM soil uses the same idea).
5. Rigid rocks: penalty contact (spring-damper, Coulomb friction) on the rim (grousers included).
6. Actuators: wheel speed PI with the motor torque limit, steering PD (heading hold), active suspension PD with a
   load-levelling loop (an assumed control law: the arm angles move to equalise the wheel loads), all torque-limited.
7. The terrain records the plastic trace of every wheel (ruts) and a grouser mark each time a grouser passes the
   bottom of a loaded wheel.

Ground made of several soils: pass a list of soils and ``soil_map(x, y) -> index`` (each wheel gets the Wong-Reece
law of the soil under its contact point). A route: ``run(..., route=[(x, y), ...])`` steers by pure pursuit along the
polyline and stops at its end; ``stop(sample) -> reason or None`` ends a run early (e.g. a traction monitor).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.spec
children.doc:
Vehicle description shared by the CAD, the multibody model and the simulator: a chassis plus corner modules
(suspension arm -> steering -> driven wheel), each with geometry, joint limits and actuator limits.

All positions are in the vehicle *assembly frame* at the reference (nominal ride height) pose: x forward, y left,
z up, origin on the ground below the geometric centre of the wheel footprint.

classes.name: Actuator
classes.doc: Torque limit [N m], speed limit [rad/s] and PD/PI gains of a joint servo.

classes.name: CornerModule
classes.doc:
One corner: suspension pivot and axis on the chassis, steering axis at the end of the arm, wheel centre.

``susp_pivot``, ``steer_origin``, ``wheel_centre`` [m] in the assembly frame; ``susp_axis`` and ``steer_axis`` unit
vectors; ``wheel_axis`` is the axle direction (+y for both sides: positive spin drives forward). Masses [kg] of the
arm, the steering module and the wheel (with its drive) and their CAD bodies are set by the vehicle definition.

children.summary: Vehicle description shared by the CAD, the multibody model and the simulator: a chassis plus corner modules (suspension arm -> steering -> driven wheel), each with geometry, joint limits and actuator ...

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.viper
children.doc:
NASA VIPER (Volatiles Investigating Polar Exploration Rover) at full scale, from public figures.

Every published number used here is listed in :data:`VIPER_SOURCES` with its source. Numbers that could not be
found are marked ``"estimate: ..."`` with the reason; they were chosen to agree with the published envelope, track,
wheelbase and wheel size, and the layout (where the mast, arrays, radiator, drill and instruments sit) follows NASA's
published photos and renders of the rover. The geometry is a parametric model built for this library from those
numbers, not a copy of any CAD model.

Caveat on the sources: from the environment this model was built in, the NASA documents could only be located with
a web search, which returned text excerpts; the PDFs themselves could not be opened, so slide or page numbers are not
given and the wording should be checked against the documents.

    from pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.viper import viper
    spec = viper()                       # VehicleSpec with the CAD (spec.cad), corners and the wheel
    spec.cad.export("viper.glb")

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vehicle.viz
children.doc:
Pictures and animations of a :class:`~.sim.VehicleRun`: the vehicle CAD posed by the multibody state (wheels roll
with their joint angles), the deformable terrain with ruts and grouser marks replayed to each instant, contact
stresses as colour maps on the wheels and the terrain, Sun shadows and the lunar sky.

    from pinneapple_simulation.vehicle import viz
    viz.render_frame(run, terrain, k, "frame.png", field="normal_stress")
    viz.animate(run, terrain, "run.gif", mp4="run.mp4", field="normal_stress", frames=120)
    viz.beauty(spec, "viper.png")

``field``: None (materials), ``"normal_stress"`` / ``"shear_stress"`` [kPa] (wheel contact arc and the peak stress
left in the ruts) or ``"sinkage"`` [mm] (rut depth).

functions.doc:
The :class:`~pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.planetary.SurfaceView` of sample ``k``.

The detailed terrain (ruts with their walls, berms and grouser marks as real geometry, optional stress maps)
covers ``half_window`` around the vehicle, shifted back by ``trail`` metres along the direction of travel so
more of the ruts behind it stay in view; a coarser far field (:func:`far_surface`, ruts included, with the
vehicle's shadow) fills ``far_margin`` metres around it and a curved annulus continues the ground to
``horizon`` metres, past the lunar horizon, so no edge of the ground mesh is visible. ``field_alpha`` and
``field_glow`` (and ``field_saturation``) set how the ruts' colour map sits on the relief (see
:class:`~pinneapple_tools.visualization.studio.planetary.SurfaceView`); e.g. 0.6 / 0.1 is a semi-transparent
map through which the rut geometry, grouser marks and Sun shading stay visible. ``field`` colours the wheels and the ruts; ``overlay=False`` keeps the
wheel colours but draws the ruts by their geometry only.

children.doc:
Wheeled planetary vehicles: a description (chassis + corner modules) with its CAD, the multibody model built from
it, and a simulator on deformable terrain with Wong-Reece wheels.

    import pinneapple as pp
    spec = pp.vehicle.viper()                                  # NASA VIPER from public figures (cited in VIPER_SOURCES)
    model = pp.vehicle.build_vehicle(spec)                     # multibody tree, masses and inertias from the CAD
    terrain = pp.terramechanics.terrain.DeformableTerrain(base, (-2, 10), (-3, 3), cell=0.01)
    run = pp.vehicle.VehicleSimulator(model, terrain, pp.terramechanics.get_soil("GRC-1")).run(30.0, speed=0.2)
    run.summary(); pp.vehicle.viz.animate(run, terrain, "run.gif", field="normal_stress")

Modules: :mod:`.spec`, :mod:`.viper`, :mod:`.build`, :mod:`.sim`, :mod:`.scenarios`, :mod:`.viz`. See
``docs/core_concepts/lunar_rover_terramechanics.md``.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vortex_domains
pinneapple_simulation.vortex_domains.bodies
children.doc:
Bodies of the VVD solver: closed polygons that move rigidly, and the generators the cases are built from.

A body is a closed polygon in its own frame plus a :class:`Motion`. Each time step the polygon is cut into straight
*panels*: the segment midpoints are the collocation points of the source sheet (no through flow) and of the vorticity
creation (no slip), and the panel normals of the wall-diffusion drift.

Every generator returns a counter-clockwise polygon with outward normals, so the solver never has to guess an
orientation.

classes.name: Motion
classes.doc:
Rigid motion ``x(t) = center(t) + R(angle(t)) x_local`` with its first derivative.

``center`` and ``angle`` are callables of time; ``velocity`` and ``omega`` are their derivatives (both default
to zero, i.e. a fixed body).
fields: center: Callable[[float], np.ndarray] = lambda t: np.zeros(2)
velocity: Callable[[float], np.ndarray] = lambda t: np.zeros(2)

classes.name: PanelSet
classes.doc: The panels of one or more bodies at one instant, in world coordinates.

methods.name: vector
methods.doc: Outward normal scaled by the panel length (the ``dS`` of the wall-diffusion kernel).

methods.name: surface_velocity_at
methods.doc: Velocity of the nearest panel's surface point, for points that sit on the wall.

classes.name: Body
classes.sig: (vertices: np.ndarray, motion: Motion | None = None, name: str = 'body', thin: bool = False)
classes.doc:
A closed polygonal body that moves rigidly.

``vertices`` are in the body's own frame (the frame :class:`Motion` maps to the world); the polygon is closed
automatically and made counter-clockwise.

methods.name: panels
methods.doc: ``(a, b, surface velocity at the midpoints)`` in world coordinates.

classes.name: Assembly
classes.sig: (bodies: Sequence[Body] | None = None)
classes.doc: A set of bodies that share one flow field.

methods.name: inside
methods.doc: Which points are inside any body (ray casting, one polygon at a time).

functions.sig: () -> Motion
functions.doc: A body that stays where it is.

functions.sig: (velocity: Sequence[float], center0: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 0.0), angle: float = 0.0, omega: float = 0.0) -> Motion
functions.doc: Constant translation (and optional constant rotation) from ``center0``.

functions.sig: (center: Sequence[float], rate: float, angle0: float = 0.0) -> Motion
functions.doc: Constant rotation about a fixed point.

functions.sig: (pivot: Sequence[float], angle_of_t: Callable[[float], float], rate_of_t: Callable[[float], float] | None = None) -> Motion
functions.doc:
A body hinged at ``pivot`` (world coordinates at ``t = 0``), turning by ``angle_of_t``.

The rate is the analytic derivative when given, otherwise a central difference of ``angle_of_t``.

functions.name: deploy
functions.sig: (from_deg: float, to_deg: float, t_start: float, duration: float) -> tuple[Any, Any]
functions.doc:
Angle and rate of a smooth ramp between two angles (radians returned).

Returns ``(angle_of_t, rate_of_t)``; both are zero outside ``[t_start, t_start + duration]``.

functions.sig: (v: np.ndarray) -> float
functions.doc: Area enclosed by a closed polygon (positive for counter-clockwise).

functions.name: polygon_centroid
functions.sig: (v: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Area centroid of a closed polygon.

functions.name: inside_polygon
functions.sig: (points: np.ndarray, vertices: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Even-odd (ray casting) point-in-polygon test, vectorised over the points.

functions.name: polygon
functions.sig: (vertices: np.ndarray, name: str = 'polygon', motion: Motion | None = None, n_refine: int = 0) -> Body
functions.doc: A body from explicit vertices (optionally subdivided into ``n_refine`` extra points per edge).

functions.name: resample_polygon
functions.sig: (vertices: np.ndarray, n: int) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``n`` points equally spaced in arclength around a closed polygon.

Cosine spacing (and any CAD curve) leaves panels next to a corner that are far shorter than the wall can
resolve; resampling makes every panel comparable, which is what the stability rule of the method wants.

functions.sig: (vertices: np.ndarray, n_refine: int) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Insert ``n_refine`` evenly spaced points on every edge of a closed polygon.

functions.sig: (diameter: float = 1.0, n: int = 120, center: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 0.0), motion: Motion | None = None, name: str = 'cylinder') -> Body
functions.doc: A circle of ``diameter`` cut into ``n`` equal panels.

functions.name: ellipse
functions.sig: (semi_x: float = 0.5, semi_y: float = 0.25, n: int = 120, center: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 0.0), angle: float = 0.0, motion: Motion | None = None, name: str = 'ellipse') -> Body
functions.doc: An ellipse, optionally turned by ``angle`` in its own frame.

functions.name: plate
functions.sig: (length: float = 0.1, thickness: float = 0.004, hinge_at: Sequence[float] = (0.0, 0.0), angle: float = 0.0, n: int = 12, motion: Motion | None = None, name: str = 'plate') -> Body
functions.doc:
A thin rectangle (a flat plate with a small thickness), hinged at its leading edge.

The ``hinge_at`` point is the origin of the body frame, so a :func:`hinge` motion turns the plate about its
leading edge.

functions.name: naca4
functions.sig: (m: float = 0.0, p: float = 0.4, t: float = 0.12, chord: float = 1.0, n: int = 120, closed_te: bool = True, motion: Motion | None = None, name: str = 'naca') -> Body
functions.doc:
A 4-digit NACA section (``m`` camber, ``p`` its position, ``t`` thickness), cosine-spaced panels.

``n`` is the total number of panels (half of them on each surface). ``closed_te`` collapses the last thickness
term to zero so the trailing edge is a single point (the classic "closed" NACA form), which is what a sharp
trailing edge needs.

functions.name: naca0012
functions.sig: (n: int = 120, chord: float = 1.0, motion: Motion | None = None, name: str = 'naca0012') -> Body
functions.doc: The symmetric NACA 0012 section the reference case uses.

functions.name: deploying_spoiler
functions.sig: (hinge_at: Sequence[float] = (0.8, 0.0), length: float = 0.1, thickness: float = 0.004, n: int = 12, angle0_deg: float = 0.0, angle1_deg: float = 90.0, t_start: float = 0.0, duration: float = 0.5, name: str = 'spoiler') -> Body
functions.doc:
A hinged spoiler that rises from flush with the surface to ``angle1_deg`` over ``duration``.

The default is the reference case: a 10 % chord spoiler whose trailing edge sits 20 % of the chord ahead of the
airfoil trailing edge, hinged at ``0.8 c`` and deploying to 90 degrees.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vortex_domains.boundary
children.doc:
The wall boundary of the VVD solver: the source sheet for no through flow, the vortex sheet for no slip.

Two conditions hold on a solid wall, and they are solved by two panel systems.

No through flow (:class:`SourceSheet`)
    A source sheet cancels the normal velocity of everything else (free stream, free domains, the bound vortex
    sheet and the body's own motion): ``A sigma = -n . (V_inf + V_others - V_body)``, with the classical ``+1/2``
    self term. On a cylinder it reproduces ``Cp = 1 - 4 sin^2(theta)`` to machine precision (see the tests).

No slip (:class:`VortexSheet`)
    A vortex sheet on the panels stands for the vorticity attached to the wall. It is solved each step so that the
    tangential velocity at every panel midpoint equals the wall's, ``B gamma = (V_body - V_others) . t``, and its
    *change* since the previous step is shed into the flow as new vortex domains (:func:`shed_change`). Nothing is
    created and nothing destroyed at the wall -- the vorticity that leaves the surface is exactly the part the
    attached sheet gave up -- which is what keeps the total circulation of the system under control.

The Kutta condition is not imposed: at a sharp trailing edge the sheet solve produces the large strength that
cannot satisfy no slip there, and shedding it is what puts the right circulation into the wake.

classes.name: SourceSheet
classes.doc: A constant-strength source sheet on the panels, enforcing ``V . n = V_body . n`` at every midpoint.

methods.name: solve
methods.sig: (panels: PanelSet, u_inf: np.ndarray, others: np.ndarray, matrix: np.ndarray | None = None) -> SourceSheet
methods.doc: Solve for the sheet that cancels the normal velocity at the midpoints.

methods.name: velocity
methods.doc: Velocity induced by the sheet at ``points``.

methods.name: at_midpoints
methods.doc: Sheet velocity at its own collocation points, from the fluid side.

methods.name: impermeability
methods.doc: Normal velocity at the midpoints, relative to the wall: zero where the sheet is doing its job.

classes.name: VortexSheet
classes.doc: A constant-strength vortex sheet on the panels: the vorticity attached to the wall.

methods.name: solve
methods.sig: (panels: PanelSet, u_inf: np.ndarray, others: np.ndarray, matrix: np.ndarray | None = None) -> VortexSheet
methods.doc: Solve for the sheet that makes the tangential velocity at the midpoints equal to the wall's.

methods.name: at_midpoints
methods.doc: Sheet velocity at its collocation points, from the fluid side (the ``+gamma/2`` half jump).

methods.name: slip
methods.doc: Tangential velocity at the midpoints, relative to the wall: zero where no slip holds.

functions.name: surface_slip
functions.sig: (panels: PanelSet, velocity_at_mid: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Tangential component of ``velocity_at_mid - V_body``, positive along the panel tangent.

functions.name: shear_slip
functions.sig: (panels: PanelSet, velocity_at_mid: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Normal component of ``velocity_at_mid - V_body`` -- the residual of the no-through-flow condition.

functions.name: edge_velocity
functions.sig: (panels: PanelSet, velocity_at_mid: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Tangential velocity of the outer flow at the wall -- the boundary layer's edge velocity ``U_e``.

It is the slip left by the potential flow (free stream, free domains and the source sheet), i.e. exactly the
velocity the boundary layer has to absorb.

functions.name: edge_gradient
functions.sig: (panels: PanelSet, u_e: np.ndarray, min_spacing: float = 0.0) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``dU_e/ds`` along the wall, by a central difference along each body's panel chain.

``min_spacing`` keeps the difference from exploding on the panels of a sharp trailing edge, which are far
shorter than anything the wall can resolve: the wall cannot create vorticity on a scale finer than the domains
that will carry it.

functions.name: vorticity_flux
functions.sig: (panels: PanelSet, u_e: np.ndarray, min_spacing: float = 0.0, limit: float | None = None) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Lighthill's wall vorticity flux ``nu dw/dn = U_e dU_e/ds``, the rate at which the wall creates vorticity.

Negative where the outer flow accelerates (the wall injects negative vorticity), positive where it decelerates,
zero at the stagnation points and at the pressure minimum -- so the boundary layer, its separation and the wake
all come out of the outer flow instead of from a free parameter. ``U_e dU_e/ds`` does not depend on which way
``s`` runs (both factors change sign together).

functions.name: create_vorticity
functions.sig: (panels: PanelSet, u_e: np.ndarray, dt: float, eps: float, offset: float = 0.6, threshold: float = 0.0, limit: float | None = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
The domains the wall creates in one step: circulation ``-U_e dU_e/ds * length * dt`` at every panel.

Returns ``(points, circulation)``. This is the only way vorticity enters the flow: the body hands it to the
fluid at the rate Lighthill's relation asks for.

children.summary: The wall boundary of the VVD solver: the source sheet for no through flow, the vortex sheet for no slip.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vortex_domains.cases
children.doc:
The cases the module is built for: a cylinder (to check the solver against published numbers) and the reference
case of the video that motivated it -- a NACA 0012 with a deploying spoiler.

Both return a :class:`Case`: the geometry, the configuration, what the run should be compared with, and a note on
what that comparison means. Nothing is run until :func:`~.study.run_study` is called.

classes.name: Case
classes.doc: A VVD problem: the bodies, the configuration, and what the result should be judged against.

methods.name: build
methods.doc: A :class:`~.solver.VVD2D` for this case.

functions.name: cylinder_case
functions.sig: (re: float = 40.0, diameter: float = 1.0, panels: int = 96, t_end: float = 10.0, reference_length: float | None = None) -> Case
functions.doc:
Flow past a circular cylinder -- the solver's verification case.

At ``Re = 40`` the flow is steady and the drag coefficient is ``1.3375`` (Dennis & Chang, *J. Fluid Mech.* 42,
1970); at ``Re = 200`` the wake sheds with a Strouhal number ``St = 0.1968`` (Williamson & Brown, *J. Fluids
Struct.* 12, 1998, ``St = 0.2731 - 1.1129/sqrt(Re) + 0.4821/Re``). Those two numbers are the references the
case carries; the tolerance is the one the verification run measured and reports, not a guess.

functions.name: spoiler_hinge
functions.sig: (chord: float = 1.0, spoiler_length: float = 0.1, trailing_gap: float = 0.2) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Where the spoiler is hinged, from the two lengths the reference case states.

The spoiler is ``spoiler_length`` (10 % of the chord) long and its trailing edge sits ``trailing_gap`` (20 % of
the chord) ahead of the airfoil's trailing edge, so the hinge is at ``x = c (1 - trailing_gap)`` on the upper
surface: flush, the spoiler covers the last tenth of the chord; deployed, it stands up from that point.

functions.name: naca0012_spoiler_case
functions.sig: (re: float = 40000.0, chord: float = 1.0, panels: int = 200, spoiler_panels: int = 24, spoiler_length: float = 0.1, deploy_angle_deg: float = 90.0, t_start: float = 0.4, deploy_time: float = 0.5, t_end: float = 1.8, alpha_deg: float = 0.0, base_gap: float = 0.0, max_domains: int = 20000) -> Case
functions.doc:
The reference case: a NACA 0012 at zero incidence, with a spoiler that deploys at ``t_start``.

The numbers are the ones the reference video states: ``Re = 4e4``, spoiler of 10 % of the chord whose trailing
edge is 20 % of the chord ahead of the airfoil's trailing edge, angle of attack 0, no-slip on the surface and
an unperturbed free stream at infinity.

Honest scope, in two parts.

*Resolution.* At ``Re = 4e4`` the boundary layer is of order ``c/sqrt(Re) = 0.005c``, thinner than the panels a
laptop-sized run can afford, so this case exercises the mechanism (moving geometry, vorticity creation,
separation off the spoiler, force history) rather than resolving the boundary layer of the real flow. The
solver's quantitative verification is on the cylinder at Re = 40 and 200, where the references exist.

*The deployment.* This is the open case of the module, and the tests and the example say so: the moving wall asks
for vorticity at a scale the panels cannot hold, so during the deployment the number of domains grows to
thousands and the run leaves its stable envelope (the reported loads diverge). Flush, before it, the case gives
the two numbers it owes -- `Cl = 0` and `Cd = 0.02` -- and those are reproducible. ``max_domains`` bounds the
cost, and the ``displacement`` check is what reports the failure.

*Trailing edge.* The panels are uniform in arclength (cosine spacing leaves panel next to the edge that are
far shorter than the wall can resolve), but the section keeps its sharp trailing edge, where the potential flow
is singular: the edge velocity reaches 15 to 50 times the free stream, and nothing here imposes a Kutta
condition to remove it. What keeps the run finite is the cap on the wall flux (``flux_limit``), which is the
honest description of the fix -- a numerical guard, not a Kutta condition. ``base_gap > 0`` blunts the base
instead; measured, it makes the wall velocity physical (``U_e = 1.2``) but the base's own corners are then the
demanding configuration, so it is not the default.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vortex_domains.domains
children.doc:
The set of vortex domains: their positions, circulations and core radii, plus the bookkeeping VVD needs.

Insertion, the core radius every domain carries (the distance to its second nearest neighbour, with a floor of a
third of the local panel length), the merge that keeps the number of domains in check, and removal with the
circulation accounted for -- a domain that leaves the field is vortex momentum that has to be reported, not
discarded silently.

The numbers are the ones the method is built on (Dynnikova's VVD scheme as documented in the reference
implementation): ``eps`` from the second neighbour, merge distance ``0.4 eps`` with the "own among strangers" rule,
and the diffusion drift clamped so a domain never jumps further than its own core in one step.

classes.name: Domains
classes.sig: (x: np.ndarray | None = None, y: np.ndarray | None = None, gamma: np.ndarray | None = None)
classes.doc: Vortex domains of a 2-D field: ``x``, ``y``, circulation ``gamma`` and core radius ``eps``.

methods.name: keep
methods.doc: Drop every domain where ``mask`` is false (positions, circulations, cores and velocities together).

methods.name: total_vorticity_moment
methods.doc: ``sum_j gamma_j (y_j, -x_j)`` -- the vorticity impulse of the field (what a force changes).

methods.name: enstrophy
methods.doc: ``sum_j gamma_j^2 / (2 pi eps_j^2)``, the discrete enstrophy.

methods.name: extend
methods.doc: Append domains at ``points`` (n, 2) with the given circulations.

methods.name: remove
methods.doc: Drop the domains where ``mask`` is true; returns their circulations.

methods.name: update_epsilon
methods.doc: Core radius = distance to the second nearest neighbour, but never below ``floor``.

methods.doc: Merge domains closer than ``factor * eps`` (and the "own among strangers" triple rule).

children.summary: The set of vortex domains: their positions, circulations and core radii, plus the bookkeeping VVD needs.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vortex_domains.fields
children.doc:
Fields of a VVD run: velocity, vorticity, pressure, stream function, streamlines, and what the wall sees.

Everything is evaluated *from the state* (domains plus the source sheet), so a field is what the simulation would
answer right now -- no interpolation of snapshots, no grid in the solver itself. The vorticity of a domain is the
Gaussian blob ``gamma / (pi eps^2) exp(-r^2/eps^2)`` it carries, the pressure is the Bernoulli form documented in
:meth:`~.solver.VVD2D.pressure`.

The stream function is that of the free domains and the free stream; the source sheet is a distribution of sources
and contributes a multi-valued potential, which is why it is left out (and said so).

classes.name: FieldGrid
classes.doc: A Cartesian block of fields, ready to plot or to save.

functions.name: grid_field
functions.sig: (sim, extent: tuple[float, float, float, float] | None = None, n: int = 160, fields: tuple[str, ...] = ('u', 'v', 'vorticity', 'pressure', 'streamfunction')) -> FieldGrid
functions.doc: Sample the simulation on an ``n x n`` grid over ``extent = (x0, x1, y0, y1)``.

functions.name: vorticity_field
functions.sig: (sim, points: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Vorticity at arbitrary ``points``.

functions.name: surface_pressure
functions.sig: (sim, panels: PanelSet | None = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: ``(midpoints, Cp)`` on the wall, ``Cp = (p - p_inf) / (rho U^2 / 2)``.

functions.name: pressure_coefficient
functions.sig: (sim, points: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: ``Cp`` at arbitrary points.

functions.name: surface_friction
functions.sig: (sim, panels: PanelSet | None = None) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: ``(midpoints, Cf)`` on the wall, with the wall shear from the vorticity of the near-wall domains.

functions.name: streamlines
functions.sig: (sim, seeds: np.ndarray, step: float = 0.02, n_steps: int = 400, stop_inside: bool = True) -> list[np.ndarray]
functions.doc: Integrate ``dx/ds = V/|V|`` from each seed, stopping when a point reaches a body or stagnates.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vortex_domains.kernels
children.doc:
Integral kernels of the viscous vortex domains (VVD) method.

Everything here is written for a 2-D field of *vortex domains* (blobs of circulation ``gamma`` and core radius
``eps``) plus a set of straight panels (the body surface) that can carry a vortex or a source sheet.

=============  ==========================================================================================
blobs          ``u(r) = sum_j gamma_j / (2 pi) * rotl(r - r_j) / (|r - r_j|^2 + eps_j^2)`` -- the regularised
               (Lamb / Oseen) kernel of Dynnikova's VVD method: finite at the centre, and equal to the point
               vortex far away
panels         the exact velocity of a constant-strength source or vortex sheet on a straight segment,
               integrated in closed form (complex logarithm, real arc-length element)
diffusion      the deterministic drift that stands in for viscosity: ``V = nu * I2 / I1`` between domains
               (Dynnikova's "vortex diffusive" velocity) and ``nu * I3 / (2 pi eps^2 - I0)`` from the walls
               ("body diffusive" velocity)
=============  ==========================================================================================

All the panel formulas are verified against a 20 000-point quadrature of the point kernels in
``tests/test_vortex_domains.py``; the reimplementation follows Dynnikova & Dynnikov, *Viscous vortex domains method
for the Navier-Stokes equations in velocity-vorticity formulation* (and the vvflow reference implementation of it,
MIT), which is cited in ``docs/guides/vortex_domains.md``.

functions.name: rotl
functions.sig: (a: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Rotate 2-vectors by +90 degrees: ``(x, y) -> (-y, x)``.

functions.name: blob_velocity
functions.sig: (points: np.ndarray, x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, gamma: np.ndarray, eps: np.ndarray, chunk: int = 1024) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc: Velocity induced at ``points`` by the vortex domains ``(x, y, gamma, eps)``, regularised Lamb kernel.

functions.name: blob_vorticity
functions.sig: (points: np.ndarray, x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, gamma: np.ndarray, eps: np.ndarray, chunk: int = 2048) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Vorticity at ``points``: each domain spreads its circulation as ``gamma / (pi eps^2) exp(-r^2/eps^2)``.

functions.name: blob_streamfunction
functions.sig: (points: np.ndarray, x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, gamma: np.ndarray, eps: np.ndarray, chunk: int = 1024) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc: Stream function of the regularised blobs, ``psi = -sum gamma/(4 pi) log(r^2 + eps^2)``.

functions.name: segment_integrals
functions.sig: (points: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``I_j = int ds / (z - zeta_j)`` over each panel, complex, in the frame ``z = x + i y``.

Real arc length element, so the differential ``d zeta`` is turned into ``ds`` by ``conj(dz)/|dz|``.

functions.name: panel_flux
functions.sig: (points: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray, strength: np.ndarray, kind: str = 'vortex', exclude_diagonal: bool = False) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Velocity at ``points`` induced by constant-strength panels ``[a_k, b_k]``.

``kind="vortex"``: ``strength`` is the sheet strength ``gamma`` (circulation per unit length),
``kind="source"``: ``strength`` is ``sigma`` (flux per unit length). Backed by the closed-form integral
:func:`segment_integrals`.

``exclude_diagonal`` drops panel ``k``'s influence on ``points[k]`` -- the collocation case, where the
principal value is supplied by the caller (``+sigma/2`` for a source sheet, ``-gamma/2`` for a vortex sheet).

functions.name: source_sheet_system
functions.sig: (mid: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray, normal: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Normal-velocity influence matrix of unit source panels, collocated at the panel midpoints.

The self-term of a flat source panel is the classical half jump, ``+1/2`` along the outward normal.

functions.name: vortex_sheet_system
functions.sig: (mid: np.ndarray, a: np.ndarray, b: np.ndarray, tangent: np.ndarray) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
Tangential-velocity influence matrix of unit vortex panels, collocated at the panel midpoints.

The self term carries the half jump the fluid side sees, ``+1/2`` along the panel tangent. That is what makes a
spinning cylinder come out with a uniform sheet equal to its surface speed
(``tests/test_vortex_domains.py``), and it is calibrated against that exact solution rather than assumed:
``+1`` there gives a sheet that is off by a factor of two.

functions.name: vortex_diffusion_drift
functions.sig: (x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, gamma: np.ndarray, eps: np.ndarray, nu: float, chunk: int = 512, same_sign: bool = True) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Dynnikova's "vortex diffusive" velocity, the drift that makes up for viscosity.

``I1 = sum_j gamma_j exp(-|rho|/eps)``, ``I2 = (1/eps) sum_j gamma_j rho/|rho| exp(-|rho|/eps)`` and
``V_d = nu * I2 / I1`` -- the velocity ``-nu grad(omega)/omega`` written as a discrete kernel estimate.
Only neighbours of the same sign contribute (as in the reference implementation): mixing signs makes the
estimate of ``grad(omega)/omega`` meaningless where the vorticity changes sign.

functions.name: wall_diffusion_drift
functions.sig: (x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, eps: np.ndarray, seg_mid: np.ndarray, seg_vector: np.ndarray, nu: float, chunk: int = 512) -> tuple[np.ndarray, np.ndarray]
functions.doc:
Dynnikova's "body diffusive" velocity: the drift produced by the wall replacing the missing half space.

``I3 = sum_k dS_k exp(-|rho_k|/eps)``, ``I0 = sum_k (|rho_k|/eps + 1)/|rho_k|^2 (rho_k . dS_k) exp(-|rho_k|/eps)``,
``W_d = nu I3 / (eps^2 (2 pi - I0))`` with ``I0`` capped at ``pi`` (the reference implementation's bound).
``dS_k`` is the outward normal of the panel scaled by its length.

functions.name: blob_pressure_sum
functions.sig: (points: np.ndarray, x: np.ndarray, y: np.ndarray, gamma: np.ndarray, velocity: np.ndarray, eps: np.ndarray, chunk: int = 512) -> np.ndarray
functions.doc:
``sum_i V_i . u_i(r)`` -- the Lagrangian unsteady term of the pressure, one pass over the domains.

``u_i`` is the velocity domain ``i`` induces at ``r`` and ``V_i`` the velocity it moves with; the sum is what
the material derivative of the potential gives in a vorticity field (the reference implementation's
``p - p_inf = (V_inf^2 - V^2)/2 + sum V_i . u_i``).

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vortex_domains.solver

classes.name: VVDConfig
classes.doc:
What a VVD run is asked for.

``re`` is the Reynolds number on ``reference_length`` and the reference velocity; ``nu = U_ref * L_ref / re``.
``dt`` follows the stability rule of the method (``dt <= 2 Re eps^2`` in ``U = L = 1`` units) when it is None.

methods.name: speed
methods.doc: Magnitude of the free stream.

methods.name: nu
methods.doc: Kinematic viscosity implied by ``re`` on the reference velocity and length.

methods.name: with_
methods.doc: A copy of this configuration with some fields replaced.

classes.name: VVD2D
classes.sig: (assembly: Assembly, config: VVDConfig | None = None, name: str = 'vvd')
classes.doc: A 2-D VVD simulation over an :class:`~.bodies.Assembly` of rigid bodies.

methods.name: eps_floor
methods.doc: Core-radius floor: a third of the mean panel, grown when the run would exceed ``max_domains``.

methods.name: induced_by_domains
methods.doc: Velocity of the free domains at ``points`` (no free stream, no sheets).

methods.name: fluid_velocity
methods.sig: (points: np.ndarray, domains: Domains | None = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: Full fluid velocity at ``points``: free stream + domains + the source sheet.

methods.name: drift
methods.sig: (points: np.ndarray, domains: Domains | None = None) -> np.ndarray
methods.doc: The two diffusive drifts (domain-domain and wall) at ``points``, clamped to the stability limit.

methods.name: step
methods.doc: Advance the flow by one time step.

methods.name: pressure
methods.doc: Pressure relative to the free stream, ``rho (V_inf^2 - |V|^2) / 2 + rho sum_i V_i . u_i``.

methods.name: wall_pressure
methods.doc: Pressure at the panel midpoints, from the fluid side of the sheets.

methods.name: run
methods.sig: (t_end: float | None = None, progress: Any = None) -> dict[str, list[float]]
methods.doc: Advance until ``t_end`` (default: the configuration's), calling ``progress(self)`` every step.

methods.name: coefficients
methods.doc: ``cl``, ``cd`` and ``cm`` at the last step, on ``reference_length`` and the reference velocity.

methods.name: series
methods.doc: The history as arrays.

methods.name: snapshot
methods.doc: A copy of everything a picture or a restart needs.

methods.name: load_snapshot
methods.doc: Restore the state of :meth:`snapshot` (the geometry is re-derived from the assembly).

functions.name: step_size
functions.sig: (panels: PanelSet, re: float, eps_factor: float = 1.0 / 3.0, safety: float = 1.0, u_scale: float = 1.0) -> float
functions.doc:
Time step: the tighter of the method's viscous rule and the advective one.

The viscous rule ``dt <= 2 Re eps^2`` is what keeps the diffusion drift stable; it is *not* the binding one at
high Reynolds number, where advecting a domain across its own core (``dt <= eps / U``) is. Taking the smaller
of the two is what lets one configuration serve both ``Re = 40`` and ``Re = 4e4``.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vortex_domains.study
children.doc:
Running a case and deciding what the run is worth: coefficients, Strouhal, physics checks, saved results.

A study is the unit the rest of PINNeAPPle consumes -- the same shape as the library's other studies: run the
physics, keep the time series, reduce it to the numbers a decision needs, and say which checks failed. The checks
here are the ones this solver can be held to:

=============================  ====================================================================================
``impermeability``             the normal velocity left at the wall (the source sheet's residual), against ``U_inf``
``no_slip``                    the tangential velocity left at the wall, against ``U_inf``
``displacement``               the largest domain step, against that domain's own core radius (the method's
                               stability criterion, ``dt <= 2 Re eps^2``)
``circulation``                the total circulation created at the walls stays bounded (nothing is destroyed)
``resolution``                 the core radius never grew beyond ``2x`` its first value because of ``max_domains``
``drag`` / ``strouhal``        against the reference the case carries, when it carries one
=============================  ====================================================================================

classes.name: StudyResult
classes.doc: What a run produced, and what can be said about it.

methods.name: save
methods.doc: Write ``study.json``, the time series and the last field to ``out_dir``.

functions.name: window_mean
functions.sig: (series: dict[str, np.ndarray], key: str, t_from: float, t_to: float) -> float
functions.doc: Mean of ``series[key]`` over ``[t_from, t_to]``.

functions.name: strouhal_number
functions.sig: (series: dict[str, np.ndarray], t_from: float | None = None, amplitude_threshold: float = 0.001) -> float | None
functions.doc:
Strouhal number ``f D / U`` of the lift signal, or ``None`` when the signal is not periodic.

The frequency is the dominant one of a Hann-windowed periodogram above ``10`` per unit time; the amplitude
threshold is what separates a shedding wake from a steady one.

functions.name: run_study
functions.sig: (case: Case, t_end: float | None = None, progress: Any = None, average_from: float | None = None) -> StudyResult
functions.doc: Run ``case`` and reduce it: mean coefficients over the last third of the run, Strouhal, the checks.

children.name: pinneapple_simulation.vortex_domains.verification
children.doc:
What this solver is checked against, and the numbers it reproduces.

The checks are of two kinds. The first four are exact or near-exact properties of the machinery (a panel integral
against a quadrature, the potential flow past a cylinder against ``Cp = 1 - 4 sin^2 theta``, the attached sheet of a
spinning cylinder against its surface speed, and the diffusion drift against the growth of a Gaussian vorticity
patch). The last two are the physics: the drag of a cylinder at ``Re = 40`` against Dennis & Chang and the Strouhal
number at ``Re = 200`` against Williamson & Brown's correlation.

``run(quick=True)`` does the cheap ones (a second); ``run()`` adds the two runs (minutes).

functions.name: check_panel_influence
functions.sig: (seed: int = 3) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: The closed-form panel integrals against a 20 000-point quadrature, away from the panels.

functions.name: check_potential_flow
functions.sig: (panels: int = 80) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: ``Cp = 1 - 4 sin^2(theta)`` on a cylinder in a uniform stream, from the source sheet alone.

functions.name: check_spinning_cylinder
functions.sig: (rate: float = 1.0, panels: int = 64) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: A cylinder spinning in a fluid at rest carries a uniform sheet equal to its surface speed.

functions.name: check_diffusion
functions.sig: (re: float = 200.0, n: int = 3000, sigma: float = 0.2) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc:
Viscosity as a drift: the diffusion velocity of a Gaussian patch must be ``2 nu r / sigma^2``.

The vorticity of a patch ``omega = exp(-r^2/sigma^2)`` has ``grad(omega)/omega = -2 r/sigma^2``, so the drift
``-nu grad(omega)/omega`` grows linearly with the radius and equals ``2 nu / sigma`` at ``r = sigma``. That is
what Dynnikova's kernel estimate of ``I2/I1`` has to reproduce, which is the whole of the viscous term.

functions.name: check_cylinder_drag
functions.sig: (re: float = 40.0, panels: int = 96, t_end: float = 10.0, progress: Any = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Steady drag of a cylinder at ``Re = 40`` against Dennis & Chang (1970): ``Cd = 1.3375``.

functions.name: check_strouhal
functions.sig: (re: float = 200.0, panels: int = 96, t_end: float = 60.0, progress: Any = None) -> dict[str, Any]
functions.doc: Shedding frequency at ``Re = 200`` against Williamson & Brown's correlation (``St = 0.1968``).

functions.name: run
functions.sig: (quick: bool = True, **kwargs) -> list[dict[str, Any]]
functions.doc: Every check, cheap ones first. ``quick=False`` adds the two cylinder runs (minutes each).

children.summary: What this solver is checked against, and the numbers it reproduces.

children.doc:
2-D viscous vortex domains (VVD): incompressible Navier-Stokes with mesh-free Lagrangian vorticity.

The method, after Dynnikova and Dynnikov: the vorticity of the flow is carried by *domains* -- blobs of circulation
``gamma`` and core radius ``eps`` -- which move with the velocity the whole field induces on them (free stream plus
the regularised Biot-Savart sum), while viscosity enters as a deterministic *drift* down the vorticity gradient,
both between the domains and from the walls. The body is a closed polygon cut into panels: a source sheet on them
keeps the flow out, and the wall hands vorticity to the fluid at the rate Lighthill's relation asks for, which is
what builds the boundary layer, its separation and the wake.

That is a solver with no mesh, no turbulence model and no user parameter that decides where vorticity goes.

* :mod:`.bodies`   -- rigid bodies (polygons, rotating and hinged) and their generators: cylinder, ellipse, plate,
  NACA 4-digit sections, a deploying spoiler.
* :mod:`.domains`  -- the set of vortex domains, their core radii, the merge that bounds their number, and removal
  that reports the circulation it takes out.
* :mod:`.kernels`  -- the integrals: the regularised blob kernel, the closed-form panel sheets, the diffusion drifts.
* :mod:`.boundary` -- the wall: source sheet for no through flow, vortex sheet for no slip, and Lighthill's flux.
* :mod:`.solver`   -- :class:`VVD2D`, the time loop, the forces and the history of a run.
* :mod:`.fields`   -- velocity, vorticity, pressure, stream function, streamlines, wall ``Cp`` and ``Cf``.
* :mod:`.cases`    -- the cylinder (verification) and the NACA 0012 with a deploying spoiler (the reference case).
* :mod:`.study`    -- run a case, reduce it to coefficients and a Strouhal number, decide on the physics checks.
* :mod:`.verification` -- what the solver is checked against, and the numbers it reproduces.

    from pinneapple_simulation.vortex_domains import cylinder_case, run_study

    result = run_study(cylinder_case(re=40, panels=96, t_end=10.0))
    print(result.summary())        # Cl, Cd, Cm, and which checks failed
    for check in result.checks:    # impermeability and displacement pass; no_slip and drag do not (see the guide)
        print(check["name"], check["ok"], check["detail"])

The two references the module is held to: the drag of a cylinder at ``Re = 40``, ``Cd = 1.3375`` (Dennis & Chang,
*J. Fluid Mech.* 42, 1970) and its shedding at ``Re = 200``, ``St = 0.1968`` (Williamson & Brown, *J. Fluids
Struct.* 12, 1998). ``python -m pinneapple_simulation.vortex_domains`` prints what this checkout reproduces
(``docs/guides/vortex_domains.md``).

doc:
pinneapple_simulation — Physics simulation back-ends and data generation.

Sub-modules
-----------
numerical_solvers  (was pinneapple_solvers)
    PDE solvers (FDM, FEM, CFD): HeatConduction3D, NavierStokes3D,
    LidDrivenCavitySolver3D, ChannelFlowSolver3D, ElasticWave3D.
    Optional bridges to OpenFOAM and FEniCS. SolverRegistry, generate_pinn_dataset.
    CAD-to-CFD pipeline (CADToCFDPipeline).

granular
    Discrete element solver for convex polyhedra and spheres with volume-based contact:
    World, Material, ForceModel, ConvexPolyhedron, bonds and fragment statistics, the
    rotating drum (power draw), the impulse wear law and fluid drag. See docs/granular_dem.md.

particle_dynamics  (was pinneapple_dynamics)
    Differentiable particle / continuum dynamics: rigid-body (RigidBody,
    RigidBodySystem), MPM (MPMSimulator), SPH (SPHParticles). All in pure
    PyTorch for autograd compatibility.

external_solvers   (was pinneapple_integrations)
    External tool bridges: OpenFOAM case staging & field extraction, MATLAB
    engine wrapper, Modelica / FMU simulation (via fmpy / OMPython), FEniCS
    workflow. All optional — graceful degradation when tool not installed.

Integration helpers
-------------------
``simulate(scenario, ...)``
    Dispatch function: routes to the appropriate solver/simulator based on
    scenario string (``"heat_3d"``, ``"ns_3d"``, ``"mpm"``, ``"sph"``, …).
``generate_data(scenario, n_samples, ...)``
    Generates a dataset of trajectories using the matching solver.

Usage
-----
>>> from pinneapple_simulation import simulate, generate_data, HeatConduction3D
>>> output = simulate("heat_3d", t_end=1.0, nx=32, ny=32, nz=32)
>>> dataset = generate_data("ns_3d", n_samples=50)
